- **Overview**: Instead of picking the reinforced digital lock on the front door, the intruder calls the building’s IT Helpdesk pretending to be an employee who just bought a new phone, convinces the clerk to register the intruder’s own smartphone as the employee’s MFA badge, walks right into the IT Lobby (SSO Dashboard), and plugs a private tunnel cable (ngrok / Tailscale) directly into the cloud and virtual server control room. Synthesizing joint reports from CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-320A, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 ("Muddled Libra"), and Google Mandiant ("UNC3944"), this scenario shows how modern identity-focused attackers bypass perimeter firewalls altogether. Instead of exploiting a software bug, the attacker calls the company’s IT Helpdesk pretending to be a real employee (vishing), convinces the helpdesk agent to reset Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) and enroll the attacker’s own phone (giving the attacker a clean, first-party MFA device on the victim’s account), logs into the corporate Single Sign-On (Okta / Entra ID) portal, searches internal SharePoint/Confluence wikis for admin runbooks, deploys a legitimate remote-access tool (AnyDesk / Tailscale, signed commercial RMM tools that do not trigger malware alerts) for persistence, and pivots into AWS/Azure cloud infrastructure and VMware ESXi hypervisors.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1556.006 (Modify Authentication Process: Multi-Factor Authentication - Credential Access / Persistence), T1078.004 (Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts - Initial Access / Lateral Movement), T1219 (Remote Access Software (Commercial RMM Tunneling) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42: Muddled Libra (Scattered Spider) Cloud Identity & VMware ESXi Intrusion Playbook (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/muddled-libra/) | CISA & FBI Joint Advisory: Scattered Spider (AA23-320A) Cybersecurity Advisory (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a) | Mandiant / Google Cloud Threat Intelligence: UNC3944: SMS Phishing, SIM Swapping, and Cloud Identity Provider Intrusions (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1621 · Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation): **OKTA MFA PUSH FATIGUE & ROGUE DEVICE ENROLLMENT** — Armed with the employee’s badge number and birthday, the caller rings the IT Helpdesk ("Hi, I got a new iPhone and lost my authenticator app") and persuades the helpdesk clerk to pair the caller’s own phone to the employee’s corporate account. Having gathered a target IT or DevOps engineer’s personal details (employee ID, date of birth, and manager name from LinkedIn or data brokers), the attacker calls the corporate IT Helpdesk impersonating that employee ("vishing", voice phishing) and claims they just got a new phone and lost their authenticator app. Persuaded by the caller, the helpdesk clerk triggers an administrative MFA reset (user.mfa.factor.activate, registering the attacker’s own smartphone or FIDO2 security key directly onto the employee’s Okta / Entra ID account so the attacker can approve their own MFA prompts at will). Unlike phishing attacks that try to steal a temporary session cookie, social-engineering the IT Helpdesk to enroll a new MFA factor on the Identity Provider (IdP) gives the attacker a permanent, legitimate MFA credential tied to their own device. In the documented Okta SystemLog exchange from Muddled Libra (UNC3944) to Core Identity & VLAN Switch, Core Identity & VLAN Switch responds with RESP Okta MFA (confirming that the MFA FACTOR ENROLL request succeeded on Core Identity & VLAN Switch and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 AUTHORIZED RMM TOOL DEPLOYMENT (SCREENCONNECT / NGROK)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ MFA FACTOR ENROLL / ⇠#1 RESP Okta MFA) from Node ① (#1 Muddled Libra (UNC3944)) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Prisma Cloud & SIEM). [Specs: OKTA EVENT=system.push.send_factor_verify_push -> user.mfa.factor.activate; TARGET ROLE=IT Helpdesk / Cloud SuperAdmin; SOURCE ANOMALY=Residential Proxy / Anonymizing VPN ASN]
  - Stage 2 (T1219 · Remote Access Software): **AUTHORIZED RMM TOOL DEPLOYMENT (SCREENCONNECT / NGROK)** — Inside the employee’s virtual office, the intruder reads the IT team’s emergency instruction manuals (Confluence / SharePoint) and installs a genuine, IT-approved remote support tool (AnyDesk / Tailscale) so even if the front-door password is changed tomorrow, they still have a private side door straight into the machine. Using the newly hijacked Single Sign-On (SSO) account, the attacker logs into the company’s virtual desktop (Citrix / Azure VDI), searches internal IT documentation (Confluence / SharePoint, documented by Mandiant UNC3944 as the primary way the group locates VPN guides, CyberArk/PAM instructions, and VMware vCenter architecture diagrams), and installs commercial Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) or mesh-VPN tools like AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Tailscale, or ngrok (chosen because these tools are digitally signed by legitimate software vendors so antivirus does not block them, and they maintain an encrypted outbound tunnel that survives even if the victim’s SSO password and MFA are later reset). Commercial RMM agents establish persistent outbound TLS/WebSocket connections to the vendor’s relay cloud, giving the attacker full interactive desktop control without deploying any custom malware binary. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 exchange from Core Identity & VLAN Switch to Okta / Entra ID SSO Portal, Okta / Entra ID SSO Portal responds with ACK PID 7488 (confirming that the RMM SCREENCONNECT request succeeded on Okta / Entra ID SSO Portal and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 SAML FEDERATION PIVOT TO AWS & VMWARE VCENTER). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ RMM SCREENCONNECT / ⇠#2 ACK PID 7488) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Okta / Entra ID SSO Portal), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Prisma Cloud & SIEM). [Specs: RMM BINARIES=ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe, fleetdeck_agent.exe, ngrok.exe; PRIVILEGE=Installed as Windows Service running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM; C2 CHANNEL=Outbound TLS :443 to tenant-specific ScreenConnect relay]
  - Stage 3 (T1078.004 · Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts): **SAML FEDERATION PIVOT TO AWS & VMWARE VCENTER** — From the IT dashboard, the intruder attaches a second "Ghost Identity Provider" to the company’s cloud account, allowing them to mint temporary cloud master keys (AssumeRole) on demand, take over VMware ESXi hypervisors, and export customer databases from S3. Combining Unit 42’s and Mandiant’s findings: pivoting through the SSO dashboard into the AWS / Azure cloud management console, the attacker invokes sts:AssumeRole (minting temporary high-privilege cloud credentials) and calls CreateSAMLProvider / UpdateAssumeRolePolicy (registering a second, attacker-controlled SAML Identity Provider inside the cloud tenant, acting as a "golden SAML" backdoor that lets the attacker mint Admin cloud sessions even after the corporate Okta/Entra tenant is locked down). Simultaneously, for on-premises infrastructure, they add their compromised account to the Active Directory ESX Admins group to take direct SSH control over VMware ESXi hypervisors and export production S3 buckets. By compromising the Single Sign-On and Active Directory identity layer that governs both cloud role federation and hypervisor authentication, the attacker moves straight from a phone call to the IT Helpdesk into full control of AWS/Azure and VMware ESXi without touching a single network firewall exploit. In the documented CloudTrail STS/IAM exchange from Okta / Entra ID SSO Portal to Admin Endpoint (RMM Persistence), Admin Endpoint (RMM Persistence) responds with RESP AKIA...Key (confirming that the ASSUMEROLE + KEY request succeeded on Admin Endpoint (RMM Persistence) and completing the final execution objective of Unit 42 & CISA, Scattered Spider (Muddled Libra): SSO MFA Fatigue, RMM & AWS/ESXi Pivot). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ASSUMEROLE + KEY / ⇠#3 RESP AKIA...Key) from Node ③ (#3 Okta / Entra ID SSO Portal) to Node ④ (#4 Admin Endpoint (RMM Persistence)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Prisma Cloud & SIEM). [Specs: AWS CLOUDTRAIL=AssumeRoleWithSAML -> iam:CreateAccessKey -> secretsmanager:GetSecretValue; HYPERVISOR PIVOT=VMware vCenter SSO & ESXi SSH Enabled; CISA ADVISORY=AA23-320A (Scattered Spider TTPs)]

### T1620: Elastic & Mandiant — APT41 (Brass Typhoon): DodgeBox, Call-Stack Spoofing & DUSTPAN Loader
- **Scenario ID**: `elastic-apt41-dustpan-stealthvector`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/elastic-apt41-dustpan-stealthvector
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=elastic-apt41-dustpan-stealthvector
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Elastic Security Labs / Mandiant · DLL Side-Loading, Synthetic Stack Frames & ChaCha20 DUSTTRAP
- **Overview**: Imagine a Russian nesting doll of disguises: first, a trusted Windows system utility (wermgr.exe) is woken up; inside it sits a hollow launcher (DUSTPAN), which unpacks an encrypted memory-only command center (STEALTHVECTOR), which in turn unlocks a modular toolkit (DUSTTRAP) that talks directly to the Windows kernel (ntdll.dll) so user-mode security cameras never see it. Synthesizing independent research from Google Mandiant (DUSTPAN & DUSTTRAP), Elastic Security Labs (DodgeBox & STEALTHVECTOR), and Trend Micro (Earth Freybug), this scenario examines the multi-stage memory-only loader chain used by APT41. Rather than putting their full backdoor in a single file that analysts could easily reverse-engineer, APT41 uses a chain of hollow loaders: a legitimate Windows process (wermgr.exe, Windows Error Reporting, documented by Trend Micro as chosen because it regularly makes outbound HTTPS connections) is spawned and injected with Mandiant’s DUSTPAN launcher, which decrypts Elastic’s STEALTHVECTOR orchestrator in memory (which overwrites ntdll.dll in RAM to wipe out user-mode EDR hooks and spoofs thread call stacks), which in turn loads the 16-plugin DUSTTRAP framework.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1574.002 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading (DodgeBox / taskhost.exe) - Defense Evasion), T1620 (Reflective Code Loading (Call-Stack Spoofing & DUSTPAN / STEALTHVECTOR) - Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Elastic Security Labs: APT41 (Brass Typhoon) DodgeBox, Call-Stack Spoofing, and STEALTHVECTOR Analysis (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs) | Mandiant / Google Cloud Threat Intelligence: APT41 DUSTPAN Loader and DUSTTRAP Multi-Stage In-Memory Plugin Ecosystem (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/apt41-us-state-governments) | The MITRE Corporation & Trend Micro Research: MITRE ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41 (Wicked Panda / Brass Typhoon / Earth Freybug) (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0096/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1574.002 · Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading): **DODGEBOX / DUSTPAN DLL SIDE-LOADING & ENV KEYING** — The outer nesting doll opens: the dropper starts the official Windows Error Reporting manager (wermgr.exe) and slips the DUSTPAN stage-1 loader into its memory. The initial persistence trigger executes the DUSTPAN stage-1 loader (a lightweight launcher documented by Mandiant that contains zero C2 domains or post-exploitation tools of its own, so if an analyst captures the file on disk they learn nothing about the final implant). DUSTPAN immediately spawns C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe (Windows Error Reporting Manager, documented by Trend Micro’s Earth Freybug research as chosen because wermgr.exe is a Microsoft-signed binary that legitimately connects to external HTTPS servers to upload crash reports, allowing C2 traffic to blend in) and injects its decryption stub into wermgr.exe’s memory. By immediately transferring execution into C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe via remote memory allocation and APC/thread hijacking, all subsequent stages execute under the process identity and digital signature of a built-in Windows telemetry binary. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 exchange from APT41 Cloudflare Worker C2 to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK Unsigned DLL (confirming that the SIDELOAD DODGEBOX request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 CALL-STACK SPOOFING & REFLECTIVE DUSTTRAP MAPPING). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SIDELOAD DODGEBOX / ⇠#1 ACK Unsigned DLL) from Node ① (#1 APT41 Cloudflare Worker C2) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & ETW Ti Sensor). [Specs: LOADER FAMILY=DodgeBox / DUSTPAN (APT41 / Brass Typhoon); SIDE-LOADED DLL=C:\ProgramData\AppService\ffmpeg.dll (Unsigned); GUARDRAIL=Environmental Keying (GetComputerNameExW Hash Check)]
  - Stage 2 (T1620 · Reflective Code Loading): **CALL-STACK SPOOFING & REFLECTIVE DUSTTRAP MAPPING** — Before opening the inner nesting doll (DUSTTRAP), the STEALTHVECTOR stage brings in a fresh, un-bugged copy of the Windows system phonebook (ntdll.dll) from disk, wiping out all the wiretaps that the endpoint’s EDR security agent had placed on the phone lines. Running inside wermgr.exe, the STEALTHVECTOR stage (analyzed by Elastic Security Labs) reads a clean copy of C:\Windows\System32\ntdll.dll from disk and overwrites the .text code section of the already-loaded ntdll.dll in RAM (because user-mode EDR agents monitor a program by placing 5-byte JMP "wiretap" hooks at the start of system functions inside ntdll.dll in memory, so pasting the clean bytes from disk right over the hooked bytes erases all of the EDR’s user-mode wiretaps). Simultaneously, it constructs synthetic thread call-stack frames (RtlUserThreadStart → BaseThreadInitThunk, so EDR memory walkers see a normal Windows call stack instead of unbacked shellcode) and ChaCha20/AES-GCM-decrypts Mandiant’s DUSTTRAP backdoor directly in memory. To unhook ntdll.dll, STEALTHVECTOR calls VirtualProtect on the in-memory ntdll.dll .text section (temporarily changing it from Read-Execute 0x20 to Read-Write-Execute 0x40), copies the clean .text bytes from the on-disk ntdll.dll file, and restores 0x20 permissions, silencing user-mode API hooks before DUSTTRAP initializes. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ STACK SPOOF + RX / ⇠#2 ALERT 312 KB RX) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Signed Host Binary (taskhost.exe)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & ETW Ti Sensor). [Specs: EVASION TECHNIQUE=Synthetic Call-Stack Spoofing (.pdata Unwind Gadget); MEMORY OPSEC=RW -> RX Transition + PE Header Zeroing (0x00); DECRYPTED IMPLANT=DUSTTRAP Multi-Plugin Backdoor (ChaCha20-Poly1305)]
  - Stage 3 (T1071.001 · Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols): **CLOUDFLARE WORKER C2 & PLUGIN EXECUTION** — With the phone lines un-tapped, the innermost doll (DUSTTRAP) snaps modular tool attachments (keylogger, credential harvester, file manager) directly into RAM as the remote operator requests them. With ntdll.dll unhooked inside wermgr.exe, the DUSTTRAP core opens a mutual-TLS channel (requiring both client and server certificates so security researchers cannot probe the C2 server or replay traffic) to APT41’s command infrastructure, and loads 16 specialized in-memory plugins (file manager, shell executor, credential harvester, Active Directory recon, streamed into RAM only when needed so the full toolkit never sits on the victim’s hard drive). Although unhooking ntdll.dll blinds user-mode API hooks inside wermgr.exe, Kernel-mode Event Tracing for Windows (EtwTiLogProtectVM) and Sysmon EventID 3 still catch the ntdll.dll permission change paired with wermgr.exe connecting to a non-Microsoft IP address. In the documented Sysmon EID 3 exchange from Signed Host Binary (taskhost.exe) to DodgeBox Stack-Spoofing & DUSTTRAP, DodgeBox Stack-Spoofing & DUSTTRAP responds with ACK TLS 1.3 (confirming that the WORKER TLS C2 request succeeded on DodgeBox Stack-Spoofing & DUSTTRAP and completing the final execution objective of Elastic & Mandiant, APT41 (Brass Typhoon): DodgeBox, Call-Stack Spoofing & DUSTPAN Loader). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ WORKER TLS C2 / ⇠#3 ACK TLS 1.3) from Node ③ (#3 Signed Host Binary (taskhost.exe)) to Node ④ (#4 DodgeBox Stack-Spoofing & DUSTTRAP), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & ETW Ti Sensor). [Specs: C2 FRONTING=HTTPS TLS 1.3 via Serverless Worker Endpoint; PLUGIN MODULES=Shell, FileOps, TokenManip, PortForward, Keylogger; TARGET ASSET=Enterprise Build & Code-Signing Server (10.10.1.15)]

### T1003.003: Microsoft & CISA — Volt Typhoon: Living-off-the-Land ntdsutil IFM & netsh Portproxy
- **Scenario ID**: `ms-volt-typhoon-lotl`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ms-volt-typhoon-lotl
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ms-volt-typhoon-lotl
- **Category**: ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Microsoft Threat Intel / CISA AA24-038A · KV-Botnet Edge Relay, WMIC, ntds.dit & netsh
- **Overview**: Imagine an infiltrator who enters a high-security facility carrying zero weapons or burglar tools in their pockets. Instead, they pick up the facility’s own maintenance clipboard (wmic.exe), use the building’s built-in port-forwarding intercom (netsh interface portproxy) to relay messages through retired home routers (KV-Botnet), and ask the facility’s official backup machine (ntdsutil.exe) to print a full copy of the master key vault (ntds.dit). Because every single action is performed by an official, factory-installed Windows utility, file-based antivirus scanners see zero foreign malware. Documented by Joint CISA/NSA/FBI/Microsoft Advisory AA24-038A, the Volt Typhoon APT group specializes in "Living off the Land" (LotL, executing attacks exclusively with built-in operating system tools so zero custom malware files ever touch the disk). Instead of using hacktools like Mimikatz that trigger antivirus immediately, Volt Typhoon routes traffic through a botnet of compromised SOHO routers (KV-Botnet at 198.51.100.14, making traffic originate from local residential or small-business IPs), runs built-in Windows administration commands (wmic, ntdsutil, netsh, all validly signed by Microsoft) from jump server SRV-MGMT-01 (10.10.15.22), extracts the entire Active Directory password database (ntds.dit) on CORP-DC01 (10.10.0.5) using ntdsutil.exe (PID 6412), and creates a stealthy port-forwarding relay via netsh.exe (PID 6890).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1003.003 (OS Credential Dumping: NTDS (ntdsutil.exe create full) - Credential Access), T1090.002 (Proxy: External Proxy (netsh interface portproxy v4tov4) - Command and Control / Lateral Movement)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Volt Typhoon targets US critical infrastructure with living-off-the-land techniques (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/05/24/volt-typhoon-targets-us-critical-infrastructure-with-living-off-the-land-techniques/) | CISA / NSA / FBI Joint Advisory: PRC State-Sponsored Actors Compromise and Maintain Persistent Access to U.S. Critical Infrastructure (AA24-038A) (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-038a) | The MITRE Corporation & Black Lotus Labs Research: MITRE ATT&CK Group G1017: Volt Typhoon (Bronze Silhouette) & KV Botnet Relay Infrastructure (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1017/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1047 · Windows Management Instrumentation): **HANDS-ON-KEYBOARD WMI DISCOVERY & LATERAL EXEC** — Rather than calling the target’s server from an overseas phone number that would raise an instant red flag, the operator routes the call through a neighborhood home router down the street (KV-Botnet 198.51.100.14) and uses the jump server’s built-in maintenance intercom (wmic process call create) to issue commands on the Domain Controller. Instead of connecting from a rented cloud VPS that threat-intelligence feeds would block, the attacker connects through a compromised small-office/home-office (SOHO) router in the same geographic region (KV-Botnet node 198.51.100.14, so geo-IP filters see normal local ISP traffic) into the IT Jump Server SRV-MGMT-01 (10.10.15.22). From SRV-MGMT-01, the operator executes wmic /node:10.10.0.5 process call create "cmd.exe /Q /c ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm"..." toward Domain Controller CORP-DC01 (10.10.0.5), causing WmiPrvSE.exe on CORP-DC01 to spawn the command under PID 6412 and return ReturnValue = 0 (confirming remote process creation over DCOM/RPC without dropping any third-party remote-execution binary). When wmic.exe connects over TCP/135 (RPC Endpoint Mapper) and dynamic DCOM ports to CORP-DC01 (10.10.0.5), the remote WMI provider host (WmiPrvSE.exe) spawns cmd.exe / ntdsutil.exe (PID 6412) under the authenticated administrator context (recording Sysmon Event ID 1 on CORP-DC01 with ParentImage = WmiPrvSE.exe). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ WMIC REMOTE EXEC / ⇠#1 ACK PID 6412) from Node ① (#1 KV-Botnet SOHO Edge Node) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & MDE). [Specs: COMMAND=wmic /node:10.10.0.5 process call create "cmd.exe /c ..."; PARENT PROCESS=C:\Windows\System32\wbem\WmiPrvSE.exe; ADVISORY REF=CISA / NSA / FBI / Microsoft AA24-038A]
  - Stage 2 (T1003.003 · OS Credential Dumping: NTDS): **OFFLINE NTDS.DIT EXTRACTION VIA NTDSUTIL IFM** — The Domain Controller keeps its master password book (ntds.dit) locked inside a glass case while Windows is running so nobody can copy the file directly. Instead of smashing the glass, the infiltrator asks the official Active Directory maintenance robot (ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm") to take a temporary backup snapshot and place an unlocked copy right into C:\Windows\Temp\tmp_ad\. Active Directory exclusively locks C:\Windows\NTDS\ntds.dit (the master database file containing the password hashes of every employee, service, and Domain Admin in the company) while the Domain Controller is running, so normal copy commands fail. Running under PID 6412 on CORP-DC01 (10.10.0.5), ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm" "create full C:\Windows\Temp\tmp_ad" (where "ac i ntds" selects the Active Directory database instance, and "ifm" / "create full" instructs Microsoft’s signed backup tool to take a Volume Shadow Copy snapshot) writes an unlocked copy of C:\Windows\Temp\tmp_ad\Active Directory\ntds.dit plus the registry\SYSTEM decryption hive (emitting ESENT Application Event ID 325 confirming the new database file was created). The ifm (Install From Media, originally designed so administrators could promote a new Domain Controller from a backup folder) command in ntdsutil.exe (PID 6412) automatically invokes vssvc.exe to snapshot the volume, extracts both Active Directory\ntds.dit and registry\SYSTEM (which holds the BootKey required to decrypt the NTLM and Kerberos keys inside ntds.dit offline), and removes the temporary shadow copy upon completion. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ NTDS.DIT CREATED / ⇠#2 ACK Event 325) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 IT Jump Server (Netsh Proxy)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & MDE). [Specs: IFM COMMAND=ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm" "create full C:\Windows\Temp\tmp_ad" q q; APPLICATION LOG=ESENT Event IDs 325, 326, 327 (Database created/detached); EXTRACTED FILES=ntds.dit + registry\SYSTEM + registry\SECURITY]
  - Stage 3 (T1090.001 · Proxy: Internal Proxy): **MULTI-HOP INTERNAL RELAY VIA NETSH PORTPROXY** — Finally, to keep a persistent hidden hallway open into the Domain Controller without installing any third-party proxy software, the infiltrator programs the Windows jump server’s built-in port forwarder (netsh interface portproxy) to quietly relay port 8443 straight to the Domain Controller’s RDP port (10.10.0.5:3389). To maintain stealthy multi-hop access and relay staged archives out through the jump server SRV-MGMT-01 (10.10.15.22), the attacker runs C:\Windows\System32\netsh.exe (PID 6890): netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=8443 connectaddress=10.10.0.5 connectport=3389 (instructing Windows’ built-in IP Helper service to forward inbound TCP port 8443 traffic directly to CORP-DC01 at 10.10.0.5:3389 without dropping any custom proxy binary to disk). When netsh.exe (PID 6890) executes the portproxy add v4tov4 command, the Windows kernel/service configuration writes the forwarding rule into HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\PortProxy\v4tov4\tcp\0.0.0.0/8443 with value 10.10.0.5/3389 (persisting the tunnel across reboots inside the native IpHlpSvc service while triggering Sysmon Event ID 13 RegistryEvent). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ NETSH PORTPROXY / ⇠#3 ACK PortProxy) from Node ③ (#3 IT Jump Server (Netsh Proxy)) to Node ④ (#4 ntdsutil.exe & vssadmin.exe), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & MDE). [Specs: LOLBIN COMMAND=netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=8443 connectport=3389; REGISTRY KEY=HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\PortProxy\v4tov4\tcp; SERVICE HOST=iphlpsvc (IP Helper Service)]

### T1098.003: Microsoft Threat Intel — Midnight Blizzard (APT29): OAuth App Persistence & EWS Exfiltration
- **Scenario ID**: `ms-midnight-blizzard-oauth`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ms-midnight-blizzard-oauth
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ms-midnight-blizzard-oauth
- **Category**: ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · Legacy Tenant Password Spray, OAuth full_access_as_app & EWS
- **Overview**: Imagine a burglar who finds a forgotten, dusty side cottage on a corporate estate (a legacy non-production test tenant) whose door still uses a simple single-key lock (no MFA). Inside that cottage, the burglar finds an old master maintenance badge (a legacy OAuth application) that happens to have cross-building authority in the main corporate headquarters. Using that badge, they mint new automated robot passes (Service Principals) granted the full_access_as_app stamp, letting them silently read any executive’s mailbox without ever needing any executive’s password. Documented by Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) and Microsoft Threat Intelligence (January 2024), this scenario illustrates how Midnight Blizzard (APT29) compromised corporate Exchange Online mailboxes through an identity-and-OAuth chain. First, the attacker used a low-and-slow residential-proxy password spray (sending only a few login attempts per IP so rate-based lockouts never trigger) to compromise a forgotten, non-production test tenant account that lacked MFA. From there, they abused an old OAuth application that had elevated permissions in the corporate environment, registered new malicious OAuth Service Principals, granted them the powerful full_access_as_app Exchange Online role (which allows reading any mailbox in the company via API without user interaction), and exfiltrated emails over EWS.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1110.003 (Brute Force: Password Spraying - Initial Access / Credential Access), T1098.003 (Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles (full_access_as_app) - Persistence / Privilege Escalation)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Midnight Blizzard: Guidance for responders on nation-state attack (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/01/25/midnight-blizzard-guidance-for-responders-on-nation-state-attack/) | CISA Emergency Directive: Emergency Directive 24-02: Mitigating the Significant Risk from Nation-State Compromise of Microsoft Corporate Email (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-24-02-mitigating-significant-risk-nation-state-compromise-microsoft-corporate-email) | Mandiant / Google Cloud Threat Intelligence: APT29 (Midnight Blizzard / Cozy Bear) Cloud Identity & Service Principal Persistence Tradecraft (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1110.003 · Brute Force: Password Spraying): **LOW-VOLUME PASSWORD SPRAY ON LEGACY TEST TENANT** — Instead of rattling the front door of the main corporate tower 1,000 times from one suspicious van, the attacker has dozens of local couriers (residential proxy IPs) try just one password at a time on a forgotten side-cottage test door that never had a two-factor keypad installed. To avoid triggering automated IP blocks or account lockouts, the attacker routes authentication requests through a rotating pool of residential proxy IPs (home internet routers in the same country as the target, making login traffic look like legitimate local employees rather than a datacenter botnet) and performs a low-volume password spray (trying just one common password at a time across a small list of accounts) against a forgotten, non-production legacy test tenant account that had never been enforced with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). Because each residential proxy IP sends only a tiny fraction of the total login attempts and stays well below the bad-password lockout threshold (e.g., 1 attempt per hour), traditional velocity-based brute-force rules do not fire, allowing the attacker to quietly log into the forgotten single-factor test account. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LEGACY TENANT SPRAY / ⇠#1 RESP ResultType 0) from Node ① (#1 Midnight Blizzard Proxy Pool) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & Defender XDR). [Specs: SPRAY CADENCE=Low-volume distributed across residential proxy IPs; ENTRY ACCOUNT=Legacy non-production test tenant account (MFA disabled); SIGN-IN LOG=AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs / SignInLogs ResultType 0]
  - Stage 2 (T1098.003 · Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles): **MALICIOUS OAUTH APP REGISTRATION & ROLE CONSENT** — Once inside the side cottage, the intruder discovers an old "Universal Maintenance App" that was accidentally given admin rights over the main corporate tower. Using that app’s authority, they print brand-new client secret keys (Add servicePrincipal credentials) and stamp them with the highest mail-reading clearance (full_access_as_app). Inside the test environment, the attacker discovers a legacy OAuth test application whose Service Principal had been granted privileged directory permissions, specifically AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All (a high-privilege Microsoft Graph permission that allows an app to grant any permission role to itself or to other apps without asking a human Global Administrator), inside the main corporate tenant. Using that legacy app, the attacker creates new malicious OAuth Service Principals, attaches new client secret keys (Add servicePrincipal credentials, creating long-lived API passwords for the app), and assigns them the Office 365 Exchange Online full_access_as_app role. In Microsoft Entra ID, an application holding AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All can call the Graph API (/servicePrincipals/{id}/appRoleAssignments) to self-assign full_access_as_app (Role ID dc890d15-9560-4a4c-9b7f-a736ec74ec40, the highest application-level Exchange permission), escalating from a forgotten test account to full tenant-wide mail access without touching a human admin’s account. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ GRANT FULL_ACCESS_AS_APP / ⇠#2 RESP Role Granted) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Microsoft Entra ID Control Plane), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & Defender XDR). [Specs: ENTRA OPERATION=Add application -> Add service principal credentials -> Add app role assignment; APP PERMISSION=full_access_as_app (dc890d15-9560-4a4c-9b7f-a736ec74ec40); PERSISTENCE=OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials token survives user password resets]
  - Stage 3 (T1528 · Steal Application Access Token): **OAUTH BEARER TOKEN EWS MAILBOX EXFILTRATION** — Holding the full_access_as_app robot pass, the attacker walks straight up to the Exchange mailroom window (outlook.office365.com/EWS/Exchange.asmx) and downloads executive inbox folders in bulk, never triggering a single phone MFA prompt on any executive’s device. Authenticating purely as the rogue OAuth application using grant_type=client_credentials (machine-to-machine authentication that uses the app’s client secret and never involves a human user login or MFA prompt), the attacker calls Exchange Web Services (https://outlook.office365.com/EWS/Exchange.asmx) through the same residential proxy pool to search and download emails from senior executive and security-team mailboxes. Because full_access_as_app is an application-level permission (Application Permission) rather than a delegated user permission (Delegated Permission), the OAuth Bearer token grants direct read/export access to any mailbox in the Exchange Online tenant without ever logging in as those users or triggering Conditional Access user-MFA policies. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ EWS MAIL EXFIL / ⇠#3 RESP 412 Items) from Node ③ (#3 Microsoft Entra ID Control Plane) to Node ④ (#4 Malicious OAuth Service Principal), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & Defender XDR). [Specs: EXFIL ENDPOINT=https://outlook.office365.com/EWS/Exchange.asmx; UNIFIED AUDIT LOG=MailItemsAccessed & ApplicationImpersonation via AppId; MITRE TECHNIQUE=T1528 (Steal Application Access Token) & T1114.002 (Remote Email Collection)]

### T1014: Microsoft & Kaspersky — Salt Typhoon (GhostEmperor): Demodex Rootkit & Telecom Core Capture
- **Scenario ID**: `ms-salt-typhoon-telecom`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ms-salt-typhoon-telecom
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ms-salt-typhoon-telecom
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Microsoft Threat Intel / Kaspersky GReAT · BYOVD Demodex Kernel Rootkit & TACACS+ Capture
- **Overview**: Imagine a telephone company’s central switching building. Instead of bugging a single office phone, the attacker slips into the core highway router (Cisco IOS XE), enables a hidden Linux maintenance room built right inside the router (Guest Shell), and taps the core fiber backbone (RADIUS / TACACS+ and packet capture pipes) so they can harvest network engineer credentials and silently copy traffic passing through the ISP. Documented by CISA, FBI, NSA, and Microsoft Threat Intelligence (2024), the Salt Typhoon APT campaign targeted major telecommunications and ISP core networks. Rather than attacking regular office workstations, Salt Typhoon compromised internet-facing edge and core routing appliances (such as Cisco IOS XE routers), abused the router’s built-in Linux container environment ("Guest Shell", a legitimate Linux environment inside the router where processes are invisible to standard router CLI commands) to run persistent implants and SSH tunnels, captured network administrator TACACS+ / RADIUS credentials in transit, and accessed sensitive core routing planes.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1014 (Rootkit (Demodex Kernel Driver & GhostSpider) - Defense Evasion / Persistence), T1552.001 (Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files (TACACS+ / RADIUS Capture) - Credential Access)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: CISA / NSA / FBI / Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Enhanced Visibility and Hardening Guidance for Communications Infrastructure (Salt Typhoon / AA24-338A) (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-338a) | Kaspersky GReAT: GhostEmperor: From ProxyLogon to Kernel Mode with Demodex Rootkit (https://securelist.com/ghostemperor-from-proxylogon-to-kernel-mode/104407/) | Cisco Talos Intelligence Group: Active Exploitation of Cisco IOS XE Software Web Management User Interface (CVE-2023-20198 & CVE-2023-20273) (https://blog.talosintelligence.com/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **BYOVD VULNERABLE SIGNED DRIVER LOAD (DSE BYPASS)** — The intruder exploits a flaw in the router’s front management web desk (webui_wsma_http) to forge a "Privilege 15 Master Engineer" badge right inside the router’s local user roster. The attacker exploits an exposed management interface or captured configuration credential on a telecom edge router (such as the Cisco IOS XE Web UI / webui_wsma_http endpoint) to execute privileged configuration commands and create a hidden local user account with privilege 15 (in Cisco IOS XE, Privilege Level 15 is the highest "enable" administrative tier, granting unrestricted control over routing tables, packet capture, and system containers). Creating a local fallback account with username <name> privilege 15 secret <hash> allows the attacker to log directly into the router with full administrative authority whenever local authentication fallback is enabled or by bypassing centralized AAA checks. In the documented Sysmon EID 6 exchange from Salt Typhoon C2 Relay to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK Event 6 (confirming that the BYOVD DRIVER LOAD request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 DEMODEX KERNEL ROOTKIT MINIFILTER & REGISTRY HIDING). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ BYOVD DRIVER LOAD / ⇠#1 ACK Event 6) from Node ① (#1 Salt Typhoon C2 Relay) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender XDR & Telecom NDR). [Specs: TECHNIQUE=Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) DSE Bypass; SYSMON EVENT=Sysmon Event ID 6 (Driver Loaded) & System EID 7045; KERNEL TARGET=ci.dll!g_CiOptions (Code Integrity) / NonPagedPoolExecute]
  - Stage 2 (T1014 · Rootkit): **DEMODEX KERNEL ROOTKIT MINIFILTER & REGISTRY HIDING** — Inside the router, there is a legitimate, factory-built Linux workshop (guestshell) meant for automation scripts. When an admin inspects the normal router command line (show processes), they cannot see inside that Linux workshop, making it the perfect hidden room to run a covert SSH tunnel. Instead of dropping files onto the router’s standard flash storage (where any network engineer running "dir flash:" would immediately spot an unfamiliar file), the attacker enables iox (Cisco’s Application Hosting framework) and runs guestshell enable (which boots a built-in Linux container inside the router, originally designed by Cisco so engineers could run Python automation scripts, but abused by the attacker because processes and files inside the Linux Guest Shell are completely hidden from standard IOS CLI commands like "show processes"). Inside the Guest Shell Linux container, the attacker has a full bash environment with network access to the router’s interfaces, allowing them to compile and run custom C2 tunnels, SSH relays, and packet sniffers inside an isolated container where no traditional endpoint EDR agent can be installed. In the documented Kernel Pool Scan exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Telecom NOC Jump Server, Telecom NOC Jump Server responds with ALERT 96 KB Ring-0 (confirming that the DEMODEX ROOTKIT request succeeded on Telecom NOC Jump Server and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 TELECOM TACACS+ CREDENTIAL CAPTURE & CORE ROUTER PIVOT). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ DEMODEX ROOTKIT / ⇠#2 ALERT 96 KB Ring-0) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Telecom NOC Jump Server), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender XDR & Telecom NDR). [Specs: ROOTKIT NAME=Demodex (GhostEmperor / Salt Typhoon); KERNEL HOOKS=FltRegisterFilter (IRP_MJ_DIRECTORY_CONTROL) & CmRegisterCallbackEx; STEALTH EFFECT=Conceals user-mode implant files, registry keys & sockets]
  - Stage 3 (T1040 · Network Sniffing): **TELECOM TACACS+ CREDENTIAL CAPTURE & CORE ROUTER PIVOT** — From their hidden room inside the highway router, the attacker clips a wiretap (EPC / tcpdump) onto the router’s management line, records the passwords of senior network engineers as they log in, and uses those keys to walk into the core switching center. From inside the compromised router, the attacker activates Embedded Packet Capture (EPC, monitor capture, the router’s built-in traffic recording feature) or runs tcpdump inside Guest Shell to sniff management-plane traffic passing through the router. They intercept TACACS+ (TCP port 49) and RADIUS (UDP port 1812) authentication packets alongside weak/obfuscated Type-7 passwords in router configs (harvesting the credentials of senior telecom engineers so the attacker can log into core MPLS/BGP backbone routers as a legitimate administrator). Because core telecom routers sit at the intersection of administrative management networks and subscriber trunks, passive packet capture on the router itself harvests authentication secrets in transit without generating noisy port scans across the internal network. In the documented Suricata TACACS+/SSH exchange from Telecom NOC Jump Server to Demodex Kernel Rootkit (Ring-0), Demodex Kernel Rootkit (Ring-0) responds with ALERT TCP/49 & :22 (confirming that the CORE ROUTER PIVOT request succeeded on Demodex Kernel Rootkit (Ring-0) and completing the final execution objective of Microsoft & Kaspersky, Salt Typhoon (GhostEmperor): Demodex Rootkit & Telecom Core Capture). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ CORE ROUTER PIVOT / ⇠#3 ALERT TCP/49 & :22) from Node ③ (#3 Telecom NOC Jump Server) to Node ④ (#4 Demodex Kernel Rootkit (Ring-0)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender XDR & Telecom NDR). [Specs: CAPTURED PROTOCOL=TACACS+ (TCP/49), RADIUS (UDP/1812) & SSH (:22); TARGET INFRASTRUCTURE=Telecom Core Routers & Lawful-Intercept Management Plane; EXFIL CHANNEL=Multi-hop encrypted TLS tunnel to 203.0.113.195:443]

### CVE-2022-38028: Microsoft Threat Intel — Forest Blizzard (APT28): Print Spooler CVE-2022-38028 & GooseEgg
- **Scenario ID**: `ms-forest-blizzard-gooseegg`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ms-forest-blizzard-gooseegg
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ms-forest-blizzard-gooseegg
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: HIGH
- **Subtitle**: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · pnms009.inf Driver Store Symlink, GooseEgg (justice.exe) & wayzgoose.dll
- **Overview**: Imagine a building where the mailroom’s high-privilege Printer Robot (spoolsv.exe, running as SYSTEM) uses a shared ledger (PnPData) to look up which driver helper (mpdwconstr.dll) it should load. Because a flaw lets a regular visitor edit the folder path in that ledger, the attacker changes the ledger to point to their own locker (wayzgoose.dll). When the Printer Robot wakes up, it loads the attacker’s library with full SYSTEM master-key authority. Documented by Microsoft Threat Intelligence (April 2024), the Forest Blizzard APT group (APT28 / STRONTIUM) used a custom post-exploitation tool named GooseEgg to escalate from a regular low-privilege user account to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM via CVE-2022-38028 in the Windows Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe, chosen because it runs as SYSTEM on every Windows machine by default). GooseEgg modifies a JavaScript constraints file (mpdw-constraints.js) used by the Microsoft XPS Document Writer printer driver, triggers the Print Spooler to corrupt permissions so a custom driver DLL (wayzgoose.dll) can be planted, and forces spoolsv.exe to load that DLL with full SYSTEM privileges.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (Print Spooler CVE-2022-38028 GooseEgg) - Privilege Escalation), T1574.001 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking (wayzgoose.dll) - Persistence / Privilege Escalation)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Analyzing Forest Blizzard’s custom post-compromise tool for exploiting CVE-2022-38028 to obtain credentials (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/04/22/analyzing-forest-blizzards-custom-post-compromise-tool-for-exploiting-cve-2022-38028-to-obtain-credentials/) | Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): CVE-2022-38028 Windows Print Spooler Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2022-38028) | The MITRE Corporation & ESET Research: MITRE ATT&CK Group G0007: APT28 (Forest Blizzard / Fancy Bear / Fighting Ursa) (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **GOOSEEGG SYMLINK & PNMS009.INF DRIVERSTORE TAMPERING** — The intruder runs a batch script (doit.bat) that edits the XPS Printer’s instruction sheet (mpdw-constraints.js) so the next time the Printer Service checks its settings, it accidentally unlocks its own protected driver cabinet. Starting from a standard low-privilege user session (which cannot install programs or read other users’ passwords), the attacker runs a batch launcher (doit.bat / justice.bat) that executes the GooseEgg binary. GooseEgg creates a custom printer driver key in the Registry and modifies mpdw-constraints.js (a JavaScript configuration file used by the built-in Microsoft XPS Document Writer printer driver to validate print ticket settings, crafted with oversized data to trigger CVE-2022-38028 when the Print Spooler reads it). When C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe (which runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM) parses the malformed mpdw-constraints.js file inside the DriverStore\FileRepository directory, a memory corruption / permission flaw (CVE-2022-38028) allows the low-privilege user to overwrite the printer driver’s PnPData / DriverFile path. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ WRITE WAYZGOOSE.DLL / ⇠#1 ACK FileCreate) from Node ① (#1 GooseEgg Batch Launcher) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2022-38028 (Windows Print Spooler EoP); EXPLOIT BINARY=justice.exe / doit.exe (HackTool:Win64/GooseEgg); MODIFIED PATH=DriverStore\FileRepository\pnms009.inf_amd64_*\MPDW-constraints.js]
  - Stage 2 (T1547.012 · Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Print Processors): **SPOOLSV.EXE LOADS WAYZGOOSE23.DLL AS SYSTEM** — Now that the printer ledger points to wayzgoose.dll, GooseEgg sends a dummy print job, waking up spoolsv.exe (SYSTEM), which dutifully loads wayzgoose.dll into its own SYSTEM-privileged memory. With the driver path redirected by the exploit, GooseEgg drops its companion malicious library (wayzgoose.dll) into a writable folder and sends an RPC print-configuration call to wake up spoolsv.exe. Because spoolsv.exe runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (the highest local operating-system account on Windows), when it calls LoadLibrary() on the registered printer driver, wayzgoose.dll is loaded directly into spoolsv.exe’s memory and executes with full SYSTEM master-key privileges. Instead of injecting memory into a SYSTEM process from the outside (which Windows Protected Process Light and EDR memory hooks block), CVE-2022-38028 tricks spoolsv.exe into voluntarily loading wayzgoose.dll as if it were an official Microsoft printer driver. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SPOOLSV LOAD DLL / ⇠#2 ACK SYSTEM Load) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 DriverStore (pnms009.inf)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR). [Specs: HOST SERVICE=C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM); MALICIOUS DLL=wayzgoose23.dll (Loaded via MPDW-constraints.js); SYSMON EVENT=Sysmon Event ID 7 (Unsigned DLL loaded by spoolsv.exe)]
  - Stage 3 (T1546.015 · Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking): **WHO.EXE SYSTEM BACKDOOR & COM SERVER HIJACK** — Running inside the SYSTEM Printer Robot, wayzgoose.dll opens a master-key backdoor service and connects out to the operator’s command center. Now executing inside spoolsv.exe as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, wayzgoose.dll launches the attacker’s post-exploitation script (who.bat, which inherits spoolsv.exe’s SYSTEM security token so every command it runs has total control of the computer), registers a persistent Windows service backdoor, and opens an outbound C2 channel so Forest Blizzard can dump LSASS credentials and move laterally. In Windows, any child process created via CreateProcess inherits the security token of its parent process by default. However, because a legitimate Print Spooler (spoolsv.exe) should only talk to printers and never spawn cmd.exe or powershell.exe, this parent-child relationship is a classic high-confidence detection signal. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 exchange from DriverStore (pnms009.inf) to spoolsv.exe -> wayzgoose23.dll, spoolsv.exe -> wayzgoose23.dll responds with ACK PID 6240 (confirming that the SPAWN WHO.EXE request succeeded on spoolsv.exe -> wayzgoose23.dll and completing the final execution objective of Microsoft Threat Intel, Forest Blizzard (APT28): Print Spooler CVE-2022-38028 & GooseEgg). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SPAWN WHO.EXE / ⇠#3 ACK PID 6240) from Node ③ (#3 DriverStore (pnms009.inf)) to Node ④ (#4 spoolsv.exe -> wayzgoose23.dll), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR). [Specs: BACKDOOR BINARY=who.exe (Spawned by spoolsv.exe as SYSTEM); PERSISTENCE=COM Server InprocServer32 Hijack + ScheduledDefrag Task; THREAT ACTOR=Forest Blizzard (APT28 / GRU Unit 26165)]

### T1539: Microsoft, Unit 42 & CISA — Star Blizzard / Storm-0539: Evilginx AiTM Cookie Theft
- **Scenario ID**: `unit42-star-blizzard-evilginx-aitm`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/unit42-star-blizzard-evilginx-aitm
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=unit42-star-blizzard-evilginx-aitm
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: HIGH
- **Subtitle**: Microsoft Threat Intel / Unit 42 / CISA AA23-341A · AiTM Reverse Proxy, ESTSAUTH Cookie & Inbox Rules
- **Overview**: Imagine a fake ATM booth placed right in front of a real bank window with a two-way mirror between them. When you walk up and type your PIN and tap your 6-digit phone MFA code, the fake booth immediately types those exact digits into the real bank window behind the glass. The real bank says: "Welcome! Here is your golden VIP Day Pass (ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT cookie)." The fake booth photocopies your golden Day Pass as it hands it to you, and now the thief can walk into the bank all day using their copy of your pass without ever needing your phone again. Documented by Microsoft Threat Intelligence, CISA, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, this scenario explains how Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing frameworks like Evilginx defeat traditional Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) such as SMS codes, authenticator apps (TOTP), and push notifications. Instead of hosting a static fake login page that only steals a password, the attacker’s Evilginx server acts as a live reverse proxy sitting between the victim’s browser and the real login.microsoftonline.com server. When the victim types their password and approves their MFA prompt, Evilginx forwards that traffic to Microsoft in real time, and intercepts the resulting ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT session cookie (the post-MFA proof-of-login token) as Microsoft sends it back.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1539 (Steal Web Session Cookie (Evilginx AiTM ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT Capture) - Credential Access), T1550.004 (Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie - Defense Evasion / Lateral Movement)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: CISA, NCSC-UK, NSA & FBI Joint Advisory: Star Blizzard (SEABORGIUM / COLDRIVER) Adversary-in-the-Middle Spear-Phishing & Session Cookie Theft (AA23-341A) (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-341a) | Microsoft Threat Intelligence: From Cookie Theft to BEC: Attackers Use AiTM Phishing Sites as Entry Point (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/07/12/from-cookie-theft-to-bec-attackers-use-aitm-phishing-sites-as-entry-point-to-further-financial-fraud/) | The MITRE Corporation & Palo Alto Unit 42: MITRE ATT&CK T1539: Steal Web Session Cookie & FIDO2 Token Binding Mitigations (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1539 · Steal Web Session Cookie): **EVILGINX AITM REVERSE-PROXY MFA INTERCEPTION** — The victim clicks a link to view a PDF document and lands at the two-way-mirror booth (Evilginx). Because the booth is relaying the real Microsoft login screen live from behind the glass, every logo, font, and custom company banner looks 100% authentic. After building trust via email, the attacker sends a link to a lookalike domain (e.g., login.micros0ft-auth-portal.com, registered with a valid Let’s Encrypt HTTPS certificate so the browser still displays a padlock icon). When the victim clicks the link, the attacker’s Evilginx server fetches the genuine login.microsoftonline.com page live in the background and rewrites the domain names inside the HTML on the fly (so the victim sees their own company’s real logo, custom background image, and live Microsoft login prompts). Unlike traditional phishing kits that host a static HTML copy of a login page (which breaks when MFA challenges or dynamic JavaScript run), an AiTM reverse proxy relays every HTTP request and response between the victim’s browser and Microsoft Entra ID in real time. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ AITM PROXY AUTH / ⇠#1 RESP ESTSAUTH Issued) from Node ① (#1 Evilginx3 AiTM Reverse Proxy) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR & Sentinel). [Specs: AITM PROXY=Evilginx3 Reverse Proxy (login.corp-verify-sso.com); CAPTURED COOKIE=ESTSAUTH & ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT (Post-MFA Token); BYPASSED CONTROL=SMS, Voice, TOTP & Push Notification MFA]
  - Stage 2 (T1550.004 · Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie): **WEB SESSION COOKIE REPLAY (PASS-THE-COOKIE)** — The victim types their password and enters the 6-digit MFA code from their phone. The man-in-the-middle booth passes both straight through the window to Microsoft in milliseconds, and when Microsoft hands back the Set-Cookie: ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT VIP pass, the booth records a copy in its database. The victim enters their corporate password and completes their real MFA challenge (typing a 6-digit Authenticator code or tapping "Approve" on a push notification). Evilginx forwards both requests straight to login.microsoftonline.com in milliseconds. Once MFA succeeds, Microsoft responds with HTTP 200 OK containing Set-Cookie: ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT=... (the master browser session cookie that Microsoft issues after both password and MFA are verified, which passes through Evilginx in plaintext because the HTTPS connection from the victim terminates on the Evilginx proxy first). Because the victim’s TLS session terminates on the attacker’s Evilginx server before Evilginx opens a second TLS session to Microsoft, Evilginx can read and save every HTTP header, including Set-Cookie: ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT and ESTSAUTH, the instant MFA completes. In the documented AADNonInteractiveSignIn exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01), Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01) responds with RESP MFA Bypassed (confirming that the COOKIE REPLAY request succeeded on Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 STEALTH INBOX RULE CREATION & BEC EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ COOKIE REPLAY / ⇠#2 RESP MFA Bypassed) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR & Sentinel). [Specs: FORENSIC ARTIFACT=Same SessionId / CorrelationId seen from 2 different IPs/ASNs; TECHNIQUE=T1550.004 (Pass the Cookie); RISK EVENT=anomalousToken / unfamiliarFeatures in Entra ID]
  - Stage 3 (T1564.008 · Hide Artifacts: Email Hiding Rules): **STEALTH INBOX RULE CREATION & BEC EXFILTRATION** — Minutes later, the attacker pastes that photocopied ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT VIP pass into their own browser in another country, walks straight into the victim’s Outlook inbox, and sets up a hidden mail-forwarding rule so they keep getting copies of every email. The attacker imports the stolen ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT cookie into their own browser using a cookie editor and opens outlook.office.com. Because holding a valid ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT cookie tells Microsoft "this browser already passed password + MFA checks", Outlook opens the victim’s mailbox immediately without asking for a password or triggering an MFA prompt on the victim’s phone. The attacker then creates a hidden Inbox rule (New-InboxRule, automatically forwarding or moving incoming security/reset emails so the victim never notices ongoing access). Why did MFA fail to stop this? Because TOTP codes and push approvals only verify the login event, not the domain in the browser bar. Only phishing-resistant FIDO2 / WebAuthn passkeys (which cryptographically bind the login signature to the exact domain name login.microsoftonline.com) or Token Protection (device-bound session cookies) defeat AiTM proxies. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ HIDE INBOX RULE / ⇠#3 RESP Rule Created) from Node ③ (#3 Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01)) to Node ④ (#4 Cookie Replay Session (Pass-the-Cookie)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR & Sentinel). [Specs: EXCHANGE AUDIT=Operation="New-InboxRule" MoveToFolder="RSS Feeds" MarkAsRead="True"; MITRE TECHNIQUE=T1564.008 (Email Hiding Rules); DEFENSE COUNTERMEASURE=FIDO2 / WebAuthn Device-Bound Passkeys + Token Protection]

### CVE-2024-20353: Cisco Talos — ArcaneDoor (UAT4356): Cisco ASA Zero-Days, Line Dancer & Line Runner
- **Scenario ID**: `talos-arcanedoor-asa`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/talos-arcanedoor-asa
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=talos-arcanedoor-asa
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Cisco Talos · CVE-2024-20353 / CVE-2024-20359, host-scan-reply Shellcode & Syslog Disable
- **Overview**: Imagine a border checkpoint guardhouse (a Cisco ASA VPN firewall) that has no security cameras inside its own booth. The attacker slips a hidden radio receiver (Line Dancer) into the guardhouse’s memory that listens for secret commands disguised inside regular traveler visa forms (/CSCOSSLC/config-auth), and welds a hidden spare key (Line Runner) into the checkpoint’s boot firmware (disk0:) so even if the building loses power and restarts, the backdoor comes right back to life. Documented by Cisco Talos, the UK NCSC, and CISA (April 2024), the ArcaneDoor espionage campaign targeted perimeter network devices, specifically Cisco Adaptive Security Appliances (ASA), using two custom implants: Line Dancer (an in-memory shellcode interpreter that hooks the firewall’s core lina process so the attacker can send commands disguised inside normal VPN login requests on port 443) and Line Runner (a persistent boot backdoor that abuses a legacy startup archive on disk0: so the implant automatically reloads even if the firewall is rebooted).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Cisco ASA CVE-2024-20353) - Initial Access), T1542.004 (Pre-OS Boot: ROMMON / Bootimage Persistence (Line Runner) - Persistence), T1562.003 (Impair Defenses: Disable Syslog & Crashdump Forensics (Line Dancer) - Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Cisco Talos Intelligence Group: ArcaneDoor — New Espionage-Focused Campaign Found Targeting Perimeter Network Devices (https://blog.talosintelligence.com/arcanedoor-new-espionage-focused-campaign-found-targeting-perimeter-network-devices/) | Cisco Security Advisories: Cisco Adaptive Security Appliance and Firepower Threat Defense Software Web Services Denial of Service and Persistence (CVE-2024-20353, CVE-2024-20359) (https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-asaftd-persist-rce-FLsNXF4h) | NCSC-UK & Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: ArcaneDoor: Espionage Campaign Targeting Perimeter Network Devices — Forensic & Detection Guidance (https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/news/arcanedoor-espionage-campaign-targeting-perimeter-network-devices)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1542 · Pre-OS Boot): **ASA ZERO-DAY EXPLOIT & LINE RUNNER FLASH PERSISTENCE** — Every day, thousands of remote employees send <config-auth> XML forms to the Cisco ASA VPN gate to log in. The attacker sends that exact same XML form, but tucks a 32-byte secret handshake and Base64 shellcode inside the <host-scan-reply> field. To control the compromised Cisco ASA firewall without opening any suspicious new network port, the attacker sends standard HTTPS POST requests on port 443 to /CSCOSSLC/config-auth (the exact URL that every remote employee’s Cisco AnyConnect VPN client connects to every morning, allowing the attacker’s command-and-control traffic to blend seamlessly into legitimate corporate VPN logins). Inside the XML body’s <host-scan-reply> tag, the attacker places a 32-byte magic identifier followed by a Base64-encoded shellcode command. Normally, the ASA’s XML parser processes <host-scan-reply> during AnyConnect posture checks. Because the Line Dancer hook intercepts the buffer inside the lina process as soon as it spots the 32-byte magic header (before standard VPN authentication even finishes), the attacker can send commands without needing a valid VPN username or password. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LINE RUNNER BOOT / ⇠#1 ACK CVE-2024-20359) from Node ① (#1 UAT4356 (Storm-1849) Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / NetFlow SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABILITIES=CVE-2024-20353 (WebVPN) & CVE-2024-20359 (Flash Preload RCE); PERSISTENT IMPLANT=Line Runner (disk0: Preload ZIP -> csco_config.lua); THREAT ACTOR=UAT4356 / Storm-1849 (ArcaneDoor Campaign)]
  - Stage 2 (T1059 · Command and Scripting Interpreter): **LINE DANCER IN-MEMORY SHELLCODE INTERPRETER** — When the Line Dancer implant inside the firewall’s lina process spots that 32-byte secret handshake, its first move is to unplug the guardhouse’s alarm bell (disabling Syslog and crash dumps) before silently running the attacker’s router commands. Inside the ASA’s main lina executable (the monolithic process that handles all firewalling, routing, and VPN sessions on a Cisco ASA), the Line Dancer memory-only implant decodes the incoming shellcode and executes it directly in RAM. Before running reconnaissance or capturing packets, Line Dancer patches the in-memory syslog logging function (temporarily silencing outbound syslog alerts so the SOC’s SIEM server never sees that someone just ran "show running-config" or started a packet capture) and disables crash dumps (so if an exploit attempt crashes a thread, no forensic core dump is written to disk). Because perimeter network appliances cannot run standard Windows/Linux EDR agents, modifying the running lina process in volatile RAM hides the implant from normal CLI checks, and can only be caught on-box by hashing the live memory text segment via verify /md5 system:memory/text. In the documented HTTPS POST scan.xml exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall, Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall responds with RESP 1,420 Bytes (confirming that the LINE DANCER C2 request succeeded on Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 SYSLOG SUPPRESSION, PCAP CAPTURE & CONFIG EXFIL). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ LINE DANCER C2 / ⇠#2 RESP 1,420 Bytes) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / NetFlow SIEM). [Specs: IN-MEMORY IMPLANT=Line Dancer (Patched into /asa/bin/lina .text); C2 XML FIELD=POST /+CSCOE+/sdesktop/scan.xml -> <host-scan-reply>; ANTI-FORENSICS=Hooks crashdump routine to force reboot on memory dump attempt]
  - Stage 3 (T1562.001 · Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools): **SYSLOG SUPPRESSION, PCAP CAPTURE & CONFIG EXFIL** — Every time a Cisco ASA firewall boots up, it automatically unzips and runs an old factory setup archive (disk0:/.private/startup-config) if one exists. Line Runner plants a booby-trapped zip file in that exact spot so every reboot automatically re-installs the backdoor. Because Line Dancer lives purely in RAM, rebooting the firewall would normally wipe it out. To survive reboots, the attacker exploits CVE-2024-20359 (a legacy feature in Cisco ASA where the boot sequence automatically looks for a leftover pre-configuration zip archive on the flash drive disk0: and runs the scripts inside it as root during startup). By planting their persistent backdoor (Line Runner) inside that legacy boot archive path, the firewall automatically re-infects its own memory every time the power is cycled. Combining Line Runner (disk0: boot persistence via CVE-2024-20359) with Line Dancer (volatile RAM command execution inside lina) gives the attacker both reboot survival and zero-footprint daily operation. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ TEXT HASH MISMATCH / ⇠#3 ALERT MODIFIED .TEXT) from Node ③ (#3 Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall) to Node ④ (#4 Line Dancer Shellcode Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / NetFlow SIEM). [Specs: DEFENSE EVASION=Suppresses ASA Syslog generation & clears command history; COLLECTION=In-memory PCAP packet capture & show running-config export; MEMORY VERIFICATION=verify /sha-512 system:memory/text detects .text modification]

### CVE-2024-21762: NCSC-NL, Talos & Mandiant — China-Nexus APT: FortiOS SSL-VPN & COATHANGER Persistent RAT
- **Scenario ID**: `talos-fortinet-coathanger-apt`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/talos-fortinet-coathanger-apt
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=talos-fortinet-coathanger-apt
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: NCSC-NL / Mandiant / Talos · CVE-2022-42475 & CVE-2024-21762, preload.so Hook & smartctl Persistence
- **Overview**: Imagine a fortress gate (a FortiGate firewall) where a burglar uses an oversized battering ram (Heap Overflow in sslvpnd) to slip inside. Once inside, the burglar hooks a tiny invisible coat hanger (ld.so.preload rootkit) onto the fortress’s coat rack so that every time an administrator runs the inspection command (ps or ls) to check if anyone is hiding in the room, the coat hanger intercepts the administrator’s glasses and erases the burglar from their field of view, and even hides a spare copy inside the emergency recovery partition (flatkc) to survive firmware updates. Documented by the Dutch Military Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD), NCTV, and Fortinet (February 2024), COATHANGER is a stealthy Remote Access Trojan (RAT) designed specifically for Fortinet FortiGate firewalls. After gaining initial entry via a heap buffer overflow in the FortiOS SSL-VPN daemon (sslvpnd, CVE-2022-42475 / CVE-2023-27997), COATHANGER hooks Linux userland libraries via /etc/ld.so.preload (forcing every program on the firewall to load the attacker’s filter library first, so the implant can hide its own files and processes from administrators) and hooks the flatkc boot unpacker so it survives firmware upgrades.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (FortiOS SSL-VPN CVE-2024-21762 / CVE-2022-42475) - Initial Access), T1574.006 (Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking (COATHANGER preload.so & smartctl) - Persistence / Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: NCSC-NL (Netherlands MIVD/AIVD): COATHANGER: Chinese Cyber Espionage Malware Targeting FortiGate Appliances (https://english.ncsc.nl/publications/publications/2024/february/6/mivd-and-aivd-alert-on-coathanger-malware) | CISA & Fortinet PSIRT: FG-IR-24-015 (CVE-2024-21762) & FG-IR-22-398 (CVE-2022-42475) FortiOS SSL-VPN RCE Advisories (https://www.fortiguard.com/psirt/FG-IR-24-015) | The MITRE Corporation & Appliance Forensics Research: MITRE ATT&CK T1574.006: Dynamic Linker Hijacking (LD_PRELOAD & /etc/ld.so.preload Rootkits) (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/006/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **FORTIOS SSLVPND HEAP OVERFLOW (CVE-2024-21762)** — The attacker sends an HTTPS request to the FortiGate VPN login gate with a falsified Content-Length label, causing the sslvpnd gatekeeper to pour extra bytes past the end of its memory bucket (Heap Overflow) and overwrite its own instruction pointer. The attacker sends a specially crafted HTTPS request with a manipulated Content-Length header or encrypted parameter (enc) to the FortiGate SSL-VPN web endpoint (/remote/logincheck or /remote/hostcheck_validate, public VPN login pages reachable from the internet without prior authentication). This triggers a heap-based buffer overflow inside the sslvpnd daemon (writing attacker-controlled bytes past the end of the allocated heap buffer to overwrite adjacent function pointers in RAM and hijack the CPU into running the attacker’s code). In FortiOS, sslvpnd and almost all system utilities are compiled into a single monolithic multi-call binary (/bin/init). By chaining Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) gadgets inside that binary, exploiting sslvpnd gives the attacker immediate code execution inside the underlying Linux OS of the firewall. In the documented FortiOS Crashlog exchange from China-Nexus APT C2 to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK CVE-2024-21762 (confirming that the SSLVPND SIGSEGV request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 COATHANGER PRELOAD.SO ROOTKIT & SMARTCTL HOOK). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SSLVPND SIGSEGV / ⇠#1 ACK CVE-2024-21762) from Node ① (#1 China-Nexus APT C2) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC NDR & Firmware Auditor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2024-21762 & CVE-2022-42475 (FortiOS sslvpnd RCE); TARGET PROCESS=/bin/sslvpnd (Runs as root on FortiOS); CRASH ARTIFACT=diagnose debug crashlog read -> Application sslvpnd signal 11]
  - Stage 2 (T1574.006 · Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking): **COATHANGER PRELOAD.SO ROOTKIT & SMARTCTL HOOK** — Once inside, COATHANGER places a filter lens (preload.so) in /etc/ld.so.preload. Whenever any program on the firewall asks Linux "What files are in /data2?" or "What processes are running?", the filter lens intercepts the answer and deletes COATHANGER’s name before showing the list. COATHANGER stores its backdoor files inside the persistent /data2/ partition and writes the path of its malicious shared library (preload.so) into /etc/ld.so.preload (a special Linux dynamic-linker configuration file that forces every single program launched on the system to load preload.so before the standard C library libc.so). Because preload.so is loaded first, it intercepts file-listing and process-listing calls (removing COATHANGER’s files and PIDs from the results so an admin inspecting the firewall sees nothing unusual). By hooking user-space libc functions like readdir(), open(), and stat() via /etc/ld.so.preload, whenever an administrator runs a diagnostic CLI command on the FortiGate, the hooked library filters out any path containing the implant’s directory before returning the output to the terminal. In the documented NCSC-NL YARA Match exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd), FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd) responds with ALERT 36 KB ELF (confirming that the COATHANGER ROOTKIT request succeeded on FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 MASQUERADED HTTPSD BEACON & VPN CREDENTIAL THEFT). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ COATHANGER ROOTKIT / ⇠#2 ALERT 36 KB ELF) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC NDR & Firmware Auditor). [Specs: ROOTKIT LIBRARY=/data2/.bd/preload.so (Injected via ptrace into init/newcli); BOOT TRIGGER=Replaced /bin/smartctl binary invokes /data2/.bd/sh; UPGRADE SURVIVAL=Hooks flatkc firmware unpacker to reinfect upgraded OS image]
  - Stage 3 (T1014 · Rootkit): **MASQUERADED HTTPSD BEACON & VPN CREDENTIAL THEFT** — Even if the IT team installs a brand-new FortiOS firmware update, COATHANGER has already tucked a backup copy of itself inside the emergency kernel unpacker (flatkc) so that as soon as the newly updated firewall reboots, it re-infects itself on startup. Normally, rebooting a FortiGate or installing a FortiOS firmware update wipes the temporary root filesystem in RAM and loads a clean image. To survive both reboots and firmware updates, COATHANGER replaces /bin/smartctl and hooks the flatkc boot binary (the low-level FortiOS unpacker that initializes the filesystem whenever the appliance boots up, causing the firewall to automatically copy the hidden backdoor from the persistent /data2 flash partition back into the freshly updated system on startup). Because standard firmware upgrades replace the main rootfs image but preserve persistent flash partitions like /data2 alongside hooked boot components, simply installing a FortiOS patch without wiping and reformatting the appliance leaves COATHANGER active. In the documented Suricata TLS Alert exchange from FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd) to COATHANGER (preload.so & smartctl), COATHANGER (preload.so & smartctl) responds with ALERT TLS 1.3 (confirming that the FORTIGATE EGRESS C2 request succeeded on COATHANGER (preload.so & smartctl) and completing the final execution objective of NCSC-NL, Talos & Mandiant, China-Nexus APT: FortiOS SSL-VPN & COATHANGER Persistent RAT). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ FORTIGATE EGRESS C2 / ⇠#3 ALERT TLS 1.3) from Node ③ (#3 FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd)) to Node ④ (#4 COATHANGER (preload.so & smartctl)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC NDR & Firmware Auditor). [Specs: MASQUERADED PROC=/bin/httpsd (Actual binary: /data2/.bd/httpsd); C2 PROTOCOL=Pinned TLS 1.2/1.3 Beacon to 198.51.100.168:443; ADVISORY REF=NCSC-NL / MIVD COATHANGER Technical Report (Feb 2024)]

### CVE-2023-46747: F5 Security & Mandiant — F5 BIG-IP TMUI AJP Request Smuggling to Root RCE
- **Scenario ID**: `f5-bigip-request-smuggling`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/f5-bigip-request-smuggling
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=f5-bigip-request-smuggling
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: F5 K000137353 / Praetorian · Apache-to-Tomcat AJP Smuggling, form_page Auth Bypass & tmsh RCE
- **Overview**: Imagine a building with a strict front-door security guard (Apache httpd) and a trusting back-office clerk (Apache Tomcat) who talk to each other over an internal pneumatic tube (AJP protocol). A visitor sends a single long envelope whose outer label says it is just a public login-page check, so the front-door guard lets it through. Inside the pneumatic tube, however, the oversized message spills over and creates a brand-new second internal work order marked REMOTE_USER = admin. The back-office clerk reads that second forged work order and believes the front guard already verified the visitor as the building’s master administrator. Documented by ProjectDiscovery, Praetorian, and CISA (October–November 2023), CVE-2023-46747 is a critical unauthenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability in the F5 BIG-IP Traffic Management User Interface (TMUI). The BIG-IP management web interface uses a two-tier architecture: a front-end Apache httpd server checks authentication and forwards requests over the binary Apache JServ Protocol (AJP) to a back-end Apache Tomcat server. By sending an HTTP request with a carefully sized header to a public .jsp page, the attacker triggers AJP Request Smuggling, injecting a forged second AJP packet straight into Tomcat with SC_A_REMOTE_USER=admin (tricking Tomcat into believing the front-end Apache server already authenticated the attacker as the master administrator).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (F5 BIG-IP TMUI AJP Smuggling CVE-2023-46747) - Initial Access), T1059.004 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell (/mgmt/tm/util/bash) - Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: F5 SIRT Security Advisory: F5 BIG-IP Configuration Utility Unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2023-46747) (https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000137353) | ProjectDiscovery & Praetorian Security Research: F5 BIG-IP Unauthenticated RCE via AJP Request Smuggling (CVE-2023-46747 Technical Deep-Dive) (https://blog.projectdiscovery.io/f5-big-ip-unauthenticated-rce-cve-2023-46747/) | NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) & CISA KEV: CVE-2023-46747 F5 BIG-IP Traffic Management User Interface (TMUI) Auth Bypass (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-46747)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **TMUI AJP REQUEST SMUGGLING (CVE-2023-46747)** — The attacker sends a request to a public login helper page (/tmui/Control/jspmap/tmui/locallb/workspace/tmshCmd.jsp) with a precisely sized HTTP header that overflows the internal AJP pneumatic tube packet, sneaking a hidden second AJP message (REMOTE_USER=admin) right behind it. The attacker sends an unauthenticated HTTPS POST request to a reachable TMUI endpoint (/tmui/Control/jspmap/tmui/locallb/workspace/tmshCmd.jsp). By carefully sizing the HTTP headers and body, mod_proxy_ajp on the front-end Apache server miscalculates the binary AJP packet boundary and forwards the attacker’s raw payload bytes as a brand-new, second AJP request (starting with the AJP magic bytes 0x12 0x34) to the back-end Tomcat server on port 8009, with the internal AJP header attribute SC_A_REMOTE_USER set to "admin" (spoofing a fully authenticated administrator session because Tomcat blindly trusts whichever username the front-end Apache proxy puts in SC_A_REMOTE_USER). In a two-tier Apache + Tomcat AJP architecture, Tomcat does not re-verify passwords; it assumes the front-end Apache server already checked the user’s login before setting SC_A_REMOTE_USER. Smuggling a raw second AJP frame inside the socket stream lets an unauthenticated attacker inject SC_A_REMOTE_USER=admin directly into Tomcat. In the documented Suricata CVE-2023-46747 exchange from Threat Actor (AJP Smuggler) to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ALERT HTTP 200 (confirming that the AJP SMUGGLING POST request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 ROGUE ADMIN ACCOUNT CREATION VIA TMSHCMD.JSP). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ AJP SMUGGLING POST / ⇠#1 ALERT HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 Threat Actor (AJP Smuggler)) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 F5 Syslog & Suricata SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-46747 (CVSS 9.8 Unauthenticated RCE); PROTOCOL FLAW=Apache mod_proxy_ajp -> Tomcat AJP13 Request Smuggling; FORGED ATTRIBUTES=REMOTEUSER=admin & REMOTEROLE=0 (Administrator)]
  - Stage 2 (T1136.001 · Create Account: Local Account): **ROGUE ADMIN ACCOUNT CREATION VIA TMSHCMD.JSP** — Fooled by the forged REMOTE_USER=admin stamp on the smuggled work order, the back-end Tomcat clerk opens the internal UserCreate ledger and registers a brand-new administrator account with full bash terminal access.
