Executing inside Tomcat under the forged REMOTE_USER=admin identity (which bypasses the outer Apache authentication filter entirely because the smuggled request was born behind the Apache gatekeeper inside the internal AJP pipe), the request invokes the internal TMUI UserCreate handler (/tmui/Control/form) to create a new local BIG-IP administrator account granted Administrator role and Advanced Shell (/bin/bash) terminal access. When Tomcat processes the smuggled /tmui/Control/form request with SC_A_REMOTE_USER=admin, it communicates with the BIG-IP master control daemon (mcpd) to write the new administrator account into /config/bigip_user.conf. In the documented BIG-IP /var/log/audit exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd), BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd) responds with ACK Audit 01070417 (confirming that the CREATE AUTH USER request succeeded on BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 ROOT BASH EXECUTION & SSL PRIVATE KEY EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ CREATE AUTH USER / ⇠#2 ACK Audit 01070417) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 F5 Syslog & Suricata SIEM). [Specs: TMSH PAYLOAD=tmsh create auth user f5_support_adm password ... shell bash role admin; AUDIT LOG=/var/log/audit -> user=admin cmd_data="create auth user"; BYPASSED LAYER=Apache PAM Authentication (mod_auth_pam_external)]
  - Stage 3 (T1059.004 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell): **ROOT BASH EXECUTION & SSL PRIVATE KEY EXFILTRATION** — With their newly minted administrator account, the attacker calls the tmsh command runner to launch bash -c as root and extract all SSL private keys and internal server credentials managed by the load balancer. Using the newly created admin account (or directly via a smuggled tmshCmd.jsp request), the attacker runs tmsh run /util bash -c "..." (abusing the Traffic Management Shell’s built-in "/util bash" utility to break out of the restricted appliance CLI into an unrestricted Linux root shell). With root access on the load balancer, they extract SSL/TLS private keys (/config/filestore/files_d/Common_d/certificate_key_d/, allowing them to decrypt HTTPS traffic for the company’s web apps) and backend server credentials. Because an F5 BIG-IP sits at the front of the datacenter terminating TLS connections and load-balancing internal servers, root access on the appliance exposes both private TLS keys and direct network paths into internal application VLANs. In the documented Auditd SYSCALL 59 exchange from BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd) to Tomcat AJP Backend & tmsh, Tomcat AJP Backend & tmsh responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the TMSH BASH RCE request succeeded on Tomcat AJP Backend & tmsh and completing the final execution objective of F5 Security & Mandiant, F5 BIG-IP TMUI AJP Request Smuggling to Root RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ TMSH BASH RCE / ⇠#3 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ③ (#3 BIG-IP Apache Frontend (httpd)) to Node ④ (#4 Tomcat AJP Backend & tmsh), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 F5 Syslog & Suricata SIEM). [Specs: BASH GADGET=tmsh create cli alias private list command /bin/bash; STOLEN ASSETS=/config/bigip.conf & /config/ssl/ssl.key/*.key; F5 MITIGATION=K000137353 Script (Block AJP Smuggling & Restrict TMUI)]

### CVE-2024-21887: Splunk STRT & Mandiant — Ivanti Connect Secure (UNC5221): Auth Bypass, RCE & ZIPLINE Backdoor
- **Scenario ID**: `splunk-ivanti-connect-secure`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/splunk-ivanti-connect-secure
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=splunk-ivanti-connect-secure
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Splunk STRT / Mandiant UNC5221 · CVE-2023-46805 + CVE-2024-21887, libdsupgrade.so ZIPLINE & CAV Tamper
- **Overview**: Imagine a secure government building where visitors must show an ID badge at the outer checkpoint before reaching any internal office. However, a hallway shortcut (../ path traversal) lets anyone walk around the outer checkpoint straight to the Python maintenance office (/api/v1/license/keys-status/). Once at the maintenance office window, the visitor hands over a form containing ; shell_command #, and the clerk types it straight into the building’s root terminal and installs a hidden translator (WIREFIRE) inside the public login page. Documented by Volexity, Mandiant, CISA (Emergency Directive 24-01), and Splunk SURGe (January 2024), this scenario traces the two-bug zero-day chain used by UTA0178 to compromise Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances. By combining CVE-2023-46805 (an authentication bypass using "../../" path traversal inside /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/../../license/keys-status/ so the outer web gatekeeper thinks the user is visiting an unauthenticated login-helper page) with CVE-2024-21887 (an OS command injection flaw where the backend Python service passes the URL parameter directly into a root popen() shell call), an unauthenticated attacker executes arbitrary root commands and implants the WIREFIRE Python webshell.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Ivanti CVE-2023-46805 & CVE-2024-21887) - Initial Access), T1574.006 (Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking (ZIPLINE LD_PRELOAD) - Persistence / Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Volexity Threat Research: Active Exploitation of Two Zero-Day Vulnerabilities in Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2023-46805 & CVE-2024-21887) (https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/01/10/active-exploitation-of-two-zero-day-vulnerabilities-in-ivanti-connect-secure/) | Mandiant & Splunk SURGe Threat Research: Cutting Edge: Suspected APT Targets Ivanti Connect Secure VPN in New Zero-Day Exploitation (UNC5221) (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/suspected-apt-targets-ivanti-zero-day) | CISA Emergency Directive: Emergency Directive 24-01: Mitigate Ivanti Connect Secure and Ivanti Policy Secure Vulnerabilities (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-24-01-mitigate-ivanti-connect-secure-and-ivanti-policy-secure-vulnerabilities)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **PATH TRAVERSAL AUTH BYPASS & RCE (CVE-2023-46805 + CVE-2024-21887)** — The outer door guard (web daemon) has a checklist that says: "Anyone walking down the /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/ hallway does not need to be logged in yet." The attacker starts down that hallway, but immediately takes two ../../ steps backward into the restricted /license/keys-status/ room, slipping right past the outer guard. In Ivanti Connect Secure, the outer web gatekeeper checks whether a requested URL starts with a public prefix like /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/ (an endpoint that must be reachable before login so users who lost their phone can submit a backup 2FA code). By requesting /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/../../license/keys-status/, the outer gatekeeper sees the allowed prefix and waves the request through without asking for a password, while the internal Python router resolves the "../../" path traversal and hands the request straight to the restricted admin-only /api/v1/license/keys-status/ endpoint. Because the authentication filter checked the raw un-normalized URI prefix (startswith("/api/v1/totp/user-backup-code")) before the backend web framework normalized "../" segments (CVE-2023-46805), any unauthenticated internet client can reach any internal REST API endpoint on the VPN appliance. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CVE-2024-21887 RCE / ⇠#1 ALERT HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 UNC5221 / UTA0178 Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)). [Specs: AUTH BYPASS=CVE-2023-46805 (/api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/../../); COMMAND INJECTION=CVE-2024-21887 (cloud-server-test-connection JSON "type"); PRIVILEGE=Unauthenticated Remote Root Execution (UID 0)]
  - Stage 2 (T1574.006 · Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking): **ZIPLINE ELF BACKDOOR IN LIBDSUPGRADE.SO & CAV TAMPERING** — Now standing at the restricted /license/keys-status/ counter without ever logging in, the attacker writes ;python -c ... # in the node-name field. The Python clerk pastes that string straight into a popen() shell command and runs it as root. Once the path-traversal request reaches /api/v1/license/keys-status/;python%20-c%20..., the backend Python handler takes the URL parameter and passes it directly into subprocess.Popen(..., shell=True) without input sanitization (CVE-2024-21887, an OS command injection flaw where untrusted URL characters are interpreted as live Linux shell commands). Inside that string, the semicolon (; which in Bash/sh terminates the legitimate license-check command and immediately executes the attacker’s python -c payload right behind it) runs the attacker’s code with full root privileges. Why did the attacker chain two CVEs? Because CVE-2024-21887 (command injection in keys-status) normally required an administrator login, and CVE-2023-46805 (path traversal) only bypassed authentication without running code. Combining both inside a single HTTP URL turns them into a 1-packet unauthenticated root RCE. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ ZIPLINE ELF HOOK / ⇠#2 ALERT 72 KB ELF) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Ivanti Connect Secure VPN), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)). [Specs: PASSIVE BACKDOOR=ZIPLINE (/home/lib/libdsupgrade.so in /home/bin/web); MAGIC TRIGGER=ASCII Header "I5033248" on TCP 443; DEFENSE EVASION=Patches cav-0.1-py2.7.egg to spoof clean ICT scan results]
  - Stage 3 (T1556 · Modify Authentication Process): **DSLOG.PM CREDENTIAL HARVESTING & INTERNAL TUNNELING** — To stay inside permanently, the attacker remounts the read-only floor tiles as writable, slips the WIREFIRE webshell into visits.py, plants the ZIPLINE LD_PRELOAD rootkit in libsecure.so, and modifies the login page JavaScript (WARPWIRE) to steal every employee’s plaintext VPN password as they log in. Synthesizing Volexity (UTA0178) and Mandiant (UNC5221) findings, with root access on the VPN appliance the attacker runs mount -o remount,rw / (temporarily unlocking the appliance’s read-only system partition so built-in files can be edited) and deploys a multi-layered malware suite: (1) Volexity’s WIREFIRE Python webshell injected directly inside visits.py (modifying an already-existing API file so basic file-count checks do not spot an extra file) and WARPWIRE JavaScript credential harvester injected into the VPN login page to steal plaintext Active Directory passwords; plus (2) Mandiant’s ZIPLINE passive backdoor loaded via LD_PRELOAD inside libsecure.so (intercepting accept() network calls inside the legitimate Ivanti web daemon). As Mandiant UNC5221 documented, the threat actor also patches ComponentIntegrity.pm (so Ivanti’s built-in Integrity Checker Tool reports "0 modified files" when an admin runs an internal self-check, which is why CISA ED 24-01 mandated running the external offline ICT snapshot tool). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ DSLOG.PM CRED STEAL / ⇠#3 ACK Cred Harvest) from Node ③ (#3 Ivanti Connect Secure VPN) to Node ④ (#4 ZIPLINE Passive Backdoor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)). [Specs: MODIFIED PERL=/home/perl/DSLog.pm & /home/webserver/htdocs/dana-na/auth/compcheckresult.cgi; STOLEN DATA=Plaintext AD Usernames, Passwords & Session Cookies; MANDIANT CLUSTER=UNC5221 (Zero-Day Espionage Actor)]

### CVE-2023-4966: Splunk STRT, Mandiant & CISA — Citrix Bleed: NetScaler OOB Memory Leak & NSC_AAAC Hijack
- **Scenario ID**: `splunk-citrix-bleed-session-hijack`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/splunk-citrix-bleed-session-hijack
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=splunk-citrix-bleed-session-hijack
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Splunk STRT / Mandiant / CISA AA23-325A · CVE-2023-4966 Host Header Leak, NSC_AAAC Cookie & VDI Pivot
- **Overview**: Imagine asking a hotel clerk to write your name on six lines of a 1-page welcome form, and then photocopy that page for you. Instead of giving a normal 10-letter name, you hand the clerk a 24,000-letter name (Host: header). The clerk’s 1-page form runs out of space after line 5, so the clerk stops writing, but when they walk over to the photocopier, they tell the machine: "Copy 147,000 letters worth of paper from my desk!" The photocopier copies the 1-page welcome form PLUS the confidential ledger sitting right next to it on the desk, which contains the active VIP room key (NSC_AAAC session cookie) of an administrator who already passed MFA. Synthesizing Assetnote’s vulnerability root-cause research, CISA/Mandiant Advisory AA23-325A, and Splunk SURGe detection telemetry, "Citrix Bleed" (CVE-2023-4966) is a memory over-read flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances. When an attacker sends an HTTP GET request to the OpenID Connect configuration page with an abnormally long Host header (~24,576 characters), the appliance constructs a JSON response using snprintf() without checking that the buffer overflowed, causing it to dump ~16 KB of raw adjacent server RAM back in the HTTP response. Inside that leaked memory sits the plaintext NSC_AAAC session cookie (the active post-MFA session token of a logged-in user or administrator).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Citrix NetScaler CVE-2023-4966) - Initial Access), T1550.004 (Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie (NSC_AAAC) - Defense Evasion / Lateral Movement)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Assetnote Security Research: Citrix Bleed: Leaking Session Tokens with CVE-2023-4966 (snprintf Heap Over-Read Root Cause) (https://www.assetnote.io/resources/research/citrix-bleed-leaking-session-tokens-with-cve-2023-4966) | Splunk SURGe Security Research: Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966) Vulnerability Analysis and Detection Guidance (https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/citrix-bleed-cve-2023-4966-vulnerability-analysis-and-detection.html) | CISA / FBI / MS-ISAC / ASD Joint Advisory: Threat Actors Exploit Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966) and Deploy LockBit 3.0 (AA23-325A) (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-325a)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **NETSCALER SNPRINTF OOB MEMORY LEAK (CVE-2023-4966)** — The attacker asks the public OpenID info desk (/oauth/idp/.well-known/openid-configuration) for its standard welcome sheet while supplying a 24,576-byte Host name. Because snprintf() reports how many bytes it wanted to write (147 KB) rather than the size of the 131 KB paper sheet, the server sends back 16 KB of raw adjacent RAM right after the welcome sheet. As reverse-engineered by Assetnote, the attacker sends an unauthenticated HTTPS GET request to /oauth/idp/.well-known/openid-configuration (a public discovery page on the Citrix NetScaler Gateway whose ns_aaa_oauthrp_send_openid_config function inserts the caller’s HTTP Host header into six JSON URL fields: issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, jwks_uri, userinfo_endpoint, and end_session_endpoint). By sending a 24,576-byte Host header, the 6 copies total ~147 KB, exceeding the server’s 131,072-byte (0x20000) stack response buffer. Because C’s snprintf() function returns how many bytes it wanted to write (147 KB) rather than how many bytes actually fit in the 128 KB buffer, NetScaler’s SSL_write transmits the 128 KB buffer PLUS ~16 KB of raw adjacent nsppe memory straight back to the attacker. In the C standard library, snprintf(buf, size, fmt...) stops writing at size bytes to prevent a crash, but returns the theoretical total length of the formatted string. Passing that unchecked return value directly to the HTTP socket writer causes an out-of-bounds memory over-read (CVE-2023-4966) from the NetScaler packet engine (nsppe). In the documented Suricata CVE-2023-4966 exchange from Threat Actor (LockBit / UNC) to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ALERT 148 KB Leak (confirming that the CITRIX BLEED GET request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 NSC_AAAC SESSION COOKIE EXTRACTION & MFA BYPASS). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CITRIX BLEED GET / ⇠#1 ALERT 148 KB Leak) from Node ① (#1 Threat Actor (LockBit / UNC)) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-4966 (Citrix Bleed OOB Memory Read); TARGET URI=GET /oauth/idp/.well-known/openid-configuration; ROOT CAUSE=Unbounded snprintf return value passed to HTTP response sender]
  - Stage 2 (T1539 · Steal Web Session Cookie): **NSC_AAAC SESSION COOKIE EXTRACTION & MFA BYPASS** — Scanning the accidentally photocopied desk pages, the attacker spots a 65-digit hexadecimal VIP wristband (NSC_AAAC) belonging to an administrator who is currently logged in. Clipping that wristband onto their own browser lets the attacker step straight into the admin’s active Citrix Virtual Desktop without any password or MFA prompt. Scanning the leaked raw memory dump with a regular expression ([0-9a-f]{32,65}), the attacker extracts a 65-character hexadecimal string: a live NSC_AAAC session cookie (the master authentication token stored in nsppe memory for a user who has already logged in and passed Multi-Factor Authentication). By pasting Cookie: NSC_AAAC=<leaked_token> into their own browser, the attacker hijacks the administrator’s active Citrix session (bypassing both the password screen and MFA completely). Because the NSC_AAAC cookie represents an active server-side AAA session in NetScaler memory, even patching the appliance or resetting the victim’s Active Directory password does not kick the attacker out unless the administrator explicitly flushes active sessions on the appliance via kill aaa session -all and kill icaconnection -all. In the documented NetScaler SSLVPN Log exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway, Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway responds with RESP IP Mismatch (confirming that the REPLAY NSC_AAAC request succeeded on Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 CITRIX ICA VDI LAUNCH & INTERNAL AD RECONNAISSANCE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ REPLAY NSC_AAAC / ⇠#2 RESP IP Mismatch) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)). [Specs: STOLEN COOKIE=NSC_AAAC=<65-byte hexadecimal session token>; VALIDATION URI=POST /logon/LogonPoint/Authentication/GetUserName; IMPACT=Complete MFA Bypass & Session Takeover (T1550.004)]
  - Stage 3 (T1550.004 · Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie): **CITRIX ICA VDI LAUNCH & INTERNAL AD RECONNAISSANCE** — Now sitting at the administrator’s virtual desk inside the building, the attacker uses the internal intercom (DCOM MMC20.Application over port 135) to command neighboring Windows servers to run commands on their behalf. Inside the hijacked Citrix Virtual Desktop (VDI) session, the attacker runs Active Directory discovery tools (adfind / SoftPerfect netscan), deploys remote management tunnels (AnyDesk / eHorus), and uses Distributed COM (DCOM, invoking the MMC20.Application COM object over RPC port 135, which instructs a remote Windows server to silently launch mmc.exe -Embedding and execute commands via Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand without creating a noisy new Windows service). Unlike PsExec or sc.exe (which register a new Windows Service and trigger System EventID 7045 on the target server), lateral movement via DCOM MMC20.Application abuses an already-registered Microsoft COM class over TCP/135. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ VDI POWERSHELL RECON / ⇠#3 ACK PID 5310) from Node ③ (#3 Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway) to Node ④ (#4 Hijacked NSC_AAAC Session), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)). [Specs: PIVOT MECHANISM=Citrix StoreFront / Gateway ICA Virtual Desktop Launch; NS.LOG ANOMALY=SSLVPN TCPCONNSTAT showing 2 client IPs for 1 username/session; CISA ADVISORY=AA23-325A (Citrix Bleed Exploitation by LockBit 3.0)]

### CVE-2023-41990: Kaspersky GReAT — Operation Triangulation: Zero-Click Font Exploit, MMIO & TriangleDB
- **Scenario ID**: `kaspersky-operation-triangulation`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/kaspersky-operation-triangulation
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=kaspersky-operation-triangulation
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kaspersky Securelist · CVE-2023-41990 ADJUST TrueType Font, CVE-2023-38606 MMIO & TriangleDB
- **Overview**: Imagine someone slips an invisible envelope under a locked door (Zero-Click iMessage), and the automatic mail-sorting machine (IMAgent) jams on a rigged font instruction (ADJUST, CVE-2023-41990) before the homeowner even knows a letter arrived. Once inside, the intruder discovers that the vault’s memory walls are protected by an unbreakable software lock (Apple PPL). Instead of fighting the software guard, the intruder walks over to a secret, undocumented maintenance panel wired directly into the silicon chip (MMIO DMA Registers, CVE-2023-38606) and orders the hardware’s own Direct Memory Access crane to lift the vault roof from the outside. Discovered and documented by Kaspersky GReAT (2023–2024), Operation Triangulation is one of the most sophisticated zero-click mobile exploit chains ever analyzed. The victim receives an invisible iMessage attachment that triggers a memory corruption bug in Apple’s TrueType font parser (the legacy ADJUST bytecode instruction, CVE-2023-41990, executing automatically inside the background IMAgent daemon without the user ever tapping or seeing a notification). Next, to bypass Apple’s hardware-enforced Page Protection Layer (PPL), the exploit writes directly to undocumented CPU Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) hardware registers (CVE-2023-38606, instructing the chip’s hardware DMA engine to overwrite protected kernel RAM from the outside) and plants the TriangleDB memory-only implant.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1203 (Exploitation for Client Execution (Zero-Click iMessage Font CVE-2023-41990) - Execution), T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (Hardware MMIO PPL Bypass CVE-2023-38606) - Privilege Escalation)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Kaspersky GReAT (Global Research & Analysis Team): Operation Triangulation: The Last (Hardware) Mystery (CVE-2023-38606 & MMIO DMA Bypass) (https://securelist.com/operation-triangulation-the-last-hardware-mystery/111669/) | Kaspersky GReAT: Dissecting TriangleDB, the Operation Triangulation iOS Implant (https://securelist.com/triangledb-iostriangulation-implant/110050/) | Apple Security Engineering, NIST NVD & CISA KEV: CVE-2023-41990 (FontParser ADJUST Instruction) & CVE-2023-38606 (Kernel MMIO) Advisories (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-38606)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1203 · Exploitation for Client Execution): **ZERO-CLICK IMESSAGE TRUETYPE ADJUST EXPLOIT (CVE-2023-41990)** — An invisible iMessage arrives while the phone is sitting untouched on a table. As the background mail-preview clerk (IMAgent) tries to render a custom font inside the attachment, an obsolete 1990s font command (ADJUST) tricks the clerk into writing outside the page boundary. The target iPhone receives an iMessage containing a disguised PDF/archive attachment with an embedded TrueType font. Even while the phone is locked in a pocket, the background daemon IMAgent (the iOS process that automatically pre-processes incoming iMessage attachments before showing a notification) parses the font using libFontParser.dylib. Inside the font, an obsolete 1990s TrueType bytecode instruction named ADJUST (opcode 0x8F/0x90, CVE-2023-41990) triggers an out-of-bounds memory write, giving the attacker instant code execution inside IMAgent with zero user clicks ("Zero-Click"). TrueType fonts are not just static shapes; they contain a Turing-complete virtual machine (font hinting bytecode) designed in the early 1990s. Abusing the legacy ADJUST instruction corrupts the C++ vtable on the heap inside IMAgent before any UI notification is ever rendered. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ IMTRANSFERAGENT C2 / ⇠#1 RESP TLS 1.3) from Node ① (#1 Triangulation Validator & C2) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky triangle_check & NDR). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-41990 (Undocumented TrueType Font ADJUST Instruction); TARGET DAEMON=IMTransferAgent (Zero-Click Execution); STAGE-1 ENGINE=JavaScriptCore NaN-Boxing 64-bit R/W Primitive]
  - Stage 2 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **XNU INTEGER OVERFLOW & HARDWARE MMIO BYPASS (CVE-2023-38606)** — Even after taking over the kernel, the chip’s hardware Page Protection Layer (PPL) blocks any software from altering protected memory pages. So the exploit talks directly to an undocumented hardware controller on the Apple Silicon die (0x206040000) and commands its hardware DMA engine to overwrite the protected RAM directly, going completely around the CPU’s software guard. Even after escalating into the iOS kernel, Apple Silicon chips enforce a hardware-backed Page Protection Layer (PPL, which blocks even the operating system kernel itself from modifying protected user-signing tables or injecting unsigned code). To bypass PPL, the exploit writes directly to undocumented physical Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) hardware registers at address 0x206040000 (CVE-2023-38606, an unmapped hardware debugging/DMA block built into the Apple A12–A16 System-on-Chip). By commanding this hardware DMA engine to write directly to physical RAM, the attacker overwrites PPL-protected kernel memory completely outside the CPU’s security checks. Because the CPU’s MMU/PPL checks only apply to memory writes executed by the CPU cores themselves, instructing an on-chip peripheral DMA engine via MMIO registers to write to physical memory bypasses PPL page-table write protection. In the documented CVE-2023-38606 MMIO exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC), IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC) responds with ALERT Ring-0 / PPL (confirming that the MMIO DMA PPL BYPASS request succeeded on IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 IN-MEMORY TRIANGLEDB IMPLANT DEPLOYMENT). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ MMIO DMA PPL BYPASS / ⇠#2 ALERT Ring-0 / PPL) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky triangle_check & NDR). [Specs: KERNEL CVE=CVE-2023-32434 (XNU mach_vm_remap Integer Overflow); HARDWARE MMIO CVE=CVE-2023-38606 (Undocumented SoC MMIO DMA PPL Bypass); ANTI-FORENSICS=Scrubs exploit attachment records from sms.db SQLite database]
  - Stage 3 (T1620 · Reflective Code Loading): **IN-MEMORY TRIANGLEDB IMPLANT DEPLOYMENT** — Once inside the vault, the exploit shreds the incoming iMessage from sms.db so the user never sees a trace, and runs the TriangleDB spyware strictly in volatile RAM, leaving behind only subtle water-meter readings (DataUsage.sqlite network byte counters) that forensic investigators can spot. With full kernel privileges, the exploit first deletes the triggering iMessage record from sms.db and attachment caches (so the victim never sees an unread message and forensic investigators cannot extract the exploit file from the phone), and then launches the TriangleDB spyware implant strictly in volatile RAM (meaning zero implant files are written to flash storage; if the phone is rebooted, the implant vanishes completely to avoid capture). Even though TriangleDB deletes its iMessage entry and runs only in RAM, iOS automatically records how many bytes of cellular/Wi-Fi data each process uses inside DataUsage.sqlite, leaving orphaned network-usage rows and timestamp gaps that Kaspersky’s triangle_check forensic tool uses to prove infection. In the documented Mach-O TriangleDB exchange from IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC) to XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers, XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers responds with ALERT 220 KB Mach-O (confirming that the LOAD TRIANGLEDB request succeeded on XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers and completing the final execution objective of Kaspersky GReAT, Operation Triangulation: Zero-Click Font Exploit, MMIO & TriangleDB). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ LOAD TRIANGLEDB / ⇠#3 ALERT 220 KB Mach-O) from Node ③ (#3 IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC)) to Node ④ (#4 XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky triangle_check & NDR). [Specs: IMPLANT NAME=TriangleDB (Memory-Resident Mach-O Spyware); OBJC CLASSES=CRConfig, CROs, CRNet, CRDB, CRFile, CRAudio; PERSISTENCE=Zero-click re-infection; disappears completely on reboot]

### CVE-2024-11859: Kaspersky GReAT — ToddyCat APT: ESET Scanner DLL Proxying (CVE-2024-11859) & TCESB Loader
- **Scenario ID**: `kaspersky-toddycat-eset-dll`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/kaspersky-toddycat-eset-dll
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=kaspersky-toddycat-eset-dll
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: HIGH
- **Subtitle**: Kaspersky Securelist · Signed ESET ecls.exe, version.dll Search-Order Hijack & TCESB In-Memory Implant
- **Overview**: Imagine a thief who brings a genuine, uniformed security officer (ESET Command Line Scanner ecls.exe) into a building, knowing that the officer has a habit of picking up whichever walkie-talkie (version.dll) is sitting on the nearest table before checking the official equipment locker (System32). The thief places a rigged walkie-talkie (version.dll) on the table right next to the officer; when the officer turns it on, the rigged walkie-talkie still forwards normal radio calls to headquarters so the officer doesn’t suspect a thing, while secretly running ToddyCat’s TCESB spy radio inside the officer’s own uniform. Documented by Kaspersky GReAT and ESET Security Advisory (CVE-2024-11859), this scenario illustrates how the ToddyCat APT group abused a legitimate, digitally signed security tool: the ESET Command Line Scanner (ecls.exe, chosen because security tools and IT administrators implicitly trust a binary signed by a major antivirus vendor). Due to a DLL search-order hijacking flaw in older versions of ecls.exe, placing a malicious DLL named version.dll in the same directory caused the trusted antivirus scanner itself to load and execute ToddyCat’s TCESB loader in memory.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1574.002 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading (ESET ecls.exe + version.dll / CVE-2024-11859) - Persistence / Defense Evasion), T1055 (Process Injection (TCESB, Samurai Backdoor & TomBerBil) - Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Kaspersky GReAT (Global Research & Analysis Team): ToddyCat: Keep Calm and Continue Espionage (Samurai, Ninja, LoFiSe & TCESB) (https://securelist.com/toddycat-keep-calm-and-continue-espionage/110698/) | ESET Security Advisories & NIST NVD: CVE-2024-11859: ESET Command Line Scanner (ecls.exe) DLL Search Order Hijacking Vulnerability (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-11859) | The MITRE Corporation: MITRE ATT&CK T1574.002: Hijack Execution Flow — DLL Side-Loading & Export Forwarding (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1574.001 · Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking): **ESET ECLS.EXE VERSION.DLL HIJACK (CVE-2024-11859)** — The attacker places a real, digitally signed ESET scanner (ecls.exe) and a forged helper library (version.dll) in the same folder (C:\ProgramData\ESET\). Because of CVE-2024-11859, the moment ecls.exe starts, it grabs the version.dll sitting right next to it instead of the real Windows System32\version.dll. The attacker drops a standalone, validly signed copy of ESET Command Line Scanner (ecls.exe, an authentic antivirus utility whose valid digital signature passes Windows AppLocker and antivirus file checks) into a writable folder like C:\ProgramData\ESET\ right next to a malicious library named version.dll. Because of CVE-2024-11859 (where ecls.exe did not restrict its DLL load path to System32), the moment ecls.exe starts, Windows loads the attacker’s version.dll from C:\ProgramData\ESET\ before checking C:\Windows\System32\version.dll. Unlike KnownDLLs (such as kernel32.dll or ntdll.dll, which Windows forces every program to load exclusively from System32), version.dll is not on the Default KnownDLLs list, so any executable that imports version.dll without specifying LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 will load a local version.dll from its own folder first. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ HIJACK VERSION.DLL / ⇠#1 ACK CVE-2024-11859) from Node ① (#1 ToddyCat C2 Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky Anti-Targeted Attack). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2024-11859 (ESET ecls.exe Insecure DLL Loading); HIJACKED DLL=C:\ProgramData\ESET\version.dll (Unsigned Proxy DLL); DLL PROXYING=Forwards 17 exports to C:\Windows\System32\version.dll]
  - Stage 2 (T1620 · Reflective Code Loading): **TCESB IN-MEMORY DECRYPTION & EDR EVASION** — If the rigged version.dll didn’t know how to answer normal version-check questions, ecls.exe would crash immediately. So the rigged DLL acts as a middleman ("Export Proxying"): it forwards every real question to C:\Windows\System32\version.dll while quietly decrypting ToddyCat’s TCESB backdoor in the background. If the attacker’s version.dll failed to answer the normal version-check functions that ecls.exe calls on startup (like GetFileVersionInfoW), ecls.exe would crash immediately with an error popup. To prevent a crash, the malicious version.dll uses DLL Export Proxying (forwarding every normal API call straight through to the real C:\Windows\System32\version.dll so ecls.exe runs smoothly), while its background thread reads an encrypted file from disk and decrypts ToddyCat’s TCESB backdoor directly into RAM. By adding linker export forwarders in the malicious DLL’s Export Address Table (pointing functions like GetFileVersionInfoW to C:\Windows\System32\version.GetFileVersionInfoW), the host program continues to work normally while the attacker’s decrypted shellcode runs in the same process memory. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ TCESB UNPACK RAM / ⇠#2 ALERT 184 KB RWX) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 ecls.exe (Signed ESET Scanner)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky Anti-Targeted Attack). [Specs: LOADER NAME=TCESB (ToddyCat ESET Loader); HOST TRUST=Executes inside ESET-signed ecls.exe (PID 5180); ENCRYPTION=AES-128-CBC / Custom XOR In-Memory Unpacking]
  - Stage 3 (T1539 · Steal Web Session Cookie): **DPAPI COOKIE THEFT & HTTPS C2 EXFILTRATION** — The malware now phones home from inside the signed ecls.exe process. However, defenders catch the trick because ecls.exe is an offline command-line file scanner, it has zero reason to ever open an outbound HTTPS connection to the internet! Running inside the memory space of the signed ecls.exe process (so process lists show a legitimate ESET security scanner), the decrypted TCESB backdoor opens an encrypted HTTPS tunnel on TCP port 443 to ToddyCat’s command-and-control server to harvest domain credentials and browser cookies. Why is this still detectable by defenders? Because ecls.exe is a standalone, offline on-demand file scanner that never connects to the internet during normal operation, meaning any Sysmon EventID 3 (NetworkConnect) log showing ecls.exe opening an outbound TCP/443 socket is an immediate indicator of compromise. In the documented Sysmon EID 3 exchange from ecls.exe (Signed ESET Scanner) to version.dll Proxy & TCESB RAM, version.dll Proxy & TCESB RAM responds with ACK TLS 1.3 (confirming that the ECLS.EXE C2 BEACON request succeeded on version.dll Proxy & TCESB RAM and completing the final execution objective of Kaspersky GReAT, ToddyCat APT: ESET Scanner DLL Proxying (CVE-2024-11859) & TCESB Loader). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ECLS.EXE C2 BEACON / ⇠#3 ACK TLS 1.3) from Node ③ (#3 ecls.exe (Signed ESET Scanner)) to Node ④ (#4 version.dll Proxy & TCESB RAM), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky Anti-Targeted Attack). [Specs: TARGET ARTIFACTS=Edge/Chrome Network\Cookies & Local State DPAPI Keys; NETWORK ANOMALY=Offline scanner ecls.exe making outbound TCP :443 connections; THREAT ACTOR=ToddyCat APT (Tracked by Kaspersky GReAT)]

### CVE-2024-21338: Kaspersky, Microsoft & Avast — Lazarus Group (Diamond Sleet): appid.sys Zero-Day & FUDModule Rootkit
- **Scenario ID**: `kaspersky-lazarus-byovd-fudmodule`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/kaspersky-lazarus-byovd-fudmodule
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=kaspersky-lazarus-byovd-fudmodule
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kaspersky GReAT / Avast / Microsoft · CVE-2024-21338 AppLocker Driver IOCTL & FUDModule DKOM Blindness
- **Overview**: In the past, attackers who wanted to cut the security cameras inside the Windows kernel had to smuggle an old, flawed third-party security guard (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver) into the building, which modern Windows blocklists immediately spot at gate. In this scenario, Lazarus Group found a zero-day flaw (CVE-2024-21338) in a guard who is already hired and pre-installed inside every Windows building (appid.sys, the built-in AppLocker driver). By whispering a forged instruction (IOCTL 0x22A018) to appid.sys, the attacker tricks the driver into flipping their own clearance badge from "Visitor (UserMode = 1)" to "Supreme Kernel Architect (KernelMode = 0)", and then quietly unplugs the EDR security agent’s cameras (Kernel Callbacks & ETW) without turning the EDR light off. Discovered by Avast and analyzed by Kaspersky and Microsoft (February 2024), this scenario shows how the Lazarus Group upgraded their FudModule rootkit. Previously, attackers had to drop a vulnerable third-party driver onto the system (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver, which Microsoft’s Vulnerable Driver Blocklist now blocks). Here, Lazarus exploited a zero-day flaw inside Windows’ own built-in AppLocker driver (appid.sys, CVE-2024-21338, pre-installed and signed by Microsoft on every Windows machine). By sending a crafted IOCTL control code (0x22A018) to appid.sys, the attacker flips their thread’s kernel privilege bit (PreviousMode = 0) and zeroes out the kernel callback tables and ETW sensors that EDR agents rely on.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (appid.sys AppLocker Zero-Day CVE-2024-21338) - Privilege Escalation / Defense Evasion), T1562.001 (Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools (FudModule DKOM Kernel Blind) - Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Avast Decoded Threat Labs: Lazarus and the FudModule Rootkit: Beyond BYOVD with an Admin-to-Kernel Zero-Day (CVE-2024-21338) (https://decoded.avast.io/janvojtesek/lazarus-and-the-fudmodule-rootkit-beyond-byovd-with-an-admin-to-kernel-zero-day/) | Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): CVE-2024-21338 Windows Kernel Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (appid.sys) (https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2024-21338) | Kaspersky GReAT & MITRE ATT&CK G0032: Lazarus Group (Diamond Sleet) KaolinRAT & FudModule Kernel Callback Blinding Analysis (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **APPID.SYS KERNEL ZERO-DAY EXPLOIT (CVE-2024-21338)** — Instead of sneaking an untrusted third-party driver file onto the disk, the attacker simply walks up to the office door of Windows’ own pre-installed AppLocker driver (\Device\AppId / appid.sys) using a LOCAL SERVICE badge. Because modern Windows blocks untrusted kernel drivers via Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) and Microsoft’s Vulnerable Driver Blocklist, the attacker does not drop any third-party .sys file onto the disk. Instead, they elevate a user-mode process to LOCAL SERVICE privileges (required because \Device\AppId’s access control list only lets LOCAL SERVICE, rather than standard Administrators, open a communication handle to it) and open a device handle to Windows’ own built-in AppLocker driver: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\appid.sys. Abusing a pre-installed inbox Windows driver (appid.sys, Living off the Land in the Kernel) completely sidesteps HVCI / Vulnerable Driver Blocklist checks because appid.sys is an official part of the Windows operating system. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ APPID.SYS IOCTL 0x22A018 / ⇠#1 RET PreviousMode=0) from Node ① (#1 Lazarus (Diamond Sleet) C2) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon & Defender XDR Sensor). [Specs: ZERO-DAY CVE=CVE-2024-21338 (Windows AppLocker Driver appid.sys EoP); IOCTL CODE=0x22A018 -> AipSmartHashImageFile Pointer Dereference; PRIMITIVE GAINED=KTHREAD.PreviousMode = 0 (Direct Kernel R/W via NtWriteVirtualMemory)]
  - Stage 2 (T1562.001 · Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools): **FUDMODULE V3 DKOM: BLINDING SYSMON, ETW-TI & EDR** — Every thread in Windows wears a tag (KTHREAD.PreviousMode) that says 1 (User Mode: check all permissions) or 0 (Kernel Mode: trust everything). By passing a forged pointer in IOCTL 0x22A018, FudModule tricks appid.sys into reaching over and flipping the attacker thread’s tag from 1 to 0. FudModule calls DeviceIoControl with control code IOCTL 0x22A018 (which invokes the internal function AipSmartHashImageFile inside appid.sys) and passes a crafted structure containing a spoofed function/object pointer (CVE-2024-21338). This tricks the kernel driver into decrementing the attacker thread’s KTHREAD.PreviousMode byte in kernel memory from 1 (UserMode, where Windows blocks the thread from touching kernel RAM) to 0 (KernelMode, telling the Windows kernel to treat every subsequent NtReadVirtualMemory and NtWriteVirtualMemory call from this thread as if it came from the kernel itself, granting unlimited Ring-0 memory read/write). When a thread calls NtWriteVirtualMemory, the kernel checks KTHREAD->PreviousMode: if it is 1 (UserMode), the kernel rejects any target address above 0x7FFFFFFEFFFF (protecting kernel space). Once CVE-2024-21338 flips PreviousMode to 0 (KernelMode), the thread can read and overwrite any address in the Windows kernel directly from user mode. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ BLIND SYSMON & ETW-TI / ⇠#2 ALERT EDR Blinded) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 appid.sys (AppLocker Driver)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon & Defender XDR Sensor). [Specs: ROOTKIT NAME=FUDModule v3 (Lazarus Group / Diamond Sleet); DKOM TARGETS=PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, ObRegisterCallbacks, EtwThreatIntProvRegHandle; EDR IMPACT=Complete telemetry blindness for Sysmon, ETW & EDR kernel drivers]
  - Stage 3 (T1003.001 · OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory): **UNMONITORED KAOLIN RAT & LSASS CREDENTIAL DUMP** — If a burglar shoots out a security camera, the guard desk immediately sees a "CAMERA OFFLINE" alarm. Instead, FudModule leaves the EDR security program running happily so its green status light stays on, while erasing its phone number from the kernel’s notification list (PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine) so the kernel never tells the EDR about new malware. Instead of killing the endpoint’s EDR security service (which would immediately set off a "Sensor Offline" alarm on the SOC dashboard), FudModule uses its new kernel read/write access (Direct Kernel Object Manipulation, DKOM) to overwrite the kernel’s PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, PspCreateThreadNotifyRoutine, and ObRegisterCallbacks arrays with zeroes (erasing the kernel notification hooks that tell the EDR whenever a new process or thread starts) and disables EtwThreatIntProvRegHandle (shutting off Microsoft’s Kernel Threat-Intelligence telemetry feed so the EDR agent stays running with a green status light, but is completely blind and deaf). By surgically zeroing out the callback pointers registered by the security vendor’s kernel driver (.sys) and flipping the ProviderEnableInfo bit on the ETW Threat-Intelligence provider, Lazarus can subsequently dump LSASS and run malware with zero EDR alerts. In the documented Zeek / Suricata NDR exchange from appid.sys (AppLocker Driver) to FUDModule v3 DKOM Engine, FUDModule v3 DKOM Engine responds with ALERT Host/NDR Gap (confirming that the KAOLIN RAT C2 request succeeded on FUDModule v3 DKOM Engine and completing the final execution objective of Kaspersky, Microsoft & Avast, Lazarus Group (Diamond Sleet): appid.sys Zero-Day & FUDModule Rootkit). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ KAOLIN RAT C2 / ⇠#3 ALERT Host/NDR Gap) from Node ③ (#3 appid.sys (AppLocker Driver)) to Node ④ (#4 FUDModule v3 DKOM Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon & Defender XDR Sensor). [Specs: RAT PAYLOAD=Kaolin RAT (Loaded in memory after DKOM blindness); LSASS ACCESS=Unrestricted PROCESS_VM_READ after ObRegisterCallbacks removal; THREAT ACTOR=Lazarus Group / Diamond Sleet (DPRK)]

### CVE-2023-42793: Mandiant & CISA — APT29 (Midnight Blizzard): JetBrains TeamCity RCE & GraphicalProton
- **Scenario ID**: `mandiant-apt29-teamcity-jetstream`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/mandiant-apt29-teamcity-jetstream
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=mandiant-apt29-teamcity-jetstream
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: CISA AA23-347A / Mandiant · CVE-2023-42793 / CVE-2024-27198 Auth Bypass, Token Minting & OneDrive C2
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security software factory (a JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD server) where the security gate has a sloppy rule written on its clipboard: "Anyone walking to a door whose name ends with /RPC2 doesn’t need to show an ID badge." The attacker walks up to the Super-Admin Key Minting machine (/app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/) and asks it to print a new master key named RPC2 (/app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2). Because the URL ends with /RPC2, the gate lets them right through, and the machine prints a permanent Super-Admin Bearer Token on the spot! Synthesizing SonarSource & Rapid7’s Java servlet root-cause analysis with the Joint CISA/FBI/NSA/NCSC & Mandiant APT29 Advisory (October 2023), this scenario shows how APT29 (Midnight Blizzard) exploited CVE-2023-42793 in on-premises JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD servers. Because an authentication wildcard flaw (/**/RPC2 inside TeamCity’s RequestInterceptors class) allowed anyone to reach internal REST paths that ended with "/RPC2" without logging in, the attacker sent a single unauthenticated POST request (/app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2) to mint a permanent administrator bearer token for User ID 1, enabled the hidden internal debug command endpoint (/app/rest/debug/processes), and deployed the GraphicalProton backdoor.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (JetBrains TeamCity CVE-2023-42793) - Initial Access), T1098.001 (Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials - Persistence)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: CISA, FBI, NSA, NCSC-UK & Mandiant: Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR / APT29) Exploiting JetBrains TeamCity CVE-2023-42793 (AA23-347A) (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-347a) | SonarSource & Rapid7 Vulnerability Research: JetBrains TeamCity Critical Auth Bypass (CVE-2023-42793): RequestInterceptors /**/RPC2 Root-Cause Analysis (https://www.sonarsource.com/blog/jetbrains-teamcity-averted-supply-chain-attack/) | NIST NVD & JetBrains Security: CVE-2023-42793 JetBrains TeamCity On-Premises Authentication Bypass & RCE (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-42793)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **TEAMCITY REST API AUTH BYPASS & TOKEN MINTING (CVE-2023-42793)** — The developer meant to exempt only the root /RPC2 path from login checks, but wrote /**/RPC2, accidentally exempting every URL in the entire server that ends with /RPC2. Requesting /app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2 tricks TeamCity into creating a new admin token named "RPC2" for User ID 1 without asking for a password. As detailed by SonarSource and Rapid7, in vulnerable TeamCity versions the RequestInterceptors authentication filter excluded any URL matching //RPC2 from login checks (intended only to exempt the legacy XML-RPC endpoint at /RPC2, but the leading "/" Ant-path wildcard accidentally exempted every URL on the server that ended with "/RPC2"). The attacker exploits this by sending an unauthenticated HTTP POST request to /app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2 (where "id:1" targets the primary built-in Super-Administrator account, and the REST API interprets the trailing "/RPC2" simply as the name to give the new token, causing TeamCity to mint and return a full Super-Admin Bearer token in the HTTP 200 response without asking for a password). Because TeamCity’s REST API endpoint for creating access tokens follows the URL template /app/rest/users/{userLocator}/tokens/{tokenName}, naming the token "RPC2" satisfies both the REST controller parameter and the /**/RPC2 authentication-bypass wildcard simultaneously (CVE-2023-42793). In the documented TeamCity Access Log exchange from APT29 (Midnight Blizzard) to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP CVE-2023-42793 (confirming that the MINT RPC2 TOKEN request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 DEBUG PROCESS RCE & CI/CD SECRET HARVESTING). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ MINT RPC2 TOKEN / ⇠#1 RESP CVE-2023-42793) from Node ① (#1 APT29 (Midnight Blizzard)) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Enterprise SIEM & EDR). [Specs: VULNERABILITIES=CVE-2023-42793 & CVE-2024-27198 (TeamCity Auth Bypass); TOKEN ENDPOINT=POST /app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2; CLEANUP STEP=DELETE /app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2 immediately after RCE]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.003 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell): **DEBUG PROCESS RCE & CI/CD SECRET HARVESTING** — Holding the freshly minted Super-Admin token, the attacker flips on a hidden "Developer Debug Terminal" switch (rest.debug.processes.enable=true), runs their operating-system commands, and then immediately shreds the RPC2 token so admins checking the active token list see nothing. Authenticating with Authorization: Bearer <token>, the attacker first sets the internal server property rest.debug.processes.enable=true (unlocking a hidden administrative diagnostic feature that is disabled by default), and then sends POST requests to /app/rest/debug/processes?exePath=cmd.exe&params=/c+... (telling the TeamCity Java server to spawn arbitrary OS commands on the underlying host). Seconds later, the attacker sends DELETE /app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2 (erasing the "RPC2" token right after creating a stealthier backdoor so an administrator checking the active tokens page in the UI sees nothing suspicious). Although deleting the RPC2 token removes it from the current UI token table, the token creation and deletion events remain recorded in logs/teamcity-activities.log and child process creations are captured by endpoint telemetry. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD, JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD responds with ACK PID 6740 (confirming that the TEAMCITY DEBUG RCE request succeeded on JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 GRAPHICALPROTON IMPLANT & ONEDRIVE GRAPH API C2). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ TEAMCITY DEBUG RCE / ⇠#2 ACK PID 6740) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Enterprise SIEM & EDR). [Specs: RCE ENDPOINT=POST /app/rest/debug/processes?exePath=cmd.exe&params=/c+...; PARENT PROCESS=C:\TeamCity\jre\bin\java.exe (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM); HARVESTED SECRETS=config\projects\*\pluginData\secure\credentials.json]
  - Stage 3 (T1102.002 · Web Service: Bidirectional Communication): **GRAPHICALPROTON IMPLANT & ONEDRIVE GRAPH API C2** — Because the CI/CD build server is the automated assembly line that deploys software to every cloud and server in the company, taking over this one room hands the attacker the master keys to cloud deployments, source code, and code-signing certificates. Because a CI/CD build server is the central factory that compiles software and deploys it into production, it stores high-privilege secrets (AWS/Azure deployment keys, GitHub SSH keys, and Authenticode code-signing certificates). As documented by Mandiant and CISA, APT29 extracts TeamCity’s encryption keys (encryption-config.xml, allowing them to decrypt every stored cloud and database password in the CI/CD database), sideloads their GraphicalProton backdoor via DLL hijacking (using Microsoft OneDrive and Dropbox Graph APIs for encrypted C2), and pivots into Active Directory. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 & 3 exchange from JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD to GraphicalProton Backdoor, GraphicalProton Backdoor responds with ACK OneDrive C2 (confirming that the GRAPHICALPROTON C2 request succeeded on GraphicalProton Backdoor and completing the final execution objective of Mandiant & CISA, APT29 (Midnight Blizzard): JetBrains TeamCity RCE & GraphicalProton). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ GRAPHICALPROTON C2 / ⇠#3 ACK OneDrive C2) from Node ③ (#3 JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD) to Node ④ (#4 GraphicalProton Backdoor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Enterprise SIEM & EDR). ### CVE-2024-1709: Splunk STRT & Huntress — ConnectWise ScreenConnect "SlashAndGrab" Auth Bypass & RMM RCE
- **Scenario ID**: `splunk-screenconnect-slashandgrab`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/splunk-screenconnect-slashandgrab
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=splunk-screenconnect-slashandgrab
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Splunk STRT / Huntress · CVE-2024-1709 /SetupWizard.aspx/ Traversal, User.xml Overwrite & .ashx RCE
- **Overview**: Imagine a smart-lock system on an office building where the "First-Time Factory Setup Screen" (/SetupWizard.aspx) is supposed to be permanently locked after Day 1. However, the guard only checks if the visitor’s request ends with the exact letters /SetupWizard.aspx. By simply adding one extra forward slash at the end (/SetupWizard.aspx/), the guard says "That doesn’t end with .aspx, go right ahead!" while the web server behind the guard still opens /SetupWizard.aspx, letting any stranger on the internet re-run the Day-1 Factory Setup Wizard, overwrite the building’s master administrator database (User.xml), and broadcast commands to every computer managed by the IT team. Synthesizing Huntress ("SlashAndGrab"), ConnectWise Security Advisory (CVE-2024-1709 & CVE-2024-1708), and Splunk SURGe (February 2024), CVE-2024-1709 is one of the simplest yet most devastating authentication bypass bugs ever found in remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. On ConnectWise ScreenConnect servers, the initial installation wizard (/SetupWizard.aspx) is supposed to be blocked once the server is configured. However, appending a trailing slash or path suffix (/SetupWizard.aspx/anything, which fools the custom security check while ASP.NET still loads SetupWizard.aspx) reopens the first-time setup wizard, allowing anyone on the internet to overwrite the server’s primary administrator database (User.xml) and push SYSTEM commands to all connected customer endpoints.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (ScreenConnect SetupWizard.aspx CVE-2024-1709) - Initial Access), T1219 (Remote Access Software (ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe Abuse) - Command and Control / Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Huntress Security Research: SlashAndGrab: ScreenConnect Post-Exploitation in the Wild (CVE-2024-1709 & CVE-2024-1708) (https://www.huntress.com/blog/slashandgrab-screen-connect-post-exploitation-in-the-wild-cve-2024-1709-cve-2024-1708) | Splunk SURGe Security Research: ConnectWise ScreenConnect Authentication Bypass (CVE-2024-1709 & CVE-2024-1708) Detection Guide (https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/connectwise-screenconnect-cve-2024-1709-cve-2024-1708.html) | ConnectWise Trust Center & CISA KEV: ConnectWise ScreenConnect 23.9.8 Security Patch Advisory (CVE-2024-1709 & CVE-2024-1708) (https://www.connectwise.com/company/trust/security-bulletins/connectwise-screenconnect-23.9.8)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **SETUPWIZARD.ASPX/ TRAVERSAL & USER.XML OVERWRITE (CVE-2024-1709)** — Adding /anything after /SetupWizard.aspx fools the security filter into thinking you are visiting a different page, while ASP.NET treats /anything as harmless PathInfo metadata and opens the First-Time Setup Wizard anyway. As reverse-engineered by Huntress, to block access to the initial setup page after Day 1, ScreenConnect’s authentication filter checked whether the requested URL ended with the exact string /SetupWizard.aspx. By simply adding a trailing slash or suffix, GET /SetupWizard.aspx/anything, the string-ending check returns false and lets the request through without authentication, while Microsoft’s ASP.NET web engine still routes the request to SetupWizard.aspx (treating the trailing "/anything" as harmless Request.PathInfo metadata, CVE-2024-1709). In ASP.NET, a URL like /Page.aspx/extra is routed to the handler for /Page.aspx with Request.PathInfo set to "/extra". Because the security check tested Request.Path instead of Request.FilePath, a single trailing "/" bypassed the lock completely. In the documented Sysmon EID 11 exchange from Threat Actor (BlackBasta / LockBit) to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ACK CVE-2024-1709 (confirming that the OVERWRITE USER.XML request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 MALICIOUS .ASHX EXTENSION UPLOAD & SYSTEM RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ OVERWRITE USER.XML / ⇠#1 ACK CVE-2024-1709) from Node ① (#1 Threat Actor (BlackBasta / LockBit)) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2024-1709 (CVSS 10.0 Authentication Bypass); BYPASS URI=GET /SetupWizard.aspx/ (or /SetupWizard.aspx/anything); MODIFIED FILE=C:\Program Files (x86)\ScreenConnect\App_Data\User.xml]
  - Stage 2 (T1505.003 · Server Software Component: Web Shell): **MALICIOUS .ASHX EXTENSION UPLOAD & SYSTEM RCE** — With the Day-1 Setup Wizard open in their browser, the attacker types in their own username and password and clicks "Finish", wiping out the company’s real IT administrators in App_Data\User.xml and making the attacker the sole super-admin. With the first-time setup wizard open in their browser, the attacker submits a new administrator username and password. ScreenConnect immediately overwrites C:\Program Files (x86)\ScreenConnect\App_Data\User.xml (the local XML database file that stores all administrator accounts and password hashes on the server, wiping out the company’s legitimate IT administrators and logging the attacker straight in as the sole Super-Admin). Furthermore, attackers can chain CVE-2024-1708 (a ZipSlip path-traversal flaw in ScreenConnect’s Extension uploader that writes .ashx webshells directly into App_Extensions\ for server-side persistence). Because the Setup Wizard was designed for a fresh installation, completing the wizard resets App_Data\User.xml from scratch and returns an authenticated administrator session cookie to the attacker’s browser. ### CVE-2024-3094: Andres Freund, Red Hat & Kaspersky — XZ Utils (liblzma) IFUNC sshd Supply Chain Backdoor
- **Scenario ID**: `xz-utils-cve-2024-3094-backdoor`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/xz-utils-cve-2024-3094-backdoor
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=xz-utils-cve-2024-3094-backdoor
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Andres Freund · Kaspersky GReAT · Red Hat · liblzma.so.5.6.1 IFUNC & RSA_public_decrypt Hook
- **Overview**: Imagine a master locksmith ("Jia Tan") who spends two years volunteering at a company that makes a tiny brass spring (liblzma.so) used inside millions of Linux tools. Right before shipping version 5.6.1, the locksmith hides a microscopic radio receiver inside a box of "broken test springs" (bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz) and rigs the factory assembly script (build-to-host.m4) to weld that receiver into the finished spring. Because Linux’s main front-door guard (sshd) wears a status badge (libsystemd.so) that uses that exact brass spring, the radio receiver wakes up inside the front-door guard’s uniform, intercepts the signature-checking pen (RSA_public_decrypt), and opens the master vault whenever anyone shows a secret Ed448 signet ring! Synthesizing Andres Freund’s initial discovery on oss-security, Kaspersky GReAT’s binary reverse engineering, and Red Hat / CISA advisories (March 2024), CVE-2024-3094 (CVSS 10.0) is one of the most sophisticated supply chain backdoors in history. During compilation of XZ Utils 5.6.0/5.6.1, obfuscated m4 scripts extracted a prebuilt object (liblzma_la-crc64-fast.o) from corrupt test files (bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz). On Linux distributions that link OpenSSH (sshd) with libsystemd.so.0 (which in turn loads liblzma.so.5), a glibc Indirect Function (IFUNC) resolver hijacks OpenSSL’s RSA_public_decrypt function pointer, allowing an attacker holding a secret Ed448 private key to execute arbitrary root commands via system() before SSH authentication even finishes.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1195.002 (Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain - Initial Access), T1574.006 (Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking (IFUNC) - Persistence / Defense Evasion), T1556 (Modify Authentication Process (sshd RSA_public_decrypt Hook) - Credential Access / Persistence)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Andres Freund (Microsoft / OpenWall oss-security): backdoor in upstream xz/liblzma leading to ssh server compromise (CVE-2024-3094) (https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2024/03/29/4) | Kaspersky GReAT (Securelist): CVE-2024-3094: Technical Analysis of the XZ Utils Backdoor & Ed448 Payload Structure (https://securelist.com/xz-backdoor-story-part-1/112354/) | Red Hat Product Security & CISA: Urgent Security Alert for Fedora 40/Rawhide & CISA CVE-2024-3094 Supply Chain Advisory (https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/urgent-security-alert-fedora-41-and-rawhide-users)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1195.002 · Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain): **M4 BUILD-TIME EXTRACTION & TRANSITIVE LIBSYSTEMD LOAD** — The malicious code is not visible in the normal C source files on GitHub; instead, a rigged build script (build-to-host.m4) unpacks a hidden binary object from a "corrupt test file" (bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz) only when building release packages, and libsystemd carries that poisoned library straight into sshd. During package compilation of XZ Utils 5.6.0 and 5.6.1, a tampered macro file named build-to-host.m4 decodes hidden shell commands from two test archives, tests/files/bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz and tests/files/good-large_compressed.lzma (hidden inside binary test files so code reviewers inspecting C source files on GitHub would see nothing suspicious), and splices a precompiled backdoor object into liblzma_la-crc64-fast.o. On Debian, Fedora, Ubuntu, and RHEL systems, the OpenSSH server (/usr/sbin/sshd) is compiled with libsystemd.so.0 support (so sshd can notify systemd when the service is ready, which transitively loads /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/liblzma.so.5.6.1 directly into every sshd process). Why did Andres Freund catch this? Because parsing the symbol tables inside the backdoored liblzma.so.5.6.1 added ~500 milliseconds (~2.3 billion CPU cycles) to every failed SSH login, which Freund spotted while profiling Debian sid with perf. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LIBLZMA 5.6.1 LOAD / ⇠#1 ACK liblzma 5.6.1) from Node ① (#1 Jia Tan / APT Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & eBPF SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2024-3094 (CVSS 10.0 Supply Chain Backdoor); TROJANIZED FILES=build-to-host.m4 & tests/files/bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz; TRANSITIVE LINK=/usr/sbin/sshd -> libsystemd.so.0 -> liblzma.so.5.6.1]
  - Stage 2 (T1574.006 · Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking): **GLIBC IFUNC RESOLVER & RSA_PUBLIC_DECRYPT GOT HIJACK** — Before sshd even runs its first line of code in main(), the Linux library loader asks liblzma which CRC64 math function fits the CPU best (IFUNC). The rigged resolver uses that early wakeup call to swap out OpenSSL’s RSA_public_decrypt phone number in memory. When a program starts on Linux, the GNU dynamic linker (ld-linux-x86-64.so.2) resolves Indirect Functions (IFUNC, a legitimate glibc feature designed to let libraries pick the fastest CPU-specific math routine before main() even begins). When the linker calls crc64_resolve() inside liblzma.so.5.6.1, the injected _get_cpuid() function checks that argv[0] is "/usr/sbin/sshd" and that debugging variables like LD_DEBUG are not set, then hooks _dl_audit_preinit to overwrite the Global Offset Table (GOT) pointer for OpenSSL’s RSA_public_decrypt (redirecting every future RSA signature check inside sshd to the backdoor’s own function). By executing inside an IFUNC resolver during dynamic linking, the backdoor modifies the in-memory GOT pointer for RSA_public_decrypt before OpenSSH’s main() function or privilege-separation sandbox even initializes. In the documented ELF IFUNC Resolver exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Linux Server (sshd :22), Linux Server (sshd :22) responds with ACK +2.3B Cycles (confirming that the IFUNC GOT HOOK request succeeded on Linux Server (sshd :22) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 ED448 SSH CERTIFICATE VERIFICATION & PRE-AUTH SYSTEM() RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ IFUNC GOT HOOK / ⇠#2 ACK +2.3B Cycles) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Linux Server (sshd :22)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & eBPF SIEM). [Specs: IFUNC ENTRYPOINT=crc64_resolve() -> _get_cpuid() in liblzma_la-crc64-fast.o; ENV EVASION CHECK=argv[0] == "/usr/sbin/sshd" && !LD_DEBUG && !LD_PROFILE; HOOKED SYMBOL=RSA_public_decrypt@plt (OpenSSL libcrypto)]
  - Stage 3 (T1556 · Modify Authentication Process): **ED448 SSH CERTIFICATE VERIFICATION & PRE-AUTH SYSTEM() RCE** — When the attacker connects over SSH, they hide an encrypted command inside the RSA public-key modulus (N) signed with their private Ed448 key. The hooked RSA_public_decrypt verifies the Ed448 signature and runs the command as root, while normal users’ SSH logins continue working normally! When the attacker connects to TCP port 22 and sends an SSH public-key authentication request (SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST), sshd calls the hooked RSA_public_decrypt() to verify the client’s key. The backdoor inspects the RSA modulus N for a magic arithmetic header (a*b + c <= 3), decrypts the embedded payload using ChaCha20, and verifies it against a hardcoded 32-byte Ed448 public key (ensuring that only the threat actor holding the matching Ed448 private key can trigger the backdoor, while all normal SSH connections pass straight through to the real RSA_public_decrypt). Once verified, the backdoor passes the decrypted command string to system() as root (UID 0). Because the hooked RSA_public_decrypt executes inside the privileged sshd monitor process before authentication completes, the command runs with full root privileges and leaves zero failed-login entries in /var/log/auth.log. In the documented Auditd SYSCALL 59 exchange from Linux Server (sshd :22) to liblzma IFUNC & GOT Hook, liblzma IFUNC & GOT Hook responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the PRE-AUTH ROOT RCE request succeeded on liblzma IFUNC & GOT Hook and completing the final execution objective of Andres Freund, Red Hat & Kaspersky, XZ Utils (liblzma) IFUNC sshd Supply Chain Backdoor). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ PRE-AUTH ROOT RCE / ⇠#3 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ③ (#3 Linux Server (sshd :22)) to Node ④ (#4 liblzma IFUNC & GOT Hook), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & eBPF SIEM). [Specs: CRYPTOGRAPHIC GATE=Ed448 Signature Verification + ChaCha20 Stream Cipher; PAYLOAD CARRIER=SSH RSA Certificate / Public Key Modulus (N); EXECUTION PRIMITIVE=system() as uid=0(root) inside privileged sshd monitor]

### CVE-2023-34362: Mandiant, Huntress & CISA — CL0P (FIN11): MOVEit Transfer SQLi, ISAPI Deserialization & LEMURLOOT
- **Scenario ID**: `cl0p-moveit-transfer-cve-2023-34362`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/cl0p-moveit-transfer-cve-2023-34362
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=cl0p-moveit-transfer-cve-2023-34362
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Mandiant · Huntress · CISA AA23-158A · guestaccess.aspx, moveitisapi.dll & human2.aspx Webshell

Synthesizing Mandiant (FIN11 / LEMURLOOT), Huntress Labs, Rapid7, and Joint CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-158A (May–June 2023), CVE-2023-34362 is the critical zero-day chain used by the CL0P ransomware group against Progress MOVEit Transfer servers worldwide. The attacker chains /guestaccess.aspx with /moveitisapi/moveitisapi.dll?action=m2 to trigger an unauthenticated SQL injection flaw, injects a Base64-encoded .NET BinaryFormatter deserialization payload into the active session database table, drops the human2.aspx (LEMURLOOT) C# webshell into C:\MOVEitTransfer\wwwroot\, and steals Azure Blob Storage keys and enterprise files.

- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **SESSION POISONING & MOVEITISAPI.DLL SQL INJECTION (CVE-2023-34362)** — First the attacker grabs a blank guest session at /guestaccess.aspx, then sends custom X-siLock-SessVar headers to /moveitisapi/moveitisapi.dll that break out of the SQL query string and rewrite the database. Why go through moveitisapi.dll instead of calling SILMachine2.aspx directly? Because MOVEit blocks external clients from passing sensitive session variables directly to SILMachine2.aspx, whereas the trusted moveitisapi.dll proxy passes X-siLock-SessVar headers right through. ### CVE-2024-6387: Qualys TRU & CISA — OpenSSH "regreSSHion": SIGALRM Async-Signal-Unsafe syslog() Heap RCE
- **Scenario ID**: `openssh-regreSSHion-cve-2024-6387`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/openssh-regreSSHion-cve-2024-6387
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=openssh-regreSSHion-cve-2024-6387
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Qualys Threat Research Unit · OpenSSH 8.5p1–9.7p1 · LoginGraceTime SIGALRM & glibc Heap Race
- **Overview**: Imagine a bank accountant (sshd main thread) who is in the middle of erasing and rearranging pages inside the master ledger (glibc free()). Suddenly, a 120-second kitchen timer (LoginGraceTime SIGALRM) rings! The accountant freezes mid-sentence with the ledger pages half-torn, and an emergency clerk (grace_alarm_handler -> sigdie) rushes in to write a "Visitor Timed Out!" note in the logbook (syslog()). However, writing that note requires grabbing a brand-new 320-byte sheet of paper (fopen("/etc/localtime") -> malloc(320)) from the exact same half-torn ledger! By timing their packets to the microsecond, the attacker tricks the emergency clerk into grabbing a rigged page that redirects the bank’s instructions (_IO_wfile_jumps) to run the attacker’s code as root. Discovered by the Qualys Threat Research Unit (July 2024), "regreSSHion" (CVE-2024-6387) is an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in OpenSSH’s server (sshd versions 8.5p1–9.7p1) on glibc-based Linux systems. An accidental October 2020 refactoring removed #ifdef DO_LOG_SAFE_IN_SIGHAND from sigdie(), reintroducing a 2006 bug (CVE-2006-5051). When a client fails to log in within LoginGraceTime (120 seconds), sshd’s SIGALRM signal handler asynchronously calls syslog(), which invokes async-signal-unsafe glibc malloc()/free() routines, allowing an attacker who interrupts an in-progress free() call to corrupt glibc _IO_FILE vtable structures and gain root RCE.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (OpenSSH SIGALRM Race CVE-2024-6387) - Initial Access), T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (Pre-Auth Root sshd) - Privilege Escalation)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Qualys Threat Research Unit (TRU): regreSSHion: RCE in OpenSSH’s server, on glibc-based Linux systems (CVE-2024-6387) (https://www.qualys.com/2024/07/01/cve-2024-6387/regresshion.txt) | The OpenSSH Project: OpenSSH 9.8 Security Advisory: Async-Signal-Unsafe sigdie() Regression (https://www.openssh.com/txt/release-9.8) | CISA & Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: CVE-2024-6387 OpenSSH regreSSHion Detection & Mitigation Guidance (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2024/07/01/etr-openssh-remote-unauthenticated-code-execution-cve-2024-6387-regresshion/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **SSH HEAP GROOMING & LOGINGRACETIME EXPIRATION** — Before the 120-second LoginGraceTime stopwatch hits zero, the attacker sends a carefully choreographed sequence of SSH public-key packets so the server’s memory ledger (glibc main_arena) is lined up with alternating 4 KB and 320-byte slots. To prepare the memory layout inside the privileged pre-authentication sshd child process, the attacker opens concurrent TCP/22 connections and sends a series of SSH2_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST packets containing crafted RSA/certificate public keys (allocating and freeing specific chunk sizes so glibc’s heap allocator arranges alternating 4 KB and 320-byte holes right before the 120-second LoginGraceTime timer expires). Why is this vulnerability called "regreSSHion"? Because OpenSSH originally fixed this exact signal-handler race in 2006 (CVE-2006-5051) by adding #ifdef DO_LOG_SAFE_IN_SIGHAND to sigdie(), but an unrelated code cleanup in October 2020 (OpenSSH 8.5p1) accidentally deleted that #ifdef guard. In the documented sshd Auth.log Flood exchange from Remote Exploit Operator to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ACK 120.000s Timeout (confirming that the LOGINGRACETIME STORM request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 SIGALRM INTERRUPTS FREE() & CALLS ASYNC-SIGNAL-UNSAFE SYSLOG()). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LOGINGRACETIME STORM / ⇠#1 ACK 120.000s Timeout) from Node ① (#1 Remote Exploit Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Auth Log & Network SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2024-6387 ("regreSSHion" — Regression of CVE-2006-5051); AFFECTED VERSIONS=OpenSSH 8.5p1 through 9.7p1 on glibc Linux; TIMER TRIGGER=LoginGraceTime (120s default) -> SIGALRM (Signal 14)]
  - Stage 2 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **SIGALRM INTERRUPTS FREE() & CALLS ASYNC-SIGNAL-UNSAFE SYSLOG()** — The attacker sends one final packet timed so that the 120-second SIGALRM bell rings while sshd is halfway through free(). The alarm handler calls syslog(), which calls fopen("/etc/localtime") -> malloc(320) on the half-updated heap pointers. The attacker times their final packet so that when the kernel delivers SIGALRM (signal 14, triggered when LoginGraceTime reaches 120 seconds), the main sshd thread is halfway through glibc’s _int_free() function (after modifying a heap chunk’s size metadata, but before updating the bin’s forward/backward pointers). The asynchronous signal handler grace_alarm_handler() calls sigdie("Timeout before authentication..."), which calls syslog() (an async-signal-unsafe C library function that internally calls __tzfile_read() -> fopen("/etc/localtime") -> malloc(320), causing glibc to allocate a 320-byte FILE structure overlapping the attacker’s packet buffer in memory). Why wasn’t OpenBSD vulnerable to CVE-2024-6387? Because OpenBSD’s syslog_r() implementation is explicitly designed to be async-signal-safe and never calls malloc() or fopen(), whereas Linux’s glibc syslog() dynamically allocates heap memory. In the documented SIGALRM / glibc Arena exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1), Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1) responds with ACK 320-Byte Overlap (confirming that the SYSLOG HEAP RACE request succeeded on Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 GLIBC _IO_FILE VTABLE HIJACK & PRE-AUTH ROOT CODE EXECUTION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SYSLOG HEAP RACE / ⇠#2 ACK 320-Byte Overlap) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Auth Log & Network SIEM). [Specs: SIGNAL HANDLER=grace_alarm_handler() -> sigdie(); UNSAFE FUNCTION=syslog() -> __tzfile_read() -> fopen() -> malloc(); HEAP PRIMITIVE=Arbitrary 320-byte chunk overlap in glibc main_arena]
  - Stage 3 (T1059.004 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell): **GLIBC _IO_FILE VTABLE HIJACK & PRE-AUTH ROOT CODE EXECUTION** — Because fopen("/etc/localtime") placed its 320-byte FILE control sheet right on top of the attacker’s buffer, the attacker overwrites the sheet’s function table (_IO_wfile_jumps) so that reading the timezone file executes /bin/sh as root. Because the 320-byte _IO_FILE structure allocated by fopen("/etc/localtime") sits inside memory controlled by the attacker’s SSH packet, the attacker crafts fake _wide_data and _vtable_offset fields pointing to glibc’s internal _IO_wfile_jumps vtable (redirecting the stream’s underflow function _IO_wfile_underflow to an arbitrary code pointer). The moment __tzfile_read() tries to read the timezone file via __uflow(), execution jumps into the attacker’s payload running inside the privileged pre-authentication sshd process (with full root UID 0 privileges, completely outside OpenSSH’s unprivileged network sandbox). Although winning the ASLR + timing race takes ~10,000 connections (roughly 3 to 6 hours against default MaxStartups), every failed attempt simply closes a child process while the master sshd daemon automatically forks fresh children. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ROOT VTABLE RCE / ⇠#3 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ③ (#3 Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1)) to Node ④ (#4 SIGALRM -> syslog() Race), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Auth Log & Network SIEM). [Specs: TARGET STRUCT=glibc struct _IO_FILE_plus (320 bytes); VTABLE GADGET=_IO_wfile_jumps -> _IO_wfile_underflow -> code pointer; PRIVILEGE LEVEL=Un-sandboxed root (UID 0) in privileged sshd process]

### CVE-2023-0669: Huntress, Mandiant & CISA — CL0P (TA505): Fortra GoAnywhere MFT LicenseServlet Deserialization RCE
- **Scenario ID**: `fortra-goanywhere-mft-cve-2023-0669-cl0p`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/fortra-goanywhere-mft-cve-2023-0669-cl0p
