- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=fortra-goanywhere-mft-cve-2023-0669-cl0p
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Huntress · Mandiant · Horizon3.ai · /goanywhere/lic/accept AES-CBC & CommonsBeanutils1 Gadget
- **Overview**: Imagine a software vault (GoAnywhere MFT) that has a special mail slot (/goanywhere/lic/accept) reserved for receiving encrypted license renewals from the manufacturer. To make sure only "official" license files are opened, the mail slot requires the package (bundle) to be locked with an AES cipher ($2). However, the developer hardcoded the exact AES password ("go@nywhereLicenseP@$$w0rd") right inside the public software binary that every customer downloads! Anyone who reads the binary can extract that password, lock a booby-trapped Java package (CommonsBeanutils1 gadget chain) with the official AES key, drop it into /goanywhere/lic/accept without logging in, and watch the server unlock and detonate it as SYSTEM. Synthesizing Horizon3.ai’s cryptographic root-cause analysis, Huntress Labs’ incident response forensics, and Mandiant / CISA advisories (February 2023), CVE-2023-0669 is the pre-authentication Java deserialization zero-day exploited by the CL0P ransomware group (TA505 / FIN11) against 130+ Fortra GoAnywhere MFT servers. Because LicenseResponseServlet (/goanywhere/lic/accept) decrypted incoming bundle parameters using a hardcoded static AES-128-CBC key and passed the plaintext directly to ObjectInputStream.readObject(), attackers sent a ysoserial CommonsBeanutils1 gadget chain to execute SYSTEM commands and deploy TrueBot and Cobalt Strike.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (GoAnywhere /lic/accept CVE-2023-0669) - Initial Access), T1059.003 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell - Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Horizon3.ai Attack Team: GoAnywhere MFT CVE-2023-0669 Pre-Auth RCE Technical Deep Dive (https://www.horizon3.ai/attack-research/attack-blogs/goanywhere-mft-cve-2023-0669-deep-dive-and-indicators-of-compromise/) | Huntress Security Research: Investigating GoAnywhere MFT RCE (CVE-2023-0669) Exploitation & Stack Traces (https://www.huntress.com/blog/investigating-goanywhere-mft-rce-cve-2023-0669) | Mandiant & CISA KEV: FIN11 / CL0P Exploitation of GoAnywhere MFT Zero-Day Deploying TrueBot & Cobalt Strike (https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **ENCRYPTED BUNDLE POST TO /GOANYWHERE/LIC/ACCEPT (CVE-2023-0669)** — Because the AES key "go@nywhereLicenseP@$$w0rd" is hardcoded inside LicenseResponseServlet, the attacker uses that exact key to encrypt their malicious Java object, adds $2 to the end, and POSTs it to /goanywhere/lic/accept without logging in. As reverse-engineered by Horizon3.ai, GoAnywhere MFT’s LicenseResponseServlet (mapped to /goanywhere/lic/accept and reachable without authentication) accepts a POST parameter named bundle. When the bundle string ends with "$2", the server decrypts it using AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding with a static 16-byte IV ("AES/CBC/PKCS5Pad") and a key derived from the hardcoded password "go@nywhereLicenseP@$$w0rd" (meaning any attacker on the internet can encrypt an arbitrary payload with that exact hardcoded key so the server treats it as a trusted license bundle, CVE-2023-0669). Encrypting a serialized Java object does not provide authentication if the encryption key is hardcoded inside the client/server software binary itself. In the documented HTTP POST / CVE-2023-0669 exchange from CL0P / TA505 Operator to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP HTTP 500 (confirming that the LIC/ACCEPT BUNDLE POST request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 COMMONSBEANUTILS1 GADGET DESERIALIZATION & SYSTEM SHELL). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LIC/ACCEPT BUNDLE POST / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 500) from Node ① (#1 CL0P / TA505 Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & GoAnywhere Log Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-0669 (Pre-Auth Java Deserialization); ENDPOINT URI=POST /goanywhere/lic/accept (bundle=...$2); HARDCODED CRYPTO=AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding + Static Key "go@nywhereLicenseP@$$w0rd"]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.003 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell): **COMMONSBEANUTILS1 GADGET DESERIALIZATION & SYSTEM SHELL** — Once decrypted, the server hands the bundle to Java’s ObjectInputStream.readObject(). Inside sits a PriorityQueue that automatically sorts its items on arrival, tricking BeanComparator into loading and running the attacker’s TemplatesImpl Java bytecode. After decrypting and Base64-decoding the bundle, LicenseTools.unserialize() passes the raw bytes into Java’s ObjectInputStream.readObject(). The attacker supplies a ysoserial CommonsBeanutils1 gadget chain (a chain of standard Java classes, java.util.PriorityQueue and org.apache.commons.beanutils.BeanComparator, already present in GoAnywhere’s classpath that automatically invokes TemplatesImpl.newTransformer() during deserialization, loading attacker-supplied Java bytecode in memory and spawning cmd.exe / powershell.exe as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM). As Huntress discovered, when the gadget chain finishes executing its payload inside readObject(), it throws a java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException that GoAnywhere writes directly into userdata/logs/goanywhere.log, giving defenders a forensic timestamp of every exploit attempt. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 + goanywhere.log exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to GoAnywhere MFT Server, GoAnywhere MFT Server responds with ACK PID 7144 (confirming that the GADGET RCE (SYSTEM) request succeeded on GoAnywhere MFT Server and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 TRUEBOT / COBALT STRIKE DEPLOYMENT & MFT VAULT EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ GADGET RCE (SYSTEM) / ⇠#2 ACK PID 7144) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 GoAnywhere MFT Server), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & GoAnywhere Log Sensor). [Specs: GADGET CHAIN=PriorityQueue -> BeanComparator -> TemplatesImpl.newTransformer(); LOG SIGNATURE=java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException in goanywhere.log; CHILD PROCESS=tomcat9.exe -> cmd.exe /c powershell -enc ...]
  - Stage 3 (T1219 · Remote Access Software): **TRUEBOT / COBALT STRIKE DEPLOYMENT & MFT VAULT EXFILTRATION** — Now running as SYSTEM inside the file-transfer server, the CL0P operators drop their TrueBot loader (rundll32.exe acl.dll,Menu) and Cobalt Strike to siphon off every sensitive file stored by the company’s customers. As documented by Mandiant (FIN11 / TA505) and Huntress, the initial PowerShell stager downloads and executes TrueBot (also tracked as Silence.Downloader, launched via rundll32.exe C:\ProgramData\acl.dll,Menu), installs NetSupport Manager RAT and Cobalt Strike beacons for redundant access, and exfiltrates sensitive customer files stored inside GoAnywhere MFT’s transfer directories. By targeting Managed File Transfer (MFT) appliances like GoAnywhere and MOVEit, CL0P bypassed endpoint EDR on user laptops and went straight to the central server where organizations store unencrypted financial, healthcare, and HR batch files. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 & 7 exchange from GoAnywhere MFT Server to CommonsBeanutils1 Deserializer, CommonsBeanutils1 Deserializer responds with ACK TrueBot DLL (confirming that the TRUEBOT DEPLOYMENT request succeeded on CommonsBeanutils1 Deserializer and completing the final execution objective of Huntress, Mandiant & CISA, CL0P (TA505): Fortra GoAnywhere MFT LicenseServlet Deserialization RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ TRUEBOT DEPLOYMENT / ⇠#3 ACK TrueBot DLL) from Node ③ (#3 GoAnywhere MFT Server) to Node ④ (#4 CommonsBeanutils1 Deserializer), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & GoAnywhere Log Sensor). [Specs: FIRST-STAGE LOADER=TrueBot (Silence.Downloader) via rundll32.exe; SECONDARY ACCESS=Cobalt Strike Beacon & NetSupport Manager RAT; EXTORTION GROUP=CL0P Ransomware / TA505 (FIN11)]

### CVE-2023-29059: CrowdStrike, Kaspersky & Mandiant — Lazarus (SmoothOperator): 3CXDesktopApp Supply Chain & Gopuram
- **Scenario ID**: `3cx-desktopapp-supply-chain-lazarus`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/3cx-desktopapp-supply-chain-lazarus
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=3cx-desktopapp-supply-chain-lazarus
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: CrowdStrike · Kaspersky GReAT · Mandiant · Trojanized ffmpeg.dll, d3dcompiler_47.dll & ICONICSTEALER
- **Overview**: Imagine a thief (Lazarus Group) who wants to break into a corporate phone system company (3CX). First, they poison an older trading program (X_TRADER) that a 3CX software engineer happens to install on their computer; that gives the thief access to 3CX’s official software factory! Inside the factory, the thief swaps out one helper library (ffmpeg.dll) inside the official 3CXDesktopApp installer before the factory stamps its genuine digital signature on the package. When thousands of companies install the update, 3CXDesktopApp.exe loads the rigged ffmpeg.dll, which reads secret encrypted instructions hidden after a 0xFEEDFACE bookmark inside a neighbor file (d3dcompiler_47.dll), checks innocent-looking icon files (icon1.ico) on GitHub to find the active command server, and steals browser passwords (ICONICSTEALER) or plants the Gopuram spyware! Synthesizing CrowdStrike (Labyrinth Chollima), Kaspersky GReAT (Gopuram), and Mandiant (UNC4736) analyses (March–April 2023), CVE-2023-29059 ("SmoothOperator") is a cascading supply chain compromise where North Korean threat actors trojanized the official Windows and macOS builds of 3CXDesktopApp (versions 18.12.407 and 18.12.416). When the validly signed 3CXDesktopApp.exe starts, it sideloads a trojanized ffmpeg.dll, which reads an RC4-encrypted shellcode blob embedded after marker 0xFEEDFACE inside d3dcompiler_47.dll, fetches AES-encrypted C2 URLs appended to .ico files on GitHub (IconStorages), and deploys ICONICSTEALER or the Gopuram backdoor in memory.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1195.002 (Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain - Initial Access), T1574.002 (Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Side-Loading (ffmpeg.dll) - Defense Evasion), T1102.001 (Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver (GitHub IconStorages .ico) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: CrowdStrike Falcon OverWatch & Threat Intelligence: CrowdStrike Detects and Prevents Active Intrusion Campaign Targeting 3CXDesktopApp Customers (https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/crowdstrike-detects-and-prevents-active-intrusion-campaign-targeting-3cxdesktopapp-customers/) | Mandiant Threat Intelligence (Google Cloud): 3CX Software Supply Chain Compromise Initiated by a Prior Software Supply Chain Compromise (UNC4736) (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) | Kaspersky GReAT (Securelist): Not just an infostealer: Gopuram backdoor deployed through 3CX supply chain attack (https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1195.002 · Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain): **TROJANIZED FFMPEG.DLL SIDE-LOADING & 0xFEEDFACE RC4 DECRYPTION** — When the user opens the validly signed 3CXDesktopApp.exe, it automatically loads ffmpeg.dll from its own folder. The rigged ffmpeg.dll opens d3dcompiler_47.dll, flips to page bookmark FE ED FA CE, and decrypts the hidden shellcode using RC4 key "3jB(2bsG#@c7". When an employee launches the legitimately signed 3CXDesktopApp.exe softphone client, Windows loads the co-located library ffmpeg.dll (which was trojanized inside 3CX’s build pipeline, CVE-2023-29059). Inside ffmpeg.dll, a malicious initialization thread creates the event AVMonitorEvent, opens the neighboring file d3dcompiler_47.dll (a legitimate-looking Direct3D shader library whose valid digital signature was stripped so an encrypted payload could be appended after the 4-byte magic marker 0xFEEDFACE), and decrypts that payload directly into RWX memory using the RC4 stream cipher with hardcoded key "3jB(2bsG#@c7". Why split the malware across three files (3CXDesktopApp.exe + ffmpeg.dll + d3dcompiler_47.dll)? Because 3CXDesktopApp.exe keeps its valid 3CX digital signature, ffmpeg.dll contains only a tiny RC4 reader with no C2 URLs, and the encrypted shellcode sits inert inside d3dcompiler_47.dll. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ TROJANIZED FFMPEG.DLL / ⇠#1 ACK RC4 Key 3jB(2bsG#@c7) from Node ① (#1 3CX Update & GitHub Dead-Drop) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / Kaspersky EDR SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-29059 (3CXDesktopApp Supply Chain Compromise); PAYLOAD MARKER=0xFEEDFACE inside d3dcompiler_47.dll; RC4 DECRYPT KEY="3jB(2bsG#@c7" (Decrypts Reflective Shellcode)]
  - Stage 2 (T1102.001 · Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver): **GITHUB ICON1.ICO DEAD-DROP RESOLVER & AES-GCM C2 EXTRACTION** — Instead of hardcoding a C2 server address that defenders could block on Day 1, the malware downloads normal-looking .ico icon files from a public GitHub repository (IconStorages) and reads an AES-encrypted web address glued to the very end of the icon file. Once decrypted in memory, the stage-2 shellcode uses a Dead Drop Resolver (MITRE T1102.001, connecting to a trusted public service like GitHub so corporate firewalls allow the traffic) by sending an HTTPS GET request to raw.githubusercontent.com/IconStorages/images/main/icon1.ico (through icon14.ico). At the very end of the valid icon image sits an appended Base64 string prefixed with "$" (which the malware extracts and decrypts using AES-GCM to reveal the real command-and-control URL, such as https://akamaicontainer.com/gl or https://msstorageboxes.com/eb). Even after GitHub took down the IconStorages repository, the shellcode also contained a fallback list of hardcoded C2 domains disguised to look like Akamai, Azure, and Microsoft storage services. In the documented Sysmon EID 22 (DNS) / HTTPS exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Enterprise Workstation (3CX), Enterprise Workstation (3CX) responds with ACK AES-GCM C2 URL (confirming that the GITHUB .ICO DEAD-DROP request succeeded on Enterprise Workstation (3CX) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 IN-MEMORY ICONICSTEALER & KASPERSKY GOPURAM BACKDOOR DEPLOYMENT). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ GITHUB .ICO DEAD-DROP / ⇠#2 ACK AES-GCM C2 URL) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Workstation (3CX)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / Kaspersky EDR SIEM). [Specs: DEAD-DROP URL=raw.githubusercontent.com/IconStorages/images/main/icon*.ico; STRING MARKER=Appended Base64 string starting with "$" at EOF of .ico; DECRYPTED C2=akamaicontainer.com / azureonlinestorage.com / msstorageboxes.com]
  - Stage 3 (T1555.003 · Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers): **IN-MEMORY ICONICSTEALER & KASPERSKY GOPURAM BACKDOOR DEPLOYMENT** — The C2 server sends back a memory-only thief (ICONICSTEALER) that raids Chrome, Edge, and Brave browser databases, and if the victim works at a cryptocurrency exchange, the operator sends in the heavy-duty Gopuram espionage backdoor. Connecting to the decrypted C2 URL with an encrypted "tutma=" cookie, the loader downloads and reflectively loads a third-stage DLL strictly in memory: ICONICSTEALER (an information stealer documented by Mandiant and CrowdStrike that enumerates the workstation and reads SQLite History and Login Data files from Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave, and Mozilla Firefox). Furthermore, as Kaspersky GReAT uncovered, on high-value cryptocurrency and financial victims the threat actor deployed Gopuram (a sophisticated modular C2 backdoor used exclusively by the Lazarus group). Mandiant subsequently traced how the 3CX supply chain attack itself began: Lazarus had earlier trojanized the website installer for Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software, which an employee at 3CX downloaded, creating a supply-chain-to-supply-chain cascade. In the documented EDR Memory / File Access exchange from Enterprise Workstation (3CX) to ffmpeg.dll & d3dcompiler_47.dll, ffmpeg.dll & d3dcompiler_47.dll responds with ACK In-Memory DLL (confirming that the ICONICSTEALER & GOPURAM request succeeded on ffmpeg.dll & d3dcompiler_47.dll and completing the final execution objective of CrowdStrike, Kaspersky & Mandiant, Lazarus (SmoothOperator): 3CXDesktopApp Supply Chain & Gopuram). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ICONICSTEALER & GOPURAM / ⇠#3 ACK In-Memory DLL) from Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Workstation (3CX)) to Node ④ (#4 ffmpeg.dll & d3dcompiler_47.dll), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / Kaspersky EDR SIEM). [Specs: STAGE 3 STEALER=ICONICSTEALER (In-Memory Browser & System Harvester); TARGETED IMPLANT=Gopuram Backdoor (Documented by Kaspersky GReAT); ATTRIBUTION=Lazarus Group / Labyrinth Chollima / UNC4736]

### CVE-2021-42287: Microsoft, CrowdStrike & Splunk — Active Directory "noPac": sAMAccountName Spoofing & KDC Impersonation
- **Scenario ID**: `nopac-samaccountname-cve-2021-42278-42287`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/nopac-samaccountname-cve-2021-42278-42287
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=nopac-samaccountname-cve-2021-42278-42287
- **Category**: ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Microsoft MSRC · CrowdStrike · Splunk SURGe · CVE-2021-42278 + CVE-2021-42287 S4U2self Domain Admin
- **Overview**: Imagine an office building where any regular employee is allowed to register up to 10 company laptops (ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 10). Normally, every laptop nametag must end with a $ symbol (FAKEPC01$). However, the badge clerk (CVE-2021-42278) forgets to check for the $ when someone renames a laptop! So the employee renames their laptop to CORP-DC01 (the exact name of the Chief Security Officer’s vault computer, minus the $), grabs a temporary lobby ticket (TGT), and immediately renames their laptop back to FAKEPC01$. Next, they hand that CORP-DC01 lobby ticket to the inner vault desk (KDC S4U2self) and ask for an Admin pass. When the vault clerk looks up CORP-DC01 and sees it no longer exists, the clerk has a quirky habit (CVE-2021-42287): "Let me add a $ to the end and check again!" Adding $ matches the real Chief Security Officer’s vault (CORP-DC01$), so the clerk prints a full Domain Admin master key for the real Domain Controller! Synthesizing Microsoft MSRC advisories, CrowdStrike Falcon Threat Intelligence, and Splunk SURGe detection research (November–December 2021), "noPac" chains two Active Directory flaws, CVE-2021-42278 (sAMAccountName spoofing) and CVE-2021-42287 (KDC $ fallback), to elevate any low-privilege domain user to Domain Administrator in seconds. The attacker creates a machine account via ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota, renames its sAMAccountName to match a Domain Controller without the trailing $, requests a Kerberos TGT, renames the account back, and uses S4U2self to trick the KDC into issuing a Domain Admin service ticket encrypted for the real CORP-DC01$ Domain Controller.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (noPac CVE-2021-42278 / 42287) - Privilege Escalation), T1558.001 (Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden/Silver S4U2self Ticket - Credential Access), T1003.006 (OS Credential Dumping: DCSync (MS-DRSR) - Credential Access)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): Active Directory sAMAccountName Spoofing (CVE-2021-42278) & KDC Pac Bypass (CVE-2021-42287) (https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2021-42287) | CrowdStrike Threat Intelligence: Understanding the Active Directory SamAccountName Spoofing / noPac Exploitation Chain (https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/) | Splunk SURGe Security Research: Detecting Active Directory noPac (CVE-2021-42278 & CVE-2021-42287) with EventID 4741 and 4781 (https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **MACHINE ACCOUNT CREATION & SAMACCOUNTNAME SPOOFING (CVE-2021-42278)** — Using the default quota that lets any user add 10 computers to the domain (ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 10), the attacker creates FAKEPC01$, strips off the $ to rename it CORP-DC01, and asks the KDC for a Kerberos TGT. By default in Active Directory, the attribute ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota is set to 10 (meaning any standard domain user can create up to 10 new computer accounts over LDAP without needing administrator rights). The attacker creates a computer account named FAKEPC01$, and then exploits CVE-2021-42278 (an LDAP validation flaw where Active Directory forgot to enforce that a computer account’s sAMAccountName must end with a trailing "$" sign when modified) to rename the computer’s sAMAccountName to CORP-DC01, matching the exact hostname of the target Domain Controller, and requests a Kerberos TGT (EventID 4768). Why didn’t Active Directory block the rename as a duplicate name? Because the real Domain Controller’s sAMAccountName is "CORP-DC01$" (with a dollar sign), so "CORP-DC01" (without a dollar sign) is treated by LDAP as a distinct string. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SPOOF DC SAMACCOUNTNAME / ⇠#1 ACK EID 4781) from Node ① (#1 Compromised Domain User) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk SIEM & Identity Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2021-42278 (AD sAMAccountName Validation Bypass); DEFAULT QUOTA=ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 10 (Standard Domain User); SPOOFED NAME=sAMAccountName = "CORP-DC01" (Stripped trailing "$")]
  - Stage 2 (T1558.001 · Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden/Silver Ticket): **RENAME BACK & KDC S4U2SELF "$" FALLBACK (CVE-2021-42287)** — While holding the CORP-DC01 TGT in their hand, the attacker renames their fake computer back to FAKEPC01$ and asks the KDC for an S4U2self service ticket. When the KDC can’t find CORP-DC01, it automatically adds $ (CORP-DC01$) and issues a ticket for the real Domain Controller! Holding the valid TGT for "CORP-DC01", the attacker renames their machine account back to FAKEPC01$ over LDAP (so no account named "CORP-DC01" exists in Active Directory anymore) and sends a Kerberos S4U2self TGS request (KRB_TGS_REQ, asking the KDC to issue a service ticket impersonating the Domain Administrator to itself). When the KDC looks up the TGT’s client name ("CORP-DC01") and fails to find it, CVE-2021-42287 triggers: kdcsvc.dll automatically appends a trailing "$" ("CORP-DC01$") and searches again, matching the real Domain Controller and encrypting a Domain Admin service ticket with the real Domain Controller’s secret key! Why is CVE-2021-42287 so critical? Because the KDC validates the incoming TGT using the attacker’s key, but encrypts the outgoing S4U2self TGS ticket (and its high-privilege Domain Admin PAC) for the real Domain Controller ("CORP-DC01$"). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ KDC "$" FALLBACK TGS / ⇠#2 ACK EID 4769) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Domain Controller (CORP-DC01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk SIEM & Identity Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2021-42287 (KDC Account Lookup "$" Fallback); KERBEROS EXTENSION=S4U2self (PA-FOR-USER = Administrator@CORP.LOCAL); ISSUED TICKET=cifs/CORP-DC01.corp.local with Domain Admin PAC]
  - Stage 3 (T1003.006 · OS Credential Dumping: DCSync): **DOMAIN CONTROLLER IMPERSONATION & NTDS.DIT DCSYNC** — The attacker walks up to the real Domain Controller (CORP-DC01) and hands over the freshly minted cifs/CORP-DC01 Domain Admin ticket, dumping every password hash in the company from NTDS.dit. Presenting the forged cifs/CORP-DC01.corp.local Kerberos service ticket (which carries a valid Privilege Attribute Certificate for the Domain Administrator signed by the KDC itself), the attacker authenticates to the Domain Controller and invokes the MS-DRSR directory replication protocol (DCSync, DrsGetNCChanges, which instructs the Domain Controller to replicate the NTLM and AES password hashes of krbtgt and all domain users from NTDS.dit). From start to finish, tools like noPac.exe and sam_the_admin.py complete all three steps automatically in under 3 seconds. In the documented WinSec EID 4662 (DCSync) exchange from Domain Controller (CORP-DC01) to KDC S4U2self Ticket Engine, KDC S4U2self Ticket Engine responds with ACK EID 4662 (confirming that the DCSYNC REPLICATION request succeeded on KDC S4U2self Ticket Engine and completing the final execution objective of Microsoft, CrowdStrike & Splunk, Active Directory "noPac": sAMAccountName Spoofing & KDC Impersonation). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ DCSYNC REPLICATION / ⇠#3 ACK EID 4662) from Node ③ (#3 Domain Controller (CORP-DC01)) to Node ④ (#4 KDC S4U2self Ticket Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk SIEM & Identity Sensor). [Specs: AUTHENTICATION=Kerberos AP-REQ with Domain Admin S4U2self Ticket; POST-EXPLOIT=MS-DRSR DrsGetNCChanges (DCSync) on CORP-DC01; COMPROMISED ASSET=krbtgt AES256/NTLM keys & Full Domain Compromise]

### CVE-2020-1472: Secura, CISA & CrowdStrike — Active Directory "Zerologon": Netlogon AES-CFB8 All-Zero IV Takeover
- **Scenario ID**: `zerologon-netlogon-cve-2020-1472`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/zerologon-netlogon-cve-2020-1472
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=zerologon-netlogon-cve-2020-1472
- **Category**: ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Secura · CISA ED 20-04 · CrowdStrike · MS-NRPC NetrServerAuthenticate3 & NetrServerPasswordSet2
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security vault door (Netlogon MS-NRPC) where the guard tests visitors by handing them a secret key calculator (AES-CFB8). Normally, scrambling an 8-digit number with a secret key produces a completely unpredictable 8-digit answer. However, the engineer who built the calculator made a fatal mistake: they wired the starting dial (Initialization Vector / IV) permanently to 0000000000000000! Because of how AES-CFB8 math works when the starting dial is all zeroes, if a visitor types in 00000000 as their challenge, there is an exact 1-in-256 chance that the encrypted answer is ALSO 00000000, no matter what the Domain Controller’s secret password is! By knocking on the door ~256 times in 3 seconds with all zeroes, the attacker gets waved right in and resets the Domain Controller’s own password to blank. Discovered by Tom Tervoort of Secura and mandated for emergency patching under CISA Emergency Directive 20-04 (August–September 2020), "Zerologon" (CVE-2020-1472, CVSS 10.0) is a catastrophic cryptographic flaw in the Windows Netlogon Remote Protocol (MS-NRPC). Because ComputeNetlogonCredential() used AES-CFB8 with a fixed all-zero 16-byte IV, supplying an 8-byte client challenge of all zeroes (0x00*8) yields an all-zero credential for 1 out of every 256 random session keys. In ~3 seconds without any domain credentials, an attacker bypasses NetrServerAuthenticate3, calls NetrServerPasswordSet2 to overwrite the Domain Controller’s CORP-DC01$ machine password with an empty string (EventID 4742), and dumps NTDS.dit via DCSync.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (Zerologon CVE-2020-1472) - Privilege Escalation), T1098 (Account Manipulation (NetrServerPasswordSet2 Empty DC Hash) - Persistence), T1003.006 (OS Credential Dumping: DCSync - Credential Access)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Secura BV (Tom Tervoort): Zerologon: Unauthenticated Domain Controller Compromise by Subverting Netlogon Cryptography (CVE-2020-1472) (https://www.secura.com/blog/zero-logon) | Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA): Emergency Directive 20-04: Mitigate Netlogon Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability from August 2020 Patch Tuesday (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-20-04-mitigate-netlogon-elevation-privilege-vulnerability-august-2020-patch) | Microsoft Threat Intelligence & CrowdStrike: Detecting CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon) via Windows EventID 5805, 4742 & Netlogon RPC Inspection (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2020/09/28/new-detections-for-cve-2020-1472-active-exploitation/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1210 · Exploitation of Remote Services): **ALL-ZERO AES-CFB8 CHALLENGE SPOOFING (CVE-2020-1472)** — Because ComputeNetlogonCredential uses AES-CFB8 with an all-zero IV, sending 8 zero bytes as the ClientChallenge has a 1-in-256 chance of producing 8 zero bytes as the ClientCredential. In less than 3 seconds, one of the 256 tries hits the jackpot! As proven by Secura, in the Netlogon handshake (NetrServerReqChallenge followed by NetrServerAuthenticate3), the client proves it knows the machine password by encrypting an 8-byte ClientChallenge using ComputeNetlogonCredential(). However, Microsoft implemented this function using AES-CFB8 (8-bit Cipher Feedback mode, which encrypts 1 byte at a time by XORing each plaintext byte with the first byte of AES applied to a 16-byte sliding window) and hardcoded the 16-byte Initialization Vector (IV) to all zeroes (0x00*16, violating the fundamental rule of cryptography that an IV must be random). When the attacker sets ClientChallenge = 0x0000000000000000, there is a 1-in-256 probability that the first AES block starts with 0x00, causing all 8 encrypted bytes to stay 0x0000000000000000! Because Netlogon has no rate-limiting or account lockout on computer accounts, an unauthenticated attacker on the network can fire ~256 RPC attempts in under 3 seconds until the random session key happens to produce the all-zero output. In the documented System EID 5805 + Zeek RPC exchange from Internal Network Attacker to Core Identity & VLAN Switch, Core Identity & VLAN Switch responds with ACK 214 RPC Tries (confirming that the NRPC ZERO-IV BRUTE request succeeded on Core Identity & VLAN Switch and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 OVERWRITING THE DOMAIN CONTROLLER PASSWORD VIA NETRSERVERPASSWORDSET2). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ NRPC ZERO-IV BRUTE / ⇠#1 ACK 214 RPC Tries) from Node ① (#1 Internal Network Attacker) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / SIEM Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2020-1472 ("Zerologon" — CVSS 10.0 MS-NRPC); CRYPTO FLAW=AES-CFB8 with All-Zero IV (1-in-256 Zero Fixed Point); RPC CALLS=NetrServerReqChallenge + NetrServerAuthenticate3 (Flags 0x212fffff)]
  - Stage 2 (T1098 · Account Manipulation): **OVERWRITING THE DOMAIN CONTROLLER PASSWORD VIA NETRSERVERPASSWORDSET2** — Even though the attacker passed the front-door check, they still don’t know what random SessionKey the Domain Controller picked. So they uncheck the "Encrypt Our Conversation" box (Flags = 0x212fffff) and tell the Domain Controller (NetrServerPasswordSet2): "Change your own CORP-DC01$ password to blank!" During the NetrServerAuthenticate3 call, the attacker clears the Netlogon Sealing flag (NegotiateFlags = 0x212fffff, telling the Domain Controller not to require RPC packet encryption on this session, which was still allowed by default in 2020 for backwards compatibility) and then invokes NetrServerPasswordSet2 with a 516-byte buffer of all zeroes. Because encrypting 516 zero bytes with AES-CFB8 and an all-zero IV also produces all zeroes, the Domain Controller overwrites its own computer account password (CORP-DC01$) in Active Directory NTDS.dit with an empty password (NTLM hash 31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0). Because this RPC call runs over an unauthenticated network pipe rather than a logged-in user session, Windows logs Security EventID 4742 ("A computer account was modified") with SubjectUserName: ANONYMOUS LOGON. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ DC$ PASSWORD WIPE / ⇠#2 ACK EID 4742) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Domain Controller (CORP-DC01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / SIEM Sensor). [Specs: RPC FUNCTION=NetrServerPasswordSet2 (ClearNewPassword = 516 Zero Bytes); NEW DC$ NTLM HASH=31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0 (Empty Password); WINDOWS EVENT=Security EventID 4742 (SubjectUserName: ANONYMOUS LOGON)]
  - Stage 3 (T1003.006 · OS Credential Dumping: DCSync): **DCSYNC DOMAIN DUMP & REGISTRY MACHINE PASSWORD RESTORATION** — Now that CORP-DC01$ has a blank password in Active Directory, the attacker logs in as CORP-DC01$ with no password, downloads every password hash in the company via DCSync, and then puts the original password back from the DC’s local registry so nobody notices the DC broke! Because a Domain Controller’s computer account (CORP-DC01$) automatically belongs to the Enterprise Domain Controllers group, the attacker authenticates over SMB/RPC as CORP\CORP-DC01$ using the empty NTLM hash (31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0) and runs DCSync (DrsGetNCChanges, dumping the Domain Administrator and krbtgt hashes from NTDS.dit). Finally, because wiping CORP-DC01$’s password in AD causes it to go out of sync with the password stored in the DC’s local registry (HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC, which would break DNS and AD replication), the attacker uses their new Domain Admin credentials to read $MACHINE.ACC and restore the original machine password. Why did Zerologon break Domain Controllers when naive attackers forgot Step 3? Because NetrServerPasswordSet2 updates NTDS.dit without updating the DC’s local LSA secret ($MACHINE.ACC), locking the DC out of its own domain until restored. In the documented WinSec EID 4624 & 4662 exchange from Domain Controller (CORP-DC01) to Netlogon AES-CFB8 & Password Reset, Netlogon AES-CFB8 & Password Reset responds with ACK NTLM 31d6cfe0... (confirming that the DC$ EMPTY-HASH DCSYNC request succeeded on Netlogon AES-CFB8 & Password Reset and completing the final execution objective of Secura, CISA & CrowdStrike, Active Directory "Zerologon": Netlogon AES-CFB8 All-Zero IV Takeover). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ DC$ EMPTY-HASH DCSYNC / ⇠#3 ACK NTLM 31d6cfe0...) from Node ③ (#3 Domain Controller (CORP-DC01)) to Node ④ (#4 Netlogon AES-CFB8 & Password Reset), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / SIEM Sensor). [Specs: REPLICATION IDENTITY=CORP\CORP-DC01$ (Enterprise Domain Controllers); CLEANUP ARTIFACT=Restores HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC; MANDATED PATCH=CISA Emergency Directive 20-04 / Secure RPC Enforcement]

### CVE-2021-34473: DEVCORE, Mandiant & CISA — Microsoft Exchange "ProxyShell": Autodiscover SSRF to MailboxExport Webshell
- **Scenario ID**: `proxyshell-exchange-cve-2021-34473`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/proxyshell-exchange-cve-2021-34473
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=proxyshell-exchange-cve-2021-34473
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Orange Tsai (DEVCORE) · CISA AA21-265A · Mandiant · CVE-2021-34473 + CVE-2021-34523 + CVE-2021-31207
- **Overview**: Imagine a corporate mailroom (Exchange Client Access Frontend :443) where a receptionist is trained to help people find their mailbox settings (/autodiscover/autodiscover.json). If someone writes /autodiscover/autodiscover.json/alice@corp.com/settings, the receptionist crosses out /autodiscover/autodiscover.json/alice@corp.com and forwards /settings to the high-security back office (Exchange Backend :444) stamped with the building’s master SYSTEM seal. Orange Tsai discovered that if you request /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com/powershell/, the receptionist gets confused by the ?@, crosses out /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com, and forwards /powershell/ straight into the restricted Admin PowerShell room! Once inside, you hand the clerk a forged ID card (X-Rps-CAT), grant yourself "Mailbox Export" rights, and export a booby-trapped email directly into the public web folder as shell.aspx! Discovered by Orange Tsai of DEVCORE (Pwn2Own 2021) and documented by Joint CISA Advisory AA21-265A, Mandiant, and Splunk SURGe, "ProxyShell" chains three Microsoft Exchange vulnerabilities into a 1-click unauthenticated SYSTEM RCE: (1) CVE-2021-34473 (pre-auth URL path confusion via /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com/powershell/ to reach the backend PowerShell endpoint as SYSTEM), (2) CVE-2021-34523 (X-Rps-CAT token deserialization to impersonate the Exchange Administrator), and (3) CVE-2021-31207 (New-MailboxExportRequest arbitrary file write to drop a polyglot .pst/.aspx webshell into C:\inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client\).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Exchange ProxyShell CVE-2021-34473) - Initial Access), T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (X-Rps-CAT Token Forgery CVE-2021-34523) - Privilege Escalation), T1505.003 (Server Software Component: Web Shell (New-MailboxExportRequest CVE-2021-31207) - Persistence)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: DEVCORE Security Research (Orange Tsai): ProxyShell: A New Attack Surface on MS Exchange Part 3 (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-31207) (https://devco.re/blog/2021/08/06/a-new-attack-surface-on-ms-exchange-part-3-ProxyShell/) | CISA & FBI Joint Advisory: Exploitation of Microsoft Exchange Server Vulnerabilities (ProxyShell) (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2021/08/21/cisa-and-fbi-release-advisory-conti-ransomware-and-proxyshell) | Huntress Labs & Mandiant: Incident Response Analysis: Detecting ProxyShell Exploitation & MailboxExportRequest Webshells (https://www.huntress.com/blog/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **AUTODISCOVER.JSON PATH CONFUSION & ACL BYPASS (CVE-2021-34473)** — Exchange’s RemoveExplicitLogonFromUrlAnchoredXml function tries to delete the email address from the URL, but a missing / check in its regex lets ?@foo.com trick it into deleting /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com, turning the URL into /powershell/! In Microsoft Exchange’s Architecture, the internet-facing Frontend Client Access Service (CAS on TCP 443) authenticates users and proxies their requests to the internal Backend server (on TCP 444) using Exchange’s own machine certificate (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM). As Orange Tsai discovered, when a URL starts with /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com/powershell/, the frontend’s Explicit-Logon parser strips "/autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com" thinking it is an email address prefix, and proxies the remaining path, /powershell/, straight to the internal Backend server with full SYSTEM authentication (CVE-2021-34473, bypassing all frontend login checks). Attackers also used an alternate form discovered in the wild: placing the path inside an HTTP cookie (Cookie: Email=autodiscover/autodiscover.json%3F@foo.com) so simple URL filters looking for "@foo.com" in the URI query string would miss it. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ AUTODISCOVER PATH BYPASS / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 ProxyShell Threat Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & Exchange Audit Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2021-34473 (Pre-Auth Path Confusion / SSRF); CRAFTED URI=/autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com/powershell/; BACKEND TARGET=https://localhost:444/powershell/ (Authenticated as SYSTEM)]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.001 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell): **POWERSHELL X-RPS-CAT IMPERSONATION & ROLE ASSIGNMENT (CVE-2021-34523)** — When the proxied request arrives in the Backend /powershell/ room, the clerk says: "I see the building’s SYSTEM stamp, but which user am I running commands for?" The attacker hands over ?X-Rps-CAT=... containing the Exchange Administrator’s SID! When the proxied request reaches the Backend PowerShell endpoint (:444/powershell/), it initially fails because the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM computer account does not have a user security token attached. Exploiting CVE-2021-34523, the attacker appends the query parameter ?X-Rps-CAT=<Base64_CommonAccessToken> (a serialized Windows CommonAccessToken structure that the Backend PowerShell module trusts without signature verification, allowing the attacker to plug in the Exchange Administrator’s Security Identifier / SID and open a full administrative Exchange PowerShell session). Inside that session, the attacker runs New-ManagementRoleAssignment -Role "Mailbox Import Export" -User "admin@corp.local". How did the attacker know the Exchange Administrator’s SID before logging in? By first sending a quick autodiscover/mapi request through the same CVE-2021-34473 proxy to convert the administrator’s email address into their legacyExchangeDN and Windows SID. In the documented MSExchange Mgmt EID 1 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Exchange Server (CAS Frontend), Exchange Server (CAS Frontend) responds with ACK EID 1 Cmdlet (confirming that the MAILBOX EXPORT CMDLET request succeeded on Exchange Server (CAS Frontend) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 NEW-MAILBOXEXPORTREQUEST ARBITRARY .ASPX WEBSHELL WRITE (CVE-2021-31207)). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ MAILBOX EXPORT CMDLET / ⇠#2 ACK EID 1 Cmdlet) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Exchange Server (CAS Frontend)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & Exchange Audit Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2021-34523 (Exchange PowerShell Backend EoP); TOKEN PARAMETER=?X-Rps-CAT=<Serialized CommonAccessToken with Admin SID>; ADMIN CMDLET=New-ManagementRoleAssignment -Role "Mailbox Import Export"]
  - Stage 3 (T1505.003 · Server Software Component: Web Shell): **NEW-MAILBOXEXPORTREQUEST ARBITRARY .ASPX WEBSHELL WRITE (CVE-2021-31207)** — Normally New-MailboxExportRequest saves a .pst email archive file. By hiding an ASPX webshell inside a draft email and telling Exchange to export that mailbox to \\127.0.0.1\c$\inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client\shell.aspx, IIS runs the email attachment as a live SYSTEM webshell! With the "Mailbox Import Export" role assigned, the attacker saves a draft email containing an encoded JScript/C# ASPX webshell, and then executes New-MailboxExportRequest -Mailbox admin@corp.local -FilePath "\\127.0.0.1\c$\inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client\shell.aspx" (CVE-2021-31207, abusing the Exchange Mailbox Replication service, which runs as SYSTEM, to write a file to any UNC path on the server). Even though the exported file is a binary .PST mailbox archive (starting with magic bytes !BDN), naming it .aspx causes IIS’s ASP.NET engine to ignore the binary PST header and execute the <script runat="server"> webshell inside it as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM! Why did the raw ASPX code have to be specially encoded inside the draft email? Because Exchange normally compresses or encodes email bodies inside a PST file; Orange Tsai used a custom UTF-7 / uncompressed attachment trick so the exact ASCII characters <%@ Page ... %> appeared intact inside the binary PST file. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 & 11 exchange from Exchange Server (CAS Frontend) to Exchange PowerShell Backend, Exchange PowerShell Backend responds with ACK SYSTEM Shell (confirming that the ASPX WEBSHELL EXEC request succeeded on Exchange PowerShell Backend and completing the final execution objective of DEVCORE, Mandiant & CISA, Microsoft Exchange "ProxyShell": Autodiscover SSRF to MailboxExport Webshell). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ASPX WEBSHELL EXEC / ⇠#3 ACK SYSTEM Shell) from Node ③ (#3 Exchange Server (CAS Frontend)) to Node ④ (#4 Exchange PowerShell Backend), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & Exchange Audit Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2021-31207 (Arbitrary File Write via MailboxExport); EXPORT CMDLET=New-MailboxExportRequest -FilePath "\\127.0.0.1\c$\...\shell.aspx"; POLYGLOT TRICK=PST file containing valid <script runat="server"> ASPX code]

### CVE-2021-34527: Microsoft, Rapid7 & Elastic — Windows "PrintNightmare": RpcAddPrinterDriverEx Remote SYSTEM RCE
- **Scenario ID**: `printnightmare-spooler-cve-2021-34527`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/printnightmare-spooler-cve-2021-34527
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=printnightmare-spooler-cve-2021-34527
- **Category**: ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Microsoft MSRC · Rapid7 · Elastic Security Labs · MS-RPRN APD_INSTALL_WARNED_DRIVER (0x8000) Bypass
- **Overview**: Imagine a corporate print room (spoolsv.exe, running as SYSTEM on every Windows server and Domain Controller) where only IT Administrators are supposed to install new printer driver software (ValidateObjectAccess). However, the rulebook for the RpcAddPrinterDriverEx command has a bizarre loophole written in the fine print: "If the caller checks the 0x8000 box (APD_INSTALL_WARNED_DRIVER), skip the ID check!" By checking that 0x8000 box and telling the Print Spooler that the printer’s "configuration helper file" (pConfigFile) is sitting on the attacker’s own shared folder (\\10.10.20.55\share\evil.dll), any regular employee can trick a Domain Controller’s Print Spooler into downloading and running evil.dll as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM! Synthesizing Microsoft MSRC advisories, Rapid7’s RPC reverse engineering, and Elastic Security Labs’ telemetry analysis (June–July 2021), "PrintNightmare" (CVE-2021-34527 / CVE-2021-1675) is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the Windows Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe). By calling RpcAddPrinterDriverEx() over \pipe\spoolss (MS-RPRN) or RpcAsyncAddPrinterDriver() (MS-PAR) with bit 0x8000 (APD_INSTALL_WARNED_DRIVER) set in dwFileCopyFlags, any authenticated domain user bypasses ValidateObjectAccess() and forces the remote server’s spoolsv.exe (SYSTEM) to copy and LoadLibraryW() an arbitrary DLL from an attacker-controlled UNC share.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation / RCE (PrintNightmare CVE-2021-34527) - Privilege Escalation / Lateral Movement), T1547.012 (Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Print Processors / Drivers - Persistence)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): Windows Print Spooler Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2021-34527 / PrintNightmare) (https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2021-34527) | Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527): Technical Analysis of MS-RPRN RpcAddPrinterDriverEx Exploitation (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2021/06/30/printnightmare-cve-2021-1675-remote-code-execution-in-windows-spooler-service/) | Elastic Security Labs & CISA: Detecting PrintNightmare via PrintService Operational EventID 316 and Sysmon EventID 7/11 (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2021/06/30/printnightmare-critical-windows-print-spooler-vulnerability)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1210 · Exploitation of Remote Services): **RPCADDPRINTERDRIVEREX AUTH BYPASS VIA 0x8000 FLAG (CVE-2021-34527)** — Normally localspl.dll checks if the caller is a Server Administrator before installing a printer driver. Setting bit 0x8000 (dwFileCopyFlags = 0x8014) jumps right over the ValidateObjectAccess() check! As reverse-engineered by Rapid7 and security researchers, the Windows Print Spooler (spoolsv.exe, which runs by default as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on all Windows workstations, member servers, and Domain Controllers) exposes the MS-RPRN RPC interface over SMB named pipe \pipe\spoolss. Inside localspl.dll’s SplAddPrinterDriverEx() function, the code checked: if ((dwFileCopyFlags & 0x8000) == 0) { ValidateObjectAccess(...); } (meaning that simply setting the flag APD_INSTALL_WARNED_DRIVER = 0x8000 inside dwFileCopyFlags caused the Print Spooler to skip the administrator permission check completely, CVE-2021-34527). Even after Microsoft patched the legacy MS-RPRN interface in June 2021 (CVE-2021-1675), researchers discovered that the asynchronous RPC interface MS-PAR (RpcAsyncAddPrinterDriver) had the exact same missing check (tracked as CVE-2021-34527). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ RPCADDPRINTERDRIVEREX / ⇠#1 RESP Flags 0x8014) from Node ① (#1 Low-Privilege Domain User) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic EDR & SIEM Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2021-34527 ("PrintNightmare" MS-RPRN / MS-PAR); BYPASS BITMASK=dwFileCopyFlags = 0x8014 (APD_INSTALL_WARNED_DRIVER = 0x8000); SKIPPED CHECK=localspl.dll!ValidateObjectAccess(SPOOLER_OBJECT_SERVER)]
  - Stage 2 (T1547.012 · Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Print Processors): **UNC DRIVER COPY & SYSTEM DLL LOAD IN SPOOLSV.EXE** — To pass Windows’ driver file checks, the attacker points the main printer driver (pDriverPath) to a real Microsoft UNIDRV.DLL already on the server, while pointing the helper configuration file (pConfigFile) to \\10.10.20.55\share\evil.dll. In the DRIVER_CONTAINER structure sent to RpcAddPrinterDriverEx(), the attacker sets pDriverPath to a genuine Microsoft inbox printer driver already on the target’s disk (such as UNIDRV.DLL so basic driver header checks pass), and sets pConfigFile to a remote SMB UNC path: \\10.10.20.55\share\evil.dll. Because the flags 0x0004 (APD_COPY_ALL_FILES) and 0x0010 (APD_COPY_FROM_DIRECTORY) are also set, spoolsv.exe reaches out over SMB, copies evil.dll into C:\Windows\System32\spool\drivers\x64\3\, and immediately calls LoadLibraryW() on it in memory. When an exploit script calls RpcAddPrinterDriverEx multiple times, Windows moves the previous copy of the DLL into backup numbered subfolders like C:\Windows\System32\spool\drivers\x64\3\Old\1\evil.dll, a classic forensic indicator on disk. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 & 11 exchange from Core Identity & VLAN Switch to Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe), Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe) responds with ACK Unsigned DLL (confirming that the SPOOLER UNSIGNED DLL request succeeded on Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 DLLMAIN SYSTEM EXECUTION & DOMAIN CONTROLLER COMPROMISE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SPOOLER UNSIGNED DLL / ⇠#2 ACK Unsigned DLL) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic EDR & SIEM Sensor). [Specs: REMOTE UNC PATH=pConfigFile = "\\10.10.20.55\share\evil.dll"; LOCAL DROP PATH=C:\Windows\System32\spool\drivers\x64\3\Old\1\evil.dll; LOADER PROCESS=C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM)]
  - Stage 3 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **DLLMAIN SYSTEM EXECUTION & DOMAIN CONTROLLER COMPROMISE** — The instant spoolsv.exe loads evil.dll to ask about printer settings, the attacker’s DllMain code runs with full SYSTEM privileges on the Domain Controller. The moment spoolsv.exe calls LoadLibraryW() and DrvConvertDevMode() on the copied configuration DLL, the attacker’s DllMain(DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH) routine executes inside the spoolsv.exe process as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (giving the attacker immediate SYSTEM code execution on the target server or Domain Controller to create a new Domain Admin account or launch a reverse shell). Why do security guides recommend disabling the Print Spooler service completely on Domain Controllers? Because a Domain Controller never needs to manage physical office paper printers, and stopping spoolsv.exe eliminates the entire MS-RPRN / MS-PAR attack surface (including both PrintNightmare and SpoolSample). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SPOOLSV CHILD SHELL / ⇠#3 ACK SYSTEM RCE) from Node ③ (#3 Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe)) to Node ④ (#4 Driver DLL Load in spoolsv.exe), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic EDR & SIEM Sensor). [Specs: EXECUTION CONTEXT=NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM inside spoolsv.exe (PID 2184); EVENT LOG TRACE=Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Admin EventID 316 / 808; HARDENING FIX=Disable Spooler service on DCs & RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators = 1]

### CVE-2023-29357: STAR Labs, Rapid7 & CISA — Microsoft SharePoint: JWT "alg:none" Auth Bypass to BCS RCE Chain
- **Scenario ID**: `sharepoint-cve-2023-29357-24955-chain`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/sharepoint-cve-2023-29357-24955-chain
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=sharepoint-cve-2023-29357-24955-chain
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: STAR Labs (Pwn2Own) · Rapid7 · CISA KEV · CVE-2023-29357 OAuth JWT Spoofing + CVE-2023-24955 .bdcm RCE
- **Overview**: Imagine a VIP corporate portal (SharePoint Server) that accepts digital passports (OAuth2 JSON Web Tokens / JWT). Every passport has a top section (Header) that tells the guard which cryptographic signature pen was used to sign it (RS256), and a bottom section (Signature). At Pwn2Own 2023, STAR Labs discovered that if you print a fake passport whose top section says "alg": "none" ("No signature pen used!") and leave the signature blank, the SharePoint guard (SPJsonWebSecurityBaseTokenHandler) says: "Well, since it says none, I don’t need to check a signature, welcome in, Farm Administrator!" Once inside as the Farm Admin, the attacker imports a custom "Business Data Connector" (.bdcm file) containing a compiled C# program (DotNetAssembly) that SharePoint loads straight into memory! Discovered by Nguyễn Tiến Giang (Jang) of STAR Labs at Pwn2Own Vancouver 2023 and documented by Microsoft MSRC, Rapid7, and CISA KEV, this scenario chains two flaws in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server: (1) CVE-2023-29357 (CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication privilege escalation via unsigned "alg": "none" OAuth2 JSON Web Tokens) and (2) CVE-2023-24955 (authenticated Remote Code Execution via Business Connectivity Services .bdcm DotNetAssembly loading inside w3wp.exe).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (SharePoint OAuth JWT alg:none CVE-2023-29357) - Initial Access), T1550.001 (Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token - Defense Evasion), T1505 (Server Software Component (BCS .bdcm DotNetAssembly RCE CVE-2023-24955) - Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: STAR Labs SG (Nguyễn Tiến Giang): SharePoint Pre-Auth RCE Chain (CVE-2023-29357 & CVE-2023-24955) Technical Writeup (https://starlabs.sg/blog/2023/09-sharepoint-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2023-29357-and-cve-2023-24955/) | Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: Analysis of SharePoint Server Elevation of Privilege (CVE-2023-29357) (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/) | Microsoft MSRC & CISA KEV: Microsoft SharePoint Server Elevation of Privilege & RCE Advisories (CVE-2023-29357 / CVE-2023-24955) (https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2023-29357)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **FORGING AN UNSIGNED OAUTH JWT WITH "ALG: NONE" (CVE-2023-29357)** — By setting "alg": "none" (eyJhbGciOiJub25l...) and "isloopback": "true" inside a self-made JWT token, the attacker tricks SharePoint into skipping cryptographic signature verification completely and handing over the list of Site Administrators. As detailed by STAR Labs and Rapid7, the attacker first sends an unauthenticated request with Authorization: Bearer to SharePoint to read the server’s Realm UUID from the HTTP 401 WWW-Authenticate response header. Next, the attacker constructs a JSON Web Token (JWT) whose header specifies {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"} (Base64 prefix eyJhbGciOiJub25l, instructing the parser that no cryptographic signature is attached) and whose payload includes "isloopback":"true" (a SharePoint-internal claim that tells the token handler to skip verifying the HTTP request’s endpoint URI) and "nameid":"00000003-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000". Because CVE-2023-29357 failed to reject the "none" algorithm when reading x5t/metadata tokens, sending this unsigned token to GET /_api/web/siteusers with header X-RequestForceAuthentication: true grants elevated app-level read access and dumps all site administrator accounts! Why is the Base64 string "eyJhbGciOiJub25l" such a reliable network detection signature? Because the ASCII JSON header {"alg":"none" always Base64URL-encodes to that exact 16-character prefix in the Authorization: Bearer header. In the documented HTTP GET / CVE-2023-29357 exchange from Remote SharePoint Exploiter to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 OK (confirming that the JWT ALG:NONE BYPASS request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 IMPERSONATING THE SHAREPOINT FARM ADMINISTRATOR). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ JWT ALG:NONE BYPASS / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200 OK) from Node ① (#1 Remote SharePoint Exploiter) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & SharePoint ULS Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-29357 (CVSS 9.8 SharePoint JWT Auth Bypass); FORGED HEADER={"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"} (eyJhbGciOiJub25l); ENUM ENDPOINT=GET /_api/web/siteusers (X-RequestForceAuthentication: true)]
  - Stage 2 (T1550.001 · Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token): **IMPERSONATING THE SHAREPOINT FARM ADMINISTRATOR** — Reading the XML response from /_api/web/siteusers, the attacker copies the Farm Administrator’s Windows SID (nameid) and issuer (nii), pastes them into a second "alg": "none" JWT, and becomes the SharePoint Farm Administrator! From the /_api/web/siteusers response, the attacker extracts a Site Collection or Farm Administrator’s UserId.NameId (their Windows Active Directory SID, e.g., s-1-5-21-...-500) and UserId.NameIdIssuer (urn:office:idp:activedirectory). The attacker then mints a second unsigned "alg":"none" JWT placing those two values into the nameid and nii claims (allowing the attacker to impersonate that specific human Administrator on any SharePoint REST API or Central Administration page without knowing their password or passing MFA). Because CVE-2023-29357 only grants SharePoint application-level administrator privileges rather than direct OS command execution, the attacker needs a post-authentication SharePoint RCE primitive (Step 3) to run operating-system commands. In the documented SharePoint ULS OAuth2 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS), SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS) responds with ACK Admin Claims (confirming that the ADMIN JWT SPOOFED request succeeded on SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 BUSINESS CONNECTIVITY SERVICES (.BDCM) ASSEMBLY RCE (CVE-2023-24955)). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ ADMIN JWT SPOOFED / ⇠#2 ACK Admin Claims) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & SharePoint ULS Sensor). [Specs: SPOOFED CLAIMS=nameid="<Admin_SID>" & nii="urn:office:idp:activedirectory"; BYPASS CLAIM="isloopback": "true" (Skips SharePoint HTTP Context URI Check); GAINED PRIVILEGE=SharePoint Site Collection & Farm Administrator]
  - Stage 3 (T1505.003 · Server Software Component: Web Shell / Server Runtime Code): **BUSINESS CONNECTIVITY SERVICES (.BDCM) ASSEMBLY RCE (CVE-2023-24955)** — Now acting as the SharePoint Farm Admin, the attacker uploads a Business Connectivity Services (.bdcm) catalog file containing a compiled C# DLL (Type="DotNetAssembly"). SharePoint loads that DLL straight into w3wp.exe and runs powershell.exe! Using the forged Farm Administrator JWT, the attacker chains CVE-2023-24955 by uploading a crafted Business Data Connectivity Model (.bdcm) XML file to SharePoint’s Business Connectivity Services (BCS) catalog. Inside the .bdcm XML, the attacker defines a LobSystem with Type="DotNetAssembly" (a BCS feature that allows SharePoint to load a compiled .NET DLL byte stream directly into the w3wp.exe worker process via Assembly.Load() and invoke its methods when an External List or Finder method is queried). The loaded C# method calls System.Diagnostics.Process.Start() to spawn powershell.exe under the high-privilege SharePoint Farm account (CORP\sp_farm). Because the malicious .NET assembly is stored inside the SharePoint SQL database and loaded directly into w3wp.exe memory via Assembly.Load(byte[]), no .aspx webshell file needs to be written to the IIS webroot on disk. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 exchange from SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS) to OAuth2 JWT Admin Context, OAuth2 JWT Admin Context responds with ACK PID 9120 (confirming that the BCS .BDCM SHELL RCE request succeeded on OAuth2 JWT Admin Context and completing the final execution objective of STAR Labs, Rapid7 & CISA, Microsoft SharePoint: JWT "alg:none" Auth Bypass to BCS RCE Chain). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ BCS .BDCM SHELL RCE / ⇠#3 ACK PID 9120) from Node ③ (#3 SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS)) to Node ④ (#4 OAuth2 JWT Admin Context), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & SharePoint ULS Sensor). [Specs: RCE GADGET=CVE-2023-24955 (BCS LobSystem Type="DotNetAssembly"); IN-MEMORY LOAD=Assembly.Load(bdcmBytes) inside SharePoint w3wp.exe; EXECUTION USER=CORP\sp_farm (SharePoint Farm Service Account)]

### CVE-2023-34048: Mandiant, VMware & CISA — UNC3886: vCenter vmdird Out-of-Bounds Write & ESXi VIRTUALPITA Backdoor
- **Scenario ID**: `vmware-vcenter-cve-2023-34048-unc3886`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/vmware-vcenter-cve-2023-34048-unc3886
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=vmware-vcenter-cve-2023-34048-unc3886
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Mandiant UNC3886 · VMSA-2023-0023 · vmdird DCERPC OOB Write, vpxuser & AF_VSOCK Backdoors
- **Overview**: Imagine a master control tower (VMware vCenter Server) that holds the master skeleton keys (vpxuser) to every apartment building (ESXi Hypervisor) in a city. Most companies put security guards (EDR agents) inside the individual apartments (Windows/Linux Guest VMs), but cannot install a guard inside the concrete foundation of the apartment building itself (ESXi Hypervisor). For two years, the espionage group UNC3886 used a zero-day flaw (CVE-2023-34048) in the control tower’s directory phone line (vmdird DCERPC) to break into vCenter, unlocked the master key safe (symkey.dat + VPX_HOST), and planted secret maintenance hatches (VIRTUALPITA & VIRTUALPIE) in the concrete foundation of every ESXi building, using internal dumbwaiter shafts (AF_VSOCK sockets) to move silently into any apartment without ever stepping out onto the street where network cameras (Firewalls / NDR) could see them! Synthesizing Mandiant (Google Cloud) threat intelligence on UNC3886, VMware Advisory VMSA-2023-0023, and CISA KEV (October 2023–June 2024), this scenario traces how UNC3886 exploited CVE-2023-34048 (CVSS 9.8 out-of-bounds heap write in vmdird DCERPC) as a zero-day for over two years. After achieving root RCE on vCenter and wiping /var/core/core.vmdird.* crash dumps, the attacker extracts and decrypts vpxuser service credentials from the VCDB PostgreSQL database using /etc/vmware-vpx/ssl/symkey.dat, lowers ESXi VIB acceptance levels, and deploys the VIRTUALPITA and VIRTUALPIE backdoors communicating over AF_VSOCK (VMCI) sockets.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (vCenter vmdird DCERPC CVE-2023-34048) - Initial Access), T1552.001 (Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files (symkey.dat & vpxuser) - Credential Access), T1547 (Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (ESXi VIB Backdoors VIRTUALPITA / VIRTUALPIE) - Persistence)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Mandiant Threat Intelligence (Google Cloud): Cloaked and Covert: Uncovering UNC3886 Espionage Operations on VMware vCenter & ESXi (CVE-2023-34048) (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/uncovering-unc3886-espionage-operations) | VMware / Broadcom Security Response: VMSA-2023-0023: VMware vCenter Server Out-of-Bounds Write Vulnerability (CVE-2023-34048) (https://support.broadcom.com/web/ecx/support-content-notification/-/external/content/SecurityAdvisories/0/23254) | Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA): CISA Adds VMware vCenter CVE-2023-34048 to Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application / Network Service): **VCENTER VMDIRD DCERPC OUT-OF-BOUNDS WRITE (CVE-2023-34048)** — The attacker sends a malformed DCERPC network request to vCenter’s directory service (vmdird on port 2012) to overwrite heap memory and run commands as root, and then deletes /var/core/core.vmdird.* crash files to cover their tracks. UNC3886 sends crafted DCERPC packets over TCP port 2012 to the VMware Directory Service daemon (/usr/lib/vmware-vmdir/sbin/vmdird) on the vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA). Due to an out-of-bounds heap write flaw in vmdird’s DCERPC protocol implementation (CVE-2023-34048), the attacker achieves unauthenticated remote code execution as root (UID 0). As Mandiant documented, because heap memory corruption often causes a worker thread of vmdird to crash before or after spawning the attacker’s shell, UNC3886 immediately runs rm -f /var/core/core.vmdird.* (deleting the core dump files on disk so storage alerts and forensic investigators do not see the exploit payload). Even if the attacker deletes the /var/core/core.vmdird.* file from disk, /var/log/vmware/vmdird/ and systemd journal logs still record the unexpected vmdird service exit/restart timestamp. In the documented VCSA Syslog / vmdird exchange from UNC3886 Threat Actor to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the VMDIRD DCERPC OOB request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 EXTRACTING & DECRYPTING ESXI "VPXUSER" CREDENTIALS FROM VCDB). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ VMDIRD DCERPC OOB / ⇠#1 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ① (#1 UNC3886 Threat Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 vSphere Syslog & SIEM Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-34048 (CVSS 9.8 vmdird DCERPC OOB Write); TARGET DAEMON=/usr/lib/vmware-vmdir/sbin/vmdird (root); ANTI-FORENSICS=Deletes /var/core/core.vmdird.* crash dumps post-RCE]
  - Stage 2 (T1552.001 · Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files): **EXTRACTING & DECRYPTING ESXI "VPXUSER" CREDENTIALS FROM VCDB** — vCenter stores the root-level vpxuser password for every ESXi hypervisor inside its local PostgreSQL database (VPX_HOST), and keeps the AES decryption key (symkey.dat) right next to it on the same server! To manage all ESXi hypervisors in the cluster, vCenter automatically creates and maintains a privileged root-equivalent account named vpxuser on every ESXi host. With root access on vCenter, UNC3886 queries the local vPostgreSQL database (psql -U postgres -d VCDB -c "SELECT ip_address, user_name, password FROM VPX_HOST;") and reads /etc/vmware-vpx/ssl/symkey.dat (the local plaintext AES symmetric key file that vCenter uses to encrypt database passwords, allowing the attacker to instantly decrypt the vpxuser password for every ESXi hypervisor in the datacenter). Compromising a single vCenter Server hands the attacker root-equivalent credentials (vpxuser) to every underlying ESXi hypervisor managed by that vCenter instance. In the documented Auditd OPEN / EXECVE exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to VMware vCenter Server (VCSA), VMware vCenter Server (VCSA) responds with ACK AES-128-CBC (confirming that the DECRYPT VPXUSER request succeeded on VMware vCenter Server (VCSA) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 DEPLOYING VIRTUALPITA & VIRTUALPIE VIB BACKDOORS OVER AF_VSOCK). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ DECRYPT VPXUSER / ⇠#2 ACK AES-128-CBC) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 VMware vCenter Server (VCSA)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 vSphere Syslog & SIEM Sensor). [Specs: DATABASE TABLE=VCDB -> VPX_HOST (Encrypted vpxuser passwords); DECRYPTION KEY=/etc/vmware-vpx/ssl/symkey.dat (AES Master Key); HARVESTED ACCOUNT=vpxuser (Root-equivalent service account on all ESXi hosts)]
  - Stage 3 (T1547 · Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Hypervisor VIB Persistence): **DEPLOYING VIRTUALPITA & VIRTUALPIE VIB BACKDOORS OVER AF_VSOCK** — Instead of opening a normal TCP port on the ESXi host that a firewall would spot, VIRTUALPITA listens on AF_VSOCK, a virtual internal cable wired directly between the ESXi hypervisor and its guest VMs. Using the decrypted vpxuser credentials, UNC3886 logs into the ESXi hypervisor, lowers its package signature requirement (esxcli software acceptance set --level=CommunitySupported), and installs an unsigned vSphere Installation Bundle (.vib) containing VIRTUALPITA (an ELF64 C backdoor disguised as /usr/libexec/setsyslog or vmsyslogd) and VIRTUALPIE. Crucially, VIRTUALPITA binds to socket family AF_VSOCK (VMware’s Virtual Machine Communication Interface, CID 2, a direct memory-to-memory communication channel between the ESXi hypervisor and its guest Virtual Machines that never touches the physical network card or TCP/IP stack, making the C2 channel completely invisible to network firewalls and NDR sensors). By chaining AF_VSOCK with CVE-2023-20867 (a VMware Tools authentication bypass in vmtoolsd), UNC3886 can push commands and transfer files from the ESXi hypervisor straight into any guest Virtual Machine without a single network packet. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ VIRTUALPITA VSOCK VIB / ⇠#3 ACK AF_VSOCK CID 2) from Node ③ (#3 VMware vCenter Server (VCSA)) to Node ④ (#4 vPostgreSQL & symkey.dat Extractor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 vSphere Syslog & SIEM Sensor). [Specs: ESXI IMPLANTS=VIRTUALPITA (ELF64) & VIRTUALPIE (Python VIB); COVERT CHANNEL=AF_VSOCK / VMCI (Hypervisor CID 2 <-> Guest VM CID); GUEST VM PIVOT=CVE-2023-20867 (vmtoolsd Guest Operations Auth Bypass)]

### CVE-2023-2868: Mandiant & CISA — UNC4841: Barracuda ESG .tar Command Injection, SALTWATER & SEASPY Backdoors
- **Scenario ID**: `barracuda-esg-cve-2023-2868-unc4841`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/barracuda-esg-cve-2023-2868-unc4841
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=barracuda-esg-cve-2023-2868-unc4841
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Mandiant UNC4841 · CISA MAR · CVE-2023-2868 Perl qx() Injection, SALTWATER bsmtp & SEASPY PCAP
- **Overview**: Imagine a corporate mail-screening machine (Barracuda Email Security Gateway) that opens every incoming .tar package before the recipient even sees the email, and writes down the name of each file inside on a Perl clipboard (qx/file '$filename'/). The espionage group UNC4841 mailed a .tar package where the file’s name itself was written as '|sh -c "curl ..."! The moment the screening machine read the label out loud, it executed the shell command as root. Once inside, UNC4841 welded a secret wiretap into the mail room’s main door (SALTWATER in bsmtp), hid a silent radio listener on the network cable (SEASPY using libpcap), and booby-trapped the building’s SQLite database (SUBMARINE) so deeply that Barracuda and CISA told every victim: "Throw the entire appliance in the trash and get a brand-new one!" Synthesizing Mandiant’s UNC4841 investigation, CISA Malware Analysis Reports (MAR-10454006), and Barracuda security advisories (May–August 2023), CVE-2023-2868 (CVSS 9.8) is a zero-click unauthenticated command injection flaw in Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG) appliances (v5.1.3–9.2.0). Sending an inbound SMTP email with a crafted .tar attachment whose member filename starts with '| triggers root command execution inside the Perl attachment scanner, deploying the SALTWATER (/usr/sbin/bsmtp), SEASPY (libpcap passive backdoor), and SUBMARINE (SQLite trigger) implants.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1566.001 (Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment (.tar CVE-2023-2868 Command Injection) - Initial Access), T1505 (Server Software Component (SALTWATER bsmtp & SEASPY libpcap Backdoors) - Persistence), T1546 (Event Triggered Execution (SUBMARINE SQLite CREATE TRIGGER Persistence) - Persistence)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Mandiant Threat Intelligence (Google Cloud): Barracuda ESG Zero-Day Vulnerability (CVE-2023-2868) Exploited Globally by Aggressive Espionage Actor UNC4841 (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/barracuda-esg-exploited-globally) | CISA & FBI Malware Analysis Report: MAR-10454006: CISA Releases Malware Analysis Reports on Barracuda Backdoors (SUBMARINE, WHIRLPOOL, SALTWATER) (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2023/07/28/cisa-releases-malware-analysis-report-submarine-malware-used-barracuda-esg-exploit) | Barracuda Networks Trust Center: Barracuda Email Security Gateway Appliance (ESG) Vulnerability CVE-2023-2868 Incident Notice (https://www.barracuda.com/company/legal/esg-vulnerability)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **MALICIOUS .TAR ATTACHMENT FILENAME INJECTION (CVE-2023-2868)** — Without any human user ever receiving or clicking the email, Barracuda’s automated attachment scanner unpacks the .tar file and passes its member filename ('|sh -c ...#) straight into a root Perl shell call. UNC4841 sends an external MIME email over SMTP port 25 containing a specially formatted .tar archive attachment. Before the email ever reaches a user’s inbox, the Barracuda ESG appliance automatically inspects the attachment using a Perl script that extracts the .tar member filenames and passes them into a shell command without escaping single quotes or pipe characters (CVE-2023-2868, where naming a file inside the tar archive '|sh -c "curl ...|sh"# closes the quoted string, pipes into /bin/sh, and comments out the rest of the command, giving the attacker instant zero-click root code execution). Because the vulnerability triggers inside the perimeter email security scanner itself before delivery, even emails addressed to non-existent or bounced recipients could trigger the exploit on unpatched appliances. In the documented SMTP .tar Attachment exchange from UNC4841 SMTP Operator to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP UID 0 (root) (confirming that the TAR FILENAME RCE request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 IMPLANTING "SALTWATER" (BSMTP) & "SEASPY" (PCAP SNIFFER)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ TAR FILENAME RCE / ⇠#1 RESP UID 0 (root)) from Node ① (#1 UNC4841 SMTP Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CISA YARA & NDR Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-2868 (CVSS 9.8 Unauthenticated SMTP .tar RCE); TRIGGER VECTOR=Inbound MIME Email with crafted .tar member filename; PERL SINK=Unsanitized filename interpolation inside Perl qx() / open()]
  - Stage 2 (T1505.003 · Server Software Component: Mail Server / Appliance Implant): **IMPLANTING "SALTWATER" (BSMTP) & "SEASPY" (PCAP SNIFFER)** — To maintain invisible access, UNC4841 trojanizes the appliance’s real mail daemon (SALTWATER in /usr/sbin/bsmtp) and runs SEASPY (BarracudaMailService), which quietly sniffs eth0 with libpcap for a magic knock packet without opening any new network port. With root access on the appliance, UNC4841 installs two stealthy backdoors analyzed by Mandiant and CISA: (1) SALTWATER (a trojanized replacement for the legitimate Barracuda SMTP daemon /usr/sbin/bsmtp that embeds six RC4-encrypted modules to execute commands, proxy traffic, and intercept emails inside the normal mail process); and (2) SEASPY (a passive C++ backdoor disguised as /usr/sbin/BarracudaMailService that uses the libpcap packet-capture library on interface eth0 to watch all normal TCP port 25 and 587 traffic for a secret magic knock sequence, meaning netstat shows zero extra listening ports on the appliance). Why use a libpcap sniffer (SEASPY) for persistence? Because even if a firewall blocks all ports except SMTP port 25, SEASPY inspects raw Ethernet frames arriving on port 25 before they reach the mail server and wakes up a reverse shell only when the attacker’s magic packet arrives. In the documented CISA MAR YARA Match exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Barracuda ESG Appliance, Barracuda ESG Appliance responds with ACK ELF64 Implants (confirming that the SALTWATER & SEASPY request succeeded on Barracuda ESG Appliance and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 DEEP PERSISTENCE VIA "SUBMARINE" & EMAIL SPOOL EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SALTWATER & SEASPY / ⇠#2 ACK ELF64 Implants) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Barracuda ESG Appliance), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CISA YARA & NDR Sensor). [Specs: SALTWATER=Trojanized /usr/sbin/bsmtp with 6 RC4-encrypted C2 modules; SEASPY=/usr/sbin/BarracudaMailService (libpcap eth0 packet sniffer); STEALTH DESIGN=Zero extra listening TCP/UDP ports visible in netstat]
  - Stage 3 (T1114.002 · Email Collection: Remote Email Collection): **DEEP PERSISTENCE VIA "SUBMARINE" & EMAIL SPOOL EXFILTRATION** — When Barracuda deployed emergency patch scripts, UNC4841 hid SUBMARINE inside a SQLite database trigger (/mail/config/config.db -> /etc/init.d/ee) so the malware resurrected itself every time the database was read, forcing victims to physically replace the appliance! When defenders and Barracuda deployed remediation patches in May 2023, UNC4841 rapidly adapted by deploying SUBMARINE (a deep-persistence rootkit that plants a malicious SQL TRIGGER inside the appliance’s core SQLite configuration database along with /etc/init.d/ee, so that whenever the appliance reads its database after a reboot or firmware update, SQLite automatically executes the attacker’s shell script as root) and exfiltrated compressed .tar.gz archives of targeted government and diplomatic mailboxes. Because UNC4841 compromised multiple layers of the appliance (SQLite triggers, kernel modules, and device SSL certificates), both Barracuda Networks and CISA issued the rare directive that all compromised ESG appliances must be completely decommissioned and replaced regardless of patch level. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SUBMARINE MAIL EXFIL / ⇠#3 RESP 112 MB .tar.gz) from Node ③ (#3 Barracuda ESG Appliance) to Node ④ (#4 SALTWATER & SEASPY Implants), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CISA YARA & NDR Sensor).
