### T1552.005: AWS Security, Unit 42 & MITRE — EC2 Reverse-Proxy SSRF to IMDSv1 (169.254.169.254) IAM Role & S3 Exfiltration
- **Scenario ID**: `aws-imdsv1-ssrf-capitalone-style`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/aws-imdsv1-ssrf-capitalone-style
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=aws-imdsv1-ssrf-capitalone-style
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: AWS Security · Unit 42 · MITRE T1552.005 · 169.254.169.254 IMDSv1 · STS Temporary Credentials & aws s3 sync
- **Overview**: Imagine an office mailroom clerk (EC2 Reverse Proxy / Web App) whose job is to fetch public brochures from any website address you write on a request slip (?url=...). Inside the building, however, there is an internal pneumatic tube at extension 169.254.169.254 (IMDSv1) that automatically dispenses a temporary master keycard (ASIA... STS IAM Role Credentials) to anyone sitting inside the building who asks for it, no questions asked! By writing http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ on the public request slip (SSRF), an outsider tricks the mailroom clerk into fetching the building’s master keycard and mailing a photocopy straight back to the street. Grounded in AWS Security’s IMDSv2 architecture documentation, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 cloud research, and MITRE ATT&CK T1552.005, this scenario demonstrates how a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) flaw on an Amazon EC2 instance with legacy IMDSv1 enabled (HttpTokens=optional) compromises the underlying cloud account. The attacker coerces the EC2 web service into sending an HTTP GET request to the link-local metadata IP (http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<RoleName>), extracts the temporary AWS STS AccessKeyId (ASIA...), SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken, and replays them from an external machine via aws s3 sync to exfiltrate private S3 buckets.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application (SSRF)): **SSRF INJECTION TO LINK-LOCAL IMDSV1 ROLE DISCOVERY** — The attacker hands the web server a URL pointing to 169.254.169.254, an internal-only IP address that only processes running inside the EC2 virtual machine can reach. The attacker sends an HTTP GET request to a URL-fetching endpoint on the EC2 web server (/api/webhook-preview?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/) (exploiting Server-Side Request Forgery so the EC2 instance itself makes an internal HTTP GET request to AWS’s link-local Instance Metadata Service at 169.254.169.254 and returns the name of its attached IAM Role, WafProxyS3ReadRole). Because 169.254.169.254 is a non-routable link-local IP (RFC 3927) answered directly by the AWS Nitro hypervisor on the local virtual network interface, external firewalls cannot see or block traffic to it once an application inside the instance is tricked into making the request. In the documented HTTP GET SSRF exchange from External Cloud Adversary to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 (WafProxyS3ReadRole) (confirming that the IMDSV1_ROLE_ENUM request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 EXTRACTION OF TEMPORARY AWS STS ROLE CREDENTIALS (ASIA...)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ IMDSV1_ROLE_ENUM / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200 (WafProxyS3ReadRole)) from Node ① (#1 External Cloud Adversary) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AWS GuardDuty & CloudTrail SIEM). [Specs: VULNERABILITY CLASS=CWE-918 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) on EC2; METADATA URI=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/; IMDS CONFIGURATION=HttpTokens: optional (IMDSv1 Enabled)]
  - Stage 2 (T1552.005 · Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API): **EXTRACTION OF TEMPORARY AWS STS ROLE CREDENTIALS (ASIA...)** — Because the instance still uses legacy IMDSv1, simply asking for the role’s folder name causes the metadata service to print out the live AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken. Appending the discovered role name to the SSRF URL (/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/WafProxyS3ReadRole) causes the IMDSv1 endpoint to return a JSON object containing temporary AWS STS credentials, AccessKeyId (starting with the prefix "ASIA", which designates temporary STS role credentials rather than permanent "AKIA" user keys), SecretAccessKey, and Token (all without requiring a preliminary HTTP PUT session token because HttpTokens is set to "optional" instead of "required"). Why does IMDSv2 stop this attack? Because IMDSv2 requires the client to first send an HTTP PUT request with a custom X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds header to obtain a secret token, and then pass that token in X-aws-ec2-metadata-token, two steps that classic GET-based SSRF vulnerabilities cannot perform. In the documented IMDSv1 CREDENTIAL_LEAK exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to EC2 Web Proxy (IMDSv1 Enabled), EC2 Web Proxy (IMDSv1 Enabled) responds with RESP 1,340 Bytes JSON (confirming that the STS_TOKEN_DUMPED request succeeded on EC2 Web Proxy (IMDSv1 Enabled) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 OFF-CLOUD CREDENTIAL REPLAY & S3 BUCKET SYNC EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ STS_TOKEN_DUMPED / ⇠#2 RESP 1,340 Bytes JSON) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 EC2 Web Proxy (IMDSv1 Enabled)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AWS GuardDuty & CloudTrail SIEM). [Specs: STS ACCESS KEY PREFIX=ASIA... (Temporary IAM Role Credentials); CREDENTIAL FIELDS=AccessKeyId + SecretAccessKey + Token (SessionToken); MITRE TECHNIQUE=T1552.005 (Cloud Instance Metadata API)]
  - Stage 3 (T1530 · Data from Cloud Storage): **OFF-CLOUD CREDENTIAL REPLAY & S3 BUCKET SYNC EXFILTRATION** — The thief takes the photocopied EC2 keycard home, plugs it into their own laptop (aws-cli), and downloads every customer file from the company’s S3 cloud vaults, setting off the "Building Keycard Used From Outside the Building!" alarm (GuardDuty). The attacker loads the stolen AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken into their local AWS CLI environment and runs aws s3 sync s3://corp-credit-applications-prod ./loot (authenticating directly to the public S3 API from their external IP 198.51.100.88 as the EC2 instance’s AssumedRole, which immediately triggers AWS GuardDuty’s UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS finding because an EC2 instance profile credential should only ever originate from an internal AWS EC2 IP). Even if an attacker steals an EC2 IAM role’s STS token, defenders can render the stolen token useless outside the VPC by attaching an aws:SourceVpce or aws:VpcSourceIp condition to the IAM role policy. In the documented CLOUDTRAIL / GUARDDUTY exchange from EC2 Web Proxy (IMDSv1 Enabled) to EC2 Instance Metadata Service, EC2 Instance Metadata Service responds with ALERT GuardDuty Severity 8.5 (confirming that the S3_SYNC_OUTSIDE_AWS request succeeded on EC2 Instance Metadata Service and completing the final execution objective of AWS Security, Unit 42 & MITRE, EC2 Reverse-Proxy SSRF to IMDSv1 (169.254.169.254) IAM Role & S3 Exfiltration). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ S3_SYNC_OUTSIDE_AWS / ⇠#3 ALERT GuardDuty Severity 8.5) from Node ③ (#3 EC2 Web Proxy (IMDSv1 Enabled)) to Node ④ (#4 EC2 Instance Metadata Service), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AWS GuardDuty & CloudTrail SIEM). [Specs: EXFIL COMMAND=aws s3 sync s3://corp-credit-applications-prod ./loot; GUARDDUTY FINDING=UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS; ARCHITECTURAL FIX=Enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required, HopLimit=1) + VPC Endpoint Policy]

### CVE-2024-21626: Snyk, OpenContainers & Sysdig — "Leaky Vessels" runc WORKDIR (/proc/self/fd/7) Host File-Descriptor Container Escape
- **Scenario ID**: `k8s-runc-cve-2024-21626-leaky-vessels`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/k8s-runc-cve-2024-21626-leaky-vessels
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=k8s-runc-cve-2024-21626-leaky-vessels
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Snyk Security Labs · OpenContainers · Sysdig Falco · runc <= 1.1.11 · /proc/self/fd/7 Host Rootfs Escape
- **Overview**: Imagine a prison guard (runc <= 1.1.11) who is escorting a new inmate (container process) into a locked isolation cell (pivot_root container filesystem). Before locking the cell door, the guard opens a clipboard folder (file descriptor 7 / fd 7) that is clipped to the main prison warden’s office hallway (/sys/fs/cgroup on the host OS). The inmate’s intake form says: "Please stand inside folder #7 (WORKDIR /proc/self/fd/7)." The guard absentmindedly lets the inmate step onto the clipboard’s hallway floor before locking the cell door and snapping the clipboard shut (O_CLOEXEC)! Even though the clipboard is closed a millisecond later, the inmate’s feet (current working directory ".") are already standing in the warden’s hallway, so walking four steps backward (cd ../../../..) puts the inmate right inside the host server’s master control room. Discovered by Snyk Security Labs (Rory McNamara) and patched by OpenContainers in January 2024 ("Leaky Vessels", CVE-2024-21626), runc versions <= 1.1.11 leaked an open file descriptor (fd 7, 8, or 9) pointing to the underlying host’s /sys/fs/cgroup directory into the container initialization step. By setting WORKDIR /proc/self/fd/7 in a malicious Dockerfile (or running runc exec --cwd /proc/self/fd/7), the container process changes its current working directory to the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup dentry before execve() closes the file descriptor, allowing relative ../../../../etc/shadow traversal and full Kubernetes worker-node root takeover.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1611 · Escape to Host): **RUNC CGROUP FILE DESCRIPTOR LEAK BEFORE PIVOT_ROOT** — While building the container’s walls, runc opens a directory handle (fd 7) to the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup folder and forgets to close it before honoring the container’s WORKDIR /proc/self/fd/7 instruction. In runc versions <= 1.1.11, the runc init process opens the host system’s /sys/fs/cgroup directory (receiving file descriptor 7, marked O_CLOEXEC so it will automatically close when execve() finally starts the container’s command) before isolating the container’s filesystem via pivot_root(). However, when the container image specifies WORKDIR /proc/self/fd/7, runc calls chdir("/proc/self/fd/7") before calling execve() (stepping directly through the still-open file descriptor 7 into the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup directory). Why didn’t O_CLOEXEC protect runc? Because O_CLOEXEC only closes file descriptors at the exact moment execve() is called, whereas runc processes the container’s WORKDIR (chdir) slightly earlier during the init setup phase while fd 7 is still open. In the documented SYSCALL chdir (80) exchange from Malicious OCI Image / Pod Spec to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK CVE-2024-21626 (confirming that the CHDIR_PROC_SELF_FD_7 request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 PERSISTENT HOST DENTRY ANCHOR IN CONTAINER CURRENT DIRECTORY). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CHDIR_PROC_SELF_FD_7 / ⇠#1 ACK CVE-2024-21626) from Node ① (#1 Malicious OCI Image / Pod Spec) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysdig / Falco eBPF Kernel Sensor). [Specs: CVE IDENTIFIER=CVE-2024-21626 ("Leaky Vessels" runc Breakout); LEAKED DESCRIPTOR=/proc/self/fd/7 -> Host /sys/fs/cgroup dentry; TRIGGER DIRECTIVE=Dockerfile WORKDIR /proc/self/fd/7 or runc exec --cwd]
  - Stage 2 (T1611 · Escape to Host): **PERSISTENT HOST DENTRY ANCHOR IN CONTAINER CURRENT DIRECTORY** — When execve() runs, file descriptor 7 snaps shut, but the container’s feet (current working directory ".") are already planted on the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup floor outside the container jail! When runc finally calls execve("/bin/sh"), the Linux kernel closes file descriptor 7 as requested by O_CLOEXEC, but the process’s kernel working directory pointer (task_struct->fs->pwd, represented by "." and /proc/self/cwd) remains anchored to the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup Virtual File System (VFS) dentry outside the container’s pivot_root boundary (causing /proc/self/cwd to display as "(unreachable)/sys/fs/cgroup"). In the Linux kernel, once a process’s fs->pwd dentry points to a mount outside its root namespace, relative path lookups starting from "." or ".." resolve along the host mount tree rather than the container’s rootfs. In the documented FALCO eBPF ALERT exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11), K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11) responds with ACK FALCO PRIORITY CRITICAL (confirming that the UNREACHABLE_HOST_CWD request succeeded on K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 RELATIVE DOT-DOT TRAVERSAL TO HOST ROOTFS & KUBELET COMPROMISE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ UNREACHABLE_HOST_CWD / ⇠#2 ACK FALCO PRIORITY CRITICAL) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysdig / Falco eBPF Kernel Sensor). [Specs: KERNEL INVARIANT=task_struct->fs->pwd survives O_CLOEXEC fd closure; CONTAINER CWD=readlink /proc/self/cwd -> (unreachable)/sys/fs/cgroup; PARENT TRAVERSAL=cd ../../../.. reaches Host Root (/) dentry]
  - Stage 3 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **RELATIVE DOT-DOT TRAVERSAL TO HOST ROOTFS & KUBELET COMPROMISE** — From /sys/fs/cgroup on the host, climbing up four parent folders (../../../../) lands the process at the host server’s real / root directory, giving full access to /etc/shadow, /etc/crontab, and Kubernetes node certificates. Because the container’s current directory (".") is /sys/fs/cgroup on the underlying Kubernetes worker node, running cd ../../../.. (or opening "../../../../etc/shadow" and "../../../../var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig" via openat(AT_FDCWD...)) walks up the host directory tree to the worker node’s real root filesystem (/), allowing the attacker to read host password hashes, write a root reverse shell into /etc/crontab, and steal the kubelet’s TLS client certificate. OpenContainers patched CVE-2024-21626 in runc 1.1.12 by marking internal cgroup descriptors O_CLOEXEC properly, closing leaked fds before chdir, and verifying via getcwd() that the working directory is not "(unreachable)" outside the container root. In the documented SYSCALL openat (257) exchange from K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11) to Leaked Host Cgroup FD (/proc/self/fd/7), Leaked Host Cgroup FD (/proc/self/fd/7) responds with ACK UID 0 HOST ESCAPE (confirming that the HOST_SHADOW_AND_KUBELET_READ request succeeded on Leaked Host Cgroup FD (/proc/self/fd/7) and completing the final execution objective of Snyk, OpenContainers & Sysdig, "Leaky Vessels" runc WORKDIR (/proc/self/fd/7) Host File-Descriptor Container Escape). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ HOST_SHADOW_AND_KUBELET_READ / ⇠#3 ACK UID 0 HOST ESCAPE) from Node ③ (#3 K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11)) to Node ④ (#4 Leaked Host Cgroup FD (/proc/self/fd/7)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysdig / Falco eBPF Kernel Sensor). [Specs: HOST ESCAPE PATH=openat(AT_FDCWD, "../../../../etc/crontab", O_WRONLY); STOLEN CREDENTIAL=/var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig & Host /etc/shadow; PATCH REMEDIATION=Upgrade runc >= 1.1.12 (verify getcwd() inside rootfs)]

### T1606.002: Microsoft Threat Intel, Wiz & CISA — Storm-0558: Acquired MSA Consumer Signing Key & Forged OWA/Exchange Online Tokens
- **Scenario ID**: `microsoft-storm-0558-msa-signing-key`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/microsoft-storm-0558-msa-signing-key
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=microsoft-storm-0558-msa-signing-key
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Microsoft Threat Intel · CISA AA23-193A · Wiz · Crash Dump MSA Key · Cross-Scope Token Validation Flaw
- **Overview**: Imagine a global hotel chain (Microsoft Cloud) that runs two completely separate divisions: a casual Public Gym (Consumer MSA / Outlook.com) and a classified Diplomatic Embassy Tower (Enterprise Azure AD / Exchange Online). Each division has its own wax signet ring (cryptographic signing key) for stamping visitor passes. One day in 2021, a Public Gym printing machine crashes, and a photo of the trash bin (crash dump) accidentally includes the Public Gym’s wax signet ring (2016 MSA consumer signing key). A spy (Storm-0558) finds that ring in the crash dump and stamps a fake VIP pass claiming to be an Embassy Ambassador. When the spy hands that pass to the Embassy Tower’s mailroom guard (Exchange Online / OWA), the guard carefully checks with a magnifying glass that the wax seal came from a real Microsoft ring, yet forgets to check that a Public Gym ring is never allowed to sign an Embassy Tower pass! Synthesizing Microsoft Threat Intelligence’s technical post-mortem, Joint CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-193A, and Wiz Research (July–September 2023), China-nexus espionage actor Storm-0558 acquired an inactive 2016 Microsoft Account (MSA) consumer signing private key that had been inadvertently written into a 2021 process crash dump. By exploiting a cross-realm signature validation bug in Outlook Web Access (OWA) and Exchange Online where enterprise relying parties verified token signatures against a shared key store without checking whether the signing key belonged to the consumer (MSA) vs. enterprise (Entra ID) trust realm, Storm-0558 forged access tokens to silently exfiltrate emails from 25 organizations including government agencies.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1552.004 · Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys): **OFFLINE TOKEN FORGERY USING CRASH-DUMP MSA SIGNING KEY** — Having recovered Microsoft’s private 2016 consumer MSA signing key from a crash dump, the spy uses it offline on their own computer to stamp fake identity tokens for government diplomats. As detailed in Microsoft’s root-cause investigation, a 2021 consumer signing service crash accidentally included private key material for a 2016 Microsoft Account (MSA) consumer signing key inside a process crash dump (which failed to be redacted due to a race condition and was later exfiltrated from a compromised engineer’s corporate environment). Storm-0558 uses this RSA private key offline to cryptographically sign forged authentication tokens populated with target enterprise user claims. Because token forgery happens 100% offline using the stolen private signing key, the attacker never sends a password guess or MFA push to Microsoft Entra ID, generating zero failed-login alerts. In the documented HTTPS OWA_AUTH exchange from Storm-0558 Forgery Engine to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 OK (confirming that the FORGED_MSA_TOKEN_PRESENTED request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 CROSS-REALM VALIDATION BYPASS IN EXCHANGE ONLINE / OWA). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ FORGED_MSA_TOKEN_PRESENTED / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200 OK) from Node ① (#1 Storm-0558 Forgery Engine) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Purview Audit & CISA AA23-193A Hunter). [Specs: KEY ORIGIN=2016 MSA Consumer Signing Key in 2021 Crash Dump; FORGED ARTIFACT=Cryptographically Signed OWA / Exchange Auth Token; MITRE TECHNIQUE=T1552.004 (Private Keys) & T1606.002 (Forge Web Credentials)]
  - Stage 2 (T1606.002 · Forge Web Credentials: SAML / OAuth Tokens): **CROSS-REALM VALIDATION BYPASS IN EXCHANGE ONLINE / OWA** — The Exchange Online guard checks that the token’s cryptographic signature matches a valid key in Microsoft’s key ring, but fails to verify whether that key belongs to the Consumer MSA ring or the Enterprise Azure AD ring! When Storm-0558 sends the forged token to Outlook Web Access (outlook.office365.com/owa/), the OWA token validation library verifies the RSA signature against a shared metadata store containing both consumer MSA keys and enterprise Azure AD (Entra ID) keys (failing to enforce scope/issuer-realm isolation that should reject a consumer MSA signing key when validating an enterprise organizational user). OWA then exchanges the forged token for live Exchange Online session tokens under AppId 00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000. As Wiz Research highlighted, cryptographic signature verification alone is insufficient in multi-tenant cloud architectures unless the verifier strictly binds each signing key ID (kid) to its authorized issuer realm. In the documented OWA TOKEN_EXCHANGE exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Exchange Online / OWA Validator, Exchange Online / OWA Validator responds with ALERT SESSION_ISSUED (confirming that the ENTERPRISE_SESSION_MINTED request succeeded on Exchange Online / OWA Validator and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 SILENT OWA MAILBOX COLLECTION & CISA AA23-193A DETECTION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ ENTERPRISE_SESSION_MINTED / ⇠#2 ALERT SESSION_ISSUED) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Exchange Online / OWA Validator), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Purview Audit & CISA AA23-193A Hunter). [Specs: VALIDATION FLAW=Missing Consumer (MSA) vs Enterprise (Entra ID) Key Realm Check; EXCHANGE APP ID=00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000 (Office 365 Exchange Online); EVASION IMPACT=Bypasses Entra ID Password + MFA + Conditional Access]
  - Stage 3 (T1114.002 · Email Collection: Remote Email Collection): **SILENT OWA MAILBOX COLLECTION & CISA AA23-193A DETECTION** — The spy silently downloads hundreds of emails through OWA, until a federal agency’s audit ledger (Purview MailItemsAccessed) reveals someone was reading mail inside the vault without ever signing the front-door guestbook (Entra SignInLogs). Routing traffic through SoftEther VPN residential exit nodes (198.51.100.119), Storm-0558 invokes /owa/service.svc?action=FindItem and action=GetItem to download sensitive diplomatic and government emails. A Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agency detects the intrusion by hunting in Microsoft Purview’s MailItemsAccessed unified audit log (spotting ClientInfoString="Client=OWA;Action=ViaProxy" and AppId 00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000 from anomalous VPN IPs with zero matching interactive Entra ID sign-ins). In response to this federal agency discovery, Microsoft revoked the compromised MSA key, patched cross-realm token validation, and made Purview MailItemsAccessed logging available across standard M365 licensing tiers. In the documented PURVIEW MailItemsAccessed exchange from Exchange Online / OWA Validator to OWA Token-Minting API (/owa/), OWA Token-Minting API (/owa/) responds with RESP 342 Items Synced (confirming that the BULK_MAIL_EXFILTRATION request succeeded on OWA Token-Minting API (/owa/) and completing the final execution objective of Microsoft Threat Intel, Wiz & CISA, Storm-0558: Acquired MSA Consumer Signing Key & Forged OWA/Exchange Online Tokens). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ BULK_MAIL_EXFILTRATION / ⇠#3 RESP 342 Items Synced) from Node ③ (#3 Exchange Online / OWA Validator) to Node ④ (#4 OWA Token-Minting API (/owa/)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Purview Audit & CISA AA23-193A Hunter). [Specs: COLLECTION API=POST /owa/service.svc?action=FindItem & action=GetItem; PURVIEW TELEMETRY=MailItemsAccessed (AppId 00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000); ADVISORY REFERENCE=CISA / FBI Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA23-193A]

### T1556.007: SpecterOps, Mandiant & Microsoft — Entra Connect (Azure AD Connect) MSOL_ DKM Decryption & Seamless SSO Silver Ticket
- **Scenario ID**: `azure-ad-connect-pass-the-certificate`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/azure-ad-connect-pass-the-certificate
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=azure-ad-connect-pass-the-certificate
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: SpecterOps · Dirk-jan Mollema · Mandiant · LocalDB mms_management_agent · DPAPI cryptKeySet & AZUREADSSOACC$
- **Overview**: Imagine a translator’s desk (Entra Connect / Azure AD Connect Server) that sits between a company’s local castle (On-Premises Active Directory) and its cloud fortress (Microsoft Entra ID). To keep both sides synchronized, the translator keeps a locked desk drawer (ADSync.mdf -> mms_management_agent LocalDB table) containing the master skeleton key to the local castle (MSOL_<hex> account with DCSync rights), and hangs the key to that drawer (DPAPI cryptKeySet) right under the desk! If an intruder compromises the translator’s server, they reach under the desk, unlock the drawer with the translator’s own magnifying glass (mcrypt.dll), grab the MSOL_ skeleton key to copy every secret in the local castle, including the AZUREADSSOACC$ bridge key, and forge golden passes straight into the cloud fortress. Synthesizing research by Dirk-jan Mollema (_dirkjan / AADInternals), SpecterOps, and Mandiant, this scenario demonstrates why Microsoft Entra Connect (formerly Azure AD Connect) is a critical Tier-0 hybrid identity asset. When an attacker gains local administrator privileges on the Entra Connect server (CORP-AADC01), they impersonate NT SERVICE\ADSync, query the local SQL Express ADSync database (mms_management_agent), load Entra Connect’s mcrypt.dll assembly to DPAPI-decrypt the on-premises MSOL_<hex> connector account password, use MSOL_ to execute a DCSync attack against the Domain Controller, and extract the AZUREADSSOACC$ computer account hash to forge Seamless SSO Kerberos Silver Tickets for any synced cloud user.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1003 · OS Credential Dumping (ADSync LocalDB)): **QUERYING ADSYNC LOCALDB (MMS_MANAGEMENT_AGENT) BLOBS** — First, the attacker steps into the shoes of the NT SERVICE\ADSync service account on the sync server and opens its private SQL LocalDB ledger (ADSync.mdf) to copy out the encrypted credential rows. After obtaining local administrator access on the Entra Connect server (CORP-AADC01), the attacker elevates to NT SERVICE\ADSync (the service account that owns the local SQL Server Express LocalDB instance and the Windows DPAPI user keyset), connects to the named pipe np:\\.\pipe\LOCALDB#...\tsql\query, and queries SELECT private_configuration_xml, encrypted_configuration FROM mms_management_agent alongside keyset_id, instance_id, and entropy from mms_server_configuration. Many organizations mistakenly place their Entra Connect server in a standard Tier-1 server OU managed by general server administrators, unaware that local admin on Entra Connect equates to Domain Admin + Cloud Global Admin. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 exchange from On-Prem Foothold Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK PID 5812 (confirming that the SQLLOCALDB_PIPE_ENUM request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 DPAPI & MCRYPT.DLL DECRYPTION OF MSOL_ CONNECTOR PASSWORD). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SQLLOCALDB_PIPE_ENUM / ⇠#1 ACK PID 5812) from Node ① (#1 On-Prem Foothold Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender for Identity & Sentinel SIEM). [Specs: DATABASE FILE=C:\Program Files\Microsoft Azure AD Sync\Data\ADSync.mdf; SQL TABLES=mms_server_configuration & mms_management_agent; SERVICE CONTEXT=NT SERVICE\ADSync (Required for LocalDB & DPAPI)]
  - Stage 2 (T1552.001 · Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files / Registry): **DPAPI & MCRYPT.DLL DECRYPTION OF MSOL_ CONNECTOR PASSWORD** — Instead of cracking the encryption by brute force, the attacker loads Entra Connect’s own decryption library (mcrypt.dll) in PowerShell and asks it to unlock the MSOL_ password using the server’s local DPAPI key. Running as NT SERVICE\ADSync, the attacker uses PowerShell reflection (or AADInternals / adconnectdump) to load C:\Program Files\Microsoft Azure AD Sync\Bin\mcrypt.dll, calls KeyManager.LoadKeySet() (which reads the DPAPI-protected AES key from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Ad Sync\Shared and unprotects it via CryptUnprotectData), and invokes DecryptBase64ToString() on encrypted_configuration to reveal the plaintext password of the on-premises connector account CORP\MSOL_9a8b7c6d5e4f. Because miiserver.exe must decrypt the MSOL_ password unattended whenever the service restarts, the entire decryption chain resides locally on the Entra Connect host. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 (ImageLoad) exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Entra Connect Server (ADSYNC), Entra Connect Server (ADSYNC) responds with ACK Signed: Microsoft (confirming that the MCRYPT_DLL_LOADED_BY_PS request succeeded on Entra Connect Server (ADSYNC) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 MSOL_ DCSYNC & AZUREADSSOACC$ SEAMLESS SSO CLOUD PIVOT). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ MCRYPT_DLL_LOADED_BY_PS / ⇠#2 ACK Signed: Microsoft) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Entra Connect Server (ADSYNC)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender for Identity & Sentinel SIEM). [Specs: CRYPTO ASSEMBLY=Microsoft.DirectoryServices.MetadirectoryServices.Cryptography.dll (mcrypt.dll); RECOVERED ACCOUNT=CORP\MSOL_9a8b7c6d5e4f (AD DS Connector Account); SYSMON INDICATOR=EventID 7: powershell.exe loading mcrypt.dll]
  - Stage 3 (T1556.007 · Modify Authentication Process: Hybrid Identity (Seamless SSO)): **MSOL_ DCSYNC & AZUREADSSOACC$ SEAMLESS SSO CLOUD PIVOT** — Because Password Hash Sync is enabled, MSOL_ has permission to copy every password hash in Active Directory (DCSync). The attacker uses MSOL_ to steal the AZUREADSSOACC$ bridge key and mints Kerberos Silver Tickets straight into Microsoft Entra ID! Because Password Hash Synchronization (PHS) requires the CORP\MSOL_9a8b7c6d5e4f account to hold Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All on the domain root, the attacker uses the decrypted MSOL_ credentials to perform a DCSync attack (MS-DRSR DRSGetNCChanges) against CORP-DC01, dumping the NTLM/AES256 hash of the AZUREADSSOACC$ computer account (the shared Kerberos trust bridge created when Entra Seamless Single Sign-On is enabled, allowing the attacker to forge Kerberos Silver Tickets holding any synchronized user’s immutableId and sid to log directly into Entra ID without knowing their password). Microsoft recommends treating Entra Connect as a Tier-0 asset, disabling Seamless SSO in favor of Primary Refresh Tokens (PRT), and rotating the AZUREADSSOACC$ Kerberos decryption key every 30 days. In the documented WinSec EID 4662 (DCSync) exchange from Entra Connect Server (ADSYNC) to DPAPI & mcrypt.dll Keyset Engine, DPAPI & mcrypt.dll Keyset Engine responds with ACK AccessMask 0x100 (confirming that the MSOL_DCSYNC_AZUREADSSOACC request succeeded on DPAPI & mcrypt.dll Keyset Engine and completing the final execution objective of SpecterOps, Mandiant & Microsoft, Entra Connect (Azure AD Connect) MSOL_ DKM Decryption & Seamless SSO Silver Ticket). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ MSOL_DCSYNC_AZUREADSSOACC / ⇠#3 ACK AccessMask 0x100) from Node ③ (#3 Entra Connect Server (ADSYNC)) to Node ④ (#4 DPAPI & mcrypt.dll Keyset Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender for Identity & Sentinel SIEM). [Specs: ON-PREM PRIVILEGE=DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All (1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2); CLOUD SSO BRIDGE=AZUREADSSOACC$ Computer Account Kerberos Key; DEFENSIVE FIX=Treat Entra Connect as Tier-0, Rotate AZUREADSSOACC$ Key Every 30 Days]

### T1098.001: Rhino Security Labs, Datadog & AWS — IAM PassRole + Lambda CreateFunction Privilege Escalation & CloudTrail StopLogging
- **Scenario ID**: `aws-cognito-iam-passrole-privesc`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/aws-cognito-iam-passrole-privesc
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=aws-cognito-iam-passrole-privesc
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Rhino Security Labs · Datadog Security Labs · MITRE Cloud · iam:PassRole + lambda:CreateFunction · AdministratorAccess
- **Overview**: Imagine a junior clerk (ci-dev-deployer) at a bank who is forbidden from opening the main vault (no iam:AttachUserPolicy permission). However, the clerk has two seemingly harmless permissions: they are allowed to build small automated mail-sorting robots (lambda:CreateFunction), and they are allowed to clip any existing employee badge onto a robot (iam:PassRole). The clerk spots the Bank President’s spare badge (LambdaAdminDeploymentRole) hanging on the wall, clips that badge onto a brand-new 5-line Python robot (metrics-health-sync-tmp), and presses the robot’s "Start" button (lambda:InvokeFunction). Wearing the President’s badge, the robot walks over to HR, promotes the junior clerk to Bank President (AdministratorAccess), and unplugs the security cameras (cloudtrail:StopLogging)! Grounded in Rhino Security Labs’ canonical AWS IAM Privilege Escalation research, Datadog Security Labs, and MITRE ATT&CK (T1098.001 / T1562.008), this scenario models one of the most common privilege escalation paths in AWS cloud environments. A compromised developer IAM user (ci-dev-deployer) lacking administrative rights abuses the intersection of iam:PassRole, lambda:CreateFunction, and lambda:InvokeFunction to create a Python Lambda function bound to a privileged service role (LambdaAdminDeploymentRole). When invoked, the Lambda function executes boto3 calls under the privileged role to attach arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess to the attacker’s IAM user and disable CloudTrail logging via cloudtrail:StopLogging.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1098.001 · Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials): **IAM PASSROLE & MALICIOUS LAMBDA FUNCTION CREATION** — The junior clerk builds a tiny Python robot (metrics-health-sync-tmp) and uses iam:PassRole to attach the LambdaAdminDeploymentRole badge to it. Using the compromised ci-dev-deployer access key, the attacker runs Pacu’s iam__privesc_scan module, discovers that the user policy permits iam:PassRole on Resource: "*" alongside lambda:CreateFunction, and invokes aws lambda create-function (binding the existing over-privileged role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/LambdaAdminDeploymentRole to a 10-line Python handler named metrics-health-sync-tmp). Why does AWS require iam:PassRole? Because compute services like Lambda, EC2, ECS, and Glue execute code using the IAM Role attached to them; if iam:PassRole is granted with a wildcard ("*"), any user who can create a compute resource can impersonate any role trusted by that service. In the documented CLOUDTRAIL CreateFunction exchange from Compromised Dev IAM User to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with RESP HTTP 201 Created (confirming that the LAMBDA_CREATE_WITH_PASSROLE request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 LAMBDA INVOCATION & ADMINISTRATORACCESS POLICY ATTACHMENT). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LAMBDA_CREATE_WITH_PASSROLE / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 201 Created) from Node ① (#1 Compromised Dev IAM User) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CloudTrail Lake & Datadog Cloud SIEM). [Specs: PRIVESC VECTOR=Rhino Security Labs Vector #13: iam:PassRole + lambda:CreateFunction; PASSED IAM ROLE=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/LambdaAdminDeploymentRole; CLOUDTRAIL EVENT=CreateFunction20150331 (runtime: python3.12)]
  - Stage 2 (T1098.003 · Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles): **LAMBDA INVOCATION & ADMINISTRATORACCESS POLICY ATTACHMENT** — The clerk presses the robot’s "Run" button (aws lambda invoke). Running with the admin role’s authority, the Python script calls iam.attach_user_policy to promote ci-dev-deployer to full AdministratorAccess. The attacker triggers the function via aws lambda invoke --function-name metrics-health-sync-tmp. Inside the AWS Lambda Firecracker microVM, the Python runtime automatically receives temporary STS credentials for LambdaAdminDeploymentRole in its environment variables and executes boto3.client("iam").attach_user_policy(UserName="ci-dev-deployer", PolicyArn="arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess") (permanently elevating the attacker’s IAM user to full AWS account administrator). In CloudTrail, the AttachUserPolicy call appears as originating from AssumedRole/LambdaAdminDeploymentRole/metrics-health-sync-tmp rather than directly from the ci-dev-deployer IAM user. In the documented CLOUDTRAIL AttachUserPolicy exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to AWS IAM & Lambda Control Plane, AWS IAM & Lambda Control Plane responds with ALERT GuardDuty High (confirming that the ADMIN_POLICY_ATTACHED request succeeded on AWS IAM & Lambda Control Plane and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 CLOUDTRAIL STOPLOGGING DEFENSE EVASION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ ADMIN_POLICY_ATTACHED / ⇠#2 ALERT GuardDuty High) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 AWS IAM & Lambda Control Plane), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CloudTrail Lake & Datadog Cloud SIEM). [Specs: API CALL=iam:AttachUserPolicy (UserName: ci-dev-deployer); GRANTED POLICY=arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess; GUARDDUTY ALERT=PrivilegeEscalation:IAMUser/AdministrativePermissions]
  - Stage 3 (T1562.008 · Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Cloud Logs): **CLOUDTRAIL STOPLOGGING DEFENSE EVASION** — Right after promoting the clerk, the robot reaches up and switches off the building’s security camera recorder (cloudtrail:StopLogging), though the camera records the exact hand that flipped the switch! To conceal follow-on data theft or resource creation, the Lambda payload (or the newly elevated ci-dev-deployer user) calls boto3.client("cloudtrail").stop_logging(Name="org-audit-trail") (halting CloudTrail management and data event delivery for the regional trail, an action that records one final StopLogging event in CloudTrail and triggers GuardDuty’s Stealth:IAMUser/CloudTrailLoggingDisabled alert). Organizations prevent even full account administrators from blinding audit logs by configuring an AWS Organizations Trail in a separate management account and applying a Service Control Policy (SCP) that explicitly denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail. In the documented CLOUDTRAIL StopLogging exchange from AWS IAM & Lambda Control Plane to Lambda Execution MicroVM (Firecracker), Lambda Execution MicroVM (Firecracker) responds with ALERT TRAIL_STOPPED (confirming that the CLOUDTRAIL_LOGGING_DISABLED request succeeded on Lambda Execution MicroVM (Firecracker) and completing the final execution objective of Rhino Security Labs, Datadog & AWS, IAM PassRole + Lambda CreateFunction Privilege Escalation & CloudTrail StopLogging). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ CLOUDTRAIL_LOGGING_DISABLED / ⇠#3 ALERT TRAIL_STOPPED) from Node ③ (#3 AWS IAM & Lambda Control Plane) to Node ④ (#4 Lambda Execution MicroVM (Firecracker)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CloudTrail Lake & Datadog Cloud SIEM). [Specs: EVASION API=cloudtrail:StopLogging (Name: org-audit-trail); MITRE TECHNIQUE=T1562.008 (Disable or Modify Cloud Logs); ARCHITECTURAL FIX=IAM Permissions Boundary + AWS Organizations SCP Denying StopLogging]

### T1610: Sysdig TRT, Permiso & Unit 42 — SCARLETEEL Operation: Kubernetes Pod RCE, AWS Terraform .tfstate Theft & Pacu Pivot
- **Scenario ID**: `sysdig-scarleteel-aws-eks-terraform`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/sysdig-scarleteel-aws-eks-terraform
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=sysdig-scarleteel-aws-eks-terraform
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Sysdig Threat Research · Permiso P0 Labs · EKS Pod RCE -> IMDS -> S3 terraform.tfstate Plaintext Keys -> Cross-Account Pivot
- **Overview**: Imagine a burglar (SCARLETEEL) who slips through an open window into a small workshop annex (Kubernetes Pod in AWS EKS). The workshop annex only has keys to a hallway supply closet (S3 DevOps Bucket). However, sitting inside that supply closet is the master architectural blueprint book (terraform.tfstate) that the building’s engineers used to construct the entire corporate campus! Because the blueprint tool (Terraform) writes down the actual cleartext combination (aws_iam_access_key.attributes.secret) of every vault it builds right inside that book, reading terraform.tfstate hands the burglar the permanent master keys to the company’s main production bank vaults across the street. Discovered and analyzed by the Sysdig Threat Research Team (SCARLETEEL & SCARLETEEL 2.0), Permiso P0 Labs, and Palo Alto Unit 42, this scenario models a sophisticated cloud-native intrusion chain that pivots from a single Kubernetes container into multi-account AWS dominance. After exploiting an internet-facing workload pod in Amazon EKS, the attacker queries the worker node’s Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254), uses the node role to download terraform.tfstate from an S3 backend bucket, extracts plaintext aws_iam_access_key secret keys belonging to privileged cross-account administrators, and uses the Pacu framework to steal proprietary source code and S3 datasets.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application (EKS Pod)): **KUBERNETES POD RCE & NODE IMDS CREDENTIAL HARVESTING** — The attacker breaks into a web container running inside Kubernetes (ml-notebook-prod), drops aws-cli into /tmp, and asks the underlying EC2 worker node’s metadata service (169.254.169.254) for its IAM role token. SCARLETEEL exploits a remote code execution flaw on a public-facing Kubernetes workload pod (ml-notebook-prod-6d8f9), downloads static binaries (aws-cli, kubectl, and trufflehog) into /tmp (triggering a Sysdig Falco container runtime drift alert), and queries http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/eks-node-role (which succeeds whenever the EKS worker node’s IMDS hop limit is left at 2 instead of restricted to 1). On Kubernetes nodes hosted on EC2, pods operate one network router hop inside the node; if HttpPutResponseHopLimit is >= 2, any compromised pod can reach the underlying EC2 worker node’s IMDS endpoint and steal the node-level IAM role. In the documented FALCO CONTAINER_DRIFT exchange from SCARLETEEL Cloud Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK FALCO WARNING (confirming that the IN_CONTAINER_TOOL_DROP request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 S3 TERRAFORM STATE (.TFSTATE) PLAINTEXT SECRET EXTRACTION). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ IN_CONTAINER_TOOL_DROP / ⇠#1 ACK FALCO WARNING) from Node ① (#1 SCARLETEEL Cloud Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysdig Secure & AWS CloudTrail SIEM). [Specs: INITIAL FOOTHOLD=Exposed Kubernetes Workload Pod in AWS EKS; HARVESTED TOKENS=K8s ServiceAccount JWT + EC2 Node Role STS Credentials; RUNTIME DRIFT=curl downloading aws-cli & trufflehog into container /tmp]
  - Stage 2 (T1552.001 · Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files (terraform.tfstate)): **S3 TERRAFORM STATE (.TFSTATE) PLAINTEXT SECRET EXTRACTION** — Using the node role to browse S3 buckets, the attacker finds terraform.tfstate, a JSON blueprint file that stores every Terraform-created IAM secret key and database password in unencrypted plaintext! Using the stolen eks-node-role credentials, the attacker lists accessible S3 buckets, spots the Infrastructure-as-Code state backend (s3://corp-devops-tfstate-prod/prod/terraform.tfstate), and streams the JSON file through grep (because whenever an engineer uses a Terraform resource like aws_iam_access_key or aws_db_instance, Terraform writes the generated SecretAccessKey and master password in cleartext inside the .tfstate JSON file). As Sysdig highlighted in their SCARLETEEL analysis, Terraform state files are a goldmine for cloud attackers: they not only contain plaintext secrets, but also map out every VPC, account ID, and S3 bucket across the organization. In the documented CLOUDTRAIL S3 GetObject exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to EKS Workload Pod (Spring/Jupyter), EKS Workload Pod (Spring/Jupyter) responds with RESP 1.8 MB JSON (confirming that the TERRAFORM_TFSTATE_READ request succeeded on EKS Workload Pod (Spring/Jupyter) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 CROSS-ACCOUNT PACU PIVOT & PROPRIETARY CODE EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ TERRAFORM_TFSTATE_READ / ⇠#2 RESP 1.8 MB JSON) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 EKS Workload Pod (Spring/Jupyter)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysdig Secure & AWS CloudTrail SIEM). [Specs: TARGET ARTIFACT=s3://corp-devops-tfstate-prod/terraform.tfstate; TERRAFORM RESOURCE=aws_iam_access_key.attributes.id & attributes.secret; ARCHITECTURAL RISK=Terraform state files store created IAM secrets in plaintext JSON]
  - Stage 3 (T1078.004 · Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts): **CROSS-ACCOUNT PACU PIVOT & PROPRIETARY CODE EXFILTRATION** — With the master terraform-org-admin key from .tfstate, the attacker loads the Pacu toolkit on Kali Linux, walks into the company’s crown-jewel production AWS account, mints backup keys, and downloads all proprietary code. The attacker imports the permanent AKIA access key extracted from terraform.tfstate into the Pacu cloud exploitation framework on their Kali Linux machine (generating a distinctive User-Agent containing "Boto3/... Linux/6.1.0-kali9-amd64"), runs iam__enum_permissions and iam__backdoor_users_keys to create persistent access keys in the peered production AWS account, and executes aws lambda get-function and aws s3 sync to steal proprietary algorithms. While SCARLETEEL sometimes deploys XMRig miners on compromised Kubernetes nodes, Sysdig proved that cryptomining is often a noisy distraction while the operators exfiltrate high-value intellectual property via S3 and Lambda APIs. In the documented CLOUDTRAIL CreateAccessKey exchange from EKS Workload Pod (Spring/Jupyter) to S3 Terraform State Backend, S3 Terraform State Backend responds with ALERT CROSS_ACCOUNT_COMPROMISE (confirming that the PACU_CROSS_ACCOUNT_BACKDOOR request succeeded on S3 Terraform State Backend and completing the final execution objective of Sysdig TRT, Permiso & Unit 42, SCARLETEEL Operation: Kubernetes Pod RCE, AWS Terraform .tfstate Theft & Pacu Pivot). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ PACU_CROSS_ACCOUNT_BACKDOOR / ⇠#3 ALERT CROSS_ACCOUNT_COMPROMISE) from Node ③ (#3 EKS Workload Pod (Spring/Jupyter)) to Node ④ (#4 S3 Terraform State Backend), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysdig Secure & AWS CloudTrail SIEM). [Specs: EXPLOITATION FRAMEWORK=Pacu (iam__enum_permissions / iam__backdoor_users_keys); EXFILTRATED ASSETS=Lambda GetFunction (.zip code) & Proprietary S3 Models; DEFENSIVE FIX=Set HopLimit=1 on EKS Nodes + Restrict S3 .tfstate Bucket via KMS/IAM]

### T1098.001: Mandiant, Wiz & Google Cloud — GCP iam.serviceAccountKeys.create & serviceAccounts.actAs Impersonation Escalation
- **Scenario ID**: `gcp-service-account-hmac-key-pivot`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/gcp-service-account-hmac-key-pivot
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=gcp-service-account-hmac-key-pivot
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Mandiant · Wiz · Rhino Security Labs · iam.serviceAccountKeys.create · Default Compute SA Editor Pivot & GCS Exfil
- **Overview**: Imagine a cloud office building (GCP Project) where every virtual machine comes with a default janitor robot (<project-number>-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com) that was accidentally given a master key to every room in the building (roles/editor). A contractor (ci-runner service account) doesn’t have access to the financial vault (gs://corp-financial-ledger-prod), but their badge allows them to print new ID cards for any robot in the building (iam.serviceAccountKeys.create). The contractor walks up to the card printer (iam.googleapis.com), prints a brand-new JSON private key card (loot_key.json) in the name of the Editor janitor robot, puts on that card, and empties the financial vault! Synthesizing research by Mandiant (Google Cloud Threat Intelligence), Wiz Research, and Rhino Security Labs, this scenario models the classic Google Cloud Platform (GCP) IAM privilege escalation chain abusing iam.serviceAccountKeys.create (or iam.serviceAccounts.actAs) against the over-privileged Default Compute Engine Service Account (<project-number>-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com). Because GCP projects historically granted the Default Compute Service Account the broad primitive role roles/editor, any identity with project-wide Service Account Key Admin permissions can mint a persistent user-managed RSA private key JSON file for that account and inherit full read/write control over Cloud Storage (GCS) and BigQuery.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1087.004 · Account Discovery: Cloud Account): **ENUMERATING PRIVILEGED DEFAULT COMPUTE SERVICE ACCOUNT** — First, the attacker lists all service accounts in the GCP project and spots <project-number>-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com, which carries project-wide roles/editor permissions. Using a compromised low-privilege CI service account (ci-runner@corp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com), the attacker runs gcloud iam service-accounts list (calling google.iam.admin.v1.ListServiceAccounts) and identifies 482910492810-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com (the Default Compute Engine Service Account that GCP automatically creates and historically binds to the primitive role roles/editor, granting read/write access to almost every service in the project). As Wiz Research documented, unless an organization explicitly enables constraints/iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts, newly created Compute Engine and App Engine default service accounts receive project-wide Editor rights. In the documented GCP ADMIN_ACTIVITY exchange from Compromised GCP Workload Caller to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 (confirming that the LIST_SERVICE_ACCOUNTS request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 MINTING USER-MANAGED RSA JSON KEY VIA CREATESERVICEACCOUNTKEY). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LIST_SERVICE_ACCOUNTS / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 Compromised GCP Workload Caller) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Google Cloud SCC & Chronicle SIEM). [Specs: TARGET IDENTITY=482910492810-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com; ATTACHED ROLE=roles/editor (Project-Wide Read/Write Primitive Role); PRIVESC PERMISSION=iam.serviceAccountKeys.create (or iam.serviceAccounts.actAs)]
  - Stage 2 (T1098.001 · Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials): **MINTING USER-MANAGED RSA JSON KEY VIA CREATESERVICEACCOUNTKEY** — Because ci-runner was granted Service Account Key Admin at the project level, it asks GCP’s IAM API to generate and download a fresh RSA private key (loot_key.json) for the Editor service account. Because the ci-runner identity holds roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin (which includes iam.serviceAccountKeys.create) scoped at the project level rather than restricted to a single non-privileged account, the attacker runs gcloud iam service-accounts keys create loot_key.json --iam-account=482910492810-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com (causing GCP IAM to generate a 2048-bit RSA key pair, store the public key on the Default Compute Service Account, and download the PKCS#8 private key in loot_key.json to the attacker’s machine). Unlike short-lived metadata tokens on a GCE VM, a user-managed service account key JSON file does not expire for 10 years by default and can be used from anywhere on the internet unless blocked by VPC Service Controls. In the documented GCP CreateServiceAccountKey exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to GCP IAM Control Plane API, GCP IAM Control Plane API responds with ALERT KEY_ID 9f8e7d6c5b (confirming that the USER_MANAGED_SA_KEY_CREATED request succeeded on GCP IAM Control Plane API and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 IMPERSONATED EDITOR AUTHENTICATION & GCS BUCKET EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ USER_MANAGED_SA_KEY_CREATED / ⇠#2 ALERT KEY_ID 9f8e7d6c5b) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 GCP IAM Control Plane API), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Google Cloud SCC & Chronicle SIEM). [Specs: AUDIT LOG METHOD=google.iam.admin.v1.CreateServiceAccountKey; CREDENTIAL TYPE=USER_MANAGED JSON Private Key (PKCS#8 RSA-2048); OAUTH EXCHANGE=Signed JWT exchanged at oauth2.googleapis.com/token for ya29.* token]
  - Stage 3 (T1530 · Data from Cloud Storage): **IMPERSONATED EDITOR AUTHENTICATION & GCS BUCKET EXFILTRATION** — The attacker signs in with loot_key.json, exchanges a signed JWT for an Editor OAuth2 bearer token (ya29.*), and copies the entire gs://corp-financial-ledger-prod bucket.
