[Specs: COMMAND 1=GET /prx/000/http/localhost/client_sec/%00/add_folder HTTP/1.1; COMMAND 2=X-AN-FILESHARE: uname=t; password=t; sp_uname=t; flags=c3248; fshare_template=../../../../etc/passwd; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Upgrade ArrayOS AG to version 9.4.0.484+ (which validates session state before honoring X-AN-FILESHARE flags) and disable unused FileShare modules on the SSL VPN gateway.; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access (T1190 - Exploit Public-Facing Application)]
  - Stage 2 (T1505.003 · Web Shell / T1090): **Stage 2: Arbitrary File Read of Gateway Configs & PHP Webshell Deployment** — Once inside the VPN gateway, the spy copies the gateway’s master password file, plants a hidden web command page, and sets up an invisible tunnel (s5n) into the corporate network. Using the CVE-2023-28461 primitive, Earth Kasha read /ca/conf/default.ampled (extracting local VPN accounts, RADIUS/LDAP secrets, and internal routing tables), wrote a PHP webshell (cals.php) into the ArrayOS web root, and launched a custom ELF SOCKS5 proxy binary (/tmp/s5n, turning the perimeter SSL VPN appliance into a transparent pivot relay into the internal corporate network). Because internal firewalls and EDRs expect user traffic to originate from the SSL VPN appliance’s internal interface IP, routing attacker traffic through /tmp/s5n blended in with legitimate remote-worker traffic. In the documented EventID 11 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Array AG SSL VPN (/prx/000/http/localhost), Array AG SSL VPN (/prx/000/http/localhost) responds with ALERT 11 (confirming that the httpd request succeeded on Array AG SSL VPN (/prx/000/http/localhost) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Internal Lateral Movement & LODEINFO / NOOPDOOR Memory Injection). ### T1542.003: BlackLotus UEFI Bootkit Baton Drop Secure Boot Bypass (CVE-2022-21894)
- **Scenario ID**: `blacklotus-uefi-bootkit-cve-2022-21894`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/blacklotus-uefi-bootkit-cve-2022-21894
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=blacklotus-uefi-bootkit-cve-2022-21894
- **Category**: KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kernel, Firmware & BYOVD · T1542.003
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security building where every morning at 6:00 AM, a robot checks that the front-door guard has a genuine badge signed by the mayor before letting the guard turn on the security cameras. A burglar brings an retired guard from two years ago, who still holds a genuine badge signed by the mayor, because the mayor forgot to put that old badge on the "revoked" list, and hands the retired guard a rigged clipboard (BCD) that tricks them into leaving the security cameras unplugged for the rest of the day. Analyzed by ESET and the subject of a joint NSA/CISA advisory in 2023, BlackLotus is an 80-kilobyte C/Assembly UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing UEFI Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. Using a "Bring Your Own Vulnerable Bootloader" (BYOVB) technique, it drops older, legitimately signed bootmgfw.efi, hvloader.efi, and winload.efi binaries onto the EFI System Partition and exploits CVE-2022-21894 ("Baton Drop") to disable Code Integrity in early boot, turn off BitLocker and HVCI, and load an unsigned kernel rootkit.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1542.003 · Bootkit): **Stage 1: EFI System Partition Staging & MOK NVRAM Variable Tampering** — The installer unlocks the hidden boot closet on the hard drive, places older signed boot guards inside, and registers its own key in a special firmware drawer that becomes invisible as soon as Windows finishes starting. Running as a local administrator, the BlackLotus installer mounted the hidden FAT32 EFI System Partition (ESP), dropped legitimate Microsoft-signed copies of bootmgfw.efi, hvloader.efi, and winload.efi (which remained trusted by UEFI Secure Boot because their hashes had not yet been added to the UEFI DBX forbidden signature database), and called ZwSetSystemEnvironmentValueEx to write a MokList UEFI NVRAM variable with the EFI_VARIABLE_BOOTSERVICE_ACCESS flag (making the variable readable during early boot but completely invisible to the running OS after ExitBootServices() is called). By setting only EFI_VARIABLE_NON_VOLATILE | EFI_VARIABLE_BOOTSERVICE_ACCESS (omitting EFI_VARIABLE_RUNTIME_ACCESS), user-mode and kernel-mode security tools running after Windows boots cannot query or delete the NVRAM variable without rebooting. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ installer.exe / ⇠#1 ACK 11) from Node ① (#1 BlackLotus User-Mode Installer) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Ring-0 Kernel Driver & Disabled HVCI). [Specs: COMMAND 1=Mountvol S: /S -> Write \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\{bootmgfw.efi, hvloader.efi, winload.efi, grubx64.efi}; COMMAND 2=ZwSetSystemEnvironmentValueEx("MokList", EFI_VARIABLE_NON_VOLATILE | EFI_VARIABLE_BOOTSERVICE_ACCESS); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Apply Microsoft UEFI Secure Boot DBX revocation updates (KB5025885) so vulnerable signed bootmanagers cannot load on Secure Boot systems.; MITRE CONTEXT=Persistence (T1542.003 - Bootkit)]
  - Stage 2 (T1562.001 · Disable or Modify Tools): **Stage 2: "Baton Drop" BCD Argument Truncation Exploit (CVE-2022-21894)** — During reboot, the older signed guard reads a deliberately cut-off instruction line on the boot clipboard, causing them to overwrite their own rulebook in memory. On the next boot, the staged vulnerable bootmgfw.efi / winload.efi parsed a custom Boot Configuration Data (BCD) store crafted by BlackLotus to trigger CVE-2022-21894 (Baton Drop, a memory corruption and argument truncation flaw in BlImgQueryCodeIntegrityBootOptions that grants arbitrary physical memory write while UEFI Boot Services are still active), allowing BlackLotus to overwrite the in-memory Secure Boot and Code Integrity state and execute its own self-signed UEFI application. Because the exploit runs after UEFI firmware verifies bootmgfw.efi’s genuine Microsoft signature but before ExitBootServices(), BlackLotus hijacks the boot chain without modifying the motherboard’s physical SPI flash. In the documented EDR exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to EFI System Partition & NVRAM (MOK), EFI System Partition & NVRAM (MOK) responds with ALERT T1562.001 (confirming that the Stage 2: "Baton Drop" BCD Argument Truncation Exploit (CVE-2022-21894) request succeeded on EFI System Partition & NVRAM (MOK) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Disabling BitLocker / HVCI & Deploying Unsigned Ring-0 Kernel Driver). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: "Baton Drop" BCD Argument Truncation Exploit (CVE-2022-21894) / ⇠#2 ALERT T1562.001) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 EFI System Partition & NVRAM (MOK)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Ring-0 Kernel Driver & Disabled HVCI). [Specs: COMMAND 1=BCD Option Injection: truncates /ov /ozz parameters inside BlImgQueryCodeIntegrityBootOptions; COMMAND 2=CVE-2022-21894 ("Baton Drop"): Arbitrary physical memory write disables UEFI Secure Boot enforcement; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Monitor TPM 2.0 Measured Boot PCR[0..7] and WBCL (Windows Boot Configuration Log) digests via remote attestation to detect unexpected bootloader hashes.; MITRE CONTEXT=Defense Evasion (T1562.001 - Disable or Modify Tools)]
  - Stage 3 (T1068 · T1068 / T1055): **Stage 3: Disabling BitLocker / HVCI & Deploying Unsigned Ring-0 Kernel Driver** — Before waking up the main Windows operating system, the bootkit cuts the wires to the hypervisor shield and slips an invisible bodyguard into the kernel. With early-boot execution control, BlackLotus patched hvloader.efi and winload.efi (OslFwpKernelSetupPhase1) in RAM to neutralize Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI / VBS) and BitLocker, mapped an unsigned 64-bit Ring-0 kernel driver into ntoskrnl.exe memory space, and injected an HTTPS C2 downloader into winlogon.exe (while the kernel driver protected the bootkit’s ESP files and registry keys from deletion). Remediation required applying Microsoft’s DBX UEFI revocation update (KB5025885), which adds the vulnerable bootloaders’ hashes to the motherboard’s UEFI NVRAM DBX, and wiping the EFI System Partition. In the documented EventID 6 exchange from EFI System Partition & NVRAM (MOK) to Vulnerable winload.efi (CVE-2022-21894), Vulnerable winload.efi (CVE-2022-21894) responds with ALERT 6 (confirming that the Stage 3: Disabling BitLocker / HVCI & Deploying Unsigned Ring-0 Kernel Driver request succeeded on Vulnerable winload.efi (CVE-2022-21894) and completing the final execution objective of BlackLotus UEFI Bootkit Baton Drop Secure Boot Bypass (CVE-2022-21894)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: Disabling BitLocker / HVCI & Deploying Unsigned Ring-0 Kernel Driver / ⇠#3 ALERT 6) from Node ③ (#3 EFI System Partition & NVRAM (MOK)) to Node ④ (#4 Vulnerable winload.efi (CVE-2022-21894)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Ring-0 Kernel Driver & Disabled HVCI). [Specs: COMMAND 1=In-memory patch of OslFwpKernelSetupPhase1 -> Disables HVCI / VBS & BitLocker; COMMAND 2=Load unsigned Ring-0 driver from ESP -> Injects HTTP C2 DLL into winlogon.exe; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Isolate affected hosts, reformat the EFI System Partition, clear custom UEFI NVRAM variables, and apply the latest DBX revocation list and firmware updates.; MITRE CONTEXT=Privilege Escalation & Command and Control (T1068 / T1055)]

### T1543.003: AuKill EDR Killer Abusing Signed Sysinternals PROCEXP152.SYS (BYOVD)
- **Scenario ID**: `aukill-edr-killer-procxp152-byovd`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/aukill-edr-killer-procxp152-byovd
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=aukill-edr-killer-procxp152-byovd
- **Category**: KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kernel, Firmware & BYOVD · T1543.003
- **Overview**: Imagine a building where normal workers are forbidden from touching the security cameras (Protected Process Light). However, an old master maintenance robot built by the building’s own manufacturer (Sysinternals PROCEXP152.SYS) has a valid master badge and will obey anyone who pushes its buttons (IOCTL 0x8335003C). A burglar wheels the old maintenance robot out of a backpack and orders it to unplug every security camera in the building. Dissected by Sophos X-Ops and Elastic Security Labs in 2023 across Medusa Locker and LockBit intrusions, AuKill is a C++ Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) tool. It drops version 16.32 of Microsoft’s signed Sysinternals Process Explorer kernel driver (PROCEXP152.SYS) into System32\drivers and issues DeviceIoControl codes 0x8335003C (open protected process handle) and 0x83350004 (close handle) to strip handles and kill PPL-protected EDR/AV services from Ring 0.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)

### T1553.002: STONESTOP & POORTRY / BURNTCIGAR WHQL-Signed Kernel Callback Wiper
- **Scenario ID**: `crowdstrike-poortry-burntcigar-byovd`

### T1036.004: BPFDoor Passive Linux Rootkit & Classic BPF Magic Packet Filter (Red Menshen)
- **Scenario ID**: `linux-bpfdoor-ebpf-socket-filter-apt`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/linux-bpfdoor-ebpf-socket-filter-apt
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=linux-bpfdoor-ebpf-socket-filter-apt
- **Category**: KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kernel, Firmware & BYOVD · T1036.004
- **Overview**: Imagine a spy hiding inside a central post office who doesn’t rent a P.O. Box (listening port) and never makes outgoing phone calls (beacons). Only when a postcard arrives with a secret watermark (0x7255) does the spy step out and unlock a side door. Unmasked by PwC Threat Intelligence (attributing it to China-nexus APT Red Menshen) and analyzed in depth by Sandfly Security and Elastic, BPFDoor is a passive Linux/Solaris implant that evaded detection for over five years across telecom and government networks. It runs from unlinked RAM storage (/dev/shm/kdmtmpflush (deleted)), spoofs its process name in ps, opens zero listening TCP/UDP ports, and attaches a classic Berkeley Packet Filter (SO_ATTACH_FILTER) to a raw socket to inspect all inbound traffic at the NIC layer for magic bytes 0x7255 (UDP/ICMP) or 0x5293 (TCP).

### T1542.001: CosmicStrand Motherboard SPI Flash UEFI Rootkit (CSMCORE -> ntoskrnl.exe Chain)
- **Scenario ID**: `kaspersky-cosmicstrand-uefi-spi-rootkit`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/kaspersky-cosmicstrand-uefi-spi-rootkit
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=kaspersky-cosmicstrand-uefi-spi-rootkit
- **Category**: KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kernel, Firmware & BYOVD · T1542.001
- **Overview**: Imagine a ghost etched directly into the silicon blueprint of a building’s foundation (SPI Flash Chip). Even if the owner bulldozes the interior walls and installs a brand-new hard drive and operating system, the moment the main power breaker is flipped on, the ghost whispers to the foundation controller (CSMCORE), who whispers to the elevator operator (bootmgfw.efi), who whispers to the floor manager (winload.efi), who finally slips a mind-control chip into the building director (ntoskrnl.exe) before the director even opens their eyes. Detailed by Kaspersky GReAT in July 2022, CosmicStrand is an advanced China-nexus UEFI firmware rootkit residing inside the physical SPI NOR flash chip of ASUS and Gigabyte H81 motherboards. Because it lives in motherboard firmware rather than on the hard drive, it survives full disk formatting and drive replacement. On every boot, its patched CSMCORE DXE driver hooks HandleProtocol to propagate a fileless in-memory hook chain through bootmgfw.efi and winload.efi directly into ntoskrnl.exe, disabling Kernel Patch Protection (PatchGuard) and deploying a Ring-0 implant.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1542.001 · System Firmware): **Stage 1: Motherboard SPI Flash Infection of CSMCORE DXE Driver (HandleProtocol Hook)** — Before the computer even knows what a hard drive is, a modified chip on the motherboard wakes up and places a tap on the firmware’s main telephone switchboard (HandleProtocol). CosmicStrand modified the UEFI firmware image stored inside the motherboard’s physical 8MB SPI NOR flash chip, specifically patching the CSMCORE DXE driver (GUID {A062CF1F-8473-4AA3-8793-600BC4FFE9A8}). When the UEFI Driver Execution Environment (DXE) loaded CSMCORE, the patched entry point jumped to shellcode appended in the .reloc section, which hooked EFI_BOOT_SERVICES.HandleProtocol (the core UEFI Boot Service function invoked later when locating and loading the OS boot manager). Because the infection resides entirely inside the motherboard’s SPI flash chip, replacing the SSD/NVMe drive or reinstalling Windows from a clean ISO has zero effect on the rootkit. In the documented EDR exchange from CosmicStrand C2 Server to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1542.001 (confirming that the Stage 1: Motherboard SPI Flash Infection of CSMCORE DXE Driver (HandleProtocol Hook) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay (bootmgfw.efi -> winload.efi)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Motherboard SPI Flash Infection of CSMCORE DXE Driver (HandleProtocol Hook) / ⇠#1 ALERT T1542.001) from Node ① (#1 CosmicStrand C2 Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Patched ntoskrnl.exe & Kernel Implant). [Specs: COMMAND 1=SPI Flash Firmware Region: Patched CSMCORE DXE driver GUID {A062CF1F-8473-4AA3-8793-600BC4FFE9A8}; COMMAND 2=Hook EFI_BOOT_SERVICES.HandleProtocol -> Intercepts loading of bootmgfw.efi; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Enable Intel Boot Guard / AMD Platform Secure Boot hardware root-of-trust and BIOS Write Protection (`BiosLock` / `BLE` + `SMM_BWP`) to prevent unauthorized SPI flash modifications.; MITRE CONTEXT=Persistence (T1542.001 - System Firmware)]
  - Stage 2 (T1542.003 · Bootkit Hooking Relay): **Stage 2: Multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay (bootmgfw.efi -> winload.efi)** — Like a baton passed in a relay race entirely in RAM, each boot component patches the next component in memory right before handing over control, without ever touching a file on the hard drive. When HandleProtocol was called during boot, CosmicStrand scanned memory for bootmgfw.efi and placed an inline hook on Archpx64TransferTo64BitApplicationAsm. When bootmgfw.efi loaded winload.efi into RAM and called that function, the hook scanned winload.efi for the byte signature of OslArchTransferToKernel (the final OS loader routine that switches the CPU into kernel execution and jumps to ntoskrnl.exe’s entry point) and hooked it in memory. Because bootmgfw.efi, winload.efi, and ntoskrnl.exe on the disk partition are never modified on disk, offline disk forensics and file-hash checks report 100% clean Microsoft system binaries. In the documented EDR exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE), Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE) responds with ALERT T1542.003 (confirming that the Stage 2: Multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay (bootmgfw.efi -> winload.efi) request succeeded on Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: PatchGuard Neutralization, ntoskrnl.exe ZwCreateSection Hook & Kernel C2). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay (bootmgfw.efi -> winload.efi) / ⇠#2 ALERT T1542.003) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Patched ntoskrnl.exe & Kernel Implant). [Specs: COMMAND 1=Hook 1 (bootmgfw.efi): Patch Archpx64TransferTo64BitApplicationAsm in RAM; COMMAND 2=Hook 2 (winload.efi): Patch OslArchTransferToKernel prior to kernel handoff; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Dump and audit motherboard SPI flash images using `CHIPSEC` (`chipsec_util spi dump`) and verify DXE driver hashes against vendor golden firmware images.; MITRE CONTEXT=Defense Evasion (T1542.003 - Bootkit Hooking Relay)]
  - Stage 3 (T1014 · Rootkit): **Stage 3: PatchGuard Neutralization, ntoskrnl.exe ZwCreateSection Hook & Kernel C2** — Right before the Windows kernel takes its first breath, the relay runner disables the kernel’s self-inspection alarm (PatchGuard) and plants a hidden radio inside the kernel’s own code pages. At the OslArchTransferToKernel handoff, before ntoskrnl.exe even executed its first instruction, CosmicStrand patched KiFilterFiberContext in ntoskrnl.exe RAM to immediately return (preventing Windows Kernel Patch Protection / PatchGuard from initializing), copied its shellcode into unused .text section slack space inside ntoskrnl.exe, and placed an inline hook on ZwCreateSection (waiting for smss.exe to map KnownDlls
tdll.dll as a signal that the OS network stack is ready before mapping its final kernel-mode C2 implant). Once Windows networking initialized, the kernel implant resolved its C2 domain via raw kernel sockets (tdi.sys) to fetch second-stage user/kernel payloads. In the documented EDR exchange from Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE) to Boot Chain (bootmgfw -> winload.efi), Boot Chain (bootmgfw -> winload.efi) responds with ALERT T1014 (confirming that the Stage 3: PatchGuard Neutralization, ntoskrnl.exe ZwCreateSection Hook & Kernel C2 request succeeded on Boot Chain (bootmgfw -> winload.efi) and completing the final execution objective of CosmicStrand Motherboard SPI Flash UEFI Rootkit (CSMCORE -> ntoskrnl.exe Chain)). ### T1068: Terminator EDR Killer Abusing Signed Zemana AntiMalware Driver (zam64.sys / CVE-2021-31728)
- **Scenario ID**: `sentinelone-terminator-zemana-byovd`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/sentinelone-terminator-zemana-byovd
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=sentinelone-terminator-zemana-byovd
- **Category**: KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kernel, Firmware & BYOVD · T1068
- **Overview**: Imagine an armored security van (zam64.sys) that promises it will only take orders from people whose names are written on its VIP clipboard. However, the van has a public window (IOCTL 0x80002010) where any stranger on the street can walk up and say, "Please write my name on the VIP clipboard!" Once their name is on the clipboard, the stranger uses the van’s roof cannon (IOCTL 0x80002048) to blast every police car on the block. Marketed on Russian cybercrime forums in May 2023 for $3,000 as a zero-day EDR bypass and rapidly reverse-engineered by SentinelOne and CrowdStrike, "Terminator" is a BYOVD wrapper abusing zam64.sys (a legitimate, Microsoft-signed kernel driver from Zemana AntiMalware vulnerable to CVE-2021-31728). Terminator drops zam64.sys under a random filename, calls DeviceIoControl with 0x80002010 to add its own PID to the driver’s internal trusted process list, and then loops 0x80002048 (ZwTerminateProcess) to kill processes belonging to 24 security vendors.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1068 · T1068 / T1036.005): **Stage 1: Dropping Randomized Signed Zemana Driver (zam64.sys) into System32\drivers** — To avoid being recognized by name at the door, the attacker paints a random 8-letter name onto the side of the signed Zemana driver before loading it. When executed with administrator privileges, Terminator.exe wrote an embedded copy of zam64.sys (a kernel driver validly signed by Zemana Ltd. and countersigned by Microsoft) into C:\Windows\System32\drivers\ using a randomly generated 5-to-10 character .sys filename (evading naive detection rules that only check if the file path ends in zam64.sys) and started the kernel service via the Service Control Manager. Regardless of the randomized .sys filename on disk, the driver’s DriverEntry routine always creates the fixed device symbolic link \\.\ZemanaAntiMalware (or \\.\B94B8021-5217-4091-96E5-6353272B9429). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Dropping Randomized Signed Zemana Driver (zam64.sys) into System32\drivers / ⇠#1 ACK 6) from Node ① (#1 Terminator.exe User-Mode Binary) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 IOCTL 0x80002048 Ring-0 Process Kill). [Specs: COMMAND 1=Drop C:\Windows\System32\drivers\<random_8_chars>.sys (SHA256 matching signed Zemana zam64.sys); COMMAND 2=CreateServiceW + StartServiceW -> Creates device symlink \\.\ZemanaAntiMalware; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Block `zam64.sys` and `zamguard64.sys` by file hash and signer certificate thumbprint rather than filename using WDAC / Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist.; MITRE CONTEXT=Privilege Escalation & Defense Evasion (T1068 / T1036.005)]
  - Stage 2 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **Stage 2: Self-Allowlisting Caller PID via Unauthenticated IOCTL 0x80002010 (CVE-2021-31728)** — The driver checks an internal VIP list before running dangerous commands, but leaves the "Add Me to the VIP List" button completely unguarded. Although zam64.sys checks an internal allowlist of trusted Process IDs before permitting privileged operations like process termination or raw disk access, it exposes IOCTL 0x80002010 (IOCTL_REGISTER_PROCESS, tracked as CVE-2021-31728, which accepts any 4-byte DWORD Process ID from user mode and appends it to the driver’s Ring-0 trusted process table without verifying the caller’s executable signature). Terminator.exe simply passed GetCurrentProcessId() to 0x80002010 to authorize itself. Once a PID is registered via 0x80002010, zam64.sys unlocks its full suite of administrative IOCTLs, including process termination, registry manipulation, and direct SCSI/disk read-write, for that caller. In the documented EDR exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Signed Zemana Driver (zam64.sys), Signed Zemana Driver (zam64.sys) responds with ALERT T1068 (confirming that the Stage 2: Self-Allowlisting Caller PID via Unauthenticated IOCTL 0x80002010 (CVE-2021-31728) request succeeded on Signed Zemana Driver (zam64.sys) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Continuous Ring-0 Termination Loop via IOCTL 0x80002048). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Self-Allowlisting Caller PID via Unauthenticated IOCTL 0x80002010 (CVE-2021-31728) / ⇠#2 ALERT T1068) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Signed Zemana Driver (zam64.sys)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 IOCTL 0x80002048 Ring-0 Process Kill). [Specs: COMMAND 1=hDev = CreateFileW("\\.\ZemanaAntiMalware", ...); COMMAND 2=myPid = GetCurrentProcessId(); DeviceIoControl(hDev, 0x80002010, &myPid, sizeof(DWORD), ...) (Registers caller in Ring-0 trusted list); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Kernel drivers must validate caller authenticity in Ring 0 using `SeLocateProcessImageName` and Windows Code Integrity verification rather than trusting a user-supplied PID registration IOCTL.; MITRE CONTEXT=Privilege Escalation (T1068 - Exploitation for Privilege Escalation)]
  - Stage 3 (T1562.001 · Disable or Modify Tools): **Stage 3: Continuous Ring-0 Termination Loop via IOCTL 0x80002048** — Now recognized as a VIP by the kernel driver, the attacker’s program runs an endless loop telling the driver to shoot down every security process that appears. In an infinite while (true) loop, Terminator.exe called CreateToolhelp32Snapshot to enumerate active processes, compared each executable name against a hardcoded array of 24 security vendors (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Defender, Sophos, Cortex XDR, Kaspersky, McAfee, Trend Micro, etc.), and sent IOCTL 0x80002048 with the matching PID (causing zam64.sys to call ZwTerminateProcess from Ring 0 and bypass User-Mode PPL protections). Modern EDRs neutralize Terminator prior to 0x80002048 by blocking the load of zam64.sys at NtLoadDriver / DriverLoad time using behavioral prevention and kernel blocklists. In the documented EDR exchange from Signed Zemana Driver (zam64.sys) to IOCTL 0x80002010 Allowlist Bypass, IOCTL 0x80002010 Allowlist Bypass responds with ALERT T1562.001 (confirming that the Stage 3: Continuous Ring-0 Termination Loop via IOCTL 0x80002048 request succeeded on IOCTL 0x80002010 Allowlist Bypass and completing the final execution objective of Terminator EDR Killer Abusing Signed Zemana AntiMalware Driver (zam64.sys / CVE-2021-31728)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: Continuous Ring-0 Termination Loop via IOCTL 0x80002048 / ⇠#3 ALERT T1562.001) from Node ③ (#3 Signed Zemana Driver (zam64.sys)) to Node ④ (#4 IOCTL 0x80002010 Allowlist Bypass), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 IOCTL 0x80002048 Ring-0 Process Kill). [Specs: COMMAND 1=CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS, 0) -> Match against 24 security vendor process names; COMMAND 2=DeviceIoControl(hDev, 0x80002048, &edrPid, sizeof(DWORD), ...) -> Ring-0 ZwTerminateProcess; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Configure EDR anti-tamper policies to block service creation and `CreateFileW` access to `\\.\ZemanaAntiMalware` before `0x80002010` can be invoked.; MITRE CONTEXT=Defense Evasion (T1562.001 - Disable or Modify Tools)]

### T1574.006: Symbiote Parasitic Linux LD_PRELOAD Rootkit & libpcap eBPF Bytecode Hooking
- **Scenario ID**: `intezer-blackberry-symbiote-linux-ldpreload`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/intezer-blackberry-symbiote-linux-ldpreload
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=intezer-blackberry-symbiote-linux-ldpreload
- **Category**: KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kernel, Firmware & BYOVD · T1574.006
- **Overview**: Imagine a parasite that doesn’t walk around the building on its own legs (so no guard ever sees an intruder on the hallway cameras). Instead, it slips a pair of augmented-reality glasses (/etc/ld.so.preload) onto every single employee in the building the moment they wake up. When an administrator looks at the room directory (ls) or the network monitor (tcpdump), the glasses digitally erase the parasite and its network wires from the administrator’s field of view. Jointly disclosed by BlackBerry and Intezer in June 2022 targeting Latin American financial institutions, Symbiote is a userland Linux rootkit compiled as a shared object (.so) library rather than a standalone executable. By injecting itself into /etc/ld.so.preload, it infects every dynamically linked process on the machine, hooking libc (fopen, getdents64, read) to conceal its files and harvest ssh/scp keystrokes, hooking pam_authenticate for backdoor root SSH access, and hooking libpcap to rewrite BPF packet filters on the fly so tcpdump cannot see its C2 traffic.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1574.006 · Dynamic Linker Hijacking): **Stage 1: Global Dynamic Linker Injection via /etc/ld.so.preload** — By adding its name to the master startup list of the Linux library loader, the malicious shared library forces every program on the server to load it first before doing anything else. Rather than running as a separate process, Symbiote was deployed as a shared library (e.g., /usr/lib/liblinux.so) and added to /etc/ld.so.preload (a system-wide configuration file read by the GNU dynamic linker /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 that forces the specified .so library to be mapped into the address space of every dynamically linked process before libc.so.6), allowing Symbiote to override standard library functions (fopen, readdir, getdents64, execve) via symbol interposition. If an administrator runs cat /etc/ld.so.preload, ls /usr/lib, or ldd /bin/ls using standard dynamically linked system binaries, Symbiote’s hooked fopen and getdents64 functions filter out its own filenames and return empty/clean results. In the documented EDR exchange from Symbiote DNS / HTTPS C2 Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1574.006 (confirming that the Stage 1: Global Dynamic Linker Injection via /etc/ld.so.preload request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: PAM Backdoor Authentication & ssh/scp libc_read Keystroke Harvesting). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Global Dynamic Linker Injection via /etc/ld.so.preload / ⇠#1 ALERT T1574.006) from Node ① (#1 Symbiote DNS / HTTPS C2 Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Hooked tcpdump / libpcap BPF Scrubber). [Specs: COMMAND 1=echo "/usr/lib/liblinux.so" > /etc/ld.so.preload; COMMAND 2=Hook glibc: fopen, fopen64, readdir, getdents64, execve (Hides /etc/ld.so.preload and liblinux.so from ls/find/ldd); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Inspect `/etc/ld.so.preload` and `/proc/1/maps` using a **statically linked** binary (such as `busybox` or a static Go security agent) that does not invoke `ld-linux.so` and therefore cannot be hooked by `LD_PRELOAD`.; MITRE CONTEXT=Persistence & Privilege Escalation (T1574.006 - Dynamic Linker Hijacking)]
  - Stage 2 (T1556.003 · Pluggable Authentication Modules): **Stage 2: PAM Backdoor Authentication & ssh/scp libc_read Keystroke Harvesting** — Because the parasite is already inside the SSH server and client programs, it listens as administrators type passwords to other servers and unlocks the front door whenever its own secret password is used. When loaded inside ssh or scp client processes, Symbiote hooked libc’s read() function to capture administrator passwords and keystrokes into an RC4-encrypted stash file (/var/tmp/.certs). When loaded inside the sshd daemon, it hooked pam_authenticate() and pam_acct_mgmt() (granting instant root SSH login whenever the attacker authenticated with a hardcoded master password, while scrubbing /var/log/auth.log and utmp/wtmp). Harvesting outbound ssh and scp credentials from compromised jump boxes allowed the attackers to pivot laterally across segmented banking infrastructure. In the documented Auth exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so), /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so) responds with ACK T1556.003 (confirming that the Stage 2: PAM Backdoor Authentication & ssh/scp libc_read Keystroke Harvesting request succeeded on /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: libpcap Function Hooking & Kernel BPF Bytecode Scrubbing Against tcpdump). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: PAM Backdoor Authentication & ssh/scp libc_read Keystroke Harvesting / ⇠#2 ACK T1556.003) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Hooked tcpdump / libpcap BPF Scrubber). [Specs: COMMAND 1=Hook ssh/scp read() -> Captures keystrokes and encrypts with RC4 into /var/tmp/.certs; COMMAND 2=Hook sshd pam_authenticate() -> If password == <hardcoded_symbiote_hash>, return PAM_SUCCESS; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Monitor `/proc/[pid]/maps` across `sshd` processes from kernel space (eBPF) for unexpected `.so` libraries loaded outside standard PAM and system library paths.; MITRE CONTEXT=Credential Access & Persistence (T1556.003 - Pluggable Authentication Modules)]
  - Stage 3 (T1014 · Rootkit / Network Capture Blindfolding): **Stage 3: libpcap Function Hooking & Kernel BPF Bytecode Scrubbing Against tcpdump** — When a forensic investigator plugs in a stethoscope (tcpdump) to listen to network traffic on the server, the parasite secretly rewrites the stethoscope’s filter so it goes deaf whenever the parasite speaks. To defeat live network forensics on the infected host, Symbiote hooked pcap_compile() in libpcap and setsockopt(..., SO_ATTACH_FILTER...) in libc. Whenever an analyst ran tcpdump or tshark, Symbiote intercepted the compiled Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) bytecode array before it was handed to the kernel and prepended its own BPF instructions (which instructed the Linux kernel to silently drop any packet matching Symbiote’s C2 ports or DNS tunneling domain before copying packets to tcpdump). Symbiote also hooked fopen("/proc/net/tcp") and removed lines matching its active connections so netstat and ss could not see its sockets either. In the documented EDR exchange from /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so) to Hooked sshd / PAM Credential Harvester, Hooked sshd / PAM Credential Harvester responds with ALERT T1014 (confirming that the Stage 3: libpcap Function Hooking & Kernel BPF Bytecode Scrubbing Against tcpdump request succeeded on Hooked sshd / PAM Credential Harvester and completing the final execution objective of Symbiote Parasitic Linux LD_PRELOAD Rootkit & libpcap eBPF Bytecode Hooking). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: libpcap Function Hooking & Kernel BPF Bytecode Scrubbing Against tcpdump / ⇠#3 ALERT T1014) from Node ③ (#3 /etc/ld.so.preload (liblinux.so)) to Node ④ (#4 Hooked sshd / PAM Credential Harvester), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Hooked tcpdump / libpcap BPF Scrubber). [Specs: COMMAND 1=Hook libpcap!pcap_compile & setsockopt(SO_ATTACH_FILTER); COMMAND 2=Prepend BPF bytecode instructions: Drop packets matching Symbiote C2 IP/Port before handing buffer to tcpdump; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Perform packet capture on an external network tap or mirror port (SPAN) rather than running `tcpdump` directly on a potentially compromised Linux host.; MITRE CONTEXT=Defense Evasion (T1014 - Rootkit / Network Capture Blindfolding)]

### T1068: Genshin Impact Anti-Cheat Driver (mhyprot2.sys) Ransomware BYOVD (CVE-2020-36603)
- **Scenario ID**: `genshin-mhyprot2-ransomware-byovd`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/genshin-mhyprot2-ransomware-byovd
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=genshin-mhyprot2-ransomware-byovd
- **Category**: KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kernel, Firmware & BYOVD · T1068
- **Overview**: Imagine a video-game referee (mhyprot2.sys) who was given a real police badge by the city (Microsoft WHCP Signature) so they could stop players from cheating on home PCs. A bank robber realizes that this referee will also obey orders inside a corporate bank vault, even if the video game isn’t installed, and commands the referee (IOCTL 0x81034000) to knock out every bank security guard in the building. Investigated by Trend Micro in August 2022 and subsequently tracked by Mandiant and Kaspersky across multiple ransomware campaigns, mhyprot2.sys (CVE-2020-36603) is the kernel-mode anti-cheat driver for the popular game Genshin Impact. Because it carries a valid digital signature from miHoYo Co., Ltd., attackers drop the standalone .sys file onto enterprise Windows servers alongside a controller binary (kill_svc.exe), complete its MT19937-64 XOR handshake via IOCTL 0x80034000, and invoke IOCTL 0x81034000 (ZwTerminateProcess in Ring 0) to mass-terminate EDR/AV processes.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

  - Stage 1 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **Stage 1: Dropping Standalone Signed mhyprot2.sys on Enterprise Domain Controller** — An attacker logs into a corporate Domain Controller that has never had a video game installed and unpacks a standalone, validly signed gaming anti-cheat driver. After compromising a server via RDP or stolen domain credentials, the ransomware operator dropped C:\Users\Public\mhyprot2.sys (a 350KB 64-bit Windows kernel driver validly signed by miHoYo Co., Ltd. and countersigned by Microsoft in 2020) and registered it as a kernel driver service via sc.exe create mhyprot2 type= kernel (loading cleanly into Ring 0 without requiring the Genshin Impact game client to be installed on the machine). Consumer anti-cheat drivers are engineered with sweeping Ring-0 process and memory inspection capabilities to catch game cheats, making them prime targets for standalone BYOVD weaponization on enterprise servers. In the documented EventID 6 exchange from kill_svc.exe Ransomware Dropper to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 6 (confirming that the Stage 1: Dropping Standalone Signed mhyprot2.sys on Enterprise Domain Controller request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Opening \.mhyprot2 & Initializing MT19937-64 Encryption Seed (IOCTL 0x80034000)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Dropping Standalone Signed mhyprot2.sys on Enterprise Domain Controller / ⇠#1 ACK 6) from Node ① (#1 kill_svc.exe Ransomware Dropper) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 IOCTL 0x81034000 Ring-0 AV Wipe & Lock).   - Stage 2 (T1027 · Obfuscated IOCTL Payloads): **Stage 2: Opening \\.\mhyprot2 & Initializing MT19937-64 Encryption Seed (IOCTL 0x80034000)** — To talk to the anti-cheat referee, the attacker’s tool sends a secret dice-roll seed (MT19937-64) that both sides use to scramble their messages. kill_svc.exe opened a handle to \\.\mhyprot2 and issued DeviceIoControl with IOCTL 0x80034000 (passing a 24-byte initialization structure that seeds the driver’s internal 64-bit Mersenne Twister MT19937-64 pseudo-random number generator, which mhyprot2.sys uses to XOR-decrypt all subsequent IOCTL request buffers and XOR-encrypt responses). Because researchers had previously reverse-engineered mhyprot2.sys’s MT19937-64 key derivation and published open-source PoCs on GitHub (evil-mhyprot-cli), ransomware developers copied the exact handshake routine directly into kill_svc.exe.   - Stage 3 (T1562.001 · T1562.001 / T1486): **Stage 3: Ring-0 ZwTerminateProcess Massacre via IOCTL 0x81034000 & Mass Encryption** — With the scrambled communication channel open, the attacker feeds the ID numbers of every antivirus guard into the anti-cheat driver, which terminates them from the kernel so the ransomware can lock the server. ### T1566.004: Black Basta Teams Vishing, Quick Assist, Backstab EDR Bypass & ChaCha20 (AA24-131A)
- **Scenario ID**: `blackbasta-qakbot-backstab-ransomware`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/blackbasta-qakbot-backstab-ransomware

- **Category**: RANSOMWARE_EXTORTION | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Ransomware & Extortion · T1566.004
- **Overview**: Imagine an extortion crew dumps 2,000 junk mail catalogs through an employee’s mail slot in five minutes. Documented in joint CISA/FBI/HHS Advisory AA24-131A and Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports on Storm-1811, Black Basta affiliates shifted from QakBot email malspam to human-operated Microsoft Teams vishing. After flooding a target’s email inbox, the attacker contacts them over external Microsoft Teams chat/voice posing as IT support, convinces them to launch the built-in Windows QuickAssist.exe utility, deploys the Backstab BYOVD tool (PROCEXP.SYS) to strip EDR handles, exfiltrates data with rclone, and encrypts network shares with ChaCha20/RSA-4096 (.basta).

### T1133: Akira Ransomware Cisco ASA VPN Breach & ESXi Hypervisor Encryption (AA24-109A)

Akira affiliates targeted WAN-facing Cisco ASA and Firepower Threat Defense (FTD) appliances, exploiting CVE-2020-3259 (an unauthenticated memory disclosure vulnerability that leaks active session tokens and credentials from ASA memory) or CVE-2023-20269 (an authorization bypass allowing brute-force and password-spray authentication against the built-in DefaultWEBVPNGroup connection profile without triggering MFA), establishing an encrypted AnyConnect VPN session. ### T1046: Play Ransomware Grixba Recon, AlphaVSS Shadow Copy Theft & Intermittent Encryption (AA23-352A)
- **Scenario ID**: `play-ransomware-grixba-vss-copy`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/play-ransomware-grixba-vss-copy
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=play-ransomware-grixba-vss-copy
- **Category**: RANSOMWARE_EXTORTION | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Ransomware & Extortion · T1046
- **Overview**: Imagine a burglar who knows that shouting "Make a shadow copy!" (vssadmin.exe) will trip the voice-activated alarm in the vault. So instead, the burglar brings a silent mechanical arm (AlphaVSS .NET COM Library) that quietly reaches into the shadow vault without making a sound, pulls out the locked master ledger (ntds.dit and SQL databases), smashes the shadow vault behind them, and then scrambles every fifth page of the remaining books. Detailed in joint CISA/FBI/ASD Advisory AA23-352A and Symantec Threat Hunter research, Play ransomware operators rely on two signature custom tools: Grixba (inf_g.exe, a .NET network and security-software enumerator packed with Costura.Fody and disguised with a SentinelOne icon) and a custom .NET VSS Copying Tool built on the AlphaVSS library (AlphaVSS.x64.dll). By calling the IVssBackupComponents COM interface directly via AlphaVSS, they snapshot and copy locked databases (ntds.dit.mdf) and delete shadow copies without ever spawning vssadmin.exe or wmic.exe, before running 1MB-stride intermittent encryption (.play).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

Play operators staged C:\Users\Public\Music\inf_g.exe (Grixba, a custom .NET reconnaissance tool compiled with Costura.Fody to embed its DLL dependencies inside a single executable and stamped with a forged SentinelOne icon and file description) and ran inf_g.exe -m:all -d:corp.local (enumerating all Active Directory computers, WMI AntivirusProduct statuses, backup software, and active user sessions into a SQLite database compressed as ExportData.zip). Staging tools specifically inside C:\Users\Public\Music\ is a consistent operational tradecraft hallmark of Play ransomware intrusions. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Play Ransomware Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the C:\Users\Public\Music\inf_g.exe -m:all -d:corp.local request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: AlphaVSS .NET Shadow Copy Mounting for Locked Database Exfiltration). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ C:\Users\Public\Music\inf_g.exe -m:all -d:corp.local / ⇠#1 ACK 1) from Node ① (#1 Play Ransomware Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AlphaVSS Shadow Access & .play Shares).   - Stage 2 (T1006 · Direct Volume Access / T1490): **Stage 2: AlphaVSS .NET Shadow Copy Mounting for Locked Database Exfiltration** — Instead of using the noisy public command-line tool (vssadmin.exe) that every security camera watches, the thief uses a direct programming interface (AlphaVSS) to quietly clone and steal locked files. To steal files locked exclusively by the OS (such as C:\Windows\NTDS\ntds.dit or live SQL Server .mdf files) and subsequently wipe recovery snapshots without triggering command-line EDR rules for vssadmin.exe or wmic.exe, Play deployed a custom .NET utility loading AlphaVSS.x64.dll and AlphaFS.dll (which wrap the native Windows IVssBackupComponents COM API to create a Volume Shadow Copy, copy locked files directly from \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy*, and delete all shadow copies programmatically). Because vssadmin.exe, wmic.exe, and powershell.exe are never spawned during this step, detection rules that rely purely on process command-line strings completely miss both the ntds.dit theft and the shadow copy deletion. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ vss_copy.exe / ⇠#2 ACK 7) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Compromised RDP / FortiOS / Exchange), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AlphaVSS Shadow Access & .play Shares). [Specs: COMMAND 1=vss_copy.exe -> Loads AlphaVSS.x64.dll (Calls IVssBackupComponents COM interface directly); COMMAND 2=Copies locked SQL .mdf & ntds.dit from \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1\ -> Deletes shadow copy; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Monitor `VSSEvent` EventID 8222 and COM instantiations of `CLSID_VssBackupComponents` (`{65EE1DBA-8FF4-4a58-AC1C-3470EE2F376A}`) by non-backup processes rather than relying solely on `vssadmin.exe` process creation rules.; MITRE CONTEXT=Collection & Defense Evasion (T1006 - Direct Volume Access / T1490)]
  - Stage 3 (T1486 · Data Encrypted for Impact): **Stage 3: WinPE APIUnhooking & Intermittent 0x100000-Byte Chunk Encryption (.play)** — To lock huge files before anyone can react, the encryptor only scrambles two or three 1-megabyte slices out of each giant file and stamps deadbeef at the bottom. Pushed via Group Policy Objects (GPO), the Play ransomware binary dynamically resolved APIs via the Process Environment Block (PEB) to evade user-mode hooks, checked if target files already contained the 0xdeadbeef footer marker, and performed intermittent encryption (encrypting only 2, 3, or 5 specific 0x100000-byte / 1MB chunks per file depending on total file size using AES and RSA-4096, appending .play, and dropping a minimalist ReadMe.txt containing only the word "PLAY" and an email address). Encrypting only a few 1MB chunks per multi-gigabyte file reduces disk I/O by over 95%, allowing Play to corrupt terabytes of storage in minutes while keeping average file-entropy scores low enough to fool naive entropy-based ransomware detectors. ### T1562.004: Rhysida Ransomware SilentKill PowerShell Preparation, PortStarter & LibTomCrypt AES-CTR (AA23-319A)
- **Scenario ID**: `rhysida-ransomware-zerologon-ps-silentskill`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/rhysida-ransomware-zerologon-ps-silentskill
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=rhysida-ransomware-zerologon-ps-silentskill
- **Category**: RANSOMWARE_EXTORTION | **Severity**: CRITICAL

Covered in joint CISA/FBI/MS-ISAC Advisory AA23-319A and Sekoia/Cisco Talos intelligence reports linking Rhysida to Vice Society (DEV-0832), Rhysida intrusions follow a disciplined three-phase playbook: (1) deploying PortStarter (a Golang backdoor that adds an inbound Windows Firewall rule via netsh for mTLS C2), (2) executing SilentKill (g.ps1, a PowerShell script that unhooks AMSI, stops 200+ AV/SQL/backup services, and enables RestrictedAdmin RDP), and (3) pushing rhysida.exe via PsExec to encrypt files using LibTomCrypt AES-256-CTR and RSA-4096 (.rhysida + CriticalBreachDetected.pdf).

### T1573.002: BianLian Custom Golang mTLS Backdoor, Built-In SOCKS5 & Pure Extortion (AA23-136A)
- **Scenario ID**: `bianlian-extortion-go-backdoor-rdp`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/bianlian-extortion-go-backdoor-rdp

- **Category**: RANSOMWARE_EXTORTION | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Ransomware & Extortion · T1573.002
- **Overview**: Imagine a modern heist crew that realizes blowing up the bank vault (ransomware encryption) sets off every alarm in the city and forces the bank to rebuild from backups anyway. Instead, they slip in quietly, install a single custom-built periscope (Golang mTLS + SOCKS5 Backdoor) that lets them peer into every room from across the ocean, photocopy every confidential legal and financial contract (rclone), and leave a quiet note on the CEO’s desk without touching a single lock. Documented in joint CISA/FBI/ASD Advisory AA23-136A and Red Canary / Avast research, BianLian shifted by 2023–2024 to a pure data-exfiltration extortion model, skipping file encryption entirely. Upon breaching an environment via RDP or edge vulnerabilities, BianLian deploys a per-victim compiled Golang backdoor that establishes a mutual TLS (mTLS) session multiplexed with hashicorp/yamux and an internal armon/go-socks5 proxy, enumerates shares with SharpShares, and exfiltrates sensitive data to Mega.io or FTP servers using a renamed rclone.exe binary (Win.exe).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1573.002 · Asymmetric Cryptography / mTLS): **Stage 1: Deploying Custom Golang mTLS Backdoor with Hardcoded X.509 Pinning** — For each target company, the attacker compiles a fresh, one-of-a-kind Go program that only talks to a single hardcoded IP address using a pair of matching digital passports (mTLS). After initial entry, BianLian dropped a uniquely compiled 64-bit Golang executable (masquerading under Windows system filenames like SystemSettingsAdminFlows.exe or Win64Ark.exe) that initiated an outbound mutual TLS (mTLS) connection directly to a hardcoded C2 IP address (embedding both the client X.509 certificate/private key and the expected C2 server certificate inside the Go binary so network middleboxes and security scanners could not intercept or probe the C2 server). Because the C2 IP and X.509 certificates are compiled directly into each binary right before deployment, every victim receives a distinct file hash. In the documented EventID 3 exchange from BianLian Extortion C2 & Mega/FTP Drop to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 3 (confirming that the SystemSettingsAdminFlows.exe request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: In-Memory Yamux Multiplexing & Built-In go-socks5 Lateral Pivot). [Specs: COMMAND 1=C:\Windows\Temp\SystemSettingsAdminFlows.exe (Golang binary with main.run & main.backconnect); COMMAND 2=mTLS Handshake: Presents embedded client X.509 cert to C2 IP:443; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Hunt for unsigned Golang binaries (`Go build ID`) executing from `C:\Windows\Temp` or `C:\ProgramData` that initiate long-lived TLS sessions to uncategorized IP literals without a preceding DNS lookup.; MITRE CONTEXT=Command and Control (T1573.002 - Asymmetric Cryptography / mTLS)]
  - Stage 2 (T1090.001 · Internal Proxy / SOCKS5): **Stage 2: In-Memory Yamux Multiplexing & Built-In go-socks5 Lateral Pivot** — Rather than installing malware on twenty different servers, the single Go program turns itself into an invisible switchboard (go-socks5), letting the attacker browse the whole network from the outside. Once the mTLS socket connected, the Golang backdoor wrapped the TLS stream in a HashiCorp Yamux connection multiplexer (github.com/hashicorp/yamux) and attached an in-memory SOCKS5 server (github.com/armon/go-socks5, allowing the external operator to route Impacket, SharpShares, LDAP queries, and SMB file reads through the single compromised host without dropping secondary implants onto target file servers). By centralizing C2 and proxying inside a single lightweight Go binary that contains zero exploit code or encryption routines, BianLian minimizes its endpoint footprint across the domain.   - Stage 3 (T1567.002 · Exfiltration to Cloud Storage / T1048): **Stage 3: Pure Data-Exfiltration Extortion via Rclone & FTP (Zero Encryption)** — Instead of locking the files, which would trip ransomware alarms, the thief disguises a cloud-sync tool as Win.exe, copies the crown jewels to Mega.io, and leaves a ransom note. Skipping file encryption completely (thereby evading all EDR behavioral ransomware sensors that watch for mass file-rename or high-entropy overwrite loops), BianLian staged a renamed copy of rclone.exe (e.g., C:\ProgramData\Win.exe) or FileZilla to stream sensitive intellectual property, financial records, and PII to Mega.io cloud storage or attacker FTP servers, leaving behind Look_at_this_file.txt demanding payment to prevent public disclosure. ### T1068: Sandworm HermeticWiper Signed EaseUS Driver (empntdrv.sys) MBR & NTFS $MFT Destruction
- **Scenario ID**: `hermeticwiper-ukraine-easeus-mbr-wipe`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/hermeticwiper-ukraine-easeus-mbr-wipe
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=hermeticwiper-ukraine-easeus-mbr-wipe
- **Category**: RANSOMWARE_EXTORTION | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Ransomware & Extortion · T1068
- **Overview**: Imagine a saboteur disguised with a genuine business license (Hermetica Digital Ltd) who wants to demolish a library’s card catalog ($MFT) and front entrance (MBR) so not a single book can ever be found again. Because the library’s operating system guards the master card catalog, the saboteur unpacks a genuine, licensed bulldozer (Signed EaseUS Partition Master Driver empntdrv.sys) from their suitcase, drives it straight into the foundation, shreds the master index with random noise, and pulls the main power plug. Discovered by ESET and analyzed by SentinelOne and CISA (AA22-057A / MAR-10375867-1) on February 23, 2022, HermeticWiper (FoxBlade) is a destructive wiper deployed by Russia’s GRU Sandworm group against Ukrainian ministries and financial institutions. Signed with a code-signing certificate issued to Hermetica Digital Ltd, the binary carries compressed 32/64-bit copies of the legitimate, Microsoft-signed EaseUS Partition Master kernel driver (empntdrv.sys) in its RCDATA resource section. It loads the driver, disables Volume Shadow Copies and crash dumps, and uses CryptGenRandom to overwrite the Master Boot Record (MBR), partition tables, and NTFS metadata ($MFT, $LogFile, $Bitmap) across \\.\PhysicalDrive0..100 before forcing a reboot.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1068 · T1068 / T1543.003): **Stage 1: Extracting & Registering Signed EaseUS Driver (empntdrv.sys) from RCDATA** — To bypass Windows protections on active disk partitions, the wiper unpacks a genuine, Microsoft-signed disk-partitioning driver hidden inside its own resource pocket. Upon execution via Active Directory GPO or WMI, HermeticWiper enabled SeLoadDriverPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, and SeShutdownPrivilege in its process token, checked the OS architecture and Windows version, decompressed an MSZIP-compressed resource (DRV_X64 / DRV_XP_X64) from its PE RCDATA section into C:\Windows\System32\drivers\<2_random_chars>dr.sys (a legitimate, Microsoft-signed copy of empntdrv.sys from EaseUS Partition Master), and loaded it into the kernel. Both the outer HermeticWiper executable (signed by Hermetica Digital Ltd until revoked) and the inner empntdrv.sys kernel driver (signed by CHENGDU YIWO Tech Development Co., Ltd.) carried valid Authenticode signatures at the time of the attack. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Extracting & Registering Signed EaseUS Driver (empntdrv.sys) from RCDATA / ⇠#1 ACK 6) from Node ① (#1 Sandworm GPO / WMI Deployment) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PhysicalDrive0 MBR & NTFS $MFT Wiped). [Specs: COMMAND 1=AdjustTokenPrivileges(SeLoadDriverPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeShutdownPrivilege); COMMAND 2=Extract RCDATA "DRV_X64" -> C:\Windows\System32\drivers\<random_2_chars>dr.sys (Signed EaseUS empntdrv.sys); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Block partition-management kernel drivers (`empntdrv.sys`, `epmntdrv.sys`, `RawDisk`) on enterprise workstations and servers using WDAC.; MITRE CONTEXT=Privilege Escalation & Defense Evasion (T1068 / T1543.003)]
  - Stage 2 (T1490 · T1490 / T1070): **Stage 2: Disabling Volume Shadow Copy (vss), Crash Dumps & Fragmenting NTFS Metadata** — Before destroying the master index, the saboteur turns off the backup camera (vss), disables the black-box flight recorder (CrashControl), and maps out every page of the NTFS file table. HermeticWiper called ChangeServiceConfigW and ControlService to disable and stop the vss (Volume Shadow Copy) service, set HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl\CrashDumpEnabled = 0 (preventing Windows from writing a MEMORY.DMP kernel crash dump when the corrupted system inevitably blue-screened, thereby denying incident responders RAM forensics), and parsed the raw NTFS boot sector and Master File Table ($MFT) to map the exact physical disk runlists of $MFT, $LogFile, $Bitmap, and C:\Windows\System32\config registry hives. By parsing the NTFS $MFT runlist fragments directly rather than using standard Windows file APIs, HermeticWiper could corrupt the exact physical sectors backing critical OS metadata even while Windows held those files locked. In the documented EventID 7040 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to HermeticWiper (conhost.dll / Hermetica), HermeticWiper (conhost.dll / Hermetica) responds with ALERT 7040 (confirming that the Stage 2: Disabling Volume Shadow Copy (vss), Crash Dumps & Fragmenting NTFS Metadata request succeeded on HermeticWiper (conhost.dll / Hermetica) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Raw \.PhysicalDrive0..100 MBR & NTFS $MFT Overwrite with CSPRNG Bytes). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Disabling Volume Shadow Copy (vss), Crash Dumps & Fragmenting NTFS Metadata / ⇠#2 ALERT 7040) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 HermeticWiper (conhost.dll / Hermetica)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PhysicalDrive0 MBR & NTFS $MFT Wiped). [Specs: COMMAND 1=ChangeServiceConfigW(hVssService, SERVICE_DISABLED) && ControlService(hVssService, SERVICE_CONTROL_STOP); COMMAND 2=RegSetValueExW("HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl", "CrashDumpEnabled", 0); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Monitor unexpected modifications to the `vss` service startup type (`SERVICE_DISABLED`) and `CrashControl\CrashDumpEnabled` registry keys.; MITRE CONTEXT=Inhibit System Recovery & Defense Evasion (T1490 / T1070)]
  - Stage 3 (T1561.002 · Disk Structure Wipe): **Stage 3: Raw \\.\PhysicalDrive0..100 MBR & NTFS $MFT Overwrite with CSPRNG Bytes** — Finally, the wiper overwrites the front door (MBR) and the master card catalog ($MFT) of every hard drive with cryptographic noise and forces an immediate reboot. Iterating through \\.\PhysicalDrive0 up to \\.\PhysicalDrive100, HermeticWiper generated cryptographically random bytes via CryptGenRandom and overwrote the Master Boot Record (MBR) (first 512 bytes of sector 0), GPT partition headers, and the mapped physical sector extents of $MFT, $LogFile, and C:\Users, before invoking ExitWindowsEx(EWX_REBOOT | EWX_FORCE) to immediately reboot the machine into an unrecoverable, unbootable state. Because the $MFT (which maps where every file resides on an NTFS volume) and $MFTMirr are overwritten with random bytes from CryptGenRandom, carving or recovering filesystem structure is rendered impossible in seconds without having to overwrite every gigabyte of the disk. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: Raw \\.\PhysicalDrive0..100 MBR & NTFS $MFT Overwrite with CSPRNG Bytes / ⇠#3 ALERT T1561.002) from Node ③ (#3 HermeticWiper (conhost.dll / Hermetica)) to Node ④ (#4 Signed EaseUS Driver (empntdrv.sys)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PhysicalDrive0 MBR & NTFS $MFT Wiped). [Specs: COMMAND 1=CreateFileW("\\.\PhysicalDrive0", GENERIC_READ | GENERIC_WRITE, ...) -> CryptGenRandom overwrite of Sector 0 (MBR); COMMAND 2=Overwrite NTFS $MFT, $LogFile, C:\Windows\System32\config\* -> ExitWindowsEx(EWX_REBOOT | EWX_FORCE); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Enforce kernel-level raw disk write protection blocking non-system processes from opening `GENERIC_WRITE` handles to `\\.\PhysicalDrive*`.; MITRE CONTEXT=Impact (T1561.002 - Disk Structure Wipe)]

### T1199: AcidRain MIPS ELF Satellite Modem Wiper (/dev/mtd MEMERASE / Viasat KA-SAT)
- **Scenario ID**: `acidrain-viasat-ka-sat-modem-wiper`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/acidrain-viasat-ka-sat-modem-wiper
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=acidrain-viasat-ka-sat-modem-wiper
- **Category**: RANSOMWARE_EXTORTION | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Ransomware & Extortion · T1199
- **Overview**: Imagine 40,000 remote satellite dishes across Europe that all listen to a single central control tower (TR-069 ACS) for automatic software updates. Saboteurs break into the control tower and broadcast a tiny self-destruct program (AcidRain / ukrop) that tells every satellite modem not just to delete its files, but to use a blowtorch (MEMERASE / MEMWRITEOOB IOCTLs) to melt the permanent flash memory chip (/dev/mtd*) holding its startup brain, turning the hardware into a dead brick. Reverse-engineered by SentinelOne (SentinelLabs) in March 2022 and addressed in joint CISA/NSA/FBI SATCOM advisories, AcidRain (ukrop) is a 32-bit big-endian MIPS ELF wiper deployed by Russian GRU threat actors against Viasat’s KA-SAT network on February 24, 2022. Pushed over the legitimate TR-069 CWMP management channel to over 40,000 SurfBeam2 satellite modems (knocking out Ukrainian communications and 5,800 German wind turbines), AcidRain exhaustively iterates Linux block devices (/dev/sd*, /dev/mmcblk*) and raw Memory Technology Devices (/dev/mtd0..99), issuing MEMUNLOCK, MEMERASE, and MEMWRITEOOB IOCTLs to permanently erase the onboard SPI NOR/NAND flash.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

  - Stage 1 (T1199 · Trusted Relationship / TR-069 Management Plane): **Stage 1: Management Plane Compromise & TR-069 CWMP Push of MIPS ELF Binary (ukrop)** — Rather than hacking 40,000 modems over the air one by one, the attackers hijack the central ground station that every modem trusts for remote management commands. After exploiting a VPN misconfiguration to enter the trusted management segment of the Viasat KA-SAT ground network, the threat actors issued mass management commands over the TR-069 (CWMP) protocol to deliver and execute a 140KB statically linked 32-bit MIPS ELF binary named ukrop (AcidRain) across tens of thousands of online SurfBeam2 satellite modems (Because ukrop had zero external library dependencies and brute-forced every conceivable Linux storage device path, it served as a universal embedded Linux/router/modem wiper In the documented Firewall exchange from Compromised SATCOM TR-069 ACS Server to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK T1199 confirming that the Stage 1: Management Plane Compromise & TR-069 CWMP Push of MIPS ELF Binary ukrop request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Block Device Enumeration /dev/sda, /dev/mmcblk & Sequential Overwrite). Because ukrop had zero external library dependencies and brute-forced every conceivable Linux storage device path, it served as a universal embedded Linux/router/modem wiper.
