On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Management Plane Compromise & TR-069 CWMP Push of MIPS ELF Binary (ukrop) / ⇠#1 ACK T1199) from Node ① (#1 Compromised SATCOM TR-069 ACS Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Bricked SPI NOR/NAND Flash & Turbines). [Specs: COMMAND 1=TR-069 CWMP Download RPC -> Pushes 32-bit MIPS ELF (/tmp/ukrop) to SurfBeam2 UT (User Terminals); COMMAND 2=Forks daemon process & iterates non-standard filesystem directories for recursive overwrite; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Cryptographically sign all firmware and management commands pushed via TR-069/CWMP and strictly segment satellite ground-station management networks with hardware MFA and command rate-limiting.; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access & Execution (T1199 - Trusted Relationship / TR-069 Management Plane)]
  - Stage 2 (T1561.002 · Disk Structure Wipe): **Stage 2: Block Device Enumeration (/dev/sda, /dev/mmcblk) & Sequential Overwrite** — First, the wiper walks through every possible hard drive, SD card, and flash partition name in the Linux dictionary and scrambles their contents. Forking into the background as root (UID 0), AcidRain first recursively overwrote files across non-essential filesystem directories, then systematically generated device paths for /dev/sda../dev/sdz, /dev/hda../dev/hdz, /dev/mmcblk0../dev/mmcblk9, and /dev/mtdblock0../dev/mtdblock99 (overwriting the first 384KB of each device and issuing BLKDISCARD, BLKSECDISCARD, and BLKZEROOUT kernel IOCTLs to erase storage blocks). By brute-forcing hundreds of device node names in a loop, AcidRain did not need to parse /proc/partitions or sysfs and worked across any embedded Linux distribution. In the documented EDR exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF), KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF) responds with ALERT T1561.002 (confirming that the Stage 2: Block Device Enumeration (/dev/sda, /dev/mmcblk) & Sequential Overwrite request succeeded on KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: Raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction via MEMUNLOCK, MEMERASE & MEMWRITEOOB). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Block Device Enumeration (/dev/sda, /dev/mmcblk) & Sequential Overwrite / ⇠#2 ALERT T1561.002) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Bricked SPI NOR/NAND Flash & Turbines). [Specs: COMMAND 1=Iterate block devices: /dev/sda..z, /dev/hda..z, /dev/mtdblock0..99, /dev/mmcblk0..9; COMMAND 2=open(dev, O_WRONLY) -> Overwrite initial sectors & issue BLKSECDISCARD / BLKDISCARD IOCTLs; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Enforce read-only SquashFS root filesystems and mandatory code-signing (`IMA/EVM`) on embedded Linux routers and SATCOM terminals.; MITRE CONTEXT=Impact (T1561.002 - Disk Structure Wipe)]
  - Stage 3 (T1495 · Firmware Corruption / T1561.001): **Stage 3: Raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction via MEMUNLOCK, MEMERASE & MEMWRITEOOB** — Finally, the wiper unlocks the raw silicon flash chip holding the modem’s bootloader (U-Boot), erases every sector, and reboots, leaving the modem unable to ever turn back on. For character-mode flash devices /dev/mtd0 through /dev/mtd99, AcidRain queried flash geometry via MEMGETINFO and then looped through every eraseblock issuing ioctl(fd, MEMUNLOCK) (unlocking software-protected flash sectors), ioctl(fd, MEMERASE) (physically erasing NOR/NAND flash blocks to 0xFF), and ioctl(fd, MEMWRITEOOB) (corrupting NAND flash Out-Of-Band ECC metadata), before invoking reboot(RB_AUTOBOOT) to permanently brick the modem. Because /dev/mtd0 holds the primary U-Boot bootloader on embedded MIPS routers and satellite modems, erasing /dev/mtd0 rendered the modems physically unbootable and required physical hardware replacement or JTAG/SPI chip reflashing. In the documented EDR exchange from KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF) to Linux MTD Subsystem (/dev/mtd0..99), Linux MTD Subsystem (/dev/mtd0..99) responds with ALERT T1495 (confirming that the Stage 3: Raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction via MEMUNLOCK, MEMERASE & MEMWRITEOOB request succeeded on Linux MTD Subsystem (/dev/mtd0..99) and completing the final execution objective of AcidRain MIPS ELF Satellite Modem Wiper (/dev/mtd MEMERASE / Viasat KA-SAT)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: Raw SPI Flash /dev/mtd0..99 Destruction via MEMUNLOCK, MEMERASE & MEMWRITEOOB / ⇠#3 ALERT T1495) from Node ③ (#3 KA-SAT SurfBeam2 Modem (ukrop ELF)) to Node ④ (#4 Linux MTD Subsystem (/dev/mtd0..99)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Bricked SPI NOR/NAND Flash & Turbines). [Specs: COMMAND 1=open("/dev/mtd0" .. "/dev/mtd99", O_RDWR); COMMAND 2=ioctl(fd, MEMUNLOCK, &ei) -> ioctl(fd, MEMERASE, &ei) -> ioctl(fd, MEMWRITEOOB, &oob) -> reboot(RB_AUTOBOOT); DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Hardware-lock bootloader flash sectors (`WP#` pin on SPI NOR flash) so software `MEMUNLOCK` / `MEMERASE` IOCTLs cannot erase the primary U-Boot bootloader partition (`/dev/mtd0`).; MITRE CONTEXT=Impact (T1495 - Firmware Corruption / T1561.001)]

### T1053.005: Sandworm ArguePatch Loader & CaddyWiper Domain-Aware Disk Wiper (T1561.001)
- **Scenario ID**: `caddywiper-arguepatch-gpo-destruction`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/caddywiper-arguepatch-gpo-destruction
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=caddywiper-arguepatch-gpo-destruction
- **Category**: RANSOMWARE_EXTORTION | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Ransomware & Extortion · T1053.005
- **Overview**: Imagine an army of demolition robots dispatched from a central radio tower (Primary Domain Controller) to tear down every building in a compound. If the first robot to wake up accidentally demolishes the central radio tower itself, none of the remaining buildings will ever receive the demolition signal! So the robot’s first instruction (DsRoleGetPrimaryDomainInformation) is: "Check if I am standing inside the central radio tower. If yes, go to sleep immediately; if no, erase every room and smash the foundation." Analyzed by ESET, Cisco Talos, and CERT-UA in March–April 2022 during Sandworm attacks against Ukrainian financial and energy organizations (including alongside Industroyer2), CaddyWiper is a compact 9KB C++ destructive wiper often loaded in memory by ArguePatch (a patched version of Hex-Rays IDA Pro’s signed/legitimate win32_remote.exe debugger server). Pushed via Active Directory GPO Scheduled Tasks, CaddyWiper first calls DsRoleGetPrimaryDomainInformation and exits immediately if running on a Primary Domain Controller (DsRole_RolePrimaryDomainController), then recursively zeroes out C:\Users and drives D:..Z: before wiping disk partition tables on \\.\PhysicalDrive9..0 via IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX (0x0007C054).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1055.012 (Process Injection: Process Hollowing - Defense Evasion / Privilege Escalation), T1106 (Native API Execution (CreateProcessW / NtUnmapViewOfSection) - Execution), T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols (HTTPS C2) - Command and Control)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw) | Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering) | Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence (https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1053.005 · Scheduled Task / T1574): **Stage 1: GPO Mass Deployment & ArguePatch Patched Debugger Loader Execution** — Using the company’s own Group Policy loudspeaker, the attacker pushes out a legitimate-looking programmer’s debugging tool (win32_remote.exe) whose startup code has been secretly rewired to unpack a wiper in RAM. From a compromised Domain Controller, Sandworm staged payloads in SYSVOL and pushed an Active Directory Group Policy Scheduled Task to execute CaddyWiper either directly (caddy.exe) or wrapped inside ArguePatch (a modified copy of Hex-Rays IDA Pro’s legitimate win32_remote.exe binary where Sandworm patched a single internal function to read, XOR-decrypt, and execute encrypted CaddyWiper shellcode directly in memory). Sandworm reused the exact same ArguePatch loader weeks later during the April 2022 electrical substation attack (Industroyer2) to schedule timed destruction of Windows servers. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Sandworm GPO Scheduled Task Push to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the win32_remote.exe request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: DsRoleGetPrimaryDomainInformation Check to Spare Domain Controllers). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ win32_remote.exe / ⇠#1 ACK 1) from Node ① (#1 Sandworm GPO Scheduled Task Push) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX Zeroing). [Specs: COMMAND 1=GPO Scheduled Task: Copy \\DC01\SYSVOL\corp.local\scripts\caddy.exe -> C:\Users\Public\; COMMAND 2=ArguePatch Loader: Patched IDA win32_remote.exe decrypts and jumps to CaddyWiper shellcode in RAM; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Audit Active Directory Group Policy Object modifications (EventID 5136) for newly added Immediate Scheduled Tasks referencing `SYSVOL` or `NETLOGON` binaries.; MITRE CONTEXT=Execution & Defense Evasion (T1053.005 - Scheduled Task / T1574)]
  - Stage 2 (T1082 · Execution Guardrails): **Stage 2: DsRoleGetPrimaryDomainInformation Check to Spare Domain Controllers** — Before lighting the fuse, the wiper checks the machine’s job title, and if the machine is the Primary Domain Controller, the wiper walks away so the Domain Controller stays alive to infect everyone else. Resolving API names dynamically on the stack to hide its Import Address Table (IAT), CaddyWiper’s very first action was calling DsRoleGetPrimaryDomainInformation(NULL, DsRolePrimaryDomainInfoBasic, &pInfo) from netapi32.dll (checking whether pInfo->MachineRole == DsRole_RolePrimaryDomainController [value 5], and immediately terminating itself without wiping anything if running on a Primary Domain Controller so Sandworm retained its Active Directory foothold and GPO distribution server). This execution guardrail explains why responders during a CaddyWiper incident often found member workstations and application servers completely bricked while the Primary Domain Controller remained up and actively pushing the malicious GPO. In the documented EDR exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to ArguePatch Loader (Patched win32_remote.exe), ArguePatch Loader (Patched win32_remote.exe) responds with ALERT T1082 (confirming that the Stage 2: DsRoleGetPrimaryDomainInformation Check to Spare Domain Controllers request succeeded on ArguePatch Loader (Patched win32_remote.exe) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: TakeOwnership Recursive File Zeroing & IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX Wipe). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: DsRoleGetPrimaryDomainInformation Check to Spare Domain Controllers / ⇠#2 ALERT T1082) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 ArguePatch Loader (Patched win32_remote.exe)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX Zeroing). [Specs: COMMAND 1=DsRoleGetPrimaryDomainInformation(NULL, DsRolePrimaryDomainInfoBasic, &pInfo); COMMAND 2=if (pInfo->MachineRole == DsRole_RolePrimaryDomainController) { ExitProcess(0); }; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Immediately unlink malicious GPOs and isolate the Primary Domain Controller (`PDC`) during a wiper outbreak, as the PDC is intentionally left intact by the malware to act as the distribution engine.; MITRE CONTEXT=Discovery & Execution Guardrails (T1082 / T1480 - Execution Guardrails)]
  - Stage 3 (T1561.001 · Disk Content Wipe / T1561.002 - Disk Structure Wipe): **Stage 3: TakeOwnership Recursive File Zeroing & IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX Wipe** — On every non-DC computer, the wiper legally transfers ownership of every file to itself, overwrites them with zeros, and then sends a single disk-layout command that erases the drive’s partition map. On member workstations and servers, CaddyWiper enabled SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege, recursively walked C:\Users and all drives from D:\ to Z:\ calling SetNamedSecurityInfoA (transferring file ownership and DACLs to the current user before overwriting every file’s contents with 0x00 null bytes), and finally looped from \\.\PhysicalDrive9 down to \\.\PhysicalDrive0 issuing DeviceIoControl with IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX (0x0007C054 passing a 1,920-byte zero-filled DRIVE_LAYOUT_INFORMATION_EX structure that instructs the Windows disk driver itself to erase the MBR/GPT partition tables). By abusing the legitimate Windows kernel disk IOCTL IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX (0x0007C054) rather than bringing a third-party kernel driver, CaddyWiper destroyed the disk partition table without needing a BYOVD driver. In the documented EDR exchange from ArguePatch Loader (Patched win32_remote.exe) to CaddyWiper (DsRole Domain Controller Check), CaddyWiper (DsRole Domain Controller Check) responds with ALERT T1561.001 (confirming that the Stage 3: TakeOwnership Recursive File Zeroing & IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX Wipe request succeeded on CaddyWiper (DsRole Domain Controller Check) and completing the final execution objective of Sandworm ArguePatch Loader & CaddyWiper Domain-Aware Disk Wiper (T1561.001)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: TakeOwnership Recursive File Zeroing & IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX Wipe / ⇠#3 ALERT T1561.001) from Node ③ (#3 ArguePatch Loader (Patched win32_remote.exe)) to Node ④ (#4 CaddyWiper (DsRole Domain Controller Check)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 IOCTL_DISK_SET_DRIVE_LAYOUT_EX Zeroing). [Specs: COMMAND 1=Recursive ACL Takeover + Zero-Fill: C:\Users\* and D:\ .. ### T1190: VulnCheck — Control Web Panel (CWP) Pre-Auth Module Dispatch to Root RCE (CVE-2026-73695..104080)
- **Scenario ID**: `vulncheck-cwp-preauth-module-dispatch-rce`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/vulncheck-cwp-preauth-module-dispatch-rce
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=vulncheck-cwp-preauth-module-dispatch-rce
- **Category**: ZERO_DAY_APPLIANCES | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Zero-Day Appliances · T1190
- **Overview**: Imagine a multi-tenant apartment building (Control Web Panel port 2083) where the front-desk guard (CWPUserIndex::__construct) tells unauthenticated visitors "Please go to the lobby login desk" (emitting an HTTP 302 Location header, CVE-2026-73696) but forgets to actually lock the inner hallway door (omitting exit()). The visitor walks straight past the desk into any tenant suite (include_once modules/$module.php, CVE-2026-73695), uses the suite maintenance panel (phpini_editor.php, CVE-2026-73697) to run commands as that tenant, and then picks up the building internal house phone (loopback API 127.0.0.1:2302, CVE-2026-77877 & CVE-2026-77878) which executes every request as the building master superintendent (root uid=0). Disclosed by VulnCheck in November 2026 ("Control Web Panel: Pre-Auth Module Dispatch to Root RCE"), this 10-CVE chain compromises Control Web Panel (CWP) instances in two network hops. First, an unauthenticated attacker enumerates a valid hosting username via an HTTP 302 vs 404 oracle on port 2083 and exploits an Execution After Redirect (EAR) flaw in UnauthenticatedFlowTrait::toLoginWithIntendedUri() (CVE-2026-73696) combined with unvalidated module LFI in services/users/index.php (CVE-2026-73695) to reach any of the 170+ user modules without a session. Second, the attacker triggers pre-auth file write or command injection in modules/phpini_editor.php (CVE-2026-73697) or modules/protected_directory.php (CVE-2026-77876) as the hosting user, and immediately relays a loopback request to the root-privileged Slim v2 User API on 127.0.0.1:2302 (/v1/restoredatabase/ CVE-2026-77877 & CVE-2026-77878, /valid_token/ CVE-2026-104080, or OAuth SQLi CVE-2026-77879 + /v1/newpass/ CVE-2026-77880) to achieve unauthenticated root RCE.
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application (Control Web Panel Pre-Auth EAR & Module LFI) - Initial Access), T1059.004 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell (phpini_editor & protected_directory Sinks) - Execution), T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (Loopback User API 127.0.0.1:2302 Root Escalation) - Privilege Escalation)
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: VulnCheck Initial Access Intelligence (CNA): Control Web Panel: Pre-Auth Module Dispatch to Root RCE (CVE-2026-73695..CVE-2026-104080) (https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/control-web-panel-pre-auth-module-dispatch-rce) | Control Web Panel (CentOS Web Panel): CWP7 ChangeLog & Security Updates (Builds 0.9.8.1210 to 0.9.8.1213+ / Patches 1.12–1.30) (https://control-webpanel.com/changelog) | NIST NVD & CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV): Control Web Panel Historical Pre-Auth RCE Context (CVE-2025-48703 & CWE-698 Execution After Redirect) (https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-48703)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1190 · Exploit Public-Facing Application): **Stage 1: Account Enumeration Oracle, Execution After Redirect (CVE-2026-73696) & Module LFI (CVE-2026-73695)** — Think of ringing apartment buzzers until one clicks (GET /labtest/ returning 302 instead of 404), and then walking past a receptionist who hands you a "Redirect to Login" slip (header Location: /login/) but never blocks you from walking into the back office (missing exit() before include_once). On port 2083, cwpsrv (nginx) routes requests matching https://host:2083/<username>/ to a dedicated per-user PHP-FPM Unix socket (returning HTTP 302 Found when the hosting account exists and HTTP 404 Not Found when the socket is absent, giving attackers a free pre-auth username oracle). When an unauthenticated caller requests /labtest/index.php?module=..., CWPUserIndex::__construct() invokes unauthenticatedFlow() and UnauthenticatedFlowTrait::toLoginWithIntendedUri() (which emits header Location: /login/?intended=... without calling exit() under CVE-2026-73696, allowing PHP execution to fall straight through to the file-scope module dispatcher). At file scope, services/users/index.php reads CWPHttpRequest::get(module) through an anti-XSS filter that leaves ../, /, and . intact and executes include_once /usr/local/cwpsrv/var/services/user_files/modules/ . $module_name . .php (bypassing setModuleVars() and checkIfModuleExists() under CVE-2026-73695 so any user module or relative .php path on disk is included pre-authentication). In the admin panel on port 2031, CWP correctly calls header(Location: /login) followed immediately by exit(), whereas the refactored user panel on port 2083 omitted exit() in UnauthenticatedFlowTrait::toLoginWithIntendedUri() and omitted checkIfModuleExists() before include_once (meaning every single HTTP request to /<valid_user>/index.php?module=<target> executes the target module inside the hosting account PHP-FPM pool before PHP flushes the cosmetic 302 redirect response). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ cwp-phpfpm: pool labtest /usr/local/cwpsrv/var/services/users/index.php?module=phpini_editor / ⇠#1 ACK 302) from Node ① (#1 External Attacker (HTTPS :2083)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Loopback User API (127.0.0.1:2302)). [Specs: COMMAND 1=curl -sk -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://cwp.corp.local:2083/labtest/  # 302 Found = valid account oracle; COMMAND 2=header("Location: /login/?intended=" . base64_encode($qs)); // CVE-2026-73696: missing exit() in UnauthenticatedFlowTrait::toLoginWithIntendedUri(); COMMAND 3=include_once "/usr/local/cwpsrv/var/services/user_files/modules/" . $module_name . ".php"; // CVE-2026-73695: ../ and / survive anti-XSS filter; DEFENSE / MITIGATION=Upgrade Control Web Panel to build 0.9.8.1212+ (patch 1.12 adds exit() after header("Location: ...") in toLoginWithIntendedUri() and checks $_SESSION["logged"] === true; patch 1.16 enforces basename() + preg_replace("/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/", "", $module) + realpath()).; MITRE CONTEXT=Initial Access (T1190 - Exploit Public-Facing Application)]
  - Stage 2 (T1059.004 · Unix Shell / Webshell Drop): **Stage 2: Pre-Auth Hosting Account RCE via phpini_editor.php (CVE-2026-73697) & protected_directory.php (CVE-2026-77876)** — Once inside the tenant suite without a key, the intruder uses two unguarded maintenance tools on the wall: a configuration notepad that saves custom text to any file path on the machine (acc=update file_put_contents) and a file-cleanup button that passes unquoted filenames straight to a system shell (acc=addlabelphpiniadv shell_exec rm -f). Because modules/phpini_editor.php executes at file scope as soon as it is included by Stage 1, an unauthenticated attacker reaches two pre-auth sinks running as the hosting user uid=1000(labtest) under CVE-2026-73697 (first, acc=update reads $_POST[file] without path validation and writes <title>=<value> lines via file_put_contents, allowing the attacker to split a quote-free PHP payload across title=<?php system($_GET[c]);//,x and value= ?>,y into /tmp/evilmod.php and execute it in-band via module=../../../../../../../tmp/evilmod&c=id; second, acc=addlabelphpiniadv reads $_POST[hfilename] via trim() and passes it unquoted into shell_exec(rm -f . $hfilename)).   - Stage 3 (T1068 · Exploitation for Privilege Escalation): **Stage 3: Single-Request Root Escalation via Loopback User API 127.0.0.1:2302 (CVE-2026-77877, CVE-2026-77878 & CVE-2026-104080)** — From the tenant apartment, the intruder picks up the internal building intercom wired to 127.0.0.1:2302: because the superintendent assumed only trusted scripts could dial that internal extension, several buttons require no passcode at all (CVE-2026-77877) and run every request directly as root (uid=0). ### T1003.003: CISA & Microsoft DFIR — Volume Shadow Copy & esentutl.exe NTDS.dit Extraction Forensics
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-ntds-dit-vssadmin-esentutl-extraction`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-ntds-dit-vssadmin-esentutl-extraction

- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security bank vault where the master ledger book (ntds.dit) is bolted to the teller desk while the bank is open, so an insider uses the building photocopy system (Volume Shadow Copy vssvc.exe) to photograph the entire room and uses the official ledger binding machine (esentutl.exe) to print a duplicate copy alongside the safe combination key (SYSTEM registry hive). Grounded in CISA Advisory AA23-075A, Microsoft ESENT Event Logging documentation, and MITRE ATT&CK T1003.003: an adversary with Domain Admin privileges creates a Volume Shadow Copy of C: on a Domain Controller via vssadmin.exe or ntdsutil.exe, copies the locked Active Directory database (C:\Windows\NTDS\ntds.dit) using esentutl.exe /y /vss, and extracts the SYSTEM registry hive for offline password hash cracking. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).

### T1134: Microsoft Sysinternals & Splunk SURGe DFIR — LSASS MiniDump via comsvcs.dll & Sysmon EventID 10
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-lsass-minidump-comsvcs-sysmon-eid10`

Grounded in Microsoft Sysinternals Sysmon Event ID 10 documentation, Splunk SURGe credential dumping research, and MITRE ATT&CK T1003.001: an attacker dumps lsass.exe process memory using the signed Windows COM+ Services DLL (rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll,MiniDump), generating a characteristic GrantedAccess mask (0x1FFFFF or 0x1410) and CallTrace signature in Sysmon EventID 10 and Security EventID 4656. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).

- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon v15 Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess) & CallTrace Analysis for LSASS Memory Dumping (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-10-processaccess) | Splunk SURGe & Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence: Detecting Credential Dumping via rundll32.exe comsvcs.dll,MiniDump & Ordinal #24 (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/) | The MITRE Corporation: MITRE ATT&CK T1003.001: OS Credential Dumping — LSASS Memory (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/)

### T1003.006: Microsoft Security Auditing & CISA DFIR — Active Directory DCSync DRSUAPI Replication (EventID 4662)
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-dcsync-drsuapi-replication-eid4662`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-dcsync-drsuapi-replication-eid4662
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-dcsync-drsuapi-replication-eid4662
- **Category**: ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Active Directory & Identity · T1003.006
- **Overview**: Imagine a regular desktop cubicle pretending to be a regional branch headquarters and calling the central bank vault over the internal synchronization phone line (MS-DRSR DRSUAPI) to request a full copy of every customer PIN and master signing key. Grounded in Microsoft Windows Security Auditing Event ID 4662 documentation, CISA AD Defense Guidance, and MITRE ATT&CK T1003.006: an attacker with Replicating Directory Changes permissions invokes the MS-DRSR (DRSUAPI) IDL_DRSGetNCChanges RPC method from a non-Domain Controller workstation to replicate the krbtgt and administrator password hashes without touching disk on the DC. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1003.006 (Microsoft Security Auditing & CISA DFIR — Active Directory DCSync DRSUAPI Replication (EventID 4662) - Credential Access (T1003.006 - OS Credential Dumping: DCSync))
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Learn — Windows Security Auditing: Security Event ID 4662 (An operation was performed on an object) & MS-DRSR IDL_DRSGetNCChanges (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4662) | CISA & NSA Joint Guidance: Detecting and Mitigating Active Directory Compromises (DCSync Extended Rights 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2) (https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/detecting-and-mitigating-active-directory-compromises) | The MITRE Corporation: MITRE ATT&CK T1003.006: OS Credential Dumping — DCSync (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/006/)

### T1546.003: Microsoft Sysmon & Mandiant DFIR — WMI Permanent Event Subscription Persistence (EventID 19 / 20 / 21)
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-wmi-event-subscription-persistence-sysmon`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-wmi-event-subscription-persistence-sysmon
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-wmi-event-subscription-persistence-sysmon
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Malware & Process Execution · T1546.003
- **Overview**: Imagine wiring a hidden motion sensor (__EventFilter) inside the building automation database (OBJECTS.DATA) and connecting it with a splice cable (__FilterToConsumerBinding) to an automated loudspeaker (CommandLineEventConsumer) that fires every 60 seconds. Grounded in Microsoft Sysinternals Sysmon v15 documentation (Event IDs 19, 20, 21), Mandiant WMI forensics research, and MITRE ATT&CK T1546.003: an adversary registers a permanent WMI Event Subscription in the root\subscription namespace consisting of an __EventFilter, a CommandLineEventConsumer, and a __FilterToConsumerBinding stored inside C:\Windows\System32\wbem\Repository\OBJECTS.DATA so scrcons.exe or wmiprvse.exe executes a payload as SYSTEM. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1546.003 (Microsoft Sysmon & Mandiant DFIR — WMI Permanent Event Subscription Persistence (EventID 19 / 20 / 21) - Persistence (T1546.003 - Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription))
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event IDs 19 (WmiEventFilter), 20 (WmiEventConsumer) & 21 (WmiEventConsumerToFilter) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-19-wmievent-wmieventfilter-activity-detected) | Mandiant / Google Cloud Threat Intelligence: Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) Offense, Defense, and Forensics (OBJECTS.DATA & EventID 5861) (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence) | The MITRE Corporation: MITRE ATT&CK T1546.003: Event Triggered Execution — WMI Event Subscription (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/003/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:
  - Stage 1 (T1546.003 · Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription): **Stage 1: WMI __EventFilter WQL Trigger Registration (Sysmon EventID 19)** — Think of installing a timer switch inside the building central control room (creating a permanent WMI __EventFilter in root\subscription with a WQL polling query, logged by Sysmon EventID 19). Using PowerShell Set-WmiInstance or mofcomp.exe, the attacker creates a permanent __EventFilter instance in the root\subscription CIM namespace with a WQL polling query (SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 60 WHERE TargetInstance ISA "Win32_PerfFormattedData_PerfOS_System"). Sysmon EventID 19 (WmiEventFilter activity detected) logs the exact Query and EventNamespace (specifically recording EventID=19 (Sysmon WmiEventFilter), Namespace=root\subscription, FilterName=SCMUpdaterFilter, WqlQuery=SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 60 WHERE TargetInstance ISA Win32_PerfFormattedData_PerfOS_System inside the Sysmon telemetry stream so DFIR investigators can attribute the exact process, principal, and timestamp). Command #1 executes Set-WmiInstance -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter -Arguments @{Name="SCMUpdaterFilter"; EventNamespace="root\cimv2"; QueryLanguage="WQL"; Query="SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 60 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_PerfFormattedData_PerfOS_System'"}, where Registers permanent WMI MOF class instances (__EventFilter WQL trigger, CommandLineEventConsumer payload, and __FilterToConsumerBinding link) inside the root\subscription namespace persisted on disk in C:\Windows\System32\wbem\Repository\OBJECTS.DATA (exact tactical and forensic purpose: Creates fileless, repository-backed SYSTEM persistence (T1546.003) during "WMI __EventFilter WQL Trigger Registration (Sysmon EventID 19)" that runs outside normal Startup folders and Services lists, detectable via Sysmon EventID 19, 20, and 21 and WMI-Activity EventID 5861). Command #2 executes Sysmon EventID 19: Operation=Created EventNamespace=root\cimv2 Name=SCMUpdaterFilter, where Executes the technical command / telemetry directive (Sysmon EventID 19: Operation=Created EventNamespace=root\cimv2 Name=SCMUpdaterFilter) via System / Runtime Execution Interface, passing the exact arguments, target paths, and protocol parameters required to carry out "WMI __EventFilter WQL Trigger Registration (Sysmon EventID 19)" (exact tactical and forensic purpose: Advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1546.003 during "WMI __EventFilter WQL Trigger Registration (Sysmon EventID 19)" (Using PowerShell Set-WmiInstance or mofcomp.exe, the attacker creates a permanent __EventFilter instance in the root\subscription CIM namespace with a WQL polling query (SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHI...) while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution).   - Stage 2 (T1546.003 · CIM Repository OBJECTS.DATA Serialization): **Stage 2: CommandLineEventConsumer & __FilterToConsumerBinding Persistence in OBJECTS.DATA (Sysmon EventID 20 & 21)** — Think of wiring that timer switch to an automated command dispatcher stored inside the master blueprint repository (registering CommandLineEventConsumer and __FilterToConsumerBinding in OBJECTS.DATA, logged by Sysmon EventID 20, 21, and WMI-Activity 5861). ### T1197: Microsoft & Mandiant DFIR — BITS Job Persistence & qmgr.db SetNotifyCmdLine Forensics (EventID 59 / 60 / 3)

- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Malware & Process Execution · T1197
- **Overview**: Imagine scheduling a recurring courier pickup with the corporate mailroom (Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service) and attaching a standing instruction (/SetNotifyCmdLine) that forces the mailroom clerk (svchost.exe) to open and run whatever package arrives. Grounded in Microsoft Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) documentation, Mandiant qmgr.db forensic research, and MITRE ATT&CK T1197: an adversary creates a persistent BITS transfer job using bitsadmin.exe and configures /SetNotifyCmdLine so svchost.exe (-k netsvcs -s BITS) repeatedly downloads and executes a payload while storing state in C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Network\Downloader\qmgr.db. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1197 (Microsoft & Mandiant DFIR — BITS Job Persistence & qmgr.db SetNotifyCmdLine Forensics (EventID 59 / 60 / 3) - Defense Evasion (T1197 - BITS Jobs))

- **Overview**: Imagine adding a recurring job to the factory master wall calendar (Scheduled Tasks) and then erasing its entry from the public index board (deleting the TaskCache\Tree SD Security Descriptor value) while leaving the internal clockwork gear (TaskCache\Tasks\{GUID}) spinning. Grounded in Microsoft Security Auditing Event ID 4698/4702 documentation, Microsoft Threat Intelligence (MSTIC) "Tarrask" research, and SANS DFIR guides: an adversary registers a SYSTEM Scheduled Task (generating Security EventID 4698, TaskScheduler EventID 106, and an XML file in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\) and then deletes the SD (Security Descriptor) registry value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache\Tree\ to hide the task from schtasks /query and Task Scheduler GUI. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1053.005 (Microsoft MSTIC & SANS DFIR — Scheduled Task Creation & TaskCache SD Descriptor Deletion (EventID 4698 / Sysmon EID 12) - Persistence (T1053.005 - Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task))

### T1021.001: SANS DFIR & Microsoft Event Log — RDP Lateral Movement, Session Reconnection & BMC Bitmap Cache Forensics
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-rdp-lateral-movement-tsclient-bitmap-cache`

### T1059.003: Mandiant, ANSSI & SANS DFIR — Application Compatibility Shimcache (AppCompatCache) & Amcache.hve Triage
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-shimcache-amcache-execution-artifact-triage`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-shimcache-amcache-execution-artifact-triage
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-shimcache-amcache-execution-artifact-triage
- **Category**: MALWARE | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Malware & Process Execution · T1059.003
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across Self-Deleting Tool (psexec64), Kernel ApphelpCacheControl, and SYSTEM Hive (AppCompatCache), unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (Amcache.hve (SHA-1 FileId)) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by AppCompatCacheParser & Amcache. Grounded in the Mandiant Application Compatibility Cache (Shimcache) Whitepaper, ANSSI Amcache.hve Analysis Guide, and SANS FOR508: even after an attacker deletes a staging binary (C:\Users\Public\psexec64.exe) and clears Event Logs, Windows preserves its LastModifiedTime and execution flag in HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCompatCache and its full SHA-1 FileId hash, PE CompileTime, and size in C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve. ### T1036.005: NIST SP 800-86 & SANS DFIR — Windows Prefetch (MAM .pf) & SRUM (SRUDB.dat) Execution & Exfiltration Trace
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-windows-prefetch-srum-network-execution-trace`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-windows-prefetch-srum-network-execution-trace

- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across Masqueraded rclone (svchost_upd), SysMain / Prefetcher Engine, and Prefetch (*.pf MAM Compressed), unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (SRUDB.dat (ESE Network Usage)) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by PECmd & SrumECmd Forensics. Grounded in SANS DFIR Windows Artifact Analysis, Microsoft System Resource Usage Monitor (SRUM) architecture, and NIST SP 800-86: when an attacker renames rclone.exe to svchost_upd.exe, runs it to exfiltrate data over HTTPS, and deletes the binary, Windows Prefetch (C:\Windows\Prefetch\SVCHOST_UPD.EXE-<Hash>.pf) records the run count, last 8 execution timestamps, and every referenced file/directory, while C:\Windows\System32\sru\SRUDB.dat logs the exact Process SID, AppId, and BytesSent. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).

### T1562.001: Microsoft PowerShell Team, CISA & Mandiant DFIR — PowerShell EventID 4104 / 4103, Engine v2.0 Downgrade & PSReadLine History
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-powershell-eid4104-4103-clm-downgrade-forensics`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-powershell-eid4104-4103-clm-downgrade-forensics
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-powershell-eid4104-4103-clm-downgrade-forensics

- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across Obfuscated PowerShell Stager, System.Management.Automation, and PowerShell Operational (4104), unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (ConsoleHost_history.txt) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by EID 400, 4103, 4104 & PSReadLine. Grounded in Microsoft PowerShell Team Logging Specifications, CISA PowerShell Security Guidance, and Mandiant DFIR research: an adversary attempts to bypass AMSI and Script Block Logging by launching powershell.exe -Version 2 (generating Windows PowerShell EventID 400 with EngineVersion=2.0 vs HostVersion=5.1), while post-exploitation commands on v5.1 hosts are captured in de-obfuscated form by EventID 4104 (ScriptBlockLogging), EventID 4103 (ModuleLogging), and %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt. - **Primary Analytical Sources**: NIST SP 800-86 & CISA Cybersecurity Advisories: Official DFIR Forensic Guidance for Microsoft PowerShell Team, CISA & Mandiant DFIR — PowerShell EventID 4104 / 4103, Engine v2.0 Downgrade & PSReadLine History (https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-86/final) | Official Platform & Vendor Security Documentation (Microsoft / Red Hat / AWS / GCP / VMware): Audit Log Schema & Forensic Artifact Specification (T1059.001) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon) | The MITRE Corporation & SigmaHQ Detection Community: MITRE ATT&CK T1059.001 & Sigma Detection Rules (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/)

### T1558.001: Microsoft Defender for Identity, CERT-FR & MITRE DFIR — Kerberos Golden Ticket Forgery Forensics (EID 4768 / 4769)
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-golden-ticket-krbtgt-eid4768-4769-lifetime-anomaly`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-golden-ticket-krbtgt-eid4768-4769-lifetime-anomaly
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-golden-ticket-krbtgt-eid4768-4769-lifetime-anomaly
- **Category**: ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Active Directory & Identity · T1558.001
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across Rubeus / Mimikatz ptt Host, Kerberos KDC TCP/UDP :88, and CORP-DC01 (kdcsvc.dll), unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (CIFS/CORP-DC01 Target Service) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by EID 4768 vs 4769 Correlation. Grounded in Microsoft Defender for Identity Kerberos analytics, CERT-FR Active Directory Golden Ticket detection guides, and MITRE ATT&CK T1558.001: after stealing the krbtgt hash, an attacker forges a custom TGT offline using Mimikatz or Rubeus and injects it via Pass-the-Ticket, producing three definitive KDC forensic anomalies on Domain Controllers: (1) an orphaned EventID 4769 (TGS-REQ) with no preceding EventID 4768 (AS-REQ), (2) a non-existent or forged Privilege Attribute Certificate (PAC) user/RID (e.g., RID 500 with fake username), and (3) a 10-year ticket lifetime or RC4 (0x17) encryption downgrade. ### T1649: SpecterOps, Microsoft ADV210003 & CISA DFIR — AD CS ESC1 SubjectAltName Spoofing & PKINIT Forensics (EID 4886 / 4768)
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-adcs-esc1-petitpotam-certificate-enrollment-eid4886`

### T1098.004: Red Hat, CISA & MITRE DFIR — Linux auditd SSH authorized_keys & PAM Module Persistence Forensics
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-linux-auditd-pam-sshd-authorized-keys-persistence`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-linux-auditd-pam-sshd-authorized-keys-persistence
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-linux-auditd-pam-sshd-authorized-keys-persistence

- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across External SSH Client (:22), sshd Daemon (PAM Stack), and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys File, unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (/lib64/security/pam_unix.so) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by Linux auditd & /var/log/secure. Grounded in the Red Hat Enterprise Linux Security & Auditd Guide, CISA Linux Incident Response Guidance, and MITRE ATT&CK T1098.004 / T1556.003: an incident responder investigates unauthorized SSH key persistence and Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) tampering on a production Linux server by correlating Linux kernel auditd SYSCALL/PATH records (openat, write, chmod on ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and /lib64/security/pam_unix.so) with /var/log/secure and /var/log/auth.log Accepted publickey Fingerprints. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).

### T1036.004: PwC, CrowdStrike & Elastic DFIR — Linux BPFDoor Raw Socket Filter, /dev/shm Masquerading & /proc/net/packet Forensics
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-linux-ebpf-bpfdoor-raw-socket-magic-packet-forensics`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-linux-ebpf-bpfdoor-raw-socket-magic-packet-forensics
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-linux-ebpf-bpfdoor-raw-socket-magic-packet-forensics
- **Category**: KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kernel, Firmware & BYOVD · T1036.004
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across Magic Packet Trigger (WAN), AF_PACKET Raw Socket Filter, and /dev/shm (deleted) Process, unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (Masqueraded [kdmtmpflush] PID) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by /proc/net/packet & ss -0pb. ### T1574.006: NCSC-NL, Red Hat & MITRE DFIR — Linux /etc/ld.so.preload Userland Rootkit & /proc/1/maps Forensics
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-linux-ld-so-preload-userland-rootkit-proc-maps`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-linux-ld-so-preload-userland-rootkit-proc-maps
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-linux-ld-so-preload-userland-rootkit-proc-maps
- **Category**: KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Kernel, Firmware & BYOVD · T1574.006
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across Rootkit Installer Process, ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 Linker, and /etc/ld.so.preload Config, unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (Hooked libc readdir/fopen) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by auditd & /proc/1/maps Check. Grounded in NCSC-NL Linux Incident Response guidelines, Red Hat Dynamic Linker (ld.so) documentation, and MITRE ATT&CK T1574.006: a userland shared-object rootkit writes the path of a malicious library (/lib64/libudev- guardian.so) into /etc/ld.so.preload so the dynamic linker (/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2) injects it into every dynamically linked process to hook readdir(), fopen(), and accept(), detectable via /proc/1/maps, LD_TRACE_LOADED_OBJECTS, and statically linked busybox/auditd. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).

### T1543.002: Freedesktop Systemd Spec & Elastic DFIR — Linux systemd Generator (/run/systemd/generator) & Unit Persistence Forensics
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-linux-systemd-generator-cron-udev-persistence`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-linux-systemd-generator-cron-udev-persistence

Grounded in the Freedesktop.org systemd.generator(7) and systemd.unit(5) specifications, Elastic Security Labs Linux persistence research, and MITRE ATT&CK T1543.002: an adversary achieves stealthy boot/daemon-reload persistence by placing a script inside /etc/systemd/system-generators/ (or a drop-in .conf inside /etc/systemd/system/<service>.service.d/) that dynamically generates an ephemeral unit in /run/systemd/generator/ whenever systemctl daemon-reload runs. ### T1098.001: AWS CIRT & CISA Cloud DFIR — AWS IAM PassRole + Lambda Privilege Escalation & StopLogging Tampering
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-aws-cloudtrail-iam-shadow-admin-passrole-lambda`

### T1528: Microsoft MSRC & Dirk-jan Mollema DFIR — Entra ID Primary Refresh Token (PRT) & Rogue Device Registration Forensics
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-entra-id-prt-roadtools-device-registration-forensics`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-entra-id-prt-roadtools-device-registration-forensics
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-entra-id-prt-roadtools-device-registration-forensics
- **Category**: CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity**: CRITICAL

- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across Rogue Device (roadtx), Entra ID DRS Service, and Registered Device Object, unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (PRT Sign-In (IncomingToken PRT)) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by Entra Audit & Sign-In Logs. Grounded in Microsoft Entra ID Primary Refresh Token (PRT) architecture documentation, Dirk-jan Mollema (ROADtools) research, and CISA Cloud Identity guidance: an attacker uses a stolen session or PRT cookie (x-ms-RefreshTokenCredential) to register a rogue Entra ID Joined device via the Device Registration Service (urn:ms-drs:enterpriseregistration.windows.net), minting a hardware-less Primary Refresh Token with an embedded MFA claim (AuthenticationRequirement="multiFactorAuthentication", IncomingTokenType="primaryRefreshToken"). Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1528 (Microsoft MSRC & Dirk-jan Mollema DFIR — Entra ID Primary Refresh Token (PRT) & Rogue Device Registration Forensics - Credential Access (T1528 - Steal Application Access Token: Entra DRS Token))
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: NIST SP 800-86 & CISA Cybersecurity Advisories: Official DFIR Forensic Guidance for Microsoft MSRC & Dirk-jan Mollema DFIR — Entra ID Primary Refresh Token (PRT) & Rogue Device Registration Forensics (https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-86/final) | Official Platform & Vendor Security Documentation (Microsoft / Red Hat / AWS / GCP / VMware): Audit Log Schema & Forensic Artifact Specification (T1528) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon) | The MITRE Corporation & SigmaHQ Detection Community: MITRE ATT&CK T1528 & Sigma Detection Rules (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/)
- **Kill-Chain Stages**:

### T1071.001: Salesforce JA3, FoxIO JA4+ & CISA DFIR — Zeek ssl.log JA3/JA4 Fingerprint & Malleable C2 Jitter Beaconing Forensics

Grounded in Salesforce JA3/JA3S specifications, FoxIO JA4+ Network Fingerprinting documentation, and CISA / Mandiant Cobalt Strike detection guides: network forensic analysts detect a custom Malleable C2 HTTPS beacon by correlating Zeek ssl.log client/server TLS fingerprints (ja3 / ja3s / ja4), X.509 certificate serial anomalies, and conn.log / http.log periodic interval jitter histograms. - **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1071.001 (Salesforce JA3, FoxIO JA4+ & CISA DFIR — Zeek ssl.log JA3/JA4 Fingerprint & Malleable C2 Jitter Beaconing Forensics - Command and Control (T1071.001 - Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols))

### T1505.004: Microsoft Exchange/IIS IR, ESET & Unit 42 DFIR — IIS HTTP.sys Kernel URI Registration & In-Memory Module Forensics

- **Subtitle**: Network & C2 Exfiltration · T1505.004
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across External Operator (:443), HTTP.sys Kernel Driver, and w3wp.exe (IIS Worker Pool), unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (applicationHost.config & GAC) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by HttpService EID 113 & netsh. Grounded in Microsoft Incident Response IIS Module guidance, ESET IIS malware research, and Unit 42 HTTP.sys analysis: a fileless .NET implant or native IIS module registers a rogue HTTP listener directly inside the Windows kernel driver HTTP.sys (bypassing IIS W3C disk webroots) or hooks IHttpModule inside w3wp.exe, detectable via Microsoft-Windows-HttpService/Operational EventID 113, netsh http show servicestate, appcmd list modules, and Sysmon EventID 7. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).

Grounded in Microsoft Threat Intelligence (MSTIC) Hafnium / ProxyLogon forensic guidance, Volexity Exchange exploitation research, and CISA Emergency Directive 21-02: an investigator correlates three Exchange-specific log sources: (1) V15\Logging\HttpProxy\Autodiscover\*.LOG showing SSRF backend cookie routing (ServerInfo~a]@), (2) the MSExchange Management event log (EventID 1) showing Set-OabVirtualDirectory or New-MailboxExportRequest with an embedded ASPX webshell in ExternalUrl/FilePath, and (3) Sysmon EventID 1 showing w3wp.exe (MSExchangeOWAAppPool) spawning cmd.exe. ### T1059.003: Microsoft SQL Server Security & Mandiant DFIR — MSSQL xp_cmdshell / Ole Automation Reconfiguration (EventID 15457) & sqlservr.exe Forensics
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-mssql-xp-cmdshell-sp-oacreate-sqlservr-audit-trace`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dfir-mssql-xp-cmdshell-sp-oacreate-sqlservr-audit-trace
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dfir-mssql-xp-cmdshell-sp-oacreate-sqlservr-audit-trace
- **Category**: NETWORK_WEB | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: Network & C2 Exfiltration · T1059.003
- **Overview**: Imagine a high-security facility where an intruder attempts to operate covertly across TDS Client (:1433 SQL), Tabular Data Stream (TDS), and sqlservr.exe (MSSQLSERVER), unaware that every system call, protocol handshake, and on-disk structural table (xplog70.dll / odsole70.dll) automatically records an immutable forensic ledger entry correlated by Application EID 15457 & Sysmon. Grounded in Microsoft SQL Server Security & Error Log documentation, Mandiant database intrusion forensics, and MITRE ATT&CK T1505.001 / T1059.003: an attacker authenticates to Microsoft SQL Server (TCP 1433) or exploits SQL injection, runs sp_configure to enable "xp_cmdshell" or "Ole Automation Procedures" (generating Windows Application EventID 15457 and SQL ERRORLOG entries), and executes OS commands that spawn cmd.exe under sqlservr.exe. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques**: T1505.001 (Microsoft SQL Server Security & Mandiant DFIR — MSSQL xp_cmdshell / Ole Automation Reconfiguration (EventID 15457) & sqlservr.exe Forensics - Execution (T1059.003 - MSSQL sp_configure Option Reconfiguration))
- **Primary Analytical Sources**: NIST SP 800-86 & CISA Cybersecurity Advisories: Official DFIR Forensic Guidance for Microsoft SQL Server Security & Mandiant DFIR — MSSQL xp_cmdshell / Ole Automation Reconfiguration (EventID 15457) & sqlservr.exe Forensics (https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-86/final) | Official Platform & Vendor Security Documentation (Microsoft / Red Hat / AWS / GCP / VMware): Audit Log Schema & Forensic Artifact Specification (T1505.001) (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon) | The MITRE Corporation & SigmaHQ Detection Community: MITRE ATT&CK T1505.001 & Sigma Detection Rules (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/001/)

### T1078: VMware/Broadcom, CISA AA23-039A & Mandiant DFIR — ESXi /var/log/shell.log, hostd.log & VMDK Hypervisor Forensics
- **Scenario ID**: `dfir-esxi-hostd-vobd-shell-log-ransomware-encryption-trace`

Grounded in VMware vSphere/ESXi Official Log Documentation, CISA Joint Advisory AA23-039A (ESXiArgs), and Mandiant hypervisor DFIR playbooks: an attacker gains SSH/SLP access to a VMware ESXi hypervisor, enumerates running guest VMs via esxcli vm process list, forcefully terminates vmx processes via esxcli vm process kill --type=force, and encrypts the backing -flat.vmdk.nvram, and .vmx files on /vmfs/volumes/<datastore>/, reconstructed via /var/log/shell.log, /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/hostd.log, and /var/log/vobd.log. ### T1611: OpenContainers Security Advisory, Snyk & CISA KEV — runc File Descriptor Leak & Host Filesystem Breakout Analysis (CVE-2024-21626)
- **Scenario ID**: `runc-leaky-vessels-cwd-fd-escape-cve-2024-21626`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/runc-leaky-vessels-cwd-fd-escape-cve-2024-21626
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=runc-leaky-vessels-cwd-fd-escape-cve-2024-21626

- **Primary Analytical Sources**: OpenContainers (runc) Official Security Advisory: GHSA-xr7r-f8xq-vfvv / CVE-2024-21626: WORKDIR File Descriptor Leak Container Escape (https://github.com/opencontainers/runc/security/advisories/GHSA-xr7r-f8xq-vfvv) | Snyk Security Labs & CISA KEV: Leaky Vessels: Deep-Dive into runc /proc/self/fd/7 Host Mount Escape (CVE-2024-21626) (https://snyk.io/blog/leaky-vessels-docker-runc-container-breakout-vulnerabilities/) | The MITRE Corporation: MITRE ATT&CK T1611: Escape to Host (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611/)

### T1195.001: PyTorch Official Security Advisory, Sonatype & MITRE T1195.001 — PyTorch torchtriton Nightly Dependency Confusion Supply Chain Attack & h4ck.cfd DNS Exfiltration
- **Scenario ID**: `pypi-pytorch-torchtriton-dependency-confusion-supply-chain`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/pypi-pytorch-torchtriton-dependency-confusion-supply-chain
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=pypi-pytorch-torchtriton-dependency-confusion-supply-chain

Grounded in the official PyTorch Security Advisory, Sonatype, and Wiz Research on the torchtriton dependency confusion attack: because pip install --extra-index-url does not give precedence to private/nightly registries over the public PyPI index, registering a higher-versioned torchtriton package on public PyPI caused pip to install a trojanized wheel containing an ELF binary (triton/runtime/triton) that exfiltrated SSH keys, AWS credentials, and /etc/passwd over encrypted DNS queries to *.h4ck.cfd. ### T1595.002: Jeffrey Appel & Microsoft Threat Intel — ARTEX Multi-Agent LLM Framework: Machine-Speed Kill-Chain Compression, Storm-0940 Spray & Defender XDR Disruption
- **Scenario ID**: `jeffreyappel-artex-llm-multi-agent-machine-speed-defender-xdr`
- **Canonical URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/jeffreyappel-artex-llm-multi-agent-machine-speed-defender-xdr
- **Interactive Simulator URL**: https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=jeffreyappel-artex-llm-multi-agent-machine-speed-defender-xdr
- **Category**: AI_LLM_MLOPS_SECURITY | **Severity**: CRITICAL
- **Subtitle**: AI, LLM Agents & MLOps Security · T1595.002
- **Overview**: Imagine a bank heist crew that replaces slow human lockpickers with a coordinated swarm of high-speed robotic arms (the ARTEX Go + Next.js LLM Planner-Worker framework): instead of inventing a brand-new laser cutter, the master robot (LLM Planner) dispatches 8 worker robots that test every door handle (nmap/curl + Storm-0940 password spray), prop open a side window (web shell + RC4 Kerberoasting), and empty the upstairs safe (Azure Key Vault SecretGet) in under 15 minutes, forcing the building security system (Microsoft Defender XDR) to slam down steel blast doors automatically (Automatic Attack Disruption) because waiting for a human guard to read the alarm log would be too late. Grounded in security researcher Jeffrey Appel’s technical analysis ("ARTEX: Old Attacks at Machine Speed, and how Microsoft Defender keeps up") and Microsoft Threat Intelligence research on Storm-0940 and AI-accelerated intrusions: threat actors deploy ARTEX (an open-source Go + Next.js multi-agent LLM penetration testing framework powered by OpenAI/DeepSeek tool-calling APIs) to orchestrate Planner-Worker sub-agents that chain external reconnaissance (nmap/curl), Storm-0940 password spraying, Kerberoasting (RC4-HMAC 0x17), web shell persistence, and Azure Key Vault secret exfiltration, compressing multi-week intrusions into minutes and requiring Microsoft Defender XDR Automatic Attack Disruption, App Governance, and KQL multi-alert burst correlation. Across this 3-step forensic reconstruction, incident responders correlate primary host, kernel, identity, and network telemetry (capturing exact Event IDs, syscall numbers, registry/filesystem structures, and protocol fields so defenders can verify root cause and scope compromise with high confidence).
